Password-based RDP needs service availability, NLA compatibility and an effective “Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services” assignment without a deny override. Restricted Admin permits hash/ticket-style network authentication only under its policy/support conditions and requires administrator access; ordinary Remote Desktop Users membership is insufficient for that mode. Ordinary RDP can place reusable credentials in the destination LSASS, whereas Restricted Admin avoids doing so but removes ordinary onward access as that user. Pass-the-Hash presents an NT hash through NTLM without first recovering plaintext. The target service must accept NTLM, the local/domain account context must be correct and the represented identity must hold that service's right. Remote UAC commonly filters network tokens for non-built-in local administrators. Domain administrators traditionally receive full remote tokens when locally authorized, but newer Administrator Protection policies can alter this; trust the observed token and operation rather than memorized defaults. Overpass-the-Hash/key-to-ticket uses an NT or AES long-term key to obtain a Kerberos TGT, then requests tickets through normal hostname/SPN flows. The process's local whoami can remain the original token while its outbound network credential represents another identity. Pass-the-Ticket imports a TGT or TGS into a logon/cache context; import success proves neither destination access nor execution. Validate the ticket client, realm, validity, SPN and resulting remote identity. After movement, verify hostname, full token, addresses, routes, listeners and ticket cache. Then repeat host credential-source checks and Block 10 domain mapping from the new identity/position. Preserve the earlier state so the chain records exactly which credential, protocol, method and authorization produced each transition. Full commands and failure routing are in Lateral Movement . Source route: PEN-200 Ch 22-24; current OffSec BOK ; Microsoft RootDSE, DirectorySearcher and PsLoggedOn documentation; current SpecterOps SharpHound CE documentation; reviewed getSH Active Directory route , current Impacket/NetExec/OpenLDAP sources and Hexdump Active Directory modules . The live Hexdump AD module was still a TODO when checked, so its minimal legacy collector cue was not treated as current syntax authority. Procedures: Stage 06 . <h2

title: 0.1.14 Tunnels and network reachability
text: id="tunnels-and-network-reachability">0.1.14 Tunnels and network reachability Draw application source → entry listener/SOCKS/TUN route → tunnel transport → pivot exit → destination before selecting a forwarding command. For a callback, draw the reverse graph separately. Identify the initiator, bind address, destination as seen by the exit, transport, DNS-resolution point, authentication hostname and cleanup objects. “The tunnel works” is too broad: process start, listener/session creation, pivot egress, local route/proxy use, application flow, name/authentication behavior and callback return are separate claims. Begin on the foothold by inspecting interfaces, routes, neighbors, DNS and local listeners. A second interface or route is a candidate vantage point, not proof that an internal service is reachable. Test one justified destination socket from the pivot. Prefer the smallest sufficient route: one explicit forward for one known TCP service; SOCKS for several TCP endpoints; a TUN/routed pivot for many ordinary clients; and command execution on the pivot itself when no forwarding is needed. SSH direction is defined by where the listener is created. -L and -D create listeners on the SSH client; destination connections exit from the SSH server. -R creates a listener on the SSH server and sends connections through the client. Remote dynamic -R PORT creates a SOCKS endpoint on the server and requires OpenSSH 7.6+ on the client issuing it. ProxyJump is an SSH-specific path, while ProxyCommand lets SSH use an existing proxy transport. ExitOnForwardFailure proves requested sockets were bound, not that the final service works. Server-side AllowTcpForwarding , PermitOpen and GatewayPorts can restrict behavior. Socat is a simple fixed relay and adds neither authentication nor encryption. sshuttle creates a transparent selected-subnet TCP/DNS-oriented route through SSH, but needs local firewall privileges and a compatible remote Python path; it is not a layer-2 or arbitrary-UDP VPN. On Windows, built-in OpenSSH retains the SSH model; Plink supports local, remote and dynamic forwards but not OpenSSH's remote-dynamic shorthand. Elevated netsh interface portproxy creates persistent TCP-only forwarding and may also need a firewall exception/IP Helper, so both rule and exception require deliberate cleanup. SOCKS only helps clients that use it. ProxyChains interposes dynamically linked socket calls and is TCP-only; static binaries, some scripts/modules, UDP, ICMP, SYN scans and pcap discovery will not transparently work. Nmap through ProxyChains therefore uses focused -sT -Pn -n , while native proxy options are preferred. A Chisel socks / R:socks remote is TCP CONNECT only. Current Chisel adds udpsocks / R:udpsocks for SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE, but that does not make ProxyChains UDP-capable and both peers/client/firewall must support the UDP path. Chisel wraps its SSH-secured channel in HTTP/WebSocket transport and is useful when the pivot can initiate permitted HTTP-like egress. Reverse SOCKS or a reverse fixed forward places the usable listener at the server side. Server fingerprint verification, client/server compatibility, target OS/architecture and runtime libraries matter. An HTTP request reaching the server without a WebSocket upgrade points to an intermediary/transport problem rather than internal routing. Ligolo-ng creates a userland routed path so normal clients can use selected internal subnets without ProxyChains. Current versions can create interfaces and routes in the console; manual TUN and OS routes remain a fallback. Its special 240.0.0.0/4 mapping exposes the selected agent's loopback when narrowly routed, while agent listeners can relay internal callbacks to the proxy host. A session alone is not enough: the correct agent, TUN interface, route and listener must all align. Raw-packet, ICMP and some UDP behavior can differ from direct networking. Kerberos reveals why route and name are different variables. Numeric IP connectivity can work while authentication fails because the client needs the target FQDN/SPN, a reachable KDC, matching realm and correct time. Decide explicitly whether DNS runs locally, through ProxyChains, at a SOCKS exit or through the pivot's resolver. Preserve a service hostname and use a separate routing address when a tool provides that option. Forward access and callback access are independent. A path that lets Kali browse an internal web service does not prove the target can reach a Kali listener. The callback may need a listener on the pivot plus SSH/Chisel/Ligolo relay. Payload delivery can need a third path. Verify each direction with a simple protocol-appropriate test before changing credentials, exploits or payloads. DNS tunneling is a conditional last-resort path, but remains in the current official BOK. dnscat2 needs client execution plus authoritative NS delegation for a controlled domain or direct DNS-server reachability. Resolver forwarding, caching, EDNS, TCP fallback and response limits affect the channel; it is slower and more conspicuous than ordinary tunnels. A DNS query arriving proves only the resolver path, not an authenticated encrypted session. DNS tunneling is not DNS spoofing, which the current exam guide prohibits. In a multihop route, validate outward from the first hop and use distinct routes/listeners. One upstream failure invalidates all deeper observations. Record route ownership, versions, bind addresses, name mappings and cleanup. The current exam guide explicitly prohibits Metasploit pivoting even though the course/BOK teaches the concept. Source route: PEN-200 Ch 19 pp583–629 and Ch 20 pp630–652; current OffSec BOK and exam guide ; reviewed getSH and Hexdump tunneling routes; current OpenSSH, Socat, ProxyChains, sshuttle, Plink, Microsoft Netsh, Chisel, Ligolo-ng and dnscat2 documentation. Procedure: Stage 07 . <h2

title: 0.1.15 Integrated attack control, stagnation and recovery
text: id="integrated-attack-control-stagnation-and-recovery">0.1.15 Integrated attack control, stagnation and recovery An unfamiliar attack is a state machine, not a linear checklist. The reusable loop is Observe → Enumerate → Interpret → Hypothesize → Validate → Exploit → Verify → Re-enumerate → Escalate/Move → Document . The purpose of the loop is to keep conclusions tied to the source position, identity and evidence that produced them. A new credential changes the authorization view; a new route changes the reachable attack surface; a new session changes the host context; and a new privilege changes which protected objects and sessions can be enumerated. Each state change routes the investigation back to the applicable earlier block. Maintain two queues. The coverage queue tracks each reachable host/endpoint/application and whether its required enumeration is complete in the current context. The hypothesis queue tracks observation, desired transition, prerequisites, cheapest discriminating test, decisive results and status. Coverage prevents tunnel vision; hypotheses prevent random command execution. A confirmed prerequisite with a direct objective transition outranks a popular technique supported only by a banner. Information-expanding tests can outrank exploit attempts when they may unlock several branches. Every candidate path should state what success and failure mean before testing. Disproven requires a valid test of the actual prerequisite. A tool error, wrong source position, missing proxy support, bad syntax or unavailable dependency is an environment/tool failure. A result that does not separate plausible explanations is inconclusive. Keeping these states distinct prevents a viable path from being abandoned for the wrong reason and prevents repeated attempts against an absent prerequisite. Warning signs include repeated tests with unchanged evidence, multiplying assumptions, increasingly exotic mechanisms without prerequisite checks, tool switching without a new hypothesis and work whose success would not advance the objective. Freeze the current host/identity/route/credential map, label the last decisive result per path, audit coverage and authenticated views, then choose a test that can change the decision. Return to a disproven path only when new evidence changes its prerequisites. For a standalone target, integrate scope/objective → TCP and bounded UDP coverage → service/web enumeration → files/configuration/identities → credential/manual weakness/exact exploit prerequisites → bounded effect → verified session → local privilege reasoning → elevated identity → final evidence and cleanup. For assumed-breach AD, integrate starting identity → DNS/time/DC/route → hosts/services and directory objects/rights → ranked identity/host transition → compatible password/hash/ticket use → verified new session/identity → authenticated re-enumeration → movement → final domain objective. Every AD edge must keep controlled identity, effective group/right, target, protocol/route and resulting state together. Source route: supplied PEN-200 Chapter 27 pp963–1017, especially the cyclic enumeration and wrap-up lessons at pp963–968 and 1015–1016; current BOK; reviewed getSH Home/AD flow and the live Hexdump report workflow. Procedure: Stage 08 . <h2

title: 0.1.16 Evidence and reproducibility
text: id="evidence-and-reproducibility">0.1.16 Evidence and reproducibility Capture access and privilege transitions when they happen: time, source position, host, identity, command/request, decisive output, effect, artifact hash and reproduction steps. Keep actual screenshots, transcripts, target details and proof material in private records. Maintain separate maps of hosts, identities, credentials, routes, hypotheses and transitions so a new state triggers the right re-enumeration rather than erasing the earlier chain. Document exploit source/version, modifications and why they were necessary. Preserve a focused diff, build/interpreter command, payload-generation command and result verification. A technically competent reader should be able to reconstruct the attack from the resulting report without relying on unexplained screenshots or a raw terminal transcript. The report is a normalized sequence of state transitions rather than a chronological terminal dump: starting state → decisive enumeration → prerequisite validation → exact action → session/identity proof → privilege/movement transition → final objective → cleanup. Retain enough failed-path evidence to explain important decisions, but do not bury the reproducible path under every inconclusive command. Screenshots require captions and nearby interpretation; they do not replace copyable steps. The current exam guide requires strict proof handling, report completeness and exact packaging. Proof-file contents must be read from the original location through an interactive target shell and captured with the target IP; control-panel submission is a separate action before the practical period ends. Target grading follows report order. The final report is an exactly named PDF inside an exactly named non-password-protected .7z no larger than 200 MB, with only PDF content accepted. Visually inspect every page, test/list the archive, compare the local and uploaded MD5 and complete final submission. Recheck the guide because these details can change. Before a mock or exam, consult the current official exam guide for evidence, tool and submission requirements. Source route: PEN-200 Ch 5 pp94–113; current official exam guide and reporting requirements; reviewed getSH Home/AD flow. OffSec's Word/LibreOffice template is the baseline. Hexdump's Markdown/Org → Pandoc/LaTeX → PDF/7z generator is a viable optional workflow only after a full local rehearsal. Procedure: Stage 08 .

title: 0.4 Recognition practice
text: id="recognition-practice">0.4 Recognition practice Strategy map | Master Notes | Study sequence These are unanswered paper exercises, not target assignments. All evidence is hypothetical and abbreviated; none records a completed attack or practical competence. Attempt a case before opening the corresponding guide. For every case, write: Your established access and the facts actually supported by the evidence. The precise recognition clue and candidate method. The missing enabling condition, the exact check you would select, and the decisive evidence you would expect. Your decision: enabled after validation, ruled out in this context, or inconclusive . State how one changed condition would change the next action. Do not substitute an attack name for prerequisite reasoning. <h2

title: 0.4.1 Case 01 — Network discovery
text: id="case-01--network-discovery">0.4.1 Case 01 — Network discovery Your starting access is a Kali workstation with an assigned target IP. A default TCP scan reports ports 22 and 80 open. Host discovery succeeds. No UDP scan or full TCP scan has been recorded. A draft note says: “The target has only SSH and HTTP; discovery is complete.” What investigation produced useful clues, and what coverage claim is unsupported? <h2

title: 0.4.2 Case 02 — Service access
text: id="case-02--service-access">0.4.2 Case 02 — Service access A supplied domain password authenticates to SMB. You can list a share and its filenames. Opening a configuration file returns access denied. No execution-capable service authorization has been checked. A draft note says: “We have remote execution and the database credentials.” Which access boundaries have actually been crossed, and which checks come next? <h2

title: 0.4.3 Case 03 — Web mapping
text: id="case-03--web-mapping">0.4.3 Case 03 — Web mapping An HTTP path-discovery run returns status 200 for many random names. A nonsense path and the home page have matching titles, sizes and body text. One export endpoint returns a different content type and a consistent application-specific response. How would you separate a useful route clue from soft-404 noise? What would you inspect before selecting an exploit? <h2

title: 0.4.4 Case 04 — Web exploitation
text: id="case-04--web-exploitation">0.4.4 Case 04 — Web exploitation An authenticated upload accepts a file with a script extension. Its returned URL downloads the exact source text rather than running it. The application stores the file on a separate static-content host. Does accepted upload establish code execution? Which conditions would have to change, and what alternative capability might still exist? <h2

title: 0.4.5 Case 05 — Credential material
text: id="case-05--credential-material">0.4.5 Case 05 — Credential material A capture contains an NTLM challenge-response exchange. A colleague proposes placing the complete captured response into a tool option that expects an NT hash. How do you classify the material? Which recovery or use paths require different prerequisites? <h2

title: 0.4.6 Case 06 — Public exploit adaptation
text: id="case-06--public-exploit-adaptation">0.4.6 Case 06 — Public exploit adaptation A reviewed public proof of concept exits with a Python import error before sending any request. The product name resembles the target banner, but the target's affected component and exact build have not been established. A draft note says: “The exploit failed, so the target is patched.” Which failure boundary was reached? What evidence is needed before making a vulnerability claim? <h2

title: 0.4.7 Case 07 — Shells and sessions
text: id="case-07--shells-and-sessions">0.4.7 Case 07 — Shells and sessions An application command primitive is confirmed. A staged payload contacts a listening socket, but no usable command session follows. The listener is a plain TCP listener, not a handler for that staged payload. Which observed result is real, what remains unproved, and how would you distinguish a handler mismatch from a blocked callback? <h2

title: 0.4.8 Case 08 — Linux privilege escalation
text: id="case-08--linux-privilege-escalation">0.4.8 Case 08 — Linux privilege escalation A low-privilege account can modify a backup script. The script contains administrative-looking commands. You have not identified a privileged scheduler, service, executable owner context or manual administrator trigger that consumes it. Why is this a candidate rather than confirmed escalation? Where would you investigate the consumer and trigger? <h2

title: 0.4.9 Case 09 — Windows privilege escalation
text: id="case-09--windows-privilege-escalation">0.4.9 Case 09 — Windows privilege escalation A service executable path contains spaces and is unquoted. All earlier executable-prefix locations are either protected from your account or occupied by existing files you cannot replace. You have not found a writable loaded dependency or service configuration right. What does the formatting clue establish? Which effective permission decides whether this particular method is available? <h2

title: 0.4.10 Case 10 — AD mapping
text: id="case-10--ad-mapping">0.4.10 Case 10 — AD mapping Your domain account can bind to LDAP. A broad query returns a size-limit warning. No service principal names appear in the returned subset. A draft note says: “The domain has no service accounts.” How would you repair enumeration coverage and preserve the distinction between an empty result and an incomplete result? <h2

title: 0.4.11 Case 11 — AD identity transition
text: id="case-11--ad-identity-transition">0.4.11 Case 11 — AD identity transition A directory account has userAccountControl value 0x00400202. For this exercise, 0x00400000 means preauthentication is not required, 0x00000200 identifies a normal account, and 0x00000002 means the account is disabled. A draft note selects the account solely because the preauthentication flag is present. Which additional flag changes the decision? What identity state and KDC result would you need before claiming a usable path? <h2

title: 0.4.12 Case 12 — Lateral movement
text: id="case-12--lateral-movement">0.4.12 Case 12 — Lateral movement The same domain password is accepted for an SMB share, but WinRM returns an authorization denial. You have not checked remote-management group membership or endpoint policy. A draft note says: “The password is wrong.” Which fact supports authentication , which result concerns authorization, and what other movement routes remain conditional? <h2

title: 0.4.13 Case 13 — Pivoting
text: id="case-13--pivoting">0.4.13 Case 13 — Pivoting An application inside a private subnet is reachable through your SOCKS proxy. An exploit's reverse connection never arrives. The payload was configured to call a workstation address for which no return route or reverse forward has been established. Why does successful proxied access not establish a working callback path? Draw the separate paths and choose the missing check. <h2

title: 0.4.14 Case 14 — Execution troubleshooting
text: id="case-14--execution-troubleshooting">0.4.14 Case 14 — Execution troubleshooting A document reaches the intended host. Office opens it in a restricted state and blocks its macro. No command process or outbound connection is observed. A draft note recommends changing listener ports repeatedly. At which boundary did execution stop? What evidence would justify investigating connectivity instead? <h2

title: 0.4.15 Case 15 — Completion and reporting
text: id="case-15--completion-and-reporting">0.4.15 Case 15 — Completion and reporting Your archive opens successfully and contains the expected screenshots and notes. In the rendered PDF, one reproduction command is clipped, and a privilege screenshot does not show the relevant host identity. A draft note says: “The archive is valid, so the report is ready.” Which checks concern file integrity, which concern reproducibility and attribution, and what must be corrected before completion? <h2

title: 0.4.16 Review after attempting a case
text: id="review-after-attempting-a-case">0.4.16 Review after attempting a case Use the topic discovery workflows to trace your proposed investigation. Compare the matching entry's discovery action, synthetic evidence, exact clue, missing checks and three decision outcomes with your answer. Record uncertainty rather than treating a plausible attack name as proof.

title: 0.3 Attack-first OSCP speedrun breakdown
text: id="attack-first-oscp-speedrun-breakdown">0.3 Attack-first OSCP speedrun breakdown Back to the index | Attack Strategy Map | Master Notes Each numbered block is a stable reference unit for notes and exam lookup. Study the blocks through the grouped attack-path units below rather than as fifteen disconnected mini-courses. This map has no time allocations and does not require the earlier chapter/class sequence. The Attack Strategy Map is the main content entry point. Its topic guides organize each objective into named methods with recognition clues, access/configuration prerequisites, checks, associated concepts, complete command examples and variants, worked reasoning, verification, failure diagnosis and linked next transitions. Use this breakdown for study order and block definitions. Teach mechanisms when they help select an attack, execute it, interpret evidence or diagnose failure. Other background is optional. For each task, work through recognition clues -> prerequisites -> method -> execution -> result interpretation -> failure diagnosis -> next action. Present popular, well-supported approaches first, then less popular but viable methods, manual checks and built-in alternatives. Explain when each is preferable and give complete usable examples. Record taught approaches in the operational procedures and cheatsheets, with necessary explanations in Master Notes. This list describes study coverage, not completed work or demonstrated competence. <h2

title: 0.3.1 Study phase before practical exploitation
text: id="study-phase-before-practical-exploitation">0.3.1 Study phase before practical exploitation Before selecting a method, use the discovery workflows . All 166 documented methods show where to investigate, a discovery action, synthetic evidence, the precise clue, missing conditions and enabled/ruled-out/ inconclusive examples. Use Recognition Practice to test that reasoning without opening the explanations first. Finish concept study across all 15 blocks before beginning practical exploitation. This phase includes full command examples, tool selection, attack prerequisites, worked attack chains, sample/saved-output interpretation, failure diagnosis and alternative approaches. Teach the attacks in enough detail to understand their execution while keeping hands-on attack activity for the later phase. Use hypothetical worked examples, paper-based changed-condition exercises and recall during concept study. Continue building Master Notes, complete procedures and extensive cheatsheets. Command examples are material to study and retain; they are not assignments to execute against a target during this phase. Defer target-based exploitation, hands-on attack drills, capstones and practical retests. Pending lab work remains recorded for later and does not block the next concept section; no live scan, flag or lab-output submission is required to progress through this document. When coverage of all grouped units and their numbered blocks has been reviewed and the learner indicates concept study is complete, select scoped labs and validate the methods through practical execution and independent retests. Record concept coverage and practical evidence separately. A request to explain a command or attack does not itself start the practical phase. <h2

title: 0.3.2 Grouped study sequence
text: id="grouped-study-sequence">0.3.2 Grouped study sequence Keep the numbered blocks separate in the reference, but study them in this dependency order: Study unit Blocks and order Attack chain 1 1 + 2 Find a reachable application, then extract names, files, permissions, credentials or access from it 2 3 + 4 Map normal web behavior, validate a weakness, then convert the primitive into useful access 3 5 Classify credentials/keys/hashes/tickets, validate compatible use and re-enumerate after success 4 6 + 7, with relevant Block 14 diagnostics Adapt a public exploit, prove execution and turn it into a reliable verified session 5 8, then 9 Apply the same control -> consumer -> identity -> trigger reasoning separately to Linux and Windows 6 13 fundamentals, then 10 -> 11 -> 12, with relevant Block 14 diagnostics Build the route, map domain rights, gain a better identity and move with the compatible authentication material 7 Remaining Block 14 Consolidate delivery, parsing, architecture, security-control, connectivity and session troubleshooting 8 15 Integrate the full attack, recover from dead ends and retain reproducible evidence Block 14 is cross-cutting: teach its relevant failure model inside Units 2, 4 and 6 when the failure can first occur, then use Unit 7 as consolidation. Block 5 is also a recurring state transition: study its credential mechanics once, then reapply them whenever another block produces authentication material. Finishing one numbered block does not mean forgetting its loop. New hostnames, routes or listeners return to Blocks 1-2; a new credential returns to Block 5 and authenticated enumeration; execution moves to Block 7; a new identity or privilege triggers re-enumeration. <h2

title: 0.3.3 Reference task index
text: id="reference-task-index">0.3.3 Reference task index Find attack surfaces Extract opportunities from services Find useful web behavior Turn application weaknesses into access Use discovered credentials and keys Adapt public exploits Obtain a reliable session Escalate on Linux Escalate on Windows Map AD attack paths Gain a more useful domain identity Move to another host Reach internal services Resolve payload execution obstacles Complete and document an unfamiliar attack <h2

title: 0.3.4 Find attack surfaces
text: id="1-find-attack-surfaces">0.3.4 Find attack surfaces Study unit: 1 of 8, first half. Continue directly into Block 2; return here whenever service enumeration discloses a new in-scope hostname, address, listener, route or source position. Situation: I have a target IP. Where can I attack? Discover exposed services, including coverage missed by limited scans. Interpret open, closed, filtered and ambiguous results. Establish application identity and select relevant enumeration. Rank the first investigations and recognize when to rescan. Skill to develop: turn scan output into decisions. <h2

title: 0.3.5 Extract opportunities from services
text: id="2-extract-opportunities-from-services">0.3.5 Extract opportunities from services Study unit: 1 of 8, second half. Enter with the Block 1 service queue and leave with evidence-labelled information/access plus a route into web behavior, credentials, public exploits or a verified session. Situation: this service is exposed. What can it give me? SMB/RPC: users, shares, files, domain clues and anonymous/authenticated access. FTP/NFS: accessible files, writable locations, permissions and credential opportunities. DNS/SNMP/SMTP: names, users, host details and configuration disclosures. SSH/RDP/WinRM: usable authentication and remote access. Databases: useful data, credentials, file access and execution where rights permit. Skill to develop: follow a service finding toward information or access. <h2

title: 0.3.6 Find useful web behavior
text: id="3-find-useful-web-behavior">0.3.6 Find useful web behavior Study unit: 2 of 8, first half. Carry observed requests, roles, parameters, files and response differences directly into Block 4. Situation: there is a website. Where is the useful behavior? Explore normal functionality, downloads, exports, uploads and account features. Discover hidden content, virtual hosts, APIs, backups and exposed configuration. Inspect requests, parameters, cookies, authentication and roles. Identify technologies and components worth investigating. Skill to develop: recognize clues through application behavior before choosing an exploit. Operational pages: HTTP and web application mapping and web mapping cheatsheet . <h2

title: 0.3.7 Turn application weaknesses into access
text: id="4-turn-application-weaknesses-into-access">0.3.7 Turn application weaknesses into access Study unit: 2 of 8, second half. Use Block 14's relevant parsing, delivery and execution diagnostics here instead of postponing them. Situation: this application behavior looks exploitable. How do I turn it into access? Traversal and file disclosure. Local/remote file inclusion and conditions for execution. Upload handling, bypasses, storage locations and execution conditions. Command injection, including blind cases. Manual SQL injection: error, UNION, boolean and time-based methods. Authentication/access-control weaknesses and relevant XSS paths. Skill to develop: move from a validated primitive to credentials, privileges, files or execution. Operational pages: web file handling , command and SQL injection , access control and XSS , and web exploitation cheatsheet . <h2

title: 0.3.8 Use discovered credentials and keys
text: id="5-use-discovered-credentials-and-keys">0.3.8 Use discovered credentials and keys Study unit: 3 of 8 and a recurring transition. Re-enter this block whenever service enumeration, web access, local escalation or AD work produces new authentication material. Situation: I found credentials or a key. What can I do with them? Identify the account and its local/domain context. Distinguish passwords, keys, stored hashes, captured responses and tickets. Crack supported material and build targeted password candidates. Test relevant reuse and interpret authentication failures. Re-enumerate accessible services and files after success. Skill to develop: distinguish a valid credential from useful access. Operational pages: credential classification, cracking and reuse and credentials/cracking cheatsheet . Re-enter this procedure after every new credential artifact. <h2

title: 0.3.9 Adapt public exploits
text: id="6-adapt-public-exploits">0.3.9 Adapt public exploits Study unit: 4 of 8, first half. Treat execution proof, callback assumptions and payload compatibility as the handoff into Block 7. Situation: there is a public exploit. Can I make it work? Check the exact software, configuration, architecture, authentication and other prerequisites. Read the relevant code and identify its assumptions. Adjust parameters, paths, requests, payloads and callbacks. Resolve dependencies and compile existing exploits. Troubleshoot and verify the actual result. Scope: retain practical use and adaptation of existing memory-corruption PoCs. Skip dedicated overflow development, stack/register/offset drills and shellcode development. Explain the mechanics necessary for the existing exploit alongside its use. Skill to develop: select and adapt a suitable public exploit and explain why it should work. Operational pages: public exploit selection and adaptation and public exploit quick sheet . Leave this block only after the exploit's effect is independently verified. <h2

title: 0.3.10 Obtain a reliable session
text: id="7-obtain-a-reliable-session">0.3.10 Obtain a reliable session Study unit: 4 of 8, second half. Apply Block 14 diagnostics for payload, listener, connectivity and session failures while they are relevant. Situation: I can execute commands. How do I get a reliable session? Choose direct execution, reverse/bind shells or authenticated remote access. Handle shell syntax, quoting, encoding, architecture and payload compatibility. Establish listeners and diagnose missing callbacks. Improve limited shells and transfer files. Verify the host, identity, privilege and network position. Skill to develop: separate execution failure, connection failure and session instability. Operational pages: shells, payloads and session repair and shell/payload quick sheet . Apply the callback ladder before replacing a payload blindly. <h2

title: 0.3.11 Escalate on Linux
text: id="8-escalate-on-linux">0.3.11 Escalate on Linux Study unit: 5 of 8, Linux track. Share the permissions/execution reasoning model with Block 9 but keep the operating-system mechanisms separate. Situation: I have a Linux shell. How do I become root? Credentials in files, histories, configuration and processes. Sudo, SUID/SGID and capabilities. Scheduled jobs, services, writable scripts, binaries and directories. PATH/environment dependencies and relevant mounts. Software/kernel exploit selection when supported by evidence. Manual validation of automated-enumerator findings. Skill to develop: trace your control into privileged execution. Operational pages: Linux privilege escalation and Linux quick sheet . Leave this block only when every candidate can be expressed as controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → verified effect. <h2

title: 0.3.12 Escalate on Windows
text: id="9-escalate-on-windows">0.3.12 Escalate on Windows Study unit: 5 of 8, Windows track. Study after Linux using the same control -> consumer -> identity -> trigger model without merging their techniques. Situation: I have a Windows shell. How do I become administrator or SYSTEM? Account context, groups, tokens, privileges and effective permissions. Stored credentials and useful configuration artifacts. Service permissions, writable binaries, unquoted paths and DLL loading. Scheduled tasks and other privileged consumers. Relevant token and software exploitation. Trigger conditions and final privilege verification. Skill to develop: establish both control over an object and a viable privileged trigger. <h2

title: 0.3.13 Map AD attack paths
text: id="10-map-ad-attack-paths">0.3.13 Map AD attack paths Study unit: 6 of 8. Study after Block 13's route/proxy fundamentals, then continue through Blocks 11 and 12 as one identity-and-movement chain. Situation: I have domain credentials. Where can this identity take me? Identify the domain, DCs, computers, accounts and groups. Enumerate shares, service accounts, permissions, sessions and host access. Collect and interpret BloodHound relationships. Validate promising edges and rank possible paths. Skill to develop: connect identity -> rights -> access -> new opportunities. <h2

title: 0.3.14 Gain a more useful domain identity
text: id="11-gain-a-more-useful-domain-identity">0.3.14 Gain a more useful domain identity Study unit: 6 of 8. Enter with a mapped relationship and leave by re-enumerating what the new identity can read, control or reach. Situation: how do I gain a more useful domain identity? AS-REP roasting and Kerberoasting. Credential access where current host privileges permit it. Account, group and directory-object permission abuse. Useful password, hash and ticket transitions. Ticket-abuse and DCSync prerequisites. Re-enumeration after every identity change. Skill to develop: explain why each transition works and what it unlocks. Operational pages: credential access , Kerberos and identity transitions , object control and domain compromise , and the AD cheatsheet . The active core follows the current BOK: password/roast paths, cached credentials, service-ticket forging and DCSync, plus the directory rights that directly enable those transitions. AD CS, delegation/RBCD and broad GPO abuse remain conditional supplements rather than core Block 11 requirements. <h2

title: 0.3.15 Move to another host
text: id="12-move-to-another-host">0.3.15 Move to another host Study unit: 6 of 8. Match password, hash or ticket to a reachable service and its authorization requirements; use the relevant Block 14 failure model immediately. Situation: I have useful credentials. How do I move to another host? SMB/service-based execution, WMI, WinRM and RDP. Password, hash and ticket authentication. Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket and Overpass-the-Hash. Authentication versus remote-access authorization. Host-specific permissions, service availability and failure diagnosis. Skill to develop: choose a movement method that matches the credential and destination. Operational pages: lateral movement , Kerberos and identity transitions , pivoting/tunneling , and the AD cheatsheet . Block 12 owns authentication-material-to-service execution; Block 13 owns the route that makes the service reachable. <h2

title: 0.3.16 Reach internal services
text: id="13-reach-internal-services">0.3.16 Reach internal services Study unit: 6 of 8, studied before Blocks 10-12. Routing is not inherently an AD technique, so retain this as a separate reference block even though it precedes the domain chain during study. Situation: the next service is behind another machine. How do I reach it? Discover internal interfaces, routes and services. Local/remote forwarding, dynamic forwarding and SOCKS. SSH tunnels and suitable alternative tunneling tools. DNS, proxy compatibility and callback routing. Diagnose each connection in the path. Skill to develop: draw and build the complete route your tools require. Operational pages: tunneling and port forwarding , pivoting cheatsheet , discovery through a SOCKS route , and lateral movement . Block 13 owns transport and reachability; Blocks 1, 2, 10 and 12 consume the new vantage point. <h2

title: 0.3.17 Resolve payload execution obstacles
text: id="14-resolve-payload-execution-obstacles">0.3.17 Resolve payload execution obstacles Study unit: cross-cutting during Units 2, 4 and 6; Unit 7 consolidates what remains. Do not wait until this point to diagnose a failure encountered earlier. Situation: the payload will not run. What needs changing? Relevant client-side delivery and required user interaction. Payload format, architecture, execution environment and dependencies. Security-control interference and justified adaptations. Metasploit modules, payloads, handlers and sessions. Tool-feature restrictions affecting practical choices. Skill to develop: isolate delivery, execution and connectivity problems. Operational pages: payload execution obstacles , payload-execution cheatsheet , shells and session repair , and pivoting . Block 14 owns the first-failed-boundary diagnosis; Blocks 4, 6, 7 and 13 own the original execution primitive, exploit, shell and route. <h2

title: 0.3.18 Complete and document an unfamiliar attack
text: id="15-complete-and-document-an-unfamiliar-attack">0.3.18 Complete and document an unfamiliar attack Study unit: 8 of 8. This is integration and independent selection, not another catalogue of attack techniques. Situation: how do I finish an unfamiliar target without losing the thread? Maintain a compact map of hosts, identities, credentials, routes and hypotheses. Prioritize tests and recover from dead ends. Capture access/privilege transitions and reproducible steps. Produce a report from retained evidence. Revisit assisted steps and test recognition on different targets. Skill to develop: integrate the techniques into an independent attack. Operational pages: integrated attack tracking and evidence , integrated attack/reporting cheatsheet , the cross-stage task index and each owning stage procedure selected by the state-change router. Block 15 owns orchestration, evidence and recovery; it does not duplicate the attack mechanics in Blocks 1–14. <h2

title: 0.3.19 Tooling map
text: id="tooling-map">0.3.19 Tooling map This table identifies tooling to cover. Exact commands, prerequisites, decisive output, failure examples and version checks accompany the individual teaching sections; it is not an installation list or a claim that these tools have been tested in the learner's environment. Tasks Tooling to cover Discovery and service investigation Nmap, service-native clients and relevant built-in utilities Web mapping and exploitation Browser, Burp Suite Community, curl, a suitable content-discovery tool and database clients Credentials John/Hashcat, relevant login clients and targeted authentication-testing tools Existing exploits SearchSploit, source inspection, interpreters, compilers and payload tools Shells and transfers Netcat, Socat, SSH/SCP, HTTP/SMB transfer methods and PowerShell Local escalation Native host checks first; LinPEAS/WinPEAS as candidate generators AD and movement Native enumeration, PowerView, BloodHound/SharpHound and relevant Impacket utilities Pivoting SSH, Chisel or another suitable tunnel, and proxy-aware clients Research the tools needed for the particular section, establish a popular baseline and cover viable alternatives with their selection criteria. Check official tool documentation for syntax and current OffSec guidance before labelling a feature exam-permitted. <h2

title: 0.3.20 Teaching and reference outputs
text: id="teaching-and-reference-outputs">0.3.20 Teaching and reference outputs Every taught section should produce: A hypothetical worked attack with prerequisites, commands, illustrative output and decisions explained. A paper-based changed-condition exercise that tests reasoning; hands-on validation follows after concept study is complete. Popular approaches first, followed by less popular but viable alternatives and failure-driven fallbacks. Master Notes explaining the necessary mechanisms. Complete operational procedures and extensive indexed cheatsheets for the approaches taught, usable with this chat closed. Preserve target-specific commands, actual credentials, flags, transcripts and assistance records in private lab records. Keep reusable public material generic and do not claim mastery or successful execution from a demonstration alone. <h2

title: 0.3.21 Sources
text: id="sources">0.3.21 Sources Hexdump OSCP modules : consult relevant sections as recurring supplements; exclude dedicated overflow development. Official Nmap reference : tool syntax and scan interpretation. OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge : published competency scope. OffSec OSCP+ exam guide : current format, restrictions and evidence requirements. This is a tutor-organized study map, not an official exam blueprint or a prediction of particular targets.

title: 6 Active Directory
text: id="6-active-directory">6 Active Directory 6.0 Quick reference | 6.5.3 Read command output Follow the numbered chapter and subsection that matches the current observation. Each interpretation row names one receiving section and the check needed there. Commands and synthetic examples remain concept-study references. <h2

title: 6.1 Connectivity and domain context
text: id="61-connectivity-and-domain-context">6.1 Connectivity and domain context §6.1 — Open 6.1: Connectivity and domain context <h2

title: 6.2 Enumeration

title: 6.2.5 Enumerate and validate effective object permissions
text: id="625-enumerate-and-validate-effective-object-permissions">6.2.5 Enumerate and validate effective object permissions §6 — AD Notes | §6.0 — Quick Reference | §6.5.3 — Read output A selected directory object and a controlled identity whose direct/nested memberships are known. Where to look: Read the target object security descriptor. Resolve the trustee SID , target object type, right, object-specific GUID, inheritance and relevant deny rules. Trace whether your controlled identity actually reaches the trustee. Expected behavior / secure boundary: Delegated administration is legitimate when narrowly scoped to intended trustees. Reading an ACL is usually not controlling its target. A powerful-looking ACE for an unrelated principal grants you nothing. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. <h2

title: 6.2.5.1 Baseline — Windows PowerShell
text: id="6251-baseline--windows-powershell">6.2.5.1 Baseline — Windows PowerShell Run: Windows PowerShell with reviewed PowerView. Requires: Read access to the selected object security descriptor; controlled trustee membership must be checked separately. Effect: Reads candidate ACEs; does not change permissions. Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight|WriteProperty|Self' } | Select-Object ObjectDN,SecurityIdentifier,ActiveDirectoryRights,ObjectAceType,AceType,IsInherited,InheritanceType What this checks: The filter selects interesting candidate ACEs, not a complete effective-access calculation. Resolve all applicable rules and the specific attribute/extended right before choosing a transition. <h2

title: 6.2.5.2 Interpret the output
text: id="6252-interpret-the-output">6.2.5.2 Interpret the output Raw/view evidence first. These are synthetic, abbreviated tool or graph-view excerpts. Graph relationship rows are a representative view, not collector console output. Version-specific wording and spacing can differ. The normalized observations below are a separate interpretation. Read §6.6.1 — SecurityIdentifier as the trustee field, §6.6.1 — ObjectAceType as the scoped operation/attribute GUID, and §6.6.1 — ActiveDirectoryRights as the represented operations. None alone establishes effective access. <summary

title: 6.2.5.2.1 Expected — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-5-2-1">6.2.5.2.1 Expected — raw evidence Command/view: Filtered Get-DomainObjectAcl projection The filtered query prints no rows. This sentence is an annotation, not program output. Decisive clue: No rows in this particular projection/filter. Supported: No candidate matching this query was displayed. Still missing: Read coverage, object scope and filter accuracy must be known before ruling out all control paths. Next check: §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions <summary

title: 6.2.5.2.2 Interesting — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-5-2-2">6.2.5.2.2 Interesting — raw evidence Command/view: Selected ACE projection (abbreviated) ObjectDN : CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test SecurityIdentifier : S-1-5-21-111-222-333-1200 ActiveDirectoryRights : WriteProperty ObjectAceType : member AceType : AccessAllowed IsInherited : False Decisive clue: member write is shown for a particular trustee SID. Supported: A group-membership write candidate exists; its connection to a controlled principal remains unverified. Still missing: Resolve the SID and check controlled direct/nested membership plus applicable deny and scope rules. Next check: §6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups <summary

title: 6.2.5.2.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-5-2-3">6.2.5.2.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence Command/view: A copy that projected the wrong trustee property ObjectDN : CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test IdentityReference : ActiveDirectoryRights : WriteProperty ObjectAceType : member Decisive clue: The projected IdentityReference value is blank. Supported: This may be a property-selection issue; it does not establish an ownerless ACE or permission denial. Still missing: Inspect the returned object before projection. Use SecurityIdentifier when that is the emitted trustee field, then resolve the principal. Next check: §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions Normalized observations: the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. ObjectDN: CN=Helpdesk,OU=Groups,DC=example,DC=test IdentityReference: EXAMPLE\Support ActiveDirectoryRights: WriteProperty ObjectAceType: member AceType: AccessAllowed Interpreted result What it establishes Required next check Continue at Support trustee A group receives the rule. Prove your identity belongs directly or through nesting. §6.2.1.1 — Baseline enumeration — users and groups member on Helpdesk A candidate group-membership modification right. Check applicable scope/deny rules and what membership would enable. §6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition WriteProperty alone The output may be incomplete or attribute-specific. Resolve its GUID; it does not mean every property is writable. §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions Stop when: Trustee, applicable right, target type and missing effective-access checks are explicit. Revisit only when: Membership, object ACL, scope or the controlled identity changes. <h2

title: 6.2.5.3 Decide and continue
text: id="6253-decide-and-continue">6.2.5.3 Decide and continue Result Decision Next numbered section Enabled after validation Effective control reaches a useful target: select a narrow permission-backed transition. §6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition Ruled out in this context The trustee is uncontrolled or the ACE does not apply: rule out this path. §6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships Inconclusive / failed check SID/GUID/inheritance is unresolved: do not perform a speculative modification. §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions <h2

title: 6.3.3 AS-REP roasting — conditions and output
text: id="633-as-rep-roasting--conditions-and-output">6.3.3 AS-REP roasting — conditions and output §6 — AD Notes | §6.0 — Quick Reference | §6.5.3 — Read output A known username/realm and KDC connectivity. A password is not required for the no-preauthentication branch; authenticated discovery is an alternative. Where to look: Inspect the account's preauthentication configuration or perform the selected-account request. Keep username existence, preauthentication setting, returned cipher and recovered password as separate evidence states. Expected behavior / secure boundary: Kerberos preauthentication is normally required. An account configured without it may expose an offline-guessable response. Strong credentials can still make guessing infeasible; receiving a response is not account compromise. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. <h2

title: 6.3.3.1 One known user, no password — Shell
text: id="6331-one-known-user-no-password--shell">6.3.3.1 One known user, no password — Shell Run: Kali / Linux with Impacket. Requires: Known target username/realm and KDC route; no password for the selected no-preauth request. Effect: Requests AS-REP material; does not recover a password by itself. impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/TARGET_USER' -no-pass -request \ -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep-TARGET_USER.hashes <h2

title: 6.3.3.2 Authenticated directory-backed discovery — Shell
text: id="6332-authenticated-directory-backed-discovery--shell">6.3.3.2 Authenticated directory-backed discovery — Shell Run: Kali / Linux with Impacket. Requires: Valid querying identity and directory/KDC route. Effect: Authenticated discovery/ticket requests; no directory modification. impacket-GetNPUsers 'DOMAIN/USER' -request \ -dc-ip DC_IP -outputfile asrep.hashes What this checks: GetNPUsers requests AS-REP material for a compatible account. The no-pass form does not submit password guesses. The authenticated form can discover/request eligible material with the supplied identity. <h2

title: 6.3.3.3 Interpret the output
text: id="6333-interpret-the-output">6.3.3.3 Interpret the output Normalized observations: the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. $krb5asrep$23$svc_legacy@example.test:SYNTHETIC_NOT_A_HASH Alternative: User svc_modern does not have UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set Interpreted result What it establishes Required next check Continue at $krb5asrep$23$ Typed RC4 AS-REP verifier, if actual complete output. Use the matching offline format; the displayed example is deliberately invalid. §6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope Preauthentication required This account is not eligible for this method now. Move to another supported clue; do not call the password invalid. §6.2.4.1 — Enumerate service accounts and SPNs KDC timeout The request did not produce account evidence. Check DC address, realm and KDC connectivity. §6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary Stop when: Eligibility, returned artifact type or the precise failed boundary is known. Revisit only when: Account preauthentication, username/realm or KDC connectivity changes. <h2

title: 6.3.3.4 Decide and continue
text: id="6334-decide-and-continue">6.3.3.4 Decide and continue Result Decision Next numbered section Enabled after validation A complete compatible verifier is returned: assess offline guessing feasibility. §6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope Ruled out in this context Preauthentication is required for that account: rule out this branch. §6.2.4.1 — Enumerate service accounts and SPNs Inconclusive / failed check Timeout or unknown principal: separate transport from spelling/realm and account existence. §6.5.1.1 — Diagnose the failed boundary <h2

title: 6.2.8 Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships
text: id="628-enumerate-using-bloodhound-and-validate-relationships">6.2.8 Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships §6 — AD Notes | §6.0 — Quick Reference | §6.5.3 — Read output A supported collector, compatible BloodHound deployment and a known collection identity. Mark only the identities and capabilities actually controlled. Where to look: Begin with directory relationships, then inspect the controlled principal's memberships and outbound control. Collect targeted local-group/session facts only where needed. For a chosen path, inspect each edge's object, source, age and missing prerequisite. Expected behavior / secure boundary: A graph contains potential relationships, including stale, inferred or incompletely collected edges. A missing edge can reflect collection gaps. DCOnly avoids host collection; it is not a complete host/session survey. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. <h2

title: 6.2.8.1 Baseline directory-only collection
text: id="6281-baseline-directory-only-collection">6.2.8.1 Baseline directory-only collection Run: Windows with compatible SharpHound CE. Requires: Domain DNS, authenticated directory context and compatible BloodHound ingestion. Effect: Collects directory relationships; DCOnly does not collect live workstation sessions. .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName domain-dconly.zip <h2

title: 6.2.8.2 Targeted host-group and session collection
text: id="6282-targeted-host-group-and-session-collection">6.2.8.2 Targeted host-group and session collection Run: Windows with compatible SharpHound CE. Requires: Explicit candidate-host file; required host connectivity and collection rights. Effect: Queries selected hosts; session collection loops and creates network activity. .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods LocalGroup --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-localgroups.zip .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --Loop --LoopDuration 00:10:00 --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-sessions.zip What this checks: The first command collects directory data. The next commands add selected-host group/session evidence. Choose the source matching the deployment; legacy and current collectors are not interchangeable. <h2

title: 6.2.8.3 Interpret the output
text: id="6283-interpret-the-output">6.2.8.3 Interpret the output Raw/view evidence first. These are synthetic, abbreviated tool or graph-view excerpts. Graph relationship rows are a representative view, not collector console output. Version-specific wording and spacing can differ. The normalized observations below are a separate interpretation. <summary

title: 6.2.8.3.1 Expected — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-8-3-1">6.2.8.3.1 Expected — raw evidence Command/view: Directory-only collection choice and graph results CollectionMethods: DCOnly Directory membership/ACL relationships: collected Live workstation sessions: not part of this collection Decisive clue: DCOnly collection scope. Supported: Directory relationships can be analyzed; no workstation session survey is implied. Still missing: A missing HasSession edge is not evidence of no logged-on users. Next check: §6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions <summary

title: 6.2.8.3.2 Interesting — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-8-3-2">6.2.8.3.2 Interesting — raw evidence Command/view: Graph relationship inspection, representative exported view analyst --MemberOf--> Support Support --AddMember--> Helpdesk Helpdesk --AdminTo--> APP01 Decisive clue: A possible identity-to-group-to-host chain. Supported: This is a path hypothesis composed of different relationship types. Still missing: Validate current membership, effective group-write permission, resulting host right, route and compatible service. Next check: §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions <summary

title: 6.2.8.3.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence
text: id="variant-6-2-8-3-3">6.2.8.3.3 Failed / inconclusive — raw evidence Command/view: Host/session collection summary, representative view APP01: session collection denied Session edges returned: 0 Directory import: completed Decisive clue: The host-derived session operation was denied. Supported: Directory ingestion succeeded while the session evidence is incomplete. Still missing: Collection permissions and freshness need validation; importing the ZIP did not repair host-query access. Next check: §6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions Normalized observations: the following is a synthetic interpretation example, not literal output from one command. Placeholder ciphers and secrets are deliberately unusable. analyst --MemberOf--> Support Support --AddMember--> Helpdesk Helpdesk --AdminTo--> APP01 APP01 --HasSession--> admin_ops Interpreted result What it establishes Required next check Continue at MemberOf / AddMember A possible identity-to-group transition. Validate current membership and exact effective group right. §6.2.5.1 — Enumerate and validate effective object permissions AdminTo APP01 A host-control candidate. Validate current host rights, reachable service and token context. §6.2.6.1 — Validate host-specific access rights HasSession admin_ops A volatile lead beyond host control. Recheck freshness and credential-source prerequisites; no automatic Domain Admin compromise. §6.2.7.1 — Enumerate and interpret sessions Stop when: One candidate path has each required edge classified and its next manual check chosen. Revisit only when: Collection scope, identity, host rights or session freshness changes. <h2

title: 6.2.8.4 Decide and continue
text: id="6284-decide-and-continue">6.2.8.4 Decide and continue Result Decision Next numbered section Enabled after validation The selected directory-object control edge is effective and useful: choose its permission-backed transition. Host and session edges use their interpretation rows above. §6.3.7.1 — Choose a permission-backed identity transition Ruled out in this context One edge is disproven: reject that chain and rank another evidence-backed lead. §6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships Inconclusive / failed check Host/session data was not collected: collect narrowly or validate manually. §6.2.8.1 — Enumerate using BloodHound and validate relationships <h2

title: 6.3.10 Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch
text: id="6310-select-an-ad-cs-delegation-or-gpo-branch">6.3.10 Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch §6 — AD Notes | §6.0 — Quick Reference | §6.5.3 — Read output A concrete service, configuration or object-right clue that selects one of these method families. These are conditional branches, not a default catalogue to run blindly. Where to look: AD CS: inspect enrollment services/templates, enrollment rights and applicable certificate/ authentication conditions. Delegation: inspect exact flags, SPNs , allowed targets and controlled principals. GPO: inspect effective links/scope, writable components, affected objects and refresh/trigger. Expected behavior / secure boundary: Certificates, delegation, trusts and linked policies can all be legitimate. A tool's vulnerable label or an isolated setting is only a candidate. The complete conjunction of effective rights, service configuration and authentication/trigger conditions determines whether a path exists. These commands are study references for a later scoped exercise. Replace placeholders for the selected environment; the output below is synthetic, not a recorded target result. Commands that collect secrets, request tickets, create sessions or change directory state require their stated prerequisites. <h2

title: 6.3.10.1 Baseline — Shell
text: id="63101-baseline--shell">6.3.10.1 Baseline — Shell Run: Kali / Linux with compatible Certipy. Requires: Directory/CA connectivity, explicit credentials and a concrete certificate-service clue. Effect: Enumerates configuration; a candidate label is not certificate issuance or account access. command -v certipy-ad || command -v certipy certipy-ad find -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -enabled -vulnerable -stdout What this checks: This command belongs only to the certificate branch after AD CS evidence is found. The full owning procedure separates template/CA enumeration, certificate requests, authentication and cleanup; GPO/delegation have different commands and prerequisites. <h2

Confirm effective CA/template rights and issuance policy. §6.3.10.1 — Select an AD CS, delegation or GPO branch Client Authentication A relevant certificate use is advertised. Check identity mapping and all conditions of the selected method. §6.3.2.1 — Classify recovered credentials and their scope Missing SAN/ACL/CA facts No complete certificate attack path is shown.
