text: id="5-why-it-works-1">3.1.6.5 Why it works One password may belong to several independently managed identities. Authentication success is useful only when associated with a precise service and allowed action. <h3

title: 3.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">3.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants Use the normal client for the observed service: ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore Local Windows account: nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares Decisive output: the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result. <summary

title: 3.1.6.6.1 Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-1">3.1.6.6.1 Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client. <summary

title: 3.1.6.6.2 Variant — one password across an authorized user list
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-2">3.1.6.6.2 Variant — one password across an authorized user list hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first. <summary

title: 3.1.6.6.3 Variant — HTTP POST form
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-3">3.1.6.6.3 Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives. <summary

title: 3.1.6.6.4 RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-4">3.1.6.6.4 RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell Use a reviewed, compatible build on the current Windows host with a known plaintext password. This creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an NT hash into a password. <h4

title: 3.1.6.6.5 Domain account: verify the new process token
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-5">3.1.6.6.5 Domain account: verify the new process token REM Domain account: verify the new process token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN <h4

title: 3.1.6.6.6 Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-6">3.1.6.6.6 Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account REM Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" <h4

title: 3.1.6.6.7 Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged
text: id="variant-3-1-6-6-7">3.1.6.6.7 Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged REM Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 Read: in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. With logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. Logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. An accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. RunasCs upstream . Native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. Neither tool guarantees an elevated token. accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. net accounts /domain Get-DomainPolicyData | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SystemAccess Password validation belongs to the existing credential procedure . Do not spray by default. If explicitly required, account for lockout threshold, duration, observation window and prior failures; use one justified candidate, stop on lockout/rate-limit evidence and preserve successful identities separately. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">3.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Identify a supported verifier/converter and build candidate structure from relevant names/policy/context rather than selecting an arbitrary hash mode. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct format/mode, complete salt/context, justified candidates and an available offline tool/backend Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Use the tool's show/result output and then validate the recovered credential in its correct context. Failure/next check: Token/separator errors imply wrong or incomplete input; no recovery means only the tested candidate space was exhausted. hashcat --example-hashes john --list=formats Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Artifact format matches SUPPORTED_MODE Candidate model: relevant words plus a justified suffix pattern Recognize this detail: A verified format and feasible candidate model enable offline recovery; a hash-shaped string alone does not. Still missing before method selection: Check complete salt/context, conversion correctness, tool backend and whether all required factors are present. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The verifier and candidate space are valid: use the selected offline strategy and verify recovered credentials. Ruled out in this context The artifact is a non-crackable token or unsupported format under this workflow: reject that mode. Inconclusive Parsing errors or an incomplete source require input repair; no recovery only exhausts the tested candidates. title: 3.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">3.1.7.5 Why it works Offline cracking compares candidate-derived values without contacting the service. Dictionary rules and masks model likely structure; infeasible keyspaces do not become useful through a different tool name. <h3

title: 3.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">3.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show -a 0 is dictionary mode. Do not use -a 3 with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. Common source examples identify NTLM as mode 1000 , Net-NTLMv2 as 5600 and KeePass as 13400 , but confirm against the installed version: hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH' <summary

title: 3.1.7.6.1 Mask and session variants
text: id="variant-3-1-7-6-1">3.1.7.6.1 Mask and session variants hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time. <summary

title: 3.1.7.6.2 Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits
text: id="variant-3-1-7-6-2">3.1.7.6.2 Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape. john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job File-to-hash converters: zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash Converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null Preserve the complete converter output. Some formats include a filename label before : that John accepts but Hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy. <h3

title: 3.1.8.2 Recognition clues

title: 3.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">3.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Look for a vault in readable backups/shares/application data, then inspect file identity and nearby factor/configuration references. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Complete database, compatible converter, and every required factor; a feasible password candidate strategy Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Open the database with all factors and distinguish vault credentials from target account credentials. Recognize this detail: The matching account name and verifier prefix identify an offline password-recovery candidate. text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">3.1.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the output schema of a justified local/domain credential source, keeping RID, machine and domain labels. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct account/domain and actual NT hash; recovery mode or an accepting NTLM service with required destination rights Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Verify source/type, identity context and the exact permitted service action. Failure/next check: Local/domain confusion, remote UAC and denied NTLM are different from an invalid hash. Use tickets only when their own prerequisites exist. head -n 3 hashes.txt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH::: Source: matched local registry extraction Recognize this detail: The source and record fields identify an NT verifier for that local account, not a captured challenge response. Still missing before method selection: Verify the actual NT field, account scope and an accepting service/client with the required destination right. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A compatible service accepts the correctly qualified hash identity: use only its verified authorization. Ruled out in this context The source produced Net-NTLMv2 or DCC2 instead: reject direct NT-hash reuse. Inconclusive An unlabeled hexadecimal value remains unknown until the source/account is resolved. title: 3.1.11.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-6">3.1.11.5 Why it works Pass-the-Hash uses a long-term NT key in an NTLM exchange; it does not convert every captured hash-like value into a reusable password equivalent. <h3

title: 3.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">3.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants Offline recovery: hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash Compatible SMB validation: nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material. <summary

title: 3.1.11.6.1 Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights
text: id="variant-3-1-11-6-1">3.1.11.6.1 Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-7">3.1.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use the saved authorized capture's structure and source context; inspect username/domain/challenge/response fields before selecting recovery. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct challenge/response formatting and feasible candidates; acquisition method must fit the allowed context Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Retain response provenance and recovered account/password mapping; confirm relevant login rights separately. Failure/next check: Incomplete captures or wrong separators break recovery. Prohibited spoofing/poisoning workflows are not an operational exam acquisition method. head -n 2 responses.txt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. USER::DOMAIN:SERVER_CHALLENGE:NT_PROOF:BLOB Recognize this detail: A challenge-bound response supports its appropriate offline verification workflow; it is not the long-term NT hash. Still missing before method selection: Check complete capture format, account mapping and feasible candidates; acquisition/relay policy is a separate issue. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A complete supported record permits offline recovery and later password validation. Ruled out in this context Using this response directly as an NT hash is the wrong mechanism: reject that authentication attempt. Inconclusive Truncated challenge/blob fields cannot support a valid recovery conclusion. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Classify the artifact and its identity context . <h3

title: 3.1.12.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-7">3.1.12.5 Why it works The captured response is bound to its challenge and exchange. It is not an NT hash for direct Pass-the-Hash; relay is a separate live protocol mechanism with additional policy and signing prerequisites. <h3

title: 3.1.12.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-7">3.1.12.6 Execute and choose variants hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash A Net-NTLMv2 response is not an NT hash and cannot be supplied to -H or -hashes . Relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights. The OSCP+ exam prohibits spoofing, including NBNS. Do not use Responder poisoning on the exam. Keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct username/salt/iteration context and feasible offline candidates Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Confirm artifact format, account mapping and current password acceptance. Failure/next check: No recovery does not disprove account existence; stale cached credentials may fail current online authentication. head -n 3 dcc2.txt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. $DCC2$ITERATIONS#USER#VERIFIER Recognize this detail: The DCC2 structure and username-associated derivation identify offline cached-logon material. title: 3.1.13.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-8">3.1.13.5 Why it works Cached interactive-logon verifiers support offline logon checks; they are not reusable NT hashes. Their derivation makes cracking materially different from NT recovery. <h3

title: 3.1.13.6 Execute and choose variants

DCC2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary PtH material. <h3

title: 3.1.14.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-9">3.1.14.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect an existing ticket/cache before collecting new material; identify its client, service, realm and validity. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context Requires: Correct principal/realm, valid lifetime, service scope, compatible cache format and naming/KDC route Action class: Credential processing and selected authentication; online guessing can affect lockout state. Stop/verify: Inspect principal, ticket service, realm and lifetime, then verify the actual service action. Failure/next check: Expired tickets, wrong hostname/SPN, cache format and time skew require different fixes; an IP-only connection can break correct Kerberos naming. klist -c FILE Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Default principal: USER@REALM Service principal: cifs/TARGET_HOST@REALM No krbtgt ticket listed Recognize this detail: This is service-scoped CIFS material, not a TGT for requesting arbitrary services. Still missing before method selection: Check lifetime, cache format, exact SPN/name, route and destination object authorization. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The matching SMB service accepts the ticket and allowed operation: use that scoped capability. Ruled out in this context A CIFS-only ticket does not enable a WinRM-specific authentication path. Inconclusive An unreadable/expired cache or unknown principal requires inspection/conversion rather than guessed reuse. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Inventory, convert and import tickets in the correct logon context . <h3

title: 3.1.14.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-9">3.1.14.5 Why it works A TGT can request service tickets ; a TGS is scoped to a service/SPN. A ticket for CIFS cannot simply be used as a WinRM credential. <h3

title: 3.1.14.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-9">3.1.14.6 Execute and choose variants Inspect before use: klist KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache Compatible client example: export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN' Verify client principal, realm, TGT versus service ticket, SPN, start/end time, clock, DNS/FQDN and routes. A readable cache does not prove authorization. Roasting, forging and detailed PtT/overpass belong to the AD procedures. <h3

title: 3.1.15 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">3.1.15 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 16 pp442–493. Hashcat examples , John documentation . Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 1.1 Discover attack surfaces
text: id="discover-attack-surfaces">1.1 Discover attack surfaces Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Discovery establishes reachable behavior from a particular source. Keep host discovery, TCP coverage, UDP coverage and application identity separate; each produces different evidence. Speedrun blocks: 1; revisit after new routes or hosts. Documented methods: 7. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 1.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">1.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 1.1.1.1 Confirm the source route
text: id="confirm-the-source-route">1.1.1.1 Confirm the source route Run from the machine that will send the scan. Keep the assigned scope explicit. ip addr ip route get TARGET nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery If A route selects the expected interface/source: Reachability still needs a probe; a route lookup alone is not a live host. → Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans . Otherwise: No response from host discovery: test the assigned host without assuming it is offline. → Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans . <h3

title: 1.1.1.2 Build a TCP port list with Nmap
text: id="build-a-tcp-port-list-with-nmap">1.1.1.2 Build a TCP port list with Nmap The command below scans all TCP ports with SYN privileges. Create the scans output directory first; use the complete connect-scan variant when unprivileged. Keep the fast initial pass distinct from full coverage. sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET If An open TCP port: Run focused service detection on the discovered ports, including nonstandard ones. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . Otherwise: Only TCP was checked: investigate UDP when the objective or DNS/SNMP/RPC clues call for it. → Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence . <h3

title: 1.1.1.3 Identify the responding application
text: id="identify-the-responding-application">1.1.1.3 Identify the responding application Keep the endpoint and raw service output; choose the matching client from its response. nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME If SMB/RPC responds: Check anonymous or known-identity share access. → Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities . If An HTTP response or redirect: Resolve the correct scheme and hostname before directory discovery. → Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . If An unrecognized listener: Send a protocol-specific probe instead of choosing an exploit by port number. → Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives . Otherwise: Results conflict with client behavior: rebuild the endpoint queue from confirmed responses. → Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue . <h2

title: 1.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">1.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with an assigned address/list and your actual source interface; no open service is assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Confirm the source interface, route and host-discovery limitations: Validate the source path and discover hosts . Separate initial TCP selection, full TCP coverage and UDP investigation: Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans ; Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence . Establish application evidence on discovered listeners, including nonstandard ports: Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks ; Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives . Save the endpoint queue and revisit it after a new identity or route: Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 1.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">1.1.3 Method families Source and reachability: Validate the source path and discover hosts , Enumerate reachable endpoints from a Windows source . Transport coverage and application identity: Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans , Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence , Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks , Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives . Evidence and re-enumeration: Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue . <h2

title: 1.1.4 Choose a method
text: id="choose-a-method">1.1.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Validate the source path and discover hosts No response, a new subnet, or uncertainty about the interface and route An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path A source-qualified reachable-host list and a defensible discovery limitation Enumerate reachable endpoints from a Windows source The useful vantage point is a Windows host without Nmap An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position A permitted Windows shell, explicit target list and built-in networking support Selected TCP reachability from the Windows network position Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans An assigned host needs an initial service queue or full TCP coverage An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage A saved TCP port-state inventory with explicit coverage Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence TCP enumeration is incomplete for the objective or DNS/SNMP/RPC clues suggest UDP An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit UDP responders and documented open/filtered uncertainty Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks A listener has a port-based label or uncertain version An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior Application and version evidence sufficient to choose service enumeration or an exploit candidate Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives A nonstandard listener, slow TCP discovery or a scanner-specific candidate An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates A validated listener/protocol candidate rather than an unverified scanner finding Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue Scanners disagree, a result is ambiguous, or a new identity changes accessible behavior An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position A selected endpoint and a test that can resolve the decision-changing uncertainty An evidence-labelled queue of endpoints, access contexts and next tests <h2

title: 1.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">1.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From the assessment host inspect the assigned interface and the route to the exact target before interpreting silence. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Record source address/interface, route and the exact responding endpoint; a missing ping response does not prove a host is down. Failure/next check: No route or wrong VPN interface is an environment failure. If only discovery is blocked, use the known-host TCP method; a SOCKS path requires a compatible connect-based client. ip addr ip route get TARGET nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. TARGET via VPN_GATEWAY dev tun0 src SOURCE_IP Nmap scan report for HOSTNAME (TARGET) Host is up Recognize this detail: The route names the intended interface/source; a responder is evidence from that source, not a global reachability claim. Still missing before method selection: Check scope, target state and whether host-discovery probes are permitted by this path. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The assigned route is correct and the selected application responds: proceed to service coverage. Ruled out in this context The route points outside the assigned VPN: repair that route before evaluating the target. Inconclusive No discovery response but a plausible route exists: the host may filter probes; test a justified selected port. If you do not yet have this clue: start with this topic's discovery workflow . <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">1.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From the Windows foothold inspect interfaces/routes, then check an assigned internal host's selected service ports. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: A permitted Windows shell, explicit target list and built-in networking support Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Associate each result with the actual Windows source and selected port; do not claim UDP or full-port coverage. Failure/next check: A false result may be routing, filtering or service absence; use route and listener evidence before deciding the service is down. Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 445 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. InterfaceAlias : ADAPTER SourceAddress : SOURCE_IP RemotePort : 445 TcpTestSucceeded : True Recognize this detail: The service is reachable from this Windows source; this can reveal a useful vantage point unavailable from Kali. Still missing before method selection: Confirm application/ authentication and whether a forward or a native client can use that route. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A protocol request works from this source: choose an authorized service client or suitable tunnel. Ruled out in this context The selected service is conclusively closed from this source: choose another observed endpoint. text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">1.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants Purpose: Test TCP reachability from a Windows host when source position or available tooling matters. Test one TCP port from the Windows source host: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS Read: TcpTestSucceeded , source and destination addresses. Use one number for PORTS. Failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem. <summary

title: 1.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">1.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: After path validation, compare a first TCP pass with explicit full-port coverage; record skipped discovery or privilege limitations. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Retain the selected port set, source context, completion/errors and raw output; follow open ports with focused application evidence. Failure/next check: Filtered is not closed. Through SOCKS use supported TCP-connect behavior and skip unsupported raw discovery/UDP; if results conflict, compare from the actual source. nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Initial selection: 22/tcp open ssh; 80/tcp open http Full selection also: 18080/tcp open unknown Recognize this detail: The high listener exists outside the first selection; its application label remains provisional. Still missing before method selection: Confirm scan completion, source, errors and application behavior on each interesting port. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A focused connection and application response confirm the listener: queue its service. Ruled out in this context The earlier result cannot be reproduced after a completed focused check: retire that stale listener hypothesis. Inconclusive Filtered ports or interrupted scans leave coverage/reachability unresolved; save the limit and choose a focused check. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate the source path and discover hosts . <h3

title: 1.1.7.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-2">1.1.7.3 Prerequisites Starting access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Required conditions: SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage. <h3

title: 1.1.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">1.1.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full <h3

title: 1.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">1.1.7.5 Why it works SYN and connect scans infer reachability differently but both cover only their selected ports. A common-port scan is a prioritization pass, not full TCP coverage. <h3

title: 1.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">1.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants Purpose: Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.1 Get initial TCP results
text: id="2-get-initial-tcp-results">1.1.7.6.1.1 Get initial TCP results sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET Coverage: 1,000 common TCP ports. Review scans/tcp-initial.nmap in a text editor. <summary

title: 1.1.7.6.1.1.1 Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports
text: id="variant-1-1-7-6-1-1-1">1.1.7.6.1.1.1 Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.2 Initial view: 1,000 common ports
text: id="initial-view-1000-common-ports">1.1.7.6.1.2 Initial view: 1,000 common ports Assigned host list, SYN scan: sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges: nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.3 Selected ports or a range
text: id="selected-ports-or-a-range">1.1.7.6.1.3 Selected ports or a range One host: replace PORTS with, for example, 25,43 or 1-1024 . sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET Find relevant services across assigned hosts: sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep A focused service sweep is not a full port map. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.4 Complete TCP coverage
text: id="3-complete-tcp-coverage">1.1.7.6.1.4 Complete TCP coverage sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET Coverage: TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs. <summary

title: 1.1.7.6.1.4.1 Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress
text: id="variant-1-1-7-6-1-4-1">1.1.7.6.1.4.1 Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.5 All TCP ports: 1-65535
text: id="all-tcp-ports-1-65535">1.1.7.6.1.5 All TCP ports: 1-65535 Connect scan: nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.6 Discovery skips a running target
text: id="discovery-skips-a-running-target">1.1.7.6.1.6 Discovery skips a running target Recheck relevant ports with response reasons: sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery: sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET -Pn assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use -sT without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.7 Timing and progress
text: id="timing-and-progress">1.1.7.6.1.7 Timing and progress Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress: sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET Faster timing on a stable path: sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET -T3 is normal timing; -T4 is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. <h5

title: 1.1.7.6.1.8 TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy
text: id="tcp-only-access-through-a-socks-proxy">1.1.7.6.1.8 TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET proxychains cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. -Pn avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it. <h3

title: 1.1.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-2">1.1.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the initial scan exposes SSH and HTTP. Test: finish full TCP selection. Illustrative output: an additional management service appears on a high port. Interpretation: add it to the queue before committing to a web-only path. <h3

title: 1.1.7.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-2">1.1.7.8 Verify the result Retain the selected port set, source context, completion/errors and raw output; follow open ports with focused application evidence. <h3

title: 1.1.7.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-2">1.1.7.9 Failure and fallback Filtered is not closed. Through SOCKS use supported TCP-connect behavior and skip unsupported raw discovery/UDP; if results conflict, compare from the actual source. <h3

title: 1.1.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-2">1.1.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A listener has a port-based label or uncertain version A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior §1.1.9 — Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks SMB/RPC endpoints, domain clues or new credentials Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter §1.2.6 — Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons §2.1.5 — Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state <h2

title: 1.1.8 Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence
text: id="probe-udp-and-resolve-ambiguous-silence">1.1.8 Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence Blocks: 1; revisit after new routes or hosts. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.1.8.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-3">1.1.8.1 Purpose and result UDP responders and documented open/filtered uncertainty. <h3

title: 1.1.8.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-3">1.1.8.2 Recognition clues TCP enumeration is incomplete for the objective or DNS/SNMP/RPC clues suggest UDP. <h4

title: 1.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">1.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect discovery results and DNS/SNMP/RPC clues, then probe a separate bounded UDP selection from the same source. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Use an application response for a confirmed service; document unresolved silence, coverage and ICMP rate-limit effects. Failure/next check: Do not translate UDP silence into a closed service. Retry a focused application-aware probe or a different permitted vantage point. sudo nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 20 --reason TARGET -oA udp-initial Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 161/udp open|filtered snmp no-response 53/udp open domain udp-response Recognize this detail: A DNS response confirms a UDP application; open|filtered SNMP silence is a candidate requiring a correctly formatted request. Still missing before method selection: Check accepted service parameters, response identity and possible ICMP rate limiting. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A service-native request returns the expected OID/record: enumerate that application. Ruled out in this context An explicit port-unreachable response rules out that UDP endpoint for this source/time. Inconclusive Silence can mean open or filtered; use a justified application-aware probe rather than declaring either. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate the source path and discover hosts . <h3

title: 1.1.8.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-3">1.1.8.3 Prerequisites Starting access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Required conditions: Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit. <h3

title: 1.1.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-3">1.1.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites sudo nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 20 --reason TARGET -oA udp-initial sudo nmap -Pn -sU -sV -p 53,161 TARGET -oA udp-focused <h3

title: 1.1.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">1.1.8.5 Why it works A UDP service may ignore an empty probe; ICMP errors and application responses distinguish states. Silence alone cannot distinguish open from filtered. <h3

title: 1.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">1.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants Purpose: Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. <h5

title: 1.1.8.6.1.1 Check UDP separately
text: id="5-check-udp-separately">1.1.8.6.1.1 Check UDP separately sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET Limit: this is a sample. open|filtered remains inconclusive; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it. <summary

title: 1.1.8.6.1.1.1 Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP
text: id="variant-1-1-8-6-1-1-1">1.1.8.6.1.1.1 Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP <h5

title: 1.1.8.6.1.2 Common-port samples
text: id="common-port-samples">1.1.8.6.1.2 Common-port samples Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted: sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET These are samples. open|filtered is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. <h5

title: 1.1.8.6.1.3 Selected ports
text: id="selected-ports">1.1.8.6.1.3 Selected ports Check a relevant UDP port/list: sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate: sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add -Pn with the same limitations as TCP. <h5

title: 1.1.8.6.1.4 Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost
text: id="full-udp-coverage-when-the-objective-justifies-the-cost">1.1.8.6.1.4 Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. <h5

title: 1.1.8.6.1.5 Combined TCP/UDP selection
text: id="combined-tcpudp-selection">1.1.8.6.1.5 Combined TCP/UDP selection Example selection: change the TCP ( T: ) and UDP ( U: ) lists for the actual question. sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan. <h3

title: 1.1.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-3">1.1.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: UDP/161 is open|filtered. Test: a correctly formatted SNMP request with a justified community. Illustrative output: system OIDs return. Interpretation: SNMP is confirmed accessible; enumerate useful branches. <h3

title: 1.1.8.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-3">1.1.8.8 Verify the result Use an application response for a confirmed service; document unresolved silence, coverage and ICMP rate-limit effects. <h3

title: 1.1.8.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-3">1.1.8.9 Failure and fallback Do not translate UDP silence into a closed service. Retry a focused application-aware probe or a different permitted vantage point. <h3

title: 1.1.8.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-3">1.1.8.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section UDP/161 evidence or an exposed management plane An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions §1.2.10 — Extract configuration and process information through SNMP A DNS server, domain name or host aliases Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer §1.2.9 — Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers RPC/NFS listeners or export information Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access §1.2.7 — Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity <h2

title: 1.1.9 Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks
text: id="identify-applications-and-validate-selected-nse-checks">1.1.9 Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks Blocks: 1; revisit after new routes or hosts. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.1.9.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-4">1.1.9.1 Purpose and result Application and version evidence sufficient to choose service enumeration or an exploit candidate. <h3

title: 1.1.9.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-4">1.1.9.2 Recognition clues A listener has a port-based label or uncertain version. <h4

title: 1.1.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-4">1.1.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Take the discovered open-port list and request protocol/version evidence rather than choosing attacks from conventional port numbers. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Preserve the responding product/version evidence and distinguish an inferred fingerprint from a confirmed vulnerable build. Failure/next check: A timeout, generic banner or scanner label leaves identity inconclusive; use native protocol clients or the unknown-port method. nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 18080/tcp open http APPLICATION_SERVER Service detection performed Recognize this detail: An HTTP response on a nonstandard port routes investigation to application mapping; a product string is still only fingerprint evidence. Still missing before method selection: Verify normal requests, hostname/TLS requirements and exact build/configuration before selecting an exploit. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Native protocol responses agree with the fingerprint: use that service's enumeration guide. Ruled out in this context A presumed SSH port instead speaks HTTP: discard the SSH-specific method for that endpoint. Inconclusive Generic banners or timeouts do not identify a build; try protocol-aware/TLS discrimination. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate the source path and discover hosts . <h3

title: 1.1.9.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-4">1.1.9.3 Prerequisites Starting access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Required conditions: A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior. <h3

title: 1.1.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-4">1.1.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME <h3

title: 1.1.9.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-4">1.1.9.5 Why it works Port numbers and banners suggest a protocol; application responses and exact configuration constrain an exploit. NSE results remain candidates when the check cannot prove the vulnerable condition. <h3

title: 1.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">1.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants Purpose: Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. <h5

title: 1.1.9.6.1.1 Identify discovered applications
text: id="4-identify-discovered-applications">1.1.9.6.1.1 Identify discovered applications nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET Next: choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability. <summary

title: 1.1.9.6.1.1.1 Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints
text: id="variant-1-1-9-6-1-1-1">1.1.9.6.1.1.1 Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints <h5

title: 1.1.9.6.1.2 Identify applications on discovered ports
text: id="identify-applications-on-discovered-ports">1.1.9.6.1.2 Identify applications on discovered ports Version probing plus the default NSE script set: use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters: nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. <h5

title: 1.1.9.6.1.3 Select a named script
text: id="select-a-named-script">1.1.9.6.1.3 Select a named script Inspect behavior locally: nmap --script-help http-headers After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s): nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. <h5

title: 1.1.9.6.1.4 OS fingerprinting and bundled probing
text: id="os-fingerprinting-and-bundled-probing">1.1.9.6.1.4 OS fingerprinting and bundled probing Estimate OS from network-stack behavior: sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET Request more tentative OS guesses: sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute: sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; -A does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful. <h3

title: 1.1.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-4">1.1.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: port 8443 is labelled HTTPS but the product is unknown. Test: version probes and a normal HTTP request. Illustrative output: a named management product and login route. Interpretation: map authentication and verify the build before exploit selection. <h3

title: 1.1.9.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-4">1.1.9.8 Verify the result Preserve the responding product/version evidence and distinguish an inferred fingerprint from a confirmed vulnerable build. <h3

title: 1.1.9.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-4">1.1.9.9 Failure and fallback A timeout, generic banner or scanner label leaves identity inconclusive; use native protocol clients or the unknown-port method. <h3

enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context §1.2.11 — Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols A DNS server, domain name or host aliases Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; title: 1.1.10 Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives
text: id="discriminate-unknown-listeners-and-use-scanner-alternatives">1.1.10 Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives Blocks: 1; revisit after new routes or hosts. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.1.10.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-5">1.1.10.1 Purpose and result A validated listener/protocol candidate rather than an unverified scanner finding. <h3

title: 1.1.10.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-5">1.1.10.2 Recognition clues A nonstandard listener, slow TCP discovery or a scanner-specific candidate. <h4

title: 1.1.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-5">1.1.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Select an unexplained listener from the saved queue, compare native connection behavior, then use focused version/TLS probes. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Confirm the endpoint through independent application behavior and preserve the rate/scope used for discovery. Failure/next check: No response may require TLS or a protocol-first request. Avoid treating speed-oriented results as complete, and keep prohibited mass vulnerability scanners outside the exam path. nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. PORT/tcp open ssl/http APPLICATION HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: https://HOSTNAME/ Recognize this detail: TLS and an HTTP redirect suggest a hostname-selected web application rather than an attack tied to the port number. Still missing before method selection: Reproduce the hostname/TLS request and confirm exact software/configuration. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A correctly addressed request produces the application: move to its normal behavior map. Ruled out in this context The banner disproves the originally assumed protocol: remove that service hypothesis. Inconclusive No banner may mean a client-first protocol, TLS or filtering; use a discriminating normal request. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate the source path and discover hosts . <h3

title: 1.1.10.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-5">1.1.10.3 Prerequisites Starting access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Required conditions: Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates. <h3

title: 1.1.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-5">1.1.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT <h3

title: 1.1.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">1.1.10.5 Why it works Fast discovery tools trade probing depth for speed. Recheck discovered ports with Nmap and a native client; a vulnerability-script label is not a complete exploit proof. <h3

title: 1.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">1.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants Use when: Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. <h5

title: 1.1.10.6.1.1 RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation
text: id="rustscan-fast-tcp-discovery-nmap-interpretation">1.1.10.6.1.1 RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation Prerequisite: RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. Coverage: only the explicit TCP range. Decisive output: a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap. <summary

title: 1.1.10.6.1.1.1 Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports
text: id="variant-1-1-10-6-1-1-1">1.1.10.6.1.1.1 Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection. <h5

title: 1.1.10.6.1.2 Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation
text: id="masscan-raw-packet-discovery-then-validation">1.1.10.6.1.2 Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation Prerequisite: root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. Choose it: for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. Failure cue: high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. <h5

title: 1.1.10.6.1.3 Unknown-port discrimination
text: id="unknown-port-discrimination">1.1.10.6.1.3 Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ Next action: route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. <h5

title: 1.1.10.6.1.4 NSE candidate checks
text: id="nse-candidate-checks">1.1.10.6.1.4 NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt The broad vuln category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt Avoid *brute* categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization . <h5

title: 1.1.10.6.1.5 Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation
text: id="nikto-bounded-web-server-candidate-generation">1.1.10.6.1.5 Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation Prerequisite: an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. Choose it: after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. Decisive output: a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt <summary

title: 1.1.10.6.1.5.1 HTTPS, host name and tuning variants
text: id="variant-1-1-10-6-1-5-1">1.1.10.6.1.5.1 HTTPS, host name and tuning variants nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect nikto -H / local documentation before relying on a copied code set. Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. <h3

title: 1.1.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-5">1.1.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: fast discovery reports an unexpected high port. Test: a focused version probe and protocol request. Illustrative output: an HTTP response appears. Interpretation: treat it as a web application regardless of its port. <h3

title: 1.1.10.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-5">1.1.10.8 Verify the result Confirm the endpoint through independent application behavior and preserve the rate/scope used for discovery. <h3

title: 1.1.10.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-5">1.1.10.9 Failure and fallback No response may require TLS or a protocol-first request. Avoid treating speed-oriented results as complete, and keep prohibited mass vulnerability scanners outside the exam path. <h3

text: id="2-recognition-clues-6">1.1.11.2 Recognition clues Scanners disagree, a result is ambiguous, or a new identity changes accessible behavior. <h4

title: 1.1.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">1.1.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Compare saved scan results with one direct connection and a service-native request for the endpoint that changes your next decision. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position Requires: A selected endpoint and a test that can resolve the decision-changing uncertainty Action class: Network probes and local output files. Stop/verify: Record which layer was demonstrated: transport, application, authentication, read/write or execution. Failure/next check: Connection success with no useful response needs a protocol-aware test; repeated identical failures without new evidence do not justify repeating the same path. nc -nvz TARGET PORT nmap -Pn -sT -p PORT --reason TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Connection to TARGET PORT succeeded PORT/tcp open SERVICE syn-ack Recognize this detail: Independent TCP reachability supports an endpoint candidate, not credentials, read permission or execution. Still missing before method selection: Identify the application and validate the particular next-layer action. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The protocol answers and the intended access check succeeds: record that specific capability. Ruled out in this context The expected protocol is absent despite a listener: reject that protocol-specific hypothesis. Inconclusive Conflicting source/time results need a controlled repeat and route comparison. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Validate the source path and discover hosts . <h3

title: 1.1.11.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-6">1.1.11.3 Prerequisites Starting access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position. Required conditions: A selected endpoint and a test that can resolve the decision-changing uncertainty. <h3

title: 1.1.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-6">1.1.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nc -nvz TARGET PORT nmap -Pn -sT -p PORT --reason TARGET <h3

title: 1.1.11.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-6">1.1.11.5 Why it works A TCP connection proves transport reachability, not successful protocol authentication or useful rights. Re-enumeration is required when identity or route changes. <h3

title: 1.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">1.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants Purpose: Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. <h5

title: 1.1.11.6.1.1 Resolve a result that changes your next action
text: id="6-resolve-a-result-that-changes-your-next-action">1.1.11.6.1.1 Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access. <summary

title: 1.1.11.6.1.1.1 Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output
text: id="variant-1-1-11-6-1-1-1">1.1.11.6.1.1.1 Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output <h5

title: 1.1.11.6.1.2 Netcat connection check
text: id="netcat-connection-check">1.1.11.6.1.2 Netcat connection check One TCP port: replace PORTS with one number. nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS Short port range: replace PORTS with a range such as 3388-3390 . nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. <h5

title: 1.1.11.6.1.3 Output and diagnostics
text: id="output-and-diagnostics">1.1.11.6.1.3 Output and diagnostics Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons: sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET Open saved .nmap or .txt output in a text editor. -oA writes .nmap , .gnmap and .xml ; -oN writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run. <h5

title: 1.1.11.6.1.4 Build the service queue
text: id="7-build-the-service-queue">1.1.11.6.1.4 Build the service queue Open the saved .nmap files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST Next: carry the complete endpoint tuple into Stage 02 service enumeration and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage. <summary

title: 1.1.11.6.1.4.1 Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established
text: id="variant-1-1-11-6-1-4-1">1.1.11.6.1.4.1 Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established open establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. closed records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. filtered leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. unfiltered means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. UDP open|filtered is inconclusive. A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. closed|filtered is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position. <h5

title: 1.1.11.6.1.5 Prioritize and know when to rescan
text: id="8-prioritize-and-know-when-to-rescan">1.1.11.6.1.5 Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed. <h3

title: 1.1.11.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-6">1.1.11.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: one scan calls a port filtered while Netcat connects. Test: repeat the focused scan and speak the application protocol. Illustrative output: a service banner returns. Interpretation: keep the application evidence and investigate timing/source differences. <h3
