title: 1.2.5 Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access
text: id="use-anonymous-or-authenticated-ftp-file-access">1.2.5 Use anonymous or authenticated FTP file access Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.5.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result">1.2.5.1 Purpose and result Retrieved files, configuration or a verified writable location. <h3

title: 1.2.5.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues">1.2.5.2 Recognition clues An FTP banner or accessible listing. <h4

title: 1.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">1.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: After identifying FTP, test the allowed anonymous context or one known credential and inspect its directory namespace. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Retrieve recognizable bytes or independently verify an uploaded canary; distinguish listing, read and write rights. Failure/next check: Login succeeds but transfers hang: diagnose the data path. A writable upload directory alone does not establish command execution. curl -v ftp://TARGET/ curl -v --user 'USER:PASSWORD' ftp://TARGET/ Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 230 Login successful LIST: application.conf; backups/ RETR application.conf: 226 Transfer complete Recognize this detail: A listing identifies candidate artifacts; a completed RETR with recognizable bytes establishes read access. Still missing before method selection: Validate the account context, file contents, data-channel reachability and any separate write/consumer conditions. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The relevant file is readable and contains a current typed secret: follow credential classification. Ruled out in this context Anonymous login is denied: rule out anonymous access, retaining authenticated FTP as a separate possibility. Inconclusive Login works but data transfer hangs: inspect active/passive data routing before concluding file access is denied. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.5.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites">1.2.5.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Anonymous login allowed or a valid FTP identity; data-channel connectivity and object-specific read/write rights. <h3

title: 1.2.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites">1.2.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -v ftp://TARGET/ curl -v --user 'USER:PASSWORD' ftp://TARGET/ <h3

title: 1.2.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">1.2.5.5 Why it works FTP authentication and directory listing do not guarantee downloads or uploads. Passive/active data channels can fail independently of the control connection; uploaded bytes need a separate execution consumer. <h3

title: 1.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">1.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: FTP usually appears on TCP/21, but trust an FTP banner or protocol response on any port. Goal: determine authentication, listable/readable content and effective write locations. <h5

title: 1.2.5.6.1.1 Baseline: anonymous access
text: id="baseline-anonymous-access">1.2.5.6.1.1 Baseline: anonymous access ftp TARGET At the prompts, try user anonymous and an email-like password. Then: status pwd ls -la binary get FILE quit If login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's passive command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. Decisive output: code 230 accepts the login; directory listings and successful RETR establish read access. Inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. Store target artifacts outside this public repository. <summary

title: 1.2.5.6.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated FTP
text: id="variant-1-2-5-6-1-1-1">1.2.5.6.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated FTP ftp TARGET Enter USER and the password when prompted. Enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access. <summary

title: 1.2.5.6.1.1.2 Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test
text: id="variant-1-2-5-6-1-1-2">1.2.5.6.1.1.2 Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER ftp://TARGET/ curl --user USER -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt Omit --user for anonymous access. Let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. Upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the FTP client after the test. <summary

title: 1.2.5.6.1.1.3 Variant — focused Nmap helpers
text: id="variant-1-2-5-6-1-1-3">1.2.5.6.1.1.3 Variant — focused Nmap helpers nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET ftp-anon checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; ftp-syst asks for server/system information. Manually confirm useful access with a protocol client. Failure cues: 530 means that login was rejected, not that FTP has no other usable identity. A listing failure after 230 may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. A successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. Next action: inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block. <h3

title: 1.2.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical">1.2.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: anonymous login succeeds. Test: list and download one relevant readable configuration. Illustrative output: an application username is present. Interpretation: classify its credential context and test only a compatible service. <h3

title: 1.2.5.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result">1.2.5.8 Verify the result Retrieve recognizable bytes or independently verify an uploaded canary; distinguish listing, read and write rights. <h3

title: 1.2.5.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback">1.2.5.9 Failure and fallback Login succeeds but transfers hang: diagnose the data path. A writable upload directory alone does not establish command execution. <h3

title: 1.2.5.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions">1.2.5.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol §3.1.5 — Classify the artifact and its identity context JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope §2.1.8 — Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts A password tied to a plausible user and service Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state §3.1.6 — Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse <h2

title: 1.2.6 Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities
text: id="enumerate-smbrpc-shares-files-and-identities">1.2.6 Enumerate SMB/RPC shares, files and identities Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.6.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-1">1.2.6.1 Purpose and result Domain/user clues, readable files or object-specific writable access. <h3

title: 1.2.6.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-1">1.2.6.2 Recognition clues SMB/RPC endpoints, domain clues or new credentials. <h4

title: 1.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">1.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Start from confirmed SMB and explicitly compare anonymous versus a known authenticated context, then open a relevant named share. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Prove the specific share/object action; a successful login or administrative indicator does not establish every remote-execution route. Failure/next check: Access denied after login usually means authorization/context. Test local/domain qualification and the exact object rather than repeating passwords. smbclient -L //TARGET -N smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Sharename Type SHARE Disk NETLOGON Disk Recognize this detail: A share name supplies a filesystem investigation target; listing it does not prove read, write or service creation. Still missing before method selection: Connect to the named share under the identity that listed it, then ls/get the exact object. Listing a share does not prove read or write. For a write candidate, verify the path operation and identify a separate execution consumer before treating it as access. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A relevant configuration can be retrieved: inspect its account/secret context. Ruled out in this context The authenticated account cannot read that object: discard the read path for this identity, not all SMB opportunities. Inconclusive Login succeeds but listing fails: check a justified known share path and separate share/NTFS authorization. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.6.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-1">1.2.6.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter. <h3

title: 1.2.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-1">1.2.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites smbclient -L //TARGET -N smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' <h3

title: 1.2.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">1.2.6.5 Why it works Session establishment, share enumeration, filesystem rights and remote execution are separate authorization layers. A credential change can reveal entirely new shares and files. <h3

title: 1.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">1.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: direct-hosted SMB commonly uses TCP/445; NetBIOS session service commonly uses TCP/139; MS-RPC endpoint mapping commonly uses TCP/135. They are related Windows surfaces but not interchangeable. Goal: distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. <h5

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1 Baseline: list shares without credentials
text: id="baseline-list-shares-without-credentials">1.2.6.6.1.1 Baseline: list shares without credentials smbclient -N -L //TARGET Decisive output: a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. It does not prove access to share contents. NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated share listing and connection
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-1">1.2.6.6.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated share listing and connection smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' The first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. Let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. Inside the share: pwd ls allinfo FILE get FILE mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit Use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. A successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.2 Variant — recursive retrieval
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-2">1.2.6.6.1.1.2 Variant — recursive retrieval smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON;prompt OFF;mget *' Run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. Search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.3 Variant — RPC null or authenticated session
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-3">1.2.6.6.1.1.3 Variant — RPC null or authenticated session rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET Useful interactive queries: srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser RID netshareenumall quit Null-session denial is common on modern systems. Authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.4 Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-4">1.2.6.6.1.1.4 Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET NetExec ( nxc ) is the current command name on recent Kali releases; older material may use crackmapexec . These tools consolidate candidates. Confirm useful shares and files with smbclient or native access. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.5 Variant — protocol, signing and time clues
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-5">1.2.6.6.1.1.5 Variant — protocol, signing and time clues nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET Signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. The older smb-os-discovery script depends on SMBv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.6 Variant — Windows built-ins
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-6">1.2.6.6.1.1.6 Variant — Windows built-ins net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE These use the current Windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. An existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors. <summary

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.7 SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-7">1.2.6.6.1.1.7 SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file Use from Kali when SMB is reachable. Choose the same domain/local identity that worked with smbclient. Suppress write probes when inventorying reads; this means a writable label is not being tested here. <h6

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.8 Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-8">1.2.6.6.1.1.8 Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file # Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --no-write-check <h6

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.9 Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-9">1.2.6.6.1.1.9 Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth # Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -r 'SHARE' --depth 2 --no-write-check <h6

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.10 Download the specific file found above
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-10">1.2.6.6.1.1.10 Download the specific file found above # Download the specific file found above smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --download 'SHARE\PATH\FILE' --no-write-check Read: a listed file must still be readable under this identity. A downloaded config/backup → classify its credential material, then test only the relevant account/service. A denied share → try another listed share or a newly obtained identity; do not infer a host-wide denial. SMBMap upstream . For broader SMB/RPC collection, use the existing enum4linux-ng baseline; authenticate explicitly when credentials exist: <h6

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.11 No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-11">1.2.6.6.1.1.11 No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates # No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates enum4linux-ng -A TARGET <h6

title: 1.2.6.6.1.1.12 Known identity: domain objects visible to this account
text: id="variant-1-2-6-6-1-1-12">1.2.6.6.1.1.12 Known identity: domain objects visible to this account # Known identity: domain objects visible to this account enum4linux-ng -A -w DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' TARGET Next: validate returned users/groups/shares with rpcclient or smbclient. A collector can return partial data despite a successful login. Failure cues: distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. A share named IPC$ is not a general file share. Guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. A share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. Next action: inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. Move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/AD blocks. <h5

title: 1.2.6.6.1.2 NetBIOS names before SMB enumeration
text: id="netbios-names-before-smb-enumeration">1.2.6.6.1.2 NetBIOS names before SMB enumeration Use when UDP/137 or SMB suggests Windows names but DNS/domain identity is unclear. # Ask the assigned host for its NetBIOS names nbtscan TARGET nmblookup -A TARGET Read: a machine name and group/domain label are leads. A workgroup label does not prove AD membership. Resolve the returned name and use the SMB/LDAP checks with the accepted identity. No reply can mean filtering or disabled NetBIOS while TCP/445 still works. Sources: upstream 1 . <h5

title: 1.2.6.6.1.3 SMB/RPC RID lookups when a normal user listing is denied
text: id="smbrpc-rid-lookups-when-a-normal-user-listing-is-denied">1.2.6.6.1.3 SMB/RPC RID lookups when a normal user listing is denied Use when the accepted identity can translate SIDs but cannot list the directory directly. Keep the queried host/domain and a bounded RID range explicit. nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --rid-brute 4000 Read: classify returned SID types—users, groups and machine accounts are different objects. The upper bound is coverage, not proof that higher RIDs contain nothing. A resolved name is not a password, service authorization or successful logon. Prefer the existing native directory/RPC listing when it is available; do not infer no accounts from a single denied enumeration method. Sources: upstream 1 . <h3

title: 1.2.6.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-1">1.2.6.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: anonymous share listing is denied but a recovered domain credential works. Test: open one relevant share and retrieve a configuration. Illustrative output: a service account secret appears. Interpretation: record its identity and re-enter credential validation. <h3

title: 1.2.6.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-1">1.2.6.8 Verify the result Prove the specific share/object action; a successful login or administrative indicator does not establish every remote-execution route. <h3

title: 1.2.6.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-1">1.2.6.9 Failure and fallback Access denied after login usually means authorization/context. Test local/domain qualification and the exact object rather than repeating passwords. <h3

title: 1.2.6.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-1">1.2.6.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol §3.1.5 — Classify the artifact and its identity context A valid domain identity and accessible file services Reachable SMB plus share/object read rights in the chosen identity context §6.2.9.7 — Read domain shares, SYSVOL and NETLOGON for useful artifacts A destination grants administrative-share write and service-control rights SMB/SCM reachability, writable required share, effective service-creation/start rights and an accepted password/hash or supported Kerberos context §6.4.4.7 — Execute through uploaded service creation using PsExec <h2

title: 1.2.7 Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity
text: id="inspect-rpcnfs-exports-and-effective-file-identity">1.2.7 Inspect RPC/NFS exports and effective file identity Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.7.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-2">1.2.7.1 Purpose and result Readable files or a controlled write with established identity semantics. <h3

title: 1.2.7.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-2">1.2.7.2 Recognition clues RPC/NFS listeners or export information. <h4

title: 1.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">1.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Follow RPC/NFS discovery with export inspection, then examine actual ownership/mapping on an allowed mount. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify the export, mapped identity, actual bytes and any created file's server-side ownership. Failure/next check: An empty showmount response does not rule out NFSv4. Mount failure may be transport/export/client-policy rather than absence of files. rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 100003 3 tcp NFS_PORT nfs Export list for TARGET: /EXPORT CLIENT_SCOPE Recognize this detail: An export lists a filesystem candidate and client policy; it does not establish file access or trusted UID 0. Still missing before method selection: Use the owning procedure to verify NFS version, allowed client, numeric identity mapping, read/write and squash/mount policy. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The relevant mapped identity can read configuration: retrieve and classify its useful artifacts. Ruled out in this context The export permits a different client scope: rule out this source's mount route. Inconclusive Empty showmount can miss NFSv4 context; confirm version/export behavior before declaring no NFS access. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.7.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-2">1.2.7.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachable RPC/NFS transports, permitted client address and an export whose UID/GID mapping grants relevant access. <h3

title: 1.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">1.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET <h3

title: 1.2.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">1.2.7.5 Why it works NFS authorization can depend on numeric IDs and export options. root_squash prevents remote UID 0 from automatically becoming server root; no_root_squash alone still needs a useful consumer or execution path. <h3

title: 1.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">1.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: rpcbind commonly appears on TCP/UDP 111 and NFS on TCP/UDP 2049, with additional dynamically assigned RPC ports. Goal: find exports, allowed client ranges and effective UID/GID-based permissions. <h5

title: 1.2.7.6.1.1 Baseline: list RPC services and exports
text: id="baseline-list-rpc-services-and-exports">1.2.7.6.1.1 Baseline: list RPC services and exports rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET Decisive output: rpcinfo maps RPC programs to versions/transports/ports. showmount -e returns exports and apparent allowed clients, but NFSv4-only servers may not expose the mount service and showmount completeness varies by implementation. <summary

title: 1.2.7.6.1.1.1 Variant — Nmap without mounting
text: id="variant-1-2-7-6-1-1-1">1.2.7.6.1.1.1 Variant — Nmap without mounting nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs TARGET The scripts can list exports, file attributes and access flags. Confirm access manually when a finding matters. <summary

title: 1.2.7.6.1.1.2 Variant — mount read-only first
text: id="variant-1-2-7-6-1-1-2">1.2.7.6.1.1.2 Variant — mount read-only first sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit If version 3 fails and version 4 is advertised, retry with -o ro,vers=4 . NFSv4 may present a pseudo-filesystem whose export path differs from showmount output. <summary

title: 1.2.7.6.1.1.3 Variant — inspect numeric ownership
text: id="variant-1-2-7-6-1-1-3">1.2.7.6.1.1.3 Variant — inspect numeric ownership ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable -ls NFS commonly authorizes Unix identities by numeric UID/GID. A matching local username is irrelevant if its number differs. root_squash usually maps remote UID 0 to an unprivileged identity; no_root_squash is dangerous but still requires a useful writable object and privileged consumption path. <summary

title: 1.2.7.6.1.1.4 Variant — bounded write verification
text: id="variant-1-2-7-6-1-1-4">1.2.7.6.1.1.4 Variant — bounded write verification sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit Use a unique harmless name only when write validation is needed and authorized. Record the resulting numeric owner/group. Success proves write in that directory, not execution or privileged ownership. Failure cues: showmount failure does not rule out NFSv4. access denied by server can mean export client restrictions or wrong path/version. permission denied after mounting is file authorization, not network failure. Do not change local UIDs or write to an export during concept study. Next action: inspect readable backups, home data, keys and configuration; record numeric ownership and actual write boundaries; send a writable/privileged-consumer hypothesis to the escalation block. <h3

title: 1.2.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-2">1.2.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an export permits the assessment client. Test: inspect ownership and a scoped read. Illustrative output: a backup configuration is readable under a matching numeric UID. Interpretation: recover its secrets; assess writes separately. <h3

title: 1.2.7.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-2">1.2.7.8 Verify the result Verify the export, mapped identity, actual bytes and any created file's server-side ownership. <h3

title: 1.2.7.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-2">1.2.7.9 Failure and fallback An empty showmount response does not rule out NFSv4. Mount failure may be transport/export/client-policy rather than absence of files. <h3

title: 1.2.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-2">1.2.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol §3.1.5 — Classify the artifact and its identity context A writable/exported filesystem or a loopback-only service with useful privileges Relevant export/mount options or service authentication; effective identity, writable path and any privileged execution consumer §5.1.18 — Exploit a permission-backed mount, NFS mapping or local service A tool/artifact must reach a target that can make an HTTP request Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination §4.2.11 — Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients <h2

title: 1.2.8 Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access
text: id="use-ssh-passwords-keys-and-forwarding-capable-access">1.2.8 Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.8.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-3">1.2.8.1 Purpose and result An authenticated shell, subsystem or forwarding capability with verified identity. <h3

title: 1.2.8.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-3">1.2.8.2 Recognition clues An SSH service and a known password, private key or agent context. <h4

title: 1.2.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">1.2.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Find SSH in service discovery, then trace a candidate password/key back to its recorded user before a bounded authentication attempt. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Run hostname and id in the resulting context; retain whether a shell, SFTP or only forwarding was actually granted. Failure/next check: Permission denied may be username, key, passphrase, policy or method mismatch. A successful banner exchange proves none of these. ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Authenticated to TARGET using publickey uid=USER_ID(USER) gid=GROUP_ID(GROUP) Recognize this detail: Accepted key authentication plus a verified shell identity establishes that specific login, not root or unrestricted forwarding. Still missing before method selection: Check actual account/shell/subsystem and separately inspect forwarding policy if a tunnel is needed. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended user can run commands: establish host/privilege/network state. Ruled out in this context The same valid key is not authorized for this user: rule out that username/key pairing. Inconclusive A passphrase prompt or host policy rejection requires key/context diagnosis; it is not evidence that all SSH access is unavailable. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.8.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-3">1.2.8.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Compatible authentication method, correct user, accepted key policy and the requested shell/subsystem permission. <h3

title: 1.2.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-3">1.2.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET <h3

title: 1.2.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">1.2.8.5 Why it works SSH authentication can succeed while shell access is restricted. Key ownership, passphrase and server authorization matter independently; forwarding is a separately controlled feature. <h3

title: 1.2.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">1.2.8.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: SSH commonly uses TCP/22. Prerequisite for access: an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. <h5

title: 1.2.8.6.1.1 Baseline: validate one known identity
text: id="baseline-validate-one-known-identity">1.2.8.6.1.1 Baseline: validate one known identity ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET Decisive output: the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. A shell prompt establishes session access as that identity. <summary

title: 1.2.8.6.1.1.1 Variant — private key
text: id="variant-1-2-8-6-1-1-1">1.2.8.6.1.1.1 Variant — private key chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET The key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. Permission denied (publickey) can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions. <summary

title: 1.2.8.6.1.1.2 Variant — discover methods for a known username
text: id="variant-1-2-8-6-1-1-2">1.2.8.6.1.1.2 Variant — discover methods for a known username nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET This starts an authentication exchange and is logged; Nmap classifies it as intrusive. Use it only when the supported methods change the next decision. <summary

title: 1.2.8.6.1.1.3 Variant — non-interactive key check
text: id="variant-1-2-8-6-1-1-3">1.2.8.6.1.1.3 Variant — non-interactive key check ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET 'id' Batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. It is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively. Failure cues: timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; Permission denied proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. A valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. Next action: after a shell, verify whoami , groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. Password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure. <h3

title: 1.2.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-3">1.2.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a disclosed private key names a local user. Test: inspect the key and authenticate to that user. Illustrative output: a shell returns with a non-root UID. Interpretation: establish Linux state and inspect allowed forwarding. <h3

title: 1.2.8.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-3">1.2.8.8 Verify the result Run hostname and id in the resulting context; retain whether a shell, SFTP or only forwarding was actually granted. <h3

title: 1.2.8.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-3">1.2.8.9 Failure and fallback Permission denied may be username, key, passphrase, policy or method mismatch. A successful banner exchange proves none of these. <h3

title: 1.2.8.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-3">1.2.8.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A new Linux foothold or an identity/privilege change A working command channel and accurate effective identity, group, mount and process context §5.1.5 — Establish Linux state and choose an escalation candidate A private key from a file read, share, repository or home directory Correct key format, passphrase if encrypted, matching server account/key authorization and accepted algorithm/policy §3.1.9 — Inspect and recover SSH private-key access SSH reaches a server that can access the needed internal service Accepted SSH identity and forwarding policy; local listener availability and SSH-server-to-destination route §6.1.3.7 — Forward a selected service through an SSH client-side listener <h2

title: 1.2.9 Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers
text: id="expand-names-through-dns-records-and-zone-transfers">1.2.9 Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.9.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-4">1.2.9.1 Purpose and result Hostnames, address relationships and possibly a zone inventory. <h3

title: 1.2.9.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-4">1.2.9.2 Recognition clues A DNS server, domain name or host aliases. <h4

title: 1.2.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-4">1.2.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use DNS-server evidence and discovered domain names to query authority and specific records before considering a transfer. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Identify responding server, record type, answer and zone authority; transfer refusal disproves only that transfer/context. Failure/next check: No answer may mean wrong server, recursion policy, transport or zone. Resolve authoritative context before retrying AXFR. dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. DOMAIN. SOA DC_HOST. HOSTMASTER. HOSTNAME.DOMAIN. A TARGET Transfer completed Recognize this detail: An authoritative zone and returned records can expose hostnames, aliases and applications needing separate enumeration. Still missing before method selection: Check each new name's scope/address and verify host/virtual-host behavior. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A permitted transfer returns a relevant new host: validate it through discovery. Ruled out in this context Transfer refused rules out AXFR on this server/zone/context; ordinary records may remain useful. Inconclusive A timeout or non-authoritative response requires authority/transport checks before any zone conclusion. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.9.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-4">1.2.9.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer. <h3

title: 1.2.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-4">1.2.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR <h3

title: 1.2.9.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-4">1.2.9.5 Why it works A DNS answer belongs to a server and zone context. AXFR exposes zone records only when the server is authoritative and permits the transfer; names become discovery or virtual-host inputs. <h3

title: 1.2.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">1.2.9.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries and TCP/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. Prerequisite: a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. <h5

title: 1.2.9.6.1.1 Baseline: query the target DNS server directly
text: id="baseline-query-the-target-dns-server-directly">1.2.9.6.1.1 Baseline: query the target DNS server directly dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN A dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT Decisive output: ANSWER records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. The aa flag supports an authoritative answer. Record status separately from the answer count. <summary

title: 1.2.9.6.1.1.1 Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer
text: id="variant-1-2-9-6-1-1-1">1.2.9.6.1.1.1 Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR A successful AXFR returns the zone records and closing SOA. Transfer failed , REFUSED or NOTAUTH only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries. <summary

title: 1.2.9.6.1.1.2 Variant — name guessing after the domain is known
text: id="variant-1-2-9-6-1-1-2">1.2.9.6.1.1.2 Variant — name guessing after the domain is known dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN Check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. Every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input. <summary

title: 1.2.9.6.1.1.3 Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range
text: id="variant-1-2-9-6-1-1-3">1.2.9.6.1.1.3 Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET Use this only when the entire SUBNET is assigned. PTR names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results. <summary

title: 1.2.9.6.1.1.4 Variant — host and Windows nslookup
text: id="variant-1-2-9-6-1-1-4">1.2.9.6.1.1.4 Variant — host and Windows nslookup host -t mx DOMAIN TARGET host -t txt DOMAIN TARGET nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=MX DOMAIN TARGET Failure cues: NXDOMAIN means that queried name does not exist in that view; NOERROR with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. Timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. A recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. Next action: add new hostnames/IPs to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints. <h3

title: 1.2.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-4">1.2.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the authoritative server permits AXFR. Test: inspect the returned A/CNAME records. Illustrative output: a previously unknown application hostname. Interpretation: confirm scope/address reachability and request that virtual host. <h3

title: 1.2.9.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-4">1.2.9.8 Verify the result Identify responding server, record type, answer and zone authority; transfer refusal disproves only that transfer/context. <h3

title: 1.2.9.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-4">1.2.9.9 Failure and fallback No answer may mean wrong server, recursion policy, transport or zone. Resolve authoritative context before retrying AXFR. <h3

title: 1.2.9.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-4">1.2.9.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section No response, a new subnet, or uncertainty about the interface and route Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path §1.1.5 — Validate the source path and discover hosts DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing §2.1.6 — Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications Domain credentials or a domain-joined foothold Correct realm/domain and account qualification; reachable DC/services, usable DNS and acceptable clock skew §6.2.9.5 — Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route <h2

title: 1.2.10 Extract configuration and process information through SNMP
text: id="extract-configuration-and-process-information-through-snmp">1.2.10 Extract configuration and process information through SNMP Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.10.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-5">1.2.10.1 Purpose and result Host, interface, software or process/configuration clues from permitted OID branches. <h3

title: 1.2.10.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-5">1.2.10.2 Recognition clues UDP/161 evidence or an exposed management plane. <h4

title: 1.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-5">1.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Take UDP/161 evidence and a justified management credential/community, then request a small known OID branch before a broad walk. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Preserve the OID, accepted security context and returned value; empty branches can reflect view restrictions. Failure/next check: Silence can mean UDP filtering, wrong community/version or denied view; change only the condition supported by evidence. snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SNMPv2-MIB::sysDescr.0 = STRING: OS_AND_BUILD SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: HOSTNAME Recognize this detail: A real OID response confirms the accepted read context and supplies software/name clues. Still missing before method selection: Determine which useful views/branches are actually readable; process data and write rights are separate. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A relevant interface/process branch returns useful data: follow the named subnet/application/credential. Ruled out in this context An explicit authorization failure rules out that security context/view. Inconclusive UDP silence can be routing, version, community or view policy; a timeout cannot choose between them. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.10.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-5">1.2.10.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: An accepted read community or SNMPv3 identity/security level; transport and view permissions. <h3

title: 1.2.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-5">1.2.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.1 <h3

title: 1.2.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">1.2.10.5 Why it works An SNMP community acts as an access selector; views can expose only some trees. A successful system OID does not grant write access or all process data. <h3

title: 1.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">1.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. Goal: turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. <h5

title: 1.2.10.6.1.1 Baseline: find a read community, then walk
text: id="baseline-find-a-read-community-then-walk">1.2.10.6.1.1 Baseline: find a read community, then walk onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 Use -v1 instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. Decisive output: returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path. <summary

title: 1.2.10.6.1.1.1 Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk
text: id="variant-1-2-10-6-1-1-1">1.2.10.6.1.1.1 Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to snmpwalk with the verified version. <summary

title: 1.2.10.6.1.1.2 Variant — high-value Windows OIDs
text: id="variant-1-2-10-6-1-1-2">1.2.10.6.1.1.2 Variant — high-value Windows OIDs snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view. <summary

title: 1.2.10.6.1.1.3 Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk
text: id="variant-1-2-10-6-1-1-3">1.2.10.6.1.1.3 Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. authNoPriv authenticates without encryption; noAuthNoPriv supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed. <summary

title: 1.2.10.6.1.1.4 Variant — focused UDP verification
text: id="variant-1-2-10-6-1-1-4">1.2.10.6.1.1.4 Variant — focused UDP verification sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET snmp-info extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community. Failure cues: UDP silence can remain open|filtered ; it does not prove that the community is wrong. Timeout: No Response can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. No Such Object means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. Next action: translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage. <h3

title: 1.2.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-5">1.2.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a system OID responds. Test: inspect the relevant interface/process branch. Illustrative output: an internal subnet and application command line. Interpretation: return the subnet to scoped discovery and classify any exposed credential. <h3

title: 1.2.10.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-5">1.2.10.8 Verify the result Preserve the OID, accepted security context and returned value; empty branches can reflect view restrictions. <h3

title: 1.2.10.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-5">1.2.10.9 Failure and fallback Silence can mean UDP filtering, wrong community/version or denied view; change only the condition supported by evidence. <h3

text: id="10-next-transitions-5">1.2.10.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section No response, a new subnet, or uncertainty about the interface and route Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path §1.1.5 — Validate the source path and discover hosts A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol §3.1.5 — Classify the artifact and its identity context A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect §4.1.5 — Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration <h2

title: 1.2.11 Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols
text: id="enumerate-smtp-identities-and-accessible-mailbox-protocols">1.2.11 Enumerate SMTP identities and accessible mailbox protocols Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.11.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-6">1.2.11.1 Purpose and result Validated mail capabilities, possible usernames or authenticated mailbox artifacts. <h3

title: 1.2.11.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-6">1.2.11.2 Recognition clues SMTP capabilities or mail-related account clues. <h4

title: 1.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">1.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Identify mail-related listeners, inspect greeting/capabilities and compare permitted user-discovery replies with a known-invalid control. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Record response/control differences and separate inferred account existence from successful mailbox authentication. Failure/next check: Uniform replies, disabled VRFY or a catch-all make username enumeration inconclusive; investigate other identity sources. nc -nv TARGET 25 Then enter the protocol dialogue: EHLO example.invalid VRFY USER VRFY INVALID_CONTROL QUIT Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 220 HOSTNAME ESMTP 250-VRFY VRFY USER -> 250 USER VRFY INVALID_CONTROL -> 550 No such user Recognize this detail: A reproducible reply difference can expose a possible mailbox identity. Still missing before method selection: Check catch-all policy and account context; recipient acceptance does not prove mailbox credentials or OS access. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Controls support a real account and compatible credentials are available: validate its permitted mailbox/service access. Ruled out in this context All recipients are accepted by catch-all behavior: discard account-existence inference from this test. Inconclusive Uniform policy replies leave usernames unknown; inspect another identity source. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.11.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-6">1.2.11.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachable SMTP/POP3/IMAP service; enumeration or mailbox access must be enabled for the selected context. <h3

title: 1.2.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-6">1.2.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nc -nv TARGET 25 <h3

title: 1.2.11.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-6">1.2.11.5 Why it works VRFY/RCPT differences may disclose account existence but catch-all policy can invalidate inference. A valid recipient is not an authenticated mailbox or operating-system login. <h3

title: 1.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">1.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: SMTP commonly uses TCP/25, submission uses 587, and implicit TLS commonly uses 465. Goal: collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. <h5

title: 1.2.11.6.1.1 Baseline: banner and capabilities
text: id="baseline-banner-and-capabilities">1.2.11.6.1.1 Baseline: banner and capabilities nc -nv TARGET PORT Then enter: EHLO example.invalid HELP VRFY USER EXPN postmaster QUIT Decisive output: 250- capability lines reveal extensions such as STARTTLS or AUTH. 250 after VRFY may support a valid mailbox; 550 commonly rejects or denies it; 252 explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists. <summary

title: 1.2.11.6.1.1.1 Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS
text: id="variant-1-2-11-6-1-1-1">1.2.11.6.1.1.1 Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet Run EHLO example.invalid after TLS negotiation. Certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism. <summary

title: 1.2.11.6.1.1.2 Variant — focused automated user checks
text: id="variant-1-2-11-6-1-1-2">1.2.11.6.1.1.2 Variant — focused automated user checks smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT RCPT testing requires an SMTP transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. Treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses. <summary

title: 1.2.11.6.1.1.3 Variant — Windows source position
text: id="variant-1-2-11-6-1-1-3">1.2.11.6.1.1.3 Variant — Windows source position Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORT This verifies TCP reachability only. Use an available Netcat/Ncat or OpenSSL client for protocol dialogue. Failure cues: multiline replies begin with NNN- and finish with NNN ; read the final line. 503 often means the command sequence is wrong. Uniform 252 or 550 responses make enumeration inconclusive. A visible AUTH method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. Next action: add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. Do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. <h5

title: 1.2.11.6.1.2 POP3 and IMAP handoff
text: id="pop3-and-imap-handoff">1.2.11.6.1.2 POP3 and IMAP handoff Mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995 -crlf -quiet # POP3S openssl s_client -connect TARGET:993 -crlf -quiet # IMAPS POP3 dialogue: CAPA USER USER PASS PASSWORD STAT LIST QUIT IMAP dialogue: a1 CAPABILITY a2 LOGIN USER PASSWORD a3 LIST "" "*" a4 LOGOUT Test one legitimately acquired credential. Capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force NSE scripts until lockout/authorization is explicitly understood. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap mail blocks. <h3

title: 1.2.11.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-6">1.2.11.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: two recipient probes produce different replies. Test: compare known-invalid controls and repeated responses. Illustrative output: only one candidate is consistently accepted. Interpretation: retain a possible username and check account context before authentication testing. <h3

text: id="8-verify-the-result-6">1.2.11.8 Verify the result Record response/control differences and separate inferred account existence from successful mailbox authentication. <h3

text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-6">1.2.11.9 Failure and fallback Uniform replies, disabled VRFY or a catch-all make username enumeration inconclusive; investigate other identity sources. <h3

title: 1.2.12 Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search
text: id="discover-ldap-naming-contexts-and-authenticated-search">1.2.12 Discover LDAP naming contexts and authenticated search Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.12.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-7">1.2.12.1 Purpose and result A directory base DN and permitted account/group/computer attributes. <h3

title: 1.2.12.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-7">1.2.12.2 Recognition clues LDAP/Kerberos listeners or a probable AD domain. <h4

title: 1.2.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-7">1.2.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Identify the directory endpoint and query RootDSE before a subtree search under a known bind identity. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Record DC, base DN, bind identity and actual returned attributes; RootDSE alone is not a complete directory dump. Failure/next check: Stronger-auth-required may mean TLS/signing policy; invalid credentials or an empty base require different fixes. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP -s base -b '' defaultNamingContext namingContexts Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. dn: defaultNamingContext: DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD Recognize this detail: RootDSE supplies the search base; it does not grant arbitrary anonymous subtree access. Still missing before method selection: Check bind identity, transport/signing requirements and read visibility on the selected objects. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A correctly authenticated scoped search returns expected objects: continue domain mapping. Ruled out in this context Anonymous subtree search is denied: reject anonymous enumeration while retaining a known-authenticated option. Inconclusive An empty result may be the wrong base/filter or ACL visibility; compare a known object. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.12.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-7">1.2.12.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachable directory; anonymous query permission or valid bind identity; required signing/TLS and naming context. <h3

title: 1.2.12.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-7">1.2.12.4 Discover and verify prerequisites ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC_IP -s base -b '' namingContexts defaultNamingContext <h3

title: 1.2.12.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-7">1.2.12.5 Why it works RootDSE can disclose naming contexts without permitting subtree enumeration. A bind identity, search base and attribute/object ACLs independently constrain results. <h3

title: 1.2.12.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-7">1.2.12.6 Execute and choose variants Recognition: LDAP commonly appears on TCP/389 or TCP/636; Global Catalog on TCP/3268 or 3269; Kerberos on TCP/UDP 88. Applications may listen elsewhere, so follow protocol evidence rather than port labels. <h5

title: 1.2.12.6.1.1 Baseline: discover naming contexts
text: id="baseline-discover-naming-contexts">1.2.12.6.1.1 Baseline: discover naming contexts Prerequisite: LDAP reachability. Coverage: RootDSE only; this can work even when directory searches require authentication. Decisive output: defaultNamingContext and dnsHostName . ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://TARGET:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext configurationNamingContext dnsHostName Convert DC=corp,DC=example into corp.example for DNS/Kerberos work. Preserve the server's exact hostname because Kerberos is name-sensitive. <summary

title: 1.2.12.6.1.1.1 LDAPS and certificate-name inspection
text: id="variant-1-2-12-6-1-1-1">1.2.12.6.1.1.1 LDAPS and certificate-name inspection openssl s_client -connect TARGET:636 -servername DC_HOST </dev/null ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldaps://DC_HOST:636 -s base -b '' defaultNamingContext dnsHostName A certificate can disclose domain/DC names. A TLS validation error is a client trust/name issue, not proof that LDAP is unavailable. <h5

title: 1.2.12.6.1.2 Anonymous directory search
text: id="anonymous-directory-search">1.2.12.6.1.2 Anonymous directory search Prerequisite: known base DN and server permitting anonymous search. Failure cue: Inappropriate authentication or Insufficient access closes only the anonymous path. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectClass=group)' cn member description <h5

title: 1.2.12.6.1.3 Authenticated search
text: id="authenticated-search">1.2.12.6.1.3 Authenticated search Prerequisite: a valid directory identity. Decisive output: objects/attributes unavailable anonymously. Avoid placing a real password in shell history when an interactive prompt is available. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 \ -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName userAccountControl <summary

title: 1.2.12.6.1.3.1 Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately
text: id="variant-1-2-12-6-1-3-1">1.2.12.6.1.3.1 Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=computer)' \ dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=group)' cn member ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf <h5

title: 1.2.12.6.1.4 Kerberos prerequisites before an attack
text: id="kerberos-prerequisites-before-an-attack">1.2.12.6.1.4 Kerberos prerequisites before an attack Kerberos failures are often name/time/route failures rather than credential failures. Establish: getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u nmap -Pn -sV -p 88,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 DC_IP -oN dc-services.txt Interpretation: resolve DOMAIN and DC_HOST consistently, keep clock skew within Kerberos tolerance, and ensure the KDC is reached through the selected route. KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN points to identity/domain naming; KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW points to time; KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED normally points to authentication material. <h5

title: 1.2.12.6.1.5 Handoff
text: id="handoff">1.2.12.6.1.5 Handoff New users, groups, computers, SPNs or domain names → domain mapping . A user confirmed without preauthentication → Kerberos and identity transitions . Valid credentials → rerun authenticated LDAP plus SMB/share/remote-access enumeration. Certificate templates/AD CS clues → AD CS and object-control abuse . <h3

title: 1.2.12.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-7">1.2.12.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: RootDSE returns a base DN. Test: attempt the permitted scoped search with the appropriate bind. Illustrative output: anonymous search is denied but a domain bind succeeds. Interpretation: continue authenticated domain mapping. <h3

title: 1.2.12.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-7">1.2.12.8 Verify the result Record DC, base DN, bind identity and actual returned attributes; RootDSE alone is not a complete directory dump. <h3

title: 1.2.12.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-7">1.2.12.9 Failure and fallback Stronger-auth-required may mean TLS/signing policy; invalid credentials or an empty base require different fixes. <h3

text: id="10-next-transitions-7">1.2.12.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section Domain credentials or a domain-joined foothold Correct realm/domain and account qualification; reachable DC/services, usable DNS and acceptable clock skew §6.2.9.5 — Establish domain identity, DC, DNS, time and route A directory bind or domain-joined identity can read relevant objects Correct search base and authentication transport; object/attribute visibility and compatible local utilities §6.2.9.6 — Enumerate directory objects with native, LDAP and PowerView approaches A user-owned SPN and a useful service-account relationship A valid domain authentication/TGT context, reachable KDC, target SPN and a feasible password/encryption candidate strategy §6.3.11.11 — Request a selected service ticket for offline service-account recovery <h2

title: 1.2.13 Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives
text: id="use-mysqlmariadb-data-and-file-primitives">1.2.13 Use MySQL/MariaDB data and file primitives Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.13.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-8">1.2.13.1 Purpose and result Useful data or a permission-backed server-side file operation. <h3

title: 1.2.13.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-8">1.2.13.2 Recognition clues A MySQL-compatible service and valid application/database credentials. <h4

title: 1.2.13.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-8">1.2.13.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use a known application/database login and inspect identity, grants and file-operation constraints before choosing an OS transition. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Database authentication and exact schema/file privileges; secure_file_priv and server filesystem identity constrain file actions Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Check current database identity, grants and actual returned data or written file through an independent observation. Failure/next check: Permission denied or a restricted file directory changes the available primitive; pivot to data/credential use or a different entry point. SELECT USER(),CURRENT_USER(),VERSION(); SHOW GRANTS; SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv'; Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. CURRENT_USER(): APP_USER@% GRANT SELECT ON APP_DB.* secure_file_priv: /RESTRICTED_DIRECTORY/ Recognize this detail: SELECT permits data investigation; absent FILE/admin rights and the restricted directory constrain file/OS hypotheses. Still missing before method selection: Check exact grants, useful tables, destination OS permissions and an execution consumer before escalating a file operation. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A useful readable table or fully validated file consumer exists: choose that precise primitive. Ruled out in this context No required FILE privilege rules out the proposed LOAD_FILE/OUTFILE chain for this account. Inconclusive Incomplete grants or unknown server path keeps file capability unresolved; inspect before selecting it. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.13.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-8">1.2.13.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Database authentication and exact schema/file privileges; secure_file_priv and server filesystem identity constrain file actions. <h3

title: 1.2.13.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-8">1.2.13.4 Discover and verify prerequisites SELECT USER(),CURRENT_USER(),VERSION(); SHOW GRANTS; SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv'; <h3

title: 1.2.13.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-8">1.2.13.5 Why it works Database rights and operating-system rights intersect. FILE permission alone does not guarantee a writable executable web directory or a usable destination. <h3

title: 1.2.13.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-8">1.2.13.6 Execute and choose variants mysql -h TARGET -P PORT -u USER -p SELECT VERSION(), USER(), CURRENT_USER(); SHOW DATABASES; SHOW GRANTS; USE DATABASE; SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE TABLE; SELECT * FROM TABLE LIMIT 20; SELECT @@secure_file_priv; Interpret: USER() shows the presented client identity; CURRENT_USER() shows the account used for privilege checking. secure_file_priv restricts server-side import/export: a directory constrains it, an empty value is unrestricted by that variable, and NULL disables these operations. The FILE privilege is still required. <summary

title: 1.2.13.6.1 MySQL variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites
text: id="variant-1-2-13-6-1">1.2.13.6.1 MySQL variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites SELECT LOAD_FILE('/path/on/database/server'); SELECT 'probe' INTO OUTFILE '/allowed/server/path/probe.txt'; Use only an authorized harmless path. LOAD_FILE returning NULL is ambiguous among missing file, permissions, size, FILE privilege and secure_file_priv . INTO OUTFILE will not overwrite an existing file. A written file becomes execution only if another privileged component consumes it. <h3

title: 1.2.13.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-8">1.2.13.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the application database login can read configuration tables. Test: inspect grants before any file operation. Illustrative output: no FILE privilege. Interpretation: use data/credential disclosure; do not assume server execution. <h3

title: 1.2.13.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-8">1.2.13.8 Verify the result Check current database identity, grants and actual returned data or written file through an independent observation. <h3

title: 1.2.13.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-8">1.2.13.9 Failure and fallback Permission denied or a restricted file directory changes the available primitive; pivot to data/credential use or a different entry point. <h3
