title: 2.1.6 Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications
text: id="discover-virtual-hosts-and-hostname-selected-applications">2.1.6 Discover virtual hosts and hostname-selected applications Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.6.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-1">2.1.6.1 Purpose and result Additional verified applications on the same address. <h3

title: 2.1.6.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-1">2.1.6.2 Recognition clues DNS names, redirects, certificate names or a default virtual-host response. <h4

title: 2.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">2.1.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Collect hostnames from redirects, certificates, DNS and source; compare named requests against an invalid-host control. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Compare candidate and nonexistent-host responses, including content and redirects; resolve to the intended scoped address. Failure/next check: A default response for every host or an SNI mismatch makes the result inconclusive; do not treat every guessed hostname as a real application. curl -sk --resolve HOSTNAME:PORT:TARGET https://HOSTNAME:PORT/ Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Host HOSTNAME: application login page Host INVALID_HOST: default server page Recognize this detail: A reproducible hostname-selected application is a new mapping target on the same address. Still missing before method selection: Send a random Host header as a negative control, compare the candidate's real response, then browse it with the correct hostname. A different status caused only by redirects or a default site is not a confirmed vhost. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The named application has distinct verified behavior: give it its own session/function map. Ruled out in this context All candidate hosts receive the same default body: discard the claimed distinct application. Inconclusive TLS routing or local DNS is wrong: fix that context before deciding a vhost is absent. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.6.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-1">2.1.6.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: A destination listener, relevant domain candidates and controlled Host/SNI routing. <h3

title: 2.1.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-1">2.1.6.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk --resolve HOSTNAME:PORT:TARGET https://HOSTNAME:PORT/ <h3

title: 2.1.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">2.1.6.5 Why it works Virtual-host routing uses the requested hostname. DNS resolution, HTTP Host and TLS SNI must be aligned when the server selects behavior at more than one layer. <h3

title: 2.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">2.1.6.6 Execute and choose variants gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt Alternative with automatic calibration: ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.DOMAIN' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json Failure cue: uniform status/length may be the default vhost. Compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map. <h3

title: 2.1.6.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-1">2.1.6.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a certificate suggests an internal application name. Test: resolve it to the assigned address while preserving SNI. Illustrative output: a separate administration interface. Interpretation: give it its own request and credential map. <h3

title: 2.1.6.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-1">2.1.6.8 Verify the result Compare candidate and nonexistent-host responses, including content and redirects; resolve to the intended scoped address. <h3

title: 2.1.6.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-1">2.1.6.9 Failure and fallback A default response for every host or an SNI mismatch makes the result inconclusive; do not treat every guessed hostname as a real application. <h3

title: 2.1.6.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-1">2.1.6.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section An HTTP endpoint, redirect or hostname-dependent response Correct scheme/port and virtual host; saved cookies/headers for authenticated comparisons §2.1.5 — Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons §2.1.7 — Map functions, roles and normal requests manually A DNS server, domain name or host aliases Reachable DNS transport and relevant authoritative zone; AXFR requires an allowed TCP zone transfer §1.2.9 — Expand names through DNS records and zone transfers <h2

title: 2.1.7 Map functions, roles and normal requests manually
text: id="map-functions-roles-and-normal-requests-manually">2.1.7 Map functions, roles and normal requests manually Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.7.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-2">2.1.7.1 Purpose and result An input/function/role map with concrete attack hypotheses. <h3

title: 2.1.7.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-2">2.1.7.2 Recognition clues Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces. <h4

title: 2.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">2.1.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Browse the site's normal account, export, upload and download features while recording requests in the browser/proxy. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Retain method, route, input location, identity and expected normal behavior; do not infer vulnerability from an interesting parameter name. Failure/next check: Expired sessions, CSRF failures and malformed requests can imitate access-control differences; reproduce a valid baseline first. curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D response-headers.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Observed browser request: GET /download?file=report.pdf Cookie: SESSION_COOKIE Recognize this detail: The normal request exposes a file-selecting input discovered through functionality, not guessed from a payload list. Still missing before method selection: Find the actual input semantics, account/role and normal response before file/read/authorization tests. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Controlled comparisons prove a useful primitive: choose its method and remaining checks. Ruled out in this context The parameter only selects an allowlisted public report: discard unrestricted-path inference. Inconclusive Unknown ownership or an expired session prevents interpreting differences; re-establish the baseline. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.7.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-2">2.1.7.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons. <h3

title: 2.1.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">2.1.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -b cookies.txt -D response-headers.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 2.1.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">2.1.7.5 Why it works The same functionality can expose different trust boundaries through object IDs, methods and roles. Changing one property while preserving request state makes differences interpretable. <h3

title: 2.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">2.1.7.6 Execute and choose variants For every visible function, capture one unchanged request in Burp Proxy history, send it to Repeater and record: METHOD PATH | CONTENT-TYPE | ACCESS CONTEXT/ROLE INPUT LOCATION + NAME | BASELINE VALUE STATUS | LENGTH/HASH | REDIRECT | MARKER/ERROR/TIME OBJECT/FUNCTION SELECTED | NEXT ONE-VARIABLE TEST Check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every JavaScript API call. Next: a browser-side restriction is not server authorization. Replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time. <h3

title: 2.1.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-2">2.1.7.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a report download accepts a numeric ID. Test: compare objects owned by two authorized study accounts. Illustrative output: a lower role receives another account's report. Interpretation: proceed to an object-authorization method. <h3

title: 2.1.7.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-2">2.1.7.8 Verify the result Retain method, route, input location, identity and expected normal behavior; do not infer vulnerability from an interesting parameter name. <h3

title: 2.1.7.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-2">2.1.7.9 Failure and fallback Expired sessions, CSRF failures and malformed requests can imitate access-control differences; reproduce a valid baseline first. <h3

title: 2.1.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-2">2.1.7.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A request selects an object by ID/path and two authorized ownership contexts are available The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access §2.2.18 — Cross an object-ownership boundary A download/path parameter or URL segment influences a local filename Untrusted path reaches a filesystem read outside its intended directory; process identity can read the requested file §2.2.5 — Read files through directory traversal An upload/import/attachment function A valid upload request and permitted account; the server accepts and stores controlled bytes §2.2.8 — Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist §2.1.9 — Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering <h2

title: 2.1.8 Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts
text: id="inspect-source-backups-configuration-and-repository-artifacts">2.1.8 Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Operational procedure | Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.8.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-3">2.1.8.1 Purpose and result Hidden functionality, version clues or typed credential artifacts. <h3

title: 2.1.8.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-3">2.1.8.2 Recognition clues JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata. <h4

title: 2.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-3">2.1.8.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect linked JavaScript/source, robots/sitemaps, relevant backups and a bounded Git metadata check from the mapped web application. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Confirm actual file/history content and distinguish a historical secret from a usable current credential. Failure/next check: A 200 soft-404 or incomplete object database is not a recovered repository. Compare known-missing paths and record missing history. curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. robots.txt: Disallow: /INTERNAL_PATH/ .git/HEAD: ref: refs/heads/main Recognize this detail: The path and Git reference are investigation leads; neither proves a working secret or complete repository. Still missing before method selection: Compare missing-path controls, retrieve actual permitted artifacts and verify recovered history/account context. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Relevant source/history is recoverable and exposes a typed artifact: inspect it through the credential workflow. Ruled out in this context The same body is returned for arbitrary missing paths: reject the apparent metadata exposure. Inconclusive HEAD without objects leaves repository recovery incomplete; document available content instead of inventing history. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.8.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-3">2.1.8.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope. <h3

title: 2.1.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-3">2.1.8.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD <h3

title: 2.1.8.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-3">2.1.8.5 Why it works Client code and repository history can preserve endpoints and removed secrets. An exposed Git HEAD proves metadata exposure; repository completeness and secret validity require separate checks. <h3

title: 2.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">2.1.8.6 Execute and choose variants curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/sitemap.xml curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/openapi.json curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/swagger.json Also inspect HTML comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked JavaScript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers. Decisive output: a path, parameter, API schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. Source disclosure is not command execution. curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/.git/config A readable HEAD / config supports exposed repository metadata. A 403 , redirect or generic template is not proof. Preserve the correct host header/base path. If authorized, recover into a new local directory with a purpose-built tool and inspect locally: git-dumper http://TARGET:PORT/.git/ repo-output git -C repo-output status git -C repo-output log --oneline --all --decorate git -C repo-output log -p --all git-dumper is an optional third-party helper; install on demand in an isolated environment only when the exposure has been confirmed. Manual object recovery is possible but slower. rg -ni 'password|passwd|token|secret|api[_-]?key|private[_-]?key' repo-output git -C repo-output log --all -S'password' --oneline git -C repo-output log --all -G'pass(word)?|secret|token' --oneline Inspect candidate commits without dumping all history: git -C repo-output show COMMIT -- PATH git -C repo-output diff COMMIT^ COMMIT -- PATH Validate freshness, identity and compatible use. Removed historical values are often rotated or environment-specific. <h3

title: 2.1.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-3">2.1.8.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: Git metadata is exposed. Test: recover only available objects and inspect history. Illustrative output: a removed database connection string. Interpretation: classify the account and validate current database access. <h3

title: 2.1.8.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-3">2.1.8.8 Verify the result Confirm actual file/history content and distinguish a historical secret from a usable current credential. <h3

title: 2.1.8.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-3">2.1.8.9 Failure and fallback A 200 soft-404 or incomplete object database is not a recovered repository. Compare known-missing paths and record missing history. <h3

text: id="10-next-transitions-3">2.1.8.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol §3.1.5 — Classify the artifact and its identity context A product/version clue, advisory or component-specific public PoC Exact vulnerable build/configuration, required access and endpoint behavior; reviewable source and a verifiable expected effect §4.1.5 — Match a public exploit to the actual component and configuration An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type §2.1.10 — Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties <h2

title: 2.1.9 Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering
text: id="discover-directories-and-files-with-controlled-response-filtering">2.1.9 Discover directories and files with controlled response filtering Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.9.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-4">2.1.9.1 Purpose and result Verified candidate routes and files. <h3

title: 2.1.9.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-4">2.1.9.2 Recognition clues An application has unlinked paths, backups or administration endpoints. <h4

title: 2.1.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-4">2.1.9.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Establish the application's missing-path response, then run a bounded content search with the existing session/host context. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Open candidates and record their actual behavior; status/length alone is only a selection clue. Failure/next check: Aggressive filters can hide genuine routes and rate limiting can fabricate differences; validate the baseline and reduce the request rate. curl -sk -D - http://TARGET:PORT/KNOWN_MISSING_PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Missing control: status=200, body=DEFAULT_ERROR Candidate /EXPORT_PATH/: status=200, body=EXPORT_FORM Recognize this detail: The candidate's actual function differs from the soft-404 control despite equal status codes. Still missing before method selection: Request a known-missing path under the same host/session and compare status, body and length. Open each distinct Gobuster/ffuf result; a uniform login page or soft-404 is a filter problem, not a directory finding. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Independent retrieval confirms an actual function: add its request to the behavior map. Ruled out in this context The candidate matches the wildcard error body: remove it from the useful queue. Inconclusive Rate limiting or session expiry distorts response size; restore stable controls before filtering. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.9.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-4">2.1.9.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: Correct base URL/session and a measured nonexistent-path response; bounded relevant wordlist. <h3

title: 2.1.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-4">2.1.9.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -D - http://TARGET:PORT/KNOWN_MISSING_PATH <h3

title: 2.1.9.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-4">2.1.9.5 Why it works Discovery enumerates names; wildcard responses, redirects and soft-404 pages can make every guess appear valid. Confirm candidates through independent retrieval and behavior. <h3

title: 2.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-4">2.1.9.6 Execute and choose variants Request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt Decisive output: manually verified routes including useful 200 , redirect, 401 , 403 and 405 responses. <summary

title: 2.1.9.6.1 Variant — technology-aware extensions
text: id="variant-2-1-9-6-1">2.1.9.6.1 Variant — technology-aware extensions gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt Choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension. <summary

title: 2.1.9.6.2 Variant — authenticated discovery
text: id="variant-2-1-9-6-2">2.1.9.6.2 Variant — authenticated discovery gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -c 'SESSION=VALUE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt Use only the cookie or header that applies. An expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect. <summary

title: 2.1.9.6.3 Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length
text: id="variant-2-1-9-6-3">2.1.9.6.3 Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST --exclude-length NOISE_LENGTH -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt Filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path. <h3

title: 2.1.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-4">2.1.9.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: every path returns 200. Test: compare the missing-path body/length before filtering. Illustrative output: one candidate has a distinct export response. Interpretation: inspect that function manually. <h3

title: 2.1.9.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-4">2.1.9.8 Verify the result Open candidates and record their actual behavior; status/length alone is only a selection clue. <h3

title: 2.1.9.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-4">2.1.9.9 Failure and fallback Aggressive filters can hide genuine routes and rate limiting can fabricate differences; validate the baseline and reduce the request rate. <h3

title: 2.1.9.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-4">2.1.9.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section Forms, downloads, exports, account functions or role-specific interfaces A normal request baseline and the relevant account/role; authorized accounts for role comparisons §2.1.7 — Map functions, roles and normal requests manually JavaScript endpoints, backup names, exposed configuration or Git metadata Readable application artifact or a complete recoverable repository; preserve the public-source scope §2.1.8 — Inspect source, backups, configuration and repository artifacts An upload/import/attachment function A valid upload request and permitted account; the server accepts and stores controlled bytes §2.2.8 — Establish upload acceptance, storage and retrieval <h2

title: 2.1.10 Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties
text: id="map-parameters-api-methods-objects-and-writable-properties">2.1.10 Map parameters, API methods, objects and writable properties Blocks: 3. Operational procedure | Operational procedure | Quick sheet <h3

title: 2.1.10.1 Purpose and result
text: id="1-purpose-and-result-5">2.1.10.1 Purpose and result A parameter/object/method inventory and testable authorization or injection hypothesis. <h3

title: 2.1.10.2 Recognition clues
text: id="2-recognition-clues-5">2.1.10.2 Recognition clues An API/schema, numeric object IDs, hidden fields or different HTTP methods. <h4

title: 2.1.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-5">2.1.10.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Capture a valid API request, inspect its schema/client code and compare allowed methods and controlled object/role contexts. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state Requires: A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type Action class: HTTP requests; selected authenticated application actions can change application state. Stop/verify: Prove which input is consumed and whether state changes persist in an independent read. Failure/next check: HTTP 400/415 may indicate encoding/schema rather than security enforcement. Keep a valid request before changing permissions-related properties. curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Object fields: id, ownerId, role Observed request: PATCH /api/profile Body: {"displayName":"VALUE"} Recognize this detail: The actual object, method and writable input are known; returned owner/role fields are only candidate security boundaries. Still missing before method selection: Determine field binding, ownership, persistence and server authorization with controlled accounts. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A protected field/action changes under a lower role and is independently verified: select its authorization method. Ruled out in this context The server ignores the sensitive field and privileges remain unchanged: reject that assignment hypothesis. Inconclusive Malformed JSON or wrong content type makes a failed request inconclusive; reproduce the valid update first. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish scheme, host, redirects and request state . <h3

title: 2.1.10.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-5">2.1.10.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A reachable HTTP application and recorded anonymous or authenticated request state. Required conditions: A valid request and explicit role/object ownership; exact input format and content type. <h3

title: 2.1.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-5">2.1.10.4 Discover and verify prerequisites curl -sk -i -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH <h3

title: 2.1.10.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-5">2.1.10.5 Why it works APIs enforce security at route, object and property boundaries. A valid JSON body can be accepted while a sensitive field is ignored; test its persisted effect separately. <h3

title: 2.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-5">2.1.10.6 Execute and choose variants GET parameter names: ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH?FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-get.json POST form parameter names: ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/PATH -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-post.json Object values with an authenticated API: ffuf -w NUMBERS -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/FUZZ' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json Decisive output: a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. Tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws. <summary

title: 2.1.10.6.1 ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request
text: id="variant-2-1-10-6-1">2.1.10.6.1 ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request Save a working raw request from the proxy as request.txt, retain its Host/cookie/body, and put FUZZ at the single parameter name/value or path being tested. Replay it once manually first. The request file does not specify TLS: choose the transport explicitly. <h4

title: 2.1.10.6.2 HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers
text: id="variant-2-1-10-6-2">2.1.10.6.2 HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers # HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto https -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-https.json <h4

title: 2.1.10.6.3 Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS
text: id="variant-2-1-10-6-3">2.1.10.6.3 Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS # Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto http -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-http.json Read: compare an outlier's status/length/body with a known missing value, then replay that exact request. A login redirect for every value → refresh the session before continuing. A one-time CSRF token → repair token handling; the saved-request flag does not refresh it automatically. ffuf request configuration . curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/login Interpretation: 405 can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. Validation errors can reveal required fields. A token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request. Build a matrix across anonymous, user A, user B and administrator contexts where available: PATH | METHOD | IDENTITY/ROLE | OBJECT/PROPERTY | RESULT | NEXT <h3

title: 2.1.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-5">2.1.10.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: an API response includes a role property. Test: compare documented writable fields and a controlled update. Illustrative output: the field is ignored and privilege is unchanged. Interpretation: that mass-assignment hypothesis is disproven; investigate other boundaries. <h3

title: 2.1.10.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-5">2.1.10.8 Verify the result Prove which input is consumed and whether state changes persist in an independent read. <h3

title: 2.1.10.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-5">2.1.10.9 Failure and fallback HTTP 400/415 may indicate encoding/schema rather than security enforcement. Keep a valid request before changing permissions-related properties. <h3

title: 2.1.10.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-5">2.1.10.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section API objects expose role, ownership or security-sensitive properties The server binds an untrusted property to a persistent security-relevant field without checking permission §2.2.20 — Modify a protected property through excessive writable fields A request selects an object by ID/path and two authorized ownership contexts are available The server accepts a lower-privilege identity's request for an object it should not access §2.2.18 — Cross an object-ownership boundary An input appears in a command-like operation or causes shell-dependent behavior Input reaches command execution with an exploitable parsing boundary; process identity/runtime can perform the selected proof §2.2.11 — Prove visible or blind operating-system command injection Database errors or controlled true/false response differences Input reaches a SQL query; a valid request and stable response baseline exist §2.2.12 — Establish SQL query influence and DBMS context Untrusted input reaches an executable HTML/JavaScript context Payload reaches a browser execution sink; any useful privileged action additionally needs a victim context, same-origin access and a valid request state §2.2.21 — Execute browser code and validate a useful same-origin action URL import, preview, webhook or fetch behavior The application server performs a controllable request; destination/protocol policy and its network position permit the selected resource §2.2.23 — Use server-side requests to inspect reachable internal behavior <h2

title: 2.1.11 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">2.1.11 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8 pp201–244. OWASP Web Security Testing Guide . Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 5.2 Escalate privileges on Windows
text: id="escalate-privileges-on-windows">5.2 Escalate privileges on Windows Strategy map | Master Notes | Operational index | Cheatsheets An administrator-group membership, enabled token privilege, writable object and effective privileged execution are different claims. Establish the precise right, consumer identity and available trigger before choosing a route. Speedrun blocks: 9. Documented methods: 13. Examples are hypothetical study material. Apply commands only to an assigned scope during the later practice phase. A method is enabled by its prerequisites; its presence here does not establish a vulnerability or practical mastery. <h2

title: 5.2.1 First pass: tools and findings
text: id="first-pass-tools-and-findings">5.2.1 First pass: tools and findings Use the branch matching the current host, identity and observed result. Tool output supplies leads; the linked procedure verifies and uses the exact condition. <h3

title: 5.2.1.1 Record the token and host context
text: id="record-the-token-and-host-context">5.2.1.1 Record the token and host context Check the current token before choosing an exploit or collector build. hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all If SeImpersonatePrivilege: Check its enabled state and the operation/access needed by that specific technique. → Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route . If SeBackupPrivilege: Inspect the permitted backup operation and the exact source it can read. → Use backup privilege to obtain protected local credential material . If Service/task activity or a useful group membership: Inspect the actual objects and ACLs. → Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions . Otherwise: No immediate token route: run the broad collector, then verify its service/file findings. → Turn automated Windows findings into manually verified candidates . <h3

title: 5.2.1.2 Run winPEAS early and save its report
text: id="run-winpeas-early-and-save-its-report">5.2.1.2 Run winPEAS early and save its report Transfer a reviewed binary matching the host architecture. The log option writes out.txt; inspect it before selecting a route. Native checks remain available if execution is blocked. winPEASx64.exe log If Modifiable service or writable service binary: Check sc qc/sdshow and the actual binary/parent ACL, service account and restart rights. → Change a privileged service's executable configuration . If Unquoted service path: Check the exact executable prefixes for write access and a privileged restartable consumer. → Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix . If A saved credential/config finding: Read the named source and classify the account/material. → Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts . Otherwise: The collector is blocked or reports no useful candidate: continue native ACL/service/task inspection. → Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions . <h3

title: 5.2.1.3 Verify the specific service/task route
text: id="verify-the-specific-servicetask-route">5.2.1.3 Verify the specific service/task route Configuration write, binary replacement, unquoted-prefix write and dependency loading require different rights. whoami /all icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" icacls "C:\Path\To" sc.exe sdshow SERVICE If Service configuration can be changed: Confirm the service runs as a stronger identity and you can cause a start/restart. → Change a privileged service's executable configuration . If Only the binary or its parent is writable: Check replacement semantics, the consumer identity and a trigger. → Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file . If A scheduled task consumes a writable file: Inspect the task principal, action and schedule. → Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers . Otherwise: The highlighted path is not effectively writable: reject that candidate and inspect another actual object. → Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions . <h2

title: 5.2.2 Discovery workflow
text: id="discovery-workflow">5.2.2 Discovery workflow Start with a Windows foothold. Administrator-group membership, a high-integrity token and a working privileged trigger are separate facts. Follow these observations into a method; the detailed recognition routes below show synthetic output and the checks still needed. Inspect whoami /all and host/process state before choosing a privilege route: Establish Windows token, host and process context . Inventory real services/tasks and inspect exact object and parent ACLs: Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions ; Change a privileged service's executable configuration ; Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers . Separate writable service configuration, replaceable binaries, unquoted prefixes and dependency loads: Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file ; Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix ; Control a privileged DLL, helper or configuration load . Follow application/history/saved-credential artifacts and exact token privileges: Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts ; Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route ; Use backup privilege to obtain protected local credential material . Match software/driver/build evidence only after validating simpler permission routes: Select a matching application, driver or kernel exploit . Decision rule: an observed clue opens a candidate. Choose it only after the missing conditions are verified; a failed check rules out that context, while unavailable evidence stays inconclusive . <h2

title: 5.2.3 Method families
text: id="method-families">5.2.3 Method families Token, ACL and credential state: Establish Windows token, host and process context , Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions , Recover Windows application, history and stored-credential artifacts . Services and privileged consumers: Change a privileged service's executable configuration , Replace a privileged service binary or consumed file , Exploit an unquoted service path with a writable earlier prefix , Control a privileged DLL, helper or configuration load , Control scheduled tasks, startup files or autostart consumers . Installer and token-backed operations: Validate elevated installer policy and administrative-token context , Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route , Use backup privilege to obtain protected local credential material . Software and candidate generation: Select a matching application, driver or kernel exploit , Turn automated Windows findings into manually verified candidates . <h2

title: 5.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access">5.2.5.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: At a new foothold inspect the complete token and host/service inventory before classifying the session as an administrator. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: A functioning command channel and the actual effective token/process context Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify represented user/SID, enabled group/privilege state and actual privileged operation. Failure/next check: A prompt title or account name is insufficient. WMIC may be absent; use the documented CIM/PowerShell alternatives. whoami /all systeminfo tasklist /svc Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. BUILTIN\Administrators: Group used for deny only Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level Recognize this detail: An Administrators SID exists but this effective process is filtered/medium-integrity. Still missing before method selection: Check actual enabled privileges and object operations in the process that will perform the action. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A higher-integrity/SYSTEM token and intended operation are verified: record that privilege state. Ruled out in this context A medium filtered token cannot perform the assumed administrative action: reject that privilege assumption. Inconclusive Username/group membership alone leaves token state unknown; inspect whoami /all. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Verify command execution, host and represented identity . <h3

title: 5.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants">5.2.5.6 Execute and choose variants hostname whoami /all systeminfo ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano tasklist /svc query user net user net localgroup Administrators driverquery /v Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName,WindowsVersion,OsBuildNumber,OsArchitecture Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Select-Object ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName Get-CimInstance Win32_SystemDriver | Select-Object Name,State,StartMode,PathName Get-LocalUser Get-LocalGroupMember Administrators Interpret: record user SID, integrity label, enabled/deny-only groups and present/enabled privileges. Administrator membership with Medium integrity is a filtered token, not a high-integrity process. Get-HotFix does not list every update; use build/KB output only to form a version hypothesis. <summary

title: 5.2.5.6.1 WMIC compatibility fallbacks
text: id="variant-5-2-5-6-1">5.2.5.6.1 WMIC compatibility fallbacks wmic qfe get HotFixID,InstalledOn wmic service get Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName wmic process get ProcessId,Name,ExecutablePath,CommandLine WMIC is deprecated and may be absent on newer systems; PowerShell CIM is the baseline. whoami /all hostname ipconfig /all After a higher token, re-enumerate protected credentials, services, tasks, sessions, listeners, routes and domain context. Preserve the command, relevant output, trigger and restoration step. For exam use, recheck the current OffSec guide: Windows full-privilege evidence requires SYSTEM, Administrator or an account with Administrator privileges, and AI/LLM use is prohibited during the exam and report phase. <h3

title: 5.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-1">5.2.6.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Take a real service/task/application path from inventory, then inspect its file, parent and separate service-object permissions. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: Correct trustee/token, object type and effective rights including parents and deny entries Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Name the exact allowed operation on the exact object and independently check a privileged consumer/trigger. Failure/next check: Generic write labels can refer to another object or an inactive group. Resolve actual effective rights before modifying anything. icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" icacls "C:\Path\To" sc.exe sdshow SERVICE Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. File: BUILTIN\Users:(RX) Parent: DOMAIN\GROUP:(M) Service-object rights: separate DACL Recognize this detail: A modifiable parent can differ from a read-only file; service configuration rights are another control plane. Still missing before method selection: Use icacls/Get-Acl on the reported object and parents. For a service also inspect sc qc/sc sdshow; for a task inspect its action/principal. Check the specific write/replace/configuration operation and its trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The intended effective operation and higher consumer are proved: select that object-control method. Ruled out in this context Only read/execute applies to the current token: reject the proposed modification. Inconclusive An ACL for an inactive or ambiguous group leaves effective access unresolved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Windows token, host and process context . <h3

title: 5.2.6.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-1">5.2.6.5 Why it works A service-object DACL controls operations such as configuration changes; the executable's filesystem ACL is separate. Parent delete/create rights can allow replacement without direct file modification. <h3

title: 5.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-1">5.2.6.6 Execute and choose variants icacls "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" sc.exe sdshow SERVICE accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\OBJECT" accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE icacls common rights: F full, M modify, RX read/execute, R read, W write, D delete. Common inheritance markers: I , OI , CI , IO , NP . File, directory, registry, service-object, task and process permissions are separate. Check whether the ACE applies to the current user or an enabled group and grants the exact required operation. Mandatory Integrity Control can still block a lower-integrity write. <h3

Interpretation: the control primitive is valid; the trigger remains missing. <h3

title: 5.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-2">5.2.7.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Follow actual application/configuration paths, PSReadLine history and saved-credential targets under the current readable user context. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: Artifact read permission and exact protecting identity/context for saved or DPAPI material Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Tie each value to a source/account/service and verify any new token with whoami /all. Failure/next check: Protected blobs, stale history and saved credentials for a different target require their own keys/context or a different route. cmdkey /list reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultUserName Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. cmdkey target: Domain:target=TARGET_HOST User: DOMAIN\USER Password: not displayed Recognize this detail: A target-bound saved credential is a possible consumer capability, not a plaintext password. Still missing before method selection: Establish protecting user/context, intended logon type and an actually permitted saved-credential or decryption route. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The matching consumer accepts the credential and the resulting token is checked: use that access. Ruled out in this context The stored entry belongs to another context/target and cannot be used here: reject that transition. Inconclusive A protected blob/listing without keys or consumer evidence leaves usable credentials unproved. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Windows token, host and process context . <h3

text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-2">5.2.7.4 Discover and verify prerequisites cmdkey /list whoami /all <h3

title: 5.2.7.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-2">5.2.7.5 Why it works A cmdkey entry proves a target-bound stored credential, not plaintext disclosure. Saved-credential use and DPAPI decryption require matching contexts; runas does not inherently bypass UAC. <h3

title: 5.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-2">5.2.7.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1 Stored credentials and PowerShell trails
text: id="stored-credentials-and-powershell-trails">5.2.7.6.1.1 Stored credentials and PowerShell trails cmdkey /list vaultcmd /list vaultcmd /listcreds:"Windows Credentials" /all $history = (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath $history Get-Content -LiteralPath $history -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\Transcription' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Id -in 4103,4104 | Select-Object -First 50 TimeCreated,Id,Message A cmdkey entry is target/context-bound and does not reveal a password. DPAPI-protected data needs the protecting user/machine context and keys. Clear-History does not necessarily clear PSReadLine's saved file. <summary

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1.1 Targeted application/file/registry search
text: id="variant-5-2-7-6-1-1-1">5.2.7.6.1.1.1 Targeted application/file/registry search reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultUserName reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v DefaultPassword reg query "HKCU\Software\SimonTatham\PuTTY\Sessions" /s dir /s /b C:\Windows\Panther\*unattend*.xml C:\Windows\System32\Sysprep\*.xml 2>nul dir /s /b C:\Users\*.kdbx C:\Users\*.rdp C:\Users\id_rsa C:\Users\*.ppk 2>nul Get-ChildItem C:\inetpub,C:\ProgramData,C:\Users -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd','.yml','.yaml','.json' } | Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionString|user id=' -CaseSensitive:$false Search from observed applications first. Classify every value by identity, format, scope and compatible service, then use the credential procedure. <summary

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1.2 Saved credential consumer
text: id="variant-5-2-7-6-1-1-2">5.2.7.6.1.1.2 Saved credential consumer runas /savecred /user:DOMAIN\USER cmd.exe Use only when cmdkey /context supports that identity and logon type. runas does not inherently bypass UAC; verify the resulting token with whoami /all . <summary

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1.3 LaZagne — recover application credentials in the current user's context
text: id="variant-5-2-7-6-1-1-3">5.2.7.6.1.1.3 LaZagne — recover application credentials in the current user's context Use a reviewed Windows build after identifying the current user and installed applications. Start with the relevant family; run broader collection only when useful. User-protected stores depend on that user's profile/decryption context; system-protected stores can need an elevated token. <h6

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1.4 Browser-store leads for the current user
text: id="variant-5-2-7-6-1-1-4">5.2.7.6.1.1.4 Browser-store leads for the current user REM Browser-store leads for the current user laZagne.exe browsers <h6

title: 5.2.7.6.1.1.5 Broader recovery, with a local text report
text: id="variant-5-2-7-6-1-1-5">5.2.7.6.1.1.5 Broader recovery, with a local text report REM Broader recovery, with a local text report laZagne.exe all -oN Read: preserve the reported application/account/source with each recovered value. Test a matching service using the credential procedure; a recovered application password is not automatically a domain password. Empty output can mean no supported store, inaccessible profile or failed decryption. Follow manual history/config/vault checks instead of assuming there are no credentials. LaZagne upstream . Get-ChildItem C:\Users,C:\ProgramData,C:\inetpub -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Name -match 'pass|cred|config|backup|unattend|\.env' } Get-ChildItem C:\Users,C:\ProgramData,C:\inetpub -File -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Extension -in '.config','.xml','.ini','.txt','.ps1','.bat','.cmd' } | Select-String -Pattern 'password|passwd|secret|token|connectionString' -CaseSensitive:$false Avoid searching the entire filesystem without a reason; scope reduces noise, access errors and sensitive-data overcollection. <h3

text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-3">5.2.8.6 Execute and choose variants Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,StartMode,PathName sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe sdshow SERVICE icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe" icacls "C:\Path\To" accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w -c "USER" SERVICE accesschk.exe -accepteula -nobanner -v -w "USER" "C:\Path\To\service.exe" Need: control of service config, exact binary/script, searched prefix, DLL/config/plugin, or relevant DACL; higher SERVICE_START_NAME ; and a start/restart/boot trigger. In PowerShell use sc.exe , because bare sc can resolve to Set-Content . Preserve BINARY_PATH_NAME , account and start mode first: sc.exe qc SERVICE sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\PAYLOAD_EXE" sc.exe stop SERVICE sc.exe start SERVICE Restore: sc.exe config SERVICE binPath= "ORIGINAL_BINARY_PATH" SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG controls binPath ; start/stop are separate rights. The space after binPath= is required. Error 1053 may mean a non-service payload ran but did not answer the Service Control Manager; verify the intended effect. <summary

Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: An earlier executable prefix is absent and creatable, service identity is higher and a start/restart trigger exists Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Confirm the earlier prefix is actually selected after the trigger and verify its resulting token. Failure/next check: A quoted path, existing protected earlier file, unwritable directory or absent trigger defeats the chain. Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,State,PathName Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. StartName: LocalSystem PathName: C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe -d Quotes around executable: absent Recognize this detail: Spaces plus absent executable quoting create candidate earlier prefixes; writable placement and trigger remain unproved. Still missing before method selection: Read the unquoted service command with sc qc. Check each earlier executable prefix for write/create access with icacls; confirm the service account and restart trigger. Spaces alone do not make the path exploitable. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A usable earlier prefix is selected at a privileged trigger: choose this parsing route. Ruled out in this context All earlier prefixes are protected, already occupied or the executable is correctly quoted: reject it. Inconclusive A scanner flag without prefix/trigger checks leaves exploitability unknown. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Windows token, host and process context . <h3

title: 5.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-6">5.2.11.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Investigate a privileged application with observed dependency failures; if permitted, filter its runtime file loads in Procmon before checking candidate directory ACLs. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: Actual controlled resolution path, compatible name/architecture/exports and a reliable privileged load trigger Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify the actual loaded path and privileged effect; a file placed on disk is not a completed chain. Failure/next check: Wrong ABI/exports, earlier trusted resolution or no load trigger blocks the method. Procmon, when accessible: filter the actual process; inspect requested .dll paths and NAME NOT FOUND results. Record the exact requested filename and every searched location. Then inspect the selected location's effective ACL with the owning procedure. Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. PROCESS CreateFile C:\SEARCH_PATH\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND Privilege and selected search order: not yet verified Recognize this detail: An actual requested missing dependency is stronger than guessing a DLL name, but does not prove an attacker-controlled resolution wins. Still missing before method selection: Validate real privilege, search precedence/KnownDLLs/manifests, directory control, ABI/exports and a load trigger. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The privileged process selects the controlled compatible dependency: choose that load route. Ruled out in this context A trusted manifest/earlier location resolves it before the writable directory: reject that path. Inconclusive No runtime visibility leaves loading behavior unresolved; retain it as a candidate rather than declaring hijack success. title: 5.2.12.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-7">5.2.12.5 Why it works RunLevel Highest selects the configured principal's highest available token; it does not mean SYSTEM. A writable user startup entry usually runs as that user. <h3

title: 5.2.12.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-7">5.2.12.6 Execute and choose variants <h5

title: 5.2.12.6.1.1 Scheduled tasks
text: id="scheduled-tasks">5.2.12.6.1.1 Scheduled tasks schtasks /query /fo LIST /v schtasks /query /tn "\FOLDER\TASK" /xml Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object { $t = $_ [pscustomobject]@{ TaskPath=$t.TaskPath; TaskName=$t.TaskName UserId=$t.Principal.UserId; RunLevel=$t.Principal.RunLevel Actions=($t.Actions | ForEach-Object { "$($_.Execute) $($_.Arguments) [wd=$($_.WorkingDirectory)]" }) -join '; ' } } icacls "C:\Path\To\task-script.ps1" icacls "C:\Path\To" schtasks /run /tn "\FOLDER\TASK" Prove action, arguments, working directory, principal, actual trigger and effective ACL. RunLevel Highest means the configured principal's highest available token, not SYSTEM. /run success means the request was accepted; verify process/effect and last-run result. <summary

title: 5.2.12.6.1.1.1 Run keys and startup consumers
text: id="variant-5-2-12-6-1-1-1">5.2.12.6.1.1.1 Run keys and startup consumers reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run dir "C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp" dir "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup" Need a modifiable consumed value/file plus a higher-privileged boot/logon/application trigger. A writable PATH directory matters only when a privileged consumer invokes an unqualified executable through that effective PATH. <h3

text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-7">5.2.12.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a writable script is named in a scheduled task. Test: inspect principal, arguments, working directory and trigger. Illustrative output: the task runs as the same low user. Interpretation: it is not a local privilege escalation under that configuration. <h3

title: 5.2.13.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-8">5.2.13.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Inspect both machine/user installer-policy values and the current token before inferring an elevated MSI or UAC-context route. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: AlwaysInstallElevated requires both effective machine/user policy values and permitted MSI execution; UAC routes require their own compatible administrator/token context Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify both relevant conditions and actual resulting token; keep UAC-context claims narrower than full privilege escalation. Failure/next check: One policy value, blocked MSI execution or an incompatible protected token defeats the assumed route. reg query HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated reg query HKCU\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated whoami /all Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. HKLM AlwaysInstallElevated REG_DWORD 0x1 HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated: value not found Recognize this detail: One policy value is insufficient; the two-policy conjunction is the key recognition condition. Still missing before method selection: For installer execution verify both applicable values and permitted MSI/runtime; assess UAC administrator/token prerequisites separately. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation Both required policies and a compatible permitted installer consumer exist: validate that route's effect. Ruled out in this context The required user policy is absent/disabled: reject this elevated-installer method. Inconclusive Policy visibility failure or unknown effective context requires another check. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Windows token, host and process context . <h3

title: 5.2.13.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-8">5.2.13.5 Why it works Both installer policies must enable the feature. UAC elevation and standard-user-to-administrator escalation have different prerequisites; a token/consent mechanism is not a universal boundary bypass. <h3

This is an unsafe installer policy, not a universal UAC bypass. whoami /groups reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin A UAC bypass normally elevates an already-administrative filtered token. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: The exact privilege and usable operation; impersonation additionally needs a compatible privileged authentication source, OS/service state and executable context Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Failure/next check: Missing token source, filtered token, protected process or driver-signing/build differences change the route; inspect the specific prerequisite. whoami /priv whoami /all Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SeImpersonatePrivilege Impersonate a client after authentication Enabled Recognize this detail: An impersonation capability is present; the privileged authentication source required by a specific tool is not established. Match the exact privilege, enabled state and token context to the technique's required API/trigger, then verify the resulting identity; the privilege name alone is not SYSTEM. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: Usable backup privilege, compatible backup API/command and a matched protected source set with a writable destination Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Verify complete matched source artifacts and exact account mapping after parsing. Failure/next check: Ordinary file-copy denial does not disprove backup semantics; missing required hives or protection can still prevent useful extraction. whoami /priv Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. SeBackupPrivilege Back up files and directories Disabled Recognize this detail: The privilege is assigned but initially disabled; permitted software may enable it for backup-semantic reads. Still missing before method selection: Check that the privilege can actually be used, supporting API/context, complete matched source set and writable output. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation A permitted backup-aware operation produces matched protected source files: select offline extraction. Ruled out in this context The token has no required privilege and no alternate read permission: reject this backup route. Inconclusive Ordinary copy denial does not settle a backup-semantic operation; verify the API rather than inferring absence. title: 5.2.17.2 Recognition clues

title: 5.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access
text: id="find-the-clue-from-your-starting-access-12">5.2.17.2.1 Find the clue from your starting access Where to investigate: Select a reviewed tool after checking host/runtime; treat each highlighted service, token or path as a lead to native evidence. Discovery action — reference example: Execution context, effects and stopping rule Host/access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups Requires: Verified current token and architecture, a compatible reviewed executable or allowed PowerShell runtime, and a writable report location Action class: Includes enumeration and permission-backed privileged execution; distinguish the selected step. Stop/verify: Read out.txt or the helper report. Use sc.exe qc/sdshow plus icacls for a service, inspect task XML/run-as for a scheduled task, or check whoami /priv for a token finding Failure/next check: Binary/script blocked or report empty: check architecture and PowerShell language/policy, then use native service/task/ACL checks. A blocked helper does not disprove the finding whoami /all $PSVersionTable $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode Illustrative evidence — synthetic, abbreviated: The excerpt may combine command fields with labelled observations from the preceding investigation; it is not a real-target transcript or a promise of exact tool formatting. Tool candidate: unquoted SERVICE path Writable earlier prefix: not checked Trigger: not checked Recognize this detail: The enumerator located a configuration clue, not the full usable chain. Still missing before method selection: Run winPEAS with log output, then inspect the exact reported service with sc qc/sc sdshow and its file with icacls. Check token highlights with whoami /priv. A collector's colored line is not the resulting elevated token. Outcome after checking Example and next decision Enabled after validation The native checks establish the complete method conditions: select its owning route. Ruled out in this context Protected prefixes or a low consumer disprove the proposed elevation: discard the finding's exploit interpretation. Inconclusive Tool blocking/partial visibility leaves enumeration incomplete; use native/application-specific checks. If you do not yet have this clue: start with Establish Windows token, host and process context . <h3

title: 5.2.17.3 Prerequisites
text: id="3-prerequisites-12">5.2.17.3 Prerequisites Starting access: A verified Windows foothold with a known token, integrity level and groups. Required conditions: Verified current token and architecture, a compatible reviewed executable or allowed PowerShell runtime, and a writable report location. <h3

title: 5.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites
text: id="4-discover-and-verify-prerequisites-12">5.2.17.4 Discover and verify prerequisites whoami /all $PSVersionTable $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode <h3

title: 5.2.17.5 Why it works
text: id="5-why-it-works-12">5.2.17.5 Why it works winPEAS, PrivescCheck, Seatbelt and PowerUp collect different evidence. Highlighted services or privileges still require exact ACL, token, identity and trigger checks. <h3

title: 5.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants
text: id="6-execute-and-choose-variants-12">5.2.17.6 Execute and choose variants winPEASx64.exe log Seatbelt.exe -group=system -outputfile="C:\Windows\Temp\seatbelt-system.txt" Seatbelt.exe -group=user -q -outputfile="C:\Windows\Temp\seatbelt-user.json" powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command ". .\PrivescCheck.ps1; Invoke-PrivescCheck -Report TXT,HTML" Import-Module .\PowerUp.ps1 Invoke-AllChecks winPEAS is broad; Seatbelt is a targeted survey and publishes source rather than official binaries; PrivescCheck evaluates the current token and skips some checks when elevated; PowerUp is useful but its upstream repository was archived. AV/script-policy failure is a tooling limitation—use native checks. Convert every highlight into: CANDIDATE | CURRENT TOKEN | CONTROLLED INPUT | EFFECTIVE RIGHT | CONSUMER | RUN-AS | TRIGGER | EXPECTED EFFECT | STATUS <h3

title: 5.2.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical
text: id="7-worked-example--hypothetical-12">5.2.17.7 Worked example — hypothetical Observation: a scanner flags an unquoted path. Test: inspect the earlier path prefixes and trigger. Illustrative output: none is writable. Interpretation: discard the exploit hypothesis and retain the configuration fact. <h3

title: 5.2.17.8 Verify the result
text: id="8-verify-the-result-12">5.2.17.8 Verify the result Read out.txt or the helper report. Use sc.exe qc/sdshow plus icacls for a service, inspect task XML/run-as for a scheduled task, or check whoami /priv for a token finding <h3

title: 5.2.17.9 Failure and fallback
text: id="9-failure-and-fallback-12">5.2.17.9 Failure and fallback Binary/script blocked or report empty: check architecture and PowerShell language/policy, then use native service/task/ACL checks. A blocked helper does not disprove the finding <h3

title: 5.2.17.10 Continue from the interpreted result
text: id="10-next-transitions-12">5.2.17.10 Continue from the interpreted result Observed result Check before proceeding Next numbered section A privileged object appears writable or an ACL tool reports a useful right Correct trustee/token, object type and effective rights including parents and deny entries §5.2.6 — Prove effective file, registry and service-object permissions Effective SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG on a higher-privileged service Configuration-change right, accessible compatible payload path and a separate start/restart trigger §5.2.8 — Change a privileged service's executable configuration whoami /priv exposes a relevant token privilege The exact privilege and usable operation; impersonation additionally needs a compatible privileged authentication source, OS/service state and executable context §5.2.14 — Select a privilege-backed impersonation or object-control route <h2

title: 5.2.18 Sources and shared concepts
text: id="sources-and-shared-concepts">5.2.18 Sources and shared concepts Supplied PEN-200 Ch 17 pp494–549. Hexdump Windows modules ; Microsoft access-control, service and token sources remain beside the operational procedure. Commands and their adjacent variant conditions are synchronized extracts of the linked operational procedures. Those procedures own complete execution details; this guide owns method selection, explanations and worked reasoning. Tool availability on the learner's Kali or a target must be checked in that environment.

title: 9.1.1 Path and Host Discovery
text: id="path-and-host-discovery">9.1.1 Path and Host Discovery ← Reference index · Next: TCP scanning | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Confirm the source path and discover explicitly assigned hosts before spending time on port coverage. <h2

title: 9.1.1.1 Check the path
text: id="1-check-the-path">9.1.1.1 Check the path From the target's working folder: mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET Read: selected interface/source address. A route lookup does not prove reachability. <summary

title: 9.1.1.1.1 Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet
text: id="variant-9-1-1-1-1">9.1.1.1.1 Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet <h3

title: 9.1.1.1.2 Host discovery
text: id="host-discovery">9.1.1.1.2 Host discovery One host: nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET Assigned list: put IPs in targets.txt , one per line. nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts Explicitly assigned subnet: nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET No response does not establish that a host is offline. A list of assigned hosts does not imply the surrounding subnet is in scope.

title: 9.1.2 TCP Scanning
text: id="tcp-scanning">9.1.2 TCP Scanning ← Reference index · Previous: Path and discovery · Next: Service identification | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. <h2

title: 9.1.2.1 Get initial TCP results
text: id="2-get-initial-tcp-results">9.1.2.1 Get initial TCP results sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET Coverage: 1,000 common TCP ports. Review scans/tcp-initial.nmap in a text editor. <summary

title: 9.1.2.1.1 Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports
text: id="variant-9-1-2-1-1">9.1.2.1.1 Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports <h3

title: 9.1.2.1.2 Initial view: 1,000 common ports
text: id="initial-view-1000-common-ports">9.1.2.1.2 Initial view: 1,000 common ports Assigned host list, SYN scan: sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges: nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. <h3

title: 9.1.2.1.3 Selected ports or a range
text: id="selected-ports-or-a-range">9.1.2.1.3 Selected ports or a range One host: replace PORTS with, for example, 25,43 or 1-1024 . sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET Find relevant services across assigned hosts: sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep A focused service sweep is not a full port map. <h2

title: 9.1.2.2 Complete TCP coverage
text: id="3-complete-tcp-coverage">9.1.2.2 Complete TCP coverage sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET Coverage: TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs. <summary

title: 9.1.2.2.1 Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress
text: id="variant-9-1-2-2-1">9.1.2.2.1 Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress <h3

title: 9.1.2.2.2 All TCP ports: 1-65535
text: id="all-tcp-ports-1-65535">9.1.2.2.2 All TCP ports: 1-65535 Connect scan: nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. <h3

title: 9.1.2.2.3 Discovery skips a running target
text: id="discovery-skips-a-running-target">9.1.2.2.3 Discovery skips a running target Recheck relevant ports with response reasons: sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery: sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET -Pn assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use -sT without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. <h3

title: 9.1.2.2.4 Timing and progress
