text: id="timing-and-progress">9.1.2.2.4 Timing and progress Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress: sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET Faster timing on a stable path: sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET -T3 is normal timing; -T4 is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. <h3

title: 9.1.2.2.5 TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy
text: id="tcp-only-access-through-a-socks-proxy">9.1.2.2.5 TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET proxychains cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. -Pn avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.

title: 9.1.3 Service Identification
text: id="service-identification">9.1.3 Service Identification ← Reference index · Previous: TCP scanning · Next: UDP scanning | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. <h2

title: 9.1.3.1 Identify discovered applications
text: id="4-identify-discovered-applications">9.1.3.1 Identify discovered applications nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET Next: choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability. <summary

title: 9.1.3.1.1 Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints
text: id="variant-9-1-3-1-1">9.1.3.1.1 Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints <h3

title: 9.1.3.1.2 Identify applications on discovered ports
text: id="identify-applications-on-discovered-ports">9.1.3.1.2 Identify applications on discovered ports Version probing plus the default NSE script set: use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters: nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. <h3

title: 9.1.3.1.3 Select a named script
text: id="select-a-named-script">9.1.3.1.3 Select a named script Inspect behavior locally: nmap --script-help http-headers After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s): nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. <h3

title: 9.1.3.1.4 OS fingerprinting and bundled probing
text: id="os-fingerprinting-and-bundled-probing">9.1.3.1.4 OS fingerprinting and bundled probing Estimate OS from network-stack behavior: sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET Request more tentative OS guesses: sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute: sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; -A does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

title: 9.1.4 UDP Scanning
text: id="udp-scanning">9.1.4 UDP Scanning ← Reference index · Previous: Service identification · Next: Results and next actions | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Sample UDP separately, preserve ambiguous states, and expand only when the objective or evidence warrants it. <h2

title: 9.1.4.1 Check UDP separately
text: id="5-check-udp-separately">9.1.4.1 Check UDP separately sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 20 -oA scans/udp-top20 TARGET Limit: this is a sample. open|filtered remains inconclusive ; expand when evidence or the objective warrants it. <summary

title: 9.1.4.1.1 Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP
text: id="variant-9-1-4-1-1">9.1.4.1.1 Variants — larger sample, selected ports, application probes and TCP + UDP <h3

title: 9.1.4.1.2 Common-port samples
text: id="common-port-samples">9.1.4.1.2 Common-port samples Expand to 100 common ports when more coverage is warranted: sudo nmap -sU -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/udp-top100 TARGET These are samples. open|filtered is inconclusive; TCP results cannot fill UDP gaps. <h3

title: 9.1.4.1.3 Selected ports
text: id="selected-ports">9.1.4.1.3 Selected ports Check a relevant UDP port/list: sudo nmap -sU -n -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-selected TARGET Add application probes to resolve a useful candidate: sudo nmap -sU -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/udp-detail TARGET A reply can resolve ambiguity; no reply can leave it inconclusive. If discovery skips an assigned running host, add -Pn with the same limitations as TCP. <h3

title: 9.1.4.1.4 Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost
text: id="full-udp-coverage-when-the-objective-justifies-the-cost">9.1.4.1.4 Full UDP coverage when the objective justifies the cost sudo nmap -sU -n -p- --stats-every 60s -oA scans/udp-all TARGET This selects UDP ports 1-65535 and may take a long time because silence requires waiting and ICMP errors may be rate-limited. It is the coverage-expansion option, not a universal first command. Continue service work in parallel and preserve the result if the scan cannot finish. <h3

title: 9.1.4.1.5 Combined TCP/UDP selection
text: id="combined-tcpudp-selection">9.1.4.1.5 Combined TCP/UDP selection Example selection: change the TCP ( T: ) and UDP ( U: ) lists for the actual question. sudo nmap -sS -sU -n -p T:22,80,445,U:53,123,161 -oA scans/tcp-udp TARGET The port lists are examples, not complete coverage. UDP waiting can extend the combined scan.

title: 9.1.5 Scan Results and Next Actions
text: id="scan-results-and-next-actions">9.1.5 Scan Results and Next Actions ← Reference index · Previous: UDP scanning · Next: Windows network checks | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. <h2

title: 9.1.5.1 Resolve a result that changes your next action
text: id="6-resolve-a-result-that-changes-your-next-action">9.1.5.1 Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access. <summary

title: 9.1.5.1.1 Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output
text: id="variant-9-1-5-1-1">9.1.5.1.1 Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output <h3

title: 9.1.5.1.2 Netcat connection check
text: id="netcat-connection-check">9.1.5.1.2 Netcat connection check One TCP port: replace PORTS with one number. nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS Short port range: replace PORTS with a range such as 3388-3390 . nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. <h3

title: 9.1.5.1.3 Output and diagnostics
text: id="output-and-diagnostics">9.1.5.1.3 Output and diagnostics Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons: sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET Open saved .nmap or .txt output in a text editor. -oA writes .nmap , .gnmap and .xml ; -oN writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run. <h2

title: 9.1.5.2 Build the service queue
text: id="7-build-the-service-queue">9.1.5.2 Build the service queue Open the saved .nmap files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST Next: carry the complete endpoint tuple into Stage 02 service enumeration and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage. <summary

title: 9.1.5.2.1 Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established
text: id="variant-9-1-5-2-1">9.1.5.2.1 Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established open establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication . closed records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. filtered leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. unfiltered means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. UDP open|filtered is inconclusive . A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. closed|filtered is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position. <h2

title: 9.1.5.3 Prioritize and know when to rescan
text: id="8-prioritize-and-know-when-to-rescan">9.1.5.3 Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed.

title: 9.1.6 Windows Network Checks
text: id="windows-network-checks">9.1.6 Windows Network Checks ← Reference index · Previous: Results and next actions · Next: RDP access | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Purpose: Test TCP reachability from a Windows host when source position or available tooling matters. Test one TCP port from the Windows source host: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORTS Read: TcpTestSucceeded , source and destination addresses. Use one number for PORTS. Failure does not distinguish a closed port, filtering or a path problem. <summary

title: 9.1.6.1 Variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list
text: id="variant-9-1-6-1">9.1.6.1 Variants — scan ports 1-1024 or a selected port list <h3

title: 9.1.6.1.1 Scan a low-port range
text: id="scan-a-low-port-range">9.1.6.1.1 Scan a low-port range 1..1024 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("DC_IP", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null <h3

title: 9.1.6.1.2 Check a selected port list
text: id="check-a-selected-port-list">9.1.6.1.2 Check a selected port list The example list can be changed to the endpoints of interest. 22,80,443,445,3389 | % {echo ((New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient).Connect("TARGET", $_)) "TCP port $_ is open"} 2>$null $_ is the current port; errors are hidden. No printed result does not prove every port is closed. Results reflect the Windows host's access and the stated port selection.

title: 9.1.7 Scanner Alternatives and Web Baseline Checks
text: id="scanner-alternatives-and-web-baseline-checks">9.1.7 Scanner Alternatives and Web Baseline Checks ← Stage index | Discovery cheatsheet | Master Notes | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Use when: Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. <h2

title: 9.1.7.1 RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation
text: id="rustscan-fast-tcp-discovery-nmap-interpretation">9.1.7.1 RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation Prerequisite: RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. Coverage: only the explicit TCP range. Decisive output: a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap. <summary

title: 9.1.7.1.1 Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports
text: id="variant-9-1-7-1-1">9.1.7.1.1 Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection. <h2

title: 9.1.7.2 Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation
text: id="masscan-raw-packet-discovery-then-validation">9.1.7.2 Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation Prerequisite: root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. Choose it: for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. Failure cue: high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. <h2

title: 9.1.7.3 Unknown-port discrimination
text: id="unknown-port-discrimination">9.1.7.3 Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ Next action: route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. <h2

title: 9.1.7.4 NSE candidate checks
text: id="nse-candidate-checks">9.1.7.4 NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt The broad vuln category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt Avoid *brute* categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization . <h2

title: 9.1.7.5 Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation
text: id="nikto-bounded-web-server-candidate-generation">9.1.7.5 Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation Prerequisite: an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. Choose it: after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. Decisive output: a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt <summary

title: 9.1.7.5.1 HTTPS, host name and tuning variants
text: id="variant-9-1-7-5-1">9.1.7.5.1 HTTPS, host name and tuning variants nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect nikto -H / local documentation before relying on a copied code set. Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision. <h2

title: 9.1.7.6 Sources
text: id="sources">9.1.7.6 Sources getSH Scan route , reviewed at source commit e1f62dd Nmap service/version detection RustScan usage Masscan README Nikto documentation Current OSCP+ exam guide

title: 9.1.0 Stage 01: Discovery and Scanning
text: id="stage-01-discovery-and-scanning">9.1.0 Stage 01: Discovery and Scanning ← Main index | Strategy map | Study methods: Discover attack surfaces Quick use: Discovery and scanning cheatsheet Paired study stage: Stage 02 service enumeration . Stage 01 produces its input queue; Stage 02 may return new hosts, listeners or routes here. Purpose: establish scope and source position, discover reachable endpoints, identify application clues, preserve coverage limits and build the next enumeration queue. Order Task Use it to 1 Path and host discovery Check the selected source/interface and discover explicitly assigned hosts 2 TCP scanning Get quick leads and complete TCP coverage 3 Service identification Probe discovered ports for application and OS clues 4 UDP scanning Check UDP separately and preserve ambiguous results 5 Results and next actions Verify decisive results and build the service queue 6 Windows network checks Test endpoints from a Windows source position 7 Scanner alternatives Use RustScan/Masscan for candidate discovery or Nikto for bounded web checks, then validate manually Exit condition: you can state the scan source, tested target/transport/ports, observed endpoints, application confidence, remaining coverage gaps and the next service-specific test, then carry that complete tuple into Stage 02 .

title: 9.2.1 FTP Enumeration
text: id="ftp-enumeration">9.2.1 FTP Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: FTP usually appears on TCP/21, but trust an FTP banner or protocol response on any port. Goal: determine authentication , listable/readable content and effective write locations. <h2

title: 9.2.1.1 Baseline: anonymous access
text: id="baseline-anonymous-access">9.2.1.1 Baseline: anonymous access ftp TARGET At the prompts, try user anonymous and an email-like password. Then: status pwd ls -la binary get FILE quit If login succeeds but listing/transfer fails, use the client's passive command to toggle data-channel mode and retry once before changing credentials. Decisive output: code 230 accepts the login; directory listings and successful RETR establish read access. Inspect downloaded backups, configuration, keys and source locally. Store target artifacts outside this public repository. <summary

title: 9.2.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated FTP
text: id="variant-9-2-1-1-1">9.2.1.1.1 Variant — authenticated FTP ftp TARGET Enter USER and the password when prompted. Enumerate from the authenticated root again; it may expose a different namespace than anonymous access. <summary

title: 9.2.1.1.2 Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test
text: id="variant-9-2-1-1-2">9.2.1.1.2 Variant — curl listing, download and bounded write test curl --list-only ftp://TARGET/ curl -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER ftp://TARGET/ curl --user USER -o FILE ftp://TARGET/path/FILE curl --user USER --upload-file ./probe.txt ftp://TARGET/path/probe.txt Omit --user for anonymous access. Let curl prompt for an authenticated password instead of placing it in shell history. Upload only a harmless uniquely named probe when write validation is necessary and authorized; remove it through the FTP client after the test. <summary

title: 9.2.1.1.3 Variant — focused Nmap helpers
text: id="variant-9-2-1-1-3">9.2.1.1.3 Variant — focused Nmap helpers nmap -sV -p PORT --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst TARGET ftp-anon checks anonymous login and may flag writable entries; ftp-syst asks for server/system information. Manually confirm useful access with a protocol client. Failure cues: 530 means that login was rejected, not that FTP has no other usable identity. A listing failure after 230 may be a data-channel/passive-mode or authorization problem. A successful upload proves write access only; it does not prove that a web server, scheduled task or privileged process consumes that file. Next action: inspect recovered files; record exact read/write boundaries; validate any new credential once against its likely service; send a writable-consumer hypothesis to the appropriate web, execution or privilege-escalation block.

title: 9.2.2 SSH Enumeration and Access Validation
text: id="ssh-enumeration-and-access-validation">9.2.2 SSH Enumeration and Access Validation ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: SSH commonly uses TCP/22. Prerequisite for access: an accepted authentication method plus a permitted account/session context. <h2

title: 9.2.2.1 Baseline: validate one known identity
text: id="baseline-validate-one-known-identity">9.2.2.1 Baseline: validate one known identity ssh -v -p PORT USER@TARGET Decisive output: the debug trace separates connection, host-key negotiation, offered authentication methods and account acceptance. A shell prompt establishes session access as that identity. <summary

title: 9.2.2.1.1 Variant — private key
text: id="variant-9-2-2-1-1">9.2.2.1.1 Variant — private key chmod 600 KEY ssh -v -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET The key must correspond to an authorized public key for that account. Permission denied (publickey) can mean wrong user, wrong key, server policy or account restrictions. <summary

title: 9.2.2.1.2 Variant — discover methods for a known username
text: id="variant-9-2-2-1-2">9.2.2.1.2 Variant — discover methods for a known username nmap -p PORT --script ssh-auth-methods --script-args "ssh.user=USER" TARGET This starts an authentication exchange and is logged; Nmap classifies it as intrusive. Use it only when the supported methods change the next decision. <summary

title: 9.2.2.1.3 Variant — non-interactive key check
text: id="variant-9-2-2-1-3">9.2.2.1.3 Variant — non-interactive key check ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 -i KEY -p PORT USER@TARGET 'id' Batch mode will not prompt for passwords or key passphrases. It is useful only when the key is already usable non-interactively. Failure cues: timeout suggests route/filtering/service issues; refusal means no accepting listener in that context; host-key failure occurs before user authentication; Permission denied proves that the attempted method/context failed, not that every credential is invalid. A valid account may still have no shell or be restricted by server policy. Next action: after a shell, verify whoami , groups, hostname and addresses, then re-enumerate locally. Password spraying and key-passphrase cracking belong to the credential-attack block, not this procedure.

title: 9.2.3 SMTP Enumeration
text: id="smtp-enumeration">9.2.3 SMTP Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: SMTP commonly uses TCP/25, submission uses 587, and implicit TLS commonly uses 465. Goal: collect banner/capabilities, mail-domain clues and only defensible user evidence. <h2

title: 9.2.3.1 Baseline: banner and capabilities
text: id="baseline-banner-and-capabilities">9.2.3.1 Baseline: banner and capabilities nc -nv TARGET PORT Then enter: EHLO example.invalid HELP VRFY USER EXPN postmaster QUIT Decisive output: 250- capability lines reveal extensions such as STARTTLS or AUTH. 250 after VRFY may support a valid mailbox; 550 commonly rejects or denies it; 252 explicitly means the server will not verify and is not proof that the user exists. <summary

title: 9.2.3.1.1 Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS
text: id="variant-9-2-3-1-1">9.2.3.1.1 Variant — STARTTLS or implicit TLS openssl s_client -connect TARGET:587 -starttls smtp -crlf -quiet openssl s_client -connect TARGET:465 -crlf -quiet Run EHLO example.invalid after TLS negotiation. Certificate names and capabilities can yield host/domain clues; authentication still requires a supported identity and mechanism. <summary

title: 9.2.3.1.2 Variant — focused automated user checks
text: id="variant-9-2-3-1-2">9.2.3.1.2 Variant — focused automated user checks smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT smtp-user-enum -M RCPT -U users.txt -t TARGET -p PORT RCPT testing requires an SMTP transaction and servers may deliberately normalize responses. Treat automation as candidate generation and manually compare decisive responses. <summary

title: 9.2.3.1.3 Variant — Windows source position
text: id="variant-9-2-3-1-3">9.2.3.1.3 Variant — Windows source position Test-NetConnection -ComputerName TARGET -Port PORT This verifies TCP reachability only. Use an available Netcat/Ncat or OpenSSL client for protocol dialogue. Failure cues: multiline replies begin with NNN- and finish with NNN ; read the final line. 503 often means the command sequence is wrong. Uniform 252 or 550 responses make enumeration inconclusive . A visible AUTH method does not mean anonymous relay or valid credentials. Next action: add confirmed/candidate names and domains to the private evidence ledger; test new names only in the later credential block. Do not send real mail or run relay checks unless the objective requires it. <h2

title: 9.2.3.2 POP3 and IMAP handoff
text: id="pop3-and-imap-handoff">9.2.3.2 POP3 and IMAP handoff Mail-access services expose mailbox capabilities and, with legitimate credentials, stored messages that may contain workflow or reset links. openssl s_client -connect TARGET:995 -crlf -quiet # POP3S openssl s_client -connect TARGET:993 -crlf -quiet # IMAPS POP3 dialogue: CAPA USER USER PASS PASSWORD STAT LIST QUIT IMAP dialogue: a1 CAPABILITY a2 LOGIN USER PASSWORD a3 LIST "" "*" a4 LOGOUT Test one legitimately acquired credential. Capability output is not authentication; avoid brute-force NSE scripts until lockout/ authorization is explicitly understood. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap mail blocks.

title: 9.2.4 DNS Enumeration
text: id="dns-enumeration">9.2.4 DNS Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: DNS uses UDP/53 for most queries and TCP/53 for operations including conventional zone transfers and oversized responses. Prerequisite: a known or inferred domain for meaningful record and name enumeration. <h2

title: 9.2.4.1 Baseline: query the target DNS server directly
text: id="baseline-query-the-target-dns-server-directly">9.2.4.1 Baseline: query the target DNS server directly dig @TARGET DOMAIN SOA dig @TARGET DOMAIN NS dig @TARGET DOMAIN A dig @TARGET DOMAIN MX dig @TARGET DOMAIN TXT Decisive output: ANSWER records disclose names, addresses, mail exchangers or text. The aa flag supports an authoritative answer. Record status separately from the answer count. <summary

title: 9.2.4.1.1 Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer
text: id="variant-9-2-4-1-1">9.2.4.1.1 Variant — reverse lookup and zone transfer dig @TARGET -x IP dig @TARGET DOMAIN AXFR A successful AXFR returns the zone records and closing SOA. Transfer failed , REFUSED or NOTAUTH only disproves an unauthenticated transfer from this source; continue ordinary queries. <summary

title: 9.2.4.1.2 Variant — name guessing after the domain is known
text: id="variant-9-2-4-1-2">9.2.4.1.2 Variant — name guessing after the domain is known dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -t std dnsrecon -d DOMAIN -n TARGET -D WORDLIST -t brt dnsenum --dnsserver TARGET DOMAIN Check wildcard behavior before trusting large result sets. Every resolved in-scope name becomes a new discovery/service-enumeration input. <summary

title: 9.2.4.1.3 Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range
text: id="variant-9-2-4-1-3">9.2.4.1.3 Variant — reverse sweep of an explicitly assigned range dnsrecon -r SUBNET -n TARGET Use this only when the entire SUBNET is assigned. PTR names are clues; resolve/scan only in-scope results. <summary

title: 9.2.4.1.4 Variant — host and Windows nslookup
text: id="variant-9-2-4-1-4">9.2.4.1.4 Variant — host and Windows nslookup host -t mx DOMAIN TARGET host -t txt DOMAIN TARGET nslookup HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=TXT HOST.DOMAIN TARGET nslookup -type=MX DOMAIN TARGET Failure cues: NXDOMAIN means that queried name does not exist in that view; NOERROR with no answer can mean the name exists but lacks that record type. Timeout can be filtering, loss or a silent/unreachable server. A recursive answer does not establish that the server is authoritative. Next action: add new hostnames/IPs to the scoped queue, correlate naming roles with observed services, and repeat discovery/service identification for those in-scope endpoints.

title: 9.2.5 NFS and Unix RPC Enumeration
text: id="nfs-and-unix-rpc-enumeration">9.2.5 NFS and Unix RPC Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: rpcbind commonly appears on TCP/UDP 111 and NFS on TCP/UDP 2049, with additional dynamically assigned RPC ports. Goal: find exports, allowed client ranges and effective UID/GID-based permissions. <h2

title: 9.2.5.1 Baseline: list RPC services and exports
text: id="baseline-list-rpc-services-and-exports">9.2.5.1 Baseline: list RPC services and exports rpcinfo -p TARGET showmount -e TARGET Decisive output: rpcinfo maps RPC programs to versions/transports/ports. showmount -e returns exports and apparent allowed clients, but NFSv4-only servers may not expose the mount service and showmount completeness varies by implementation. <summary

title: 9.2.5.1.1 Variant — Nmap without mounting
text: id="variant-9-2-5-1-1">9.2.5.1.1 Variant — Nmap without mounting nmap -sV -p 111,2049 --script nfs-showmount,nfs-ls,nfs-statfs TARGET The scripts can list exports, file attributes and access flags. Confirm access manually when a finding matters. <summary

title: 9.2.5.1.2 Variant — mount read-only first
text: id="variant-9-2-5-1-2">9.2.5.1.2 Variant — mount read-only first sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-audit sudo mount -t nfs -o ro,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -ls sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit If version 3 fails and version 4 is advertised, retry with -o ro,vers=4 . NFSv4 may present a pseudo-filesystem whose export path differs from showmount output. <summary

title: 9.2.5.1.3 Variant — inspect numeric ownership
text: id="variant-9-2-5-1-3">9.2.5.1.3 Variant — inspect numeric ownership ls -lan /mnt/nfs-audit find /mnt/nfs-audit -maxdepth 3 -type f -readable -ls NFS commonly authorizes Unix identities by numeric UID/GID. A matching local username is irrelevant if its number differs. root_squash usually maps remote UID 0 to an unprivileged identity; no_root_squash is dangerous but still requires a useful writable object and privileged consumption path. <summary

title: 9.2.5.1.4 Variant — bounded write verification
text: id="variant-9-2-5-1-4">9.2.5.1.4 Variant — bounded write verification sudo mount -t nfs -o rw,vers=3,nolock TARGET:/EXPORT /mnt/nfs-audit touch /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file ls -ln /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file rm /mnt/nfs-audit/probe-file sudo umount /mnt/nfs-audit Use a unique harmless name only when write validation is needed and authorized. Record the resulting numeric owner/group. Success proves write in that directory, not execution or privileged ownership. Failure cues: showmount failure does not rule out NFSv4. access denied by server can mean export client restrictions or wrong path/version. permission denied after mounting is file authorization , not network failure. Do not change local UIDs or write to an export during concept study. Next action: inspect readable backups, home data, keys and configuration; record numeric ownership and actual write boundaries; send a writable/privileged-consumer hypothesis to the escalation block.

title: 9.2.6 SMB and MS-RPC Enumeration
text: id="smb-and-ms-rpc-enumeration">9.2.6 SMB and MS-RPC Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: direct-hosted SMB commonly uses TCP/445; NetBIOS session service commonly uses TCP/139; MS-RPC endpoint mapping commonly uses TCP/135. They are related Windows surfaces but not interchangeable. Goal: distinguish null, guest and authenticated contexts; enumerate shares, files, users, groups, domain/workgroup clues and actual permissions. <h2

title: 9.2.6.1 Baseline: list shares without credentials
text: id="baseline-list-shares-without-credentials">9.2.6.1 Baseline: list shares without credentials smbclient -N -L //TARGET Decisive output: a share list proves that this access context can enumerate names. It does not prove access to share contents. NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED means this context was denied; repeat after obtaining a legitimate credential. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.1 Variant — authenticated share listing and connection
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-1">9.2.6.1.1 Variant — authenticated share listing and connection smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'TARGET/USER' smbclient -L //TARGET -U 'guest%' The first two forms use a domain identity, the third makes a local target account explicit, and the fourth tests a guest account with an empty password. Let the client prompt for non-empty passwords. Inside the share: pwd ls allinfo FILE get FILE mkdir probe-dir rmdir probe-dir exit Use a harmless uniquely named directory only when write permission must be verified. A successful create/remove establishes share-level write access, not code execution. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.2 Variant — recursive retrieval
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-2">9.2.6.1.2 Variant — recursive retrieval smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN/USER' -c 'recurse ON;prompt OFF;mget *' Run from a dedicated local evidence directory and review expected volume first. Search downloaded configuration, scripts, backups, keys and unattended-install files locally; never publish recovered data. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.3 Variant — RPC null or authenticated session
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-3">9.2.6.1.3 Variant — RPC null or authenticated session rpcclient -U '' -N TARGET rpcclient -U 'DOMAIN/USER' TARGET Useful interactive queries: srvinfo enumdomains enumdomusers enumdomgroups queryuser RID netshareenumall quit Null-session denial is common on modern systems. Authenticated output must be labelled with the identity that produced it. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.4 Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-4">9.2.6.1.4 Variant — fast permission summary and consolidated candidates nxc smb TARGET -u USER -p PASSWORD --shares enum4linux-ng -A TARGET NetExec ( nxc ) is the current command name on recent Kali releases; older material may use crackmapexec . These tools consolidate candidates. Confirm useful shares and files with smbclient or native access. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.5 Variant — protocol, signing and time clues
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-5">9.2.6.1.5 Variant — protocol, signing and time clues nmap -p 139,445 --script smb-protocols,smb2-security-mode,smb2-time TARGET Signing and dialect results affect later relay/exploit decisions but are not vulnerabilities by themselves. The older smb-os-discovery script depends on SMBv1 behavior and may not identify modern hosts reliably. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.6 Variant — Windows built-ins
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-6">9.2.6.1.6 Variant — Windows built-ins net view \\TARGET /all Get-ChildItem \\TARGET\SHARE Get-Content \\TARGET\SHARE\FILE These use the current Windows logon context unless alternate credentials or mappings are established. An existing connection to the same server under another identity can cause credential-conflict errors. <summary

title: 9.2.6.1.7 SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-7">9.2.6.1.7 SMBMap — map rights, then read one useful file Use from Kali when SMB is reachable. Choose the same domain/local identity that worked with smbclient. Suppress write probes when inventorying reads; this means a writable label is not being tested here. <h3

title: 9.2.6.1.8 Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-8">9.2.6.1.8 Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file # Known domain account: enumerate share access without creating a probe file smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --no-write-check <h3

title: 9.2.6.1.9 Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-9">9.2.6.1.9 Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth # Inspect the selected share to a bounded depth smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' -r 'SHARE' --depth 2 --no-write-check <h3

title: 9.2.6.1.10 Download the specific file found above
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-10">9.2.6.1.10 Download the specific file found above # Download the specific file found above smbmap -H TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --download 'SHARE\PATH\FILE' --no-write-check Read: a listed file must still be readable under this identity. A downloaded config/backup → classify its credential material, then test only the relevant account/service. A denied share → try another listed share or a newly obtained identity; do not infer a host-wide denial. SMBMap upstream . For broader SMB/RPC collection, use the existing enum4linux-ng baseline; authenticate explicitly when credentials exist: <h3

title: 9.2.6.1.11 No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-11">9.2.6.1.11 No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates # No credentials: anonymous RPC/SMB candidates enum4linux-ng -A TARGET <h3

title: 9.2.6.1.12 Known identity: domain objects visible to this account
text: id="variant-9-2-6-1-12">9.2.6.1.12 Known identity: domain objects visible to this account # Known identity: domain objects visible to this account enum4linux-ng -A -w DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' TARGET Next: validate returned users/groups/shares with rpcclient or smbclient. A collector can return partial data despite a successful login. Failure cues: distinguish connection failure, authentication failure, share enumeration denial and file authorization denial. A share named IPC$ is not a general file share. Guest acceptance may look like success while returning a restricted namespace. A share marked writable still needs a consumer/trigger before it becomes an execution path. Next action: inspect readable content, record per-share rights, validate names/domain clues, and re-run authenticated enumeration whenever identity changes. Move file-consumer hypotheses to web/execution/escalation and signing/relay hypotheses to the later credential/AD blocks. <h2

title: 9.2.6.2 NetBIOS names before SMB enumeration
text: id="netbios-names-before-smb-enumeration">9.2.6.2 NetBIOS names before SMB enumeration Use when UDP/137 or SMB suggests Windows names but DNS/domain identity is unclear. # Ask the assigned host for its NetBIOS names nbtscan TARGET nmblookup -A TARGET Read: a machine name and group/domain label are leads. A workgroup label does not prove AD membership. Resolve the returned name and use the SMB/LDAP checks with the accepted identity. No reply can mean filtering or disabled NetBIOS while TCP/445 still works. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.6.3 SMB/RPC RID lookups when a normal user listing is denied
text: id="smbrpc-rid-lookups-when-a-normal-user-listing-is-denied">9.2.6.3 SMB/RPC RID lookups when a normal user listing is denied Use when the accepted identity can translate SIDs but cannot list the directory directly. Keep the queried host/domain and a bounded RID range explicit. nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --rid-brute 4000 Read: classify returned SID types—users, groups and machine accounts are different objects. The upper bound is coverage, not proof that higher RIDs contain nothing. A resolved name is not a password, service authorization or successful logon. Prefer the existing native directory/RPC listing when it is available; do not infer no accounts from a single denied enumeration method. Sources: upstream 1 .

title: 9.2.7 SNMP Enumeration
text: id="snmp-enumeration">9.2.7 SNMP Enumeration ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: SNMP queries commonly use UDP/161. Versions 1 and 2c authenticate with a community string sent without modern transport protection; version 3 can provide user-based authentication and privacy. Goal: turn a valid read context into host, interface, route, process, software, user and listener clues. <h2

title: 9.2.7.1 Baseline: find a read community, then walk
text: id="baseline-find-a-read-community-then-walk">9.2.7.1 Baseline: find a read community, then walk onesixtyone -c COMMUNITY_FILE TARGET snmpwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 Use -v1 instead when version 1 is indicated. Start with the standard system tree before a huge full walk. Decisive output: returned OID/value pairs prove that the selected version/community can read those objects. Hostnames, interfaces, routes, users, processes and locally listening ports become new hypotheses to validate through the appropriate service or post-access path. <summary

title: 9.2.7.1.1 Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk
text: id="variant-9-2-7-1-1">9.2.7.1.1 Variant — efficient v2c bulk walk snmpbulkwalk -v2c -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 Bulk requests reduce round trips but require SNMPv2c or later. If the agent rejects them, fall back to snmpwalk with the verified version. <summary

title: 9.2.7.1.2 Variant — high-value Windows OIDs
text: id="variant-9-2-7-1-2">9.2.7.1.2 Variant — high-value Windows OIDs snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2 snmpwalk -v1 -c COMMUNITY TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3 These target user names, running process names, installed software and TCP listener ports. Availability depends on the agent and exposed MIB view. <summary

title: 9.2.7.1.3 Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk
text: id="variant-9-2-7-1-3">9.2.7.1.3 Variant — SNMPv3 authenticated and private walk snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u USER -a SHA -A AUTH_PASSWORD -x AES -X PRIV_PASSWORD TARGET 1.3.6.1.2.1 The security level, authentication algorithm, privacy algorithm and credentials must match the configured SNMPv3 user. authNoPriv authenticates without encryption; noAuthNoPriv supplies neither and should be used only when that exact configuration is observed. <summary

title: 9.2.7.1.4 Variant — focused UDP verification
text: id="variant-9-2-7-1-4">9.2.7.1.4 Variant — focused UDP verification sudo nmap -sU -sV -p 161 --script snmp-info TARGET snmp-info extracts basic SNMPv3 engine information without proving a usable v1/v2c community. Failure cues: UDP silence can remain open|filtered ; it does not prove that the community is wrong. Timeout: No Response can be version mismatch, wrong community, filtering, loss or an unavailable OID view. No Such Object means the queried OID is absent/not exposed, not that the whole service failed. Do not use a discovered write community to change configuration during enumeration. Next action: translate output into exact host/service/user hypotheses, scan newly disclosed in-scope addresses/listeners from the proper source position, and keep configuration-changing SNMP actions outside this stage.

title: 9.2.8 Database Enumeration and Privilege Boundaries
text: id="database-enumeration-and-privilege-boundaries">9.2.8 Database Enumeration and Privilege Boundaries ← Stage index · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: common ports include MSSQL 1433, MySQL/MariaDB 3306 and PostgreSQL 5432, but instances can use other ports. Goal: establish database identity, authentication context, databases/schemas/tables, granted rights, useful data, server-side file access and command execution only where explicit privileges permit it. Database administrator and operating-system administrator are different identities. Server-side file/program features act in the database server's filesystem and service-account context, not Kali's. <h2

title: 9.2.8.1 MySQL / MariaDB
text: id="mysql--mariadb">9.2.8.1 MySQL / MariaDB mysql -h TARGET -P PORT -u USER -p SELECT VERSION(), USER(), CURRENT_USER(); SHOW DATABASES; SHOW GRANTS; USE DATABASE; SHOW TABLES; DESCRIBE TABLE; SELECT * FROM TABLE LIMIT 20; SELECT @@secure_file_priv; Interpret: USER() shows the presented client identity; CURRENT_USER() shows the account used for privilege checking. secure_file_priv restricts server-side import/export: a directory constrains it, an empty value is unrestricted by that variable, and NULL disables these operations. The FILE privilege is still required. <summary

title: 9.2.8.1.1 MySQL variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites
text: id="variant-9-2-8-1-1">9.2.8.1.1 MySQL variant — validate server-side file read/write prerequisites SELECT LOAD_FILE('/path/on/database/server'); SELECT 'probe' INTO OUTFILE '/allowed/server/path/probe.txt'; Use only an authorized harmless path. LOAD_FILE returning NULL is ambiguous among missing file, permissions, size, FILE privilege and secure_file_priv . INTO OUTFILE will not overwrite an existing file. A written file becomes execution only if another privileged component consumes it. <h2

title: 9.2.8.2 Microsoft SQL Server
text: id="microsoft-sql-server">9.2.8.2 Microsoft SQL Server impacket-mssqlclient 'USER@TARGET' impacket-mssqlclient 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' -windows-auth Let the tool prompt for the password. At the SQL prompt: SELECT @@VERSION; SELECT SYSTEM_USER; SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin'); SELECT name FROM sys.databases; USE DATABASE; SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES; SELECT TOP 20 * FROM SCHEMA.TABLE; Interpret: IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') returns 1 , 0 or NULL ; NULL is not success. Impacket also exposes helpers such as enum_impersonate and xp_cmdshell depending on version and rights. <summary

title: 9.2.8.2.1 MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary
text: id="variant-9-2-8-2-1">9.2.8.2.1 MSSQL variant — command-execution boundary EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; xp_cmdshell is disabled by default on new installations. Enabling it generally requires high privilege and changes server configuration; do not enable it merely to enumerate. When available, a sysadmin's child process normally runs as the SQL Server service account; an authorized non-sysadmin may use a configured proxy. Verify returned identity before choosing the next action. <h2

title: 9.2.8.3 PostgreSQL
text: id="postgresql">9.2.8.3 PostgreSQL psql -h TARGET -p PORT -U USER -d postgres \conninfo \l \du \dn \dt *.* SELECT version(), current_user, session_user; SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb FROM pg_roles; <summary

title: 9.2.8.3.1 PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary
text: id="variant-9-2-8-3-1">9.2.8.3.1 PostgreSQL variant — server file/program privilege boundary SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_read_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_write_server_files', 'member'); SELECT pg_has_role(current_user, 'pg_execute_server_program', 'member'); Server-side COPY ... FROM/TO 'file' uses the PostgreSQL server's filesystem and service identity. COPY ... PROGRAM executes on the server and requires superuser or the corresponding predefined role. Client-side \copy reads/writes the client filesystem and is not the same primitive. Failure cues: connection refusal/timeout is network or listener context; login rejection is authentication/context; an empty database list may be visibility limits; object denial is authorization . Query only bounded rows first. Never assume that reading application credentials or obtaining database admin implies OS execution. Next action: identify application accounts, hashes/credentials, paths and linked systems; record the precise grant enabling any file or execution primitive; validate recovered credentials in the later credential block and re-enumerate after any identity change. <h2

title: 9.2.8.4 Redis
text: id="redis">9.2.8.4 Redis nmap -Pn -sV --script redis-info -p PORT TARGET redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT PING redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT INFO redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL WHOAMI redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT ACL LIST Authenticated when a password is legitimately known: redis-cli -h TARGET -p PORT --askpass PONG proves an accessible Redis command surface, not write/file/execution permission. Check ACLs, mode, bind/protected-mode and persistence/module configuration before reasoning about an effect. Do not run CONFIG SET , write keys or load modules during enumeration. <h2

title: 9.2.8.5 Oracle TNS/SID triage
text: id="oracle-tnssid-triage">9.2.8.5 Oracle TNS/SID triage nmap -Pn -sV --script oracle-tns-version -p 1521 TARGET nmap -Pn --script oracle-sid-brute -p 1521 TARGET A discovered SID /service name is a namespace clue, not credentials. Continue with an installed Oracle client only when a legitimate identity is available; preserve listener/version/SID evidence and do not treat a conventional port as Oracle proof. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap Oracle block. <h2

title: 9.2.8.6 MongoDB — inspect readable databases with mongosh
text: id="mongodb--inspect-readable-databases-with-mongosh">9.2.8.6 MongoDB — inspect readable databases with mongosh Use when the service is MongoDB, commonly TCP/27017. Current installations use mongosh ; the old mongo binary may be absent. <h3

title: 9.2.8.6.1 Reachable service without known credentials
text: id="variant-9-2-8-6-1">9.2.8.6.1 Reachable service without known credentials # Reachable service without known credentials mongosh --host TARGET --port PORT <h3

title: 9.2.8.6.2 Known account; -p prompts rather than storing the password in the command
text: id="variant-9-2-8-6-2">9.2.8.6.2 Known account; -p prompts rather than storing the password in the command # Known account; -p prompts rather than storing the password in the command mongosh --host TARGET --port PORT -u USER -p --authenticationDatabase admin Inside mongosh, choose the real database/collection: show dbs use DATABASE show collections db.getCollection('COLLECTION').find().limit(5) db.getCollection('users').findOne({username: 'USER'}) Read: returned documents prove that identity can read those collections. An empty database list can reflect authorization, not an empty server. Classify recovered secrets and use the matching service. Login/operator injection is an application query issue, distinct from direct DB access. Do not overwrite account records just because the repo contains an update example. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.8.7 SQLite — inspect a recovered application database
text: id="sqlite--inspect-a-recovered-application-database">9.2.8.7 SQLite — inspect a recovered application database Use when a downloaded/local application file is SQLite. It is a file format, not a remote listener. file app.db sqlite3 -readonly app.db .tables .schema users PRAGMA table_info(users); SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5; .quit Read: identify the schema and credential format before choosing a recovery mode. Keep the database's provenance and any required WAL/SHM companions; a locked/incomplete copy can give misleading results. Recovered passwords/hashes → the credential procedure, not an assumption of OS or domain access. Sources: upstream 1 .

title: 9.2.9 Windows Remote-Access Validation
text: id="windows-remote-access-validation">9.2.9 Windows Remote-Access Validation ← Stage index · RDP access procedure · Cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognize: RDP commonly uses TCP/3389; WinRM commonly uses 5985/HTTP and 5986/HTTPS. Goal: determine whether one known credential is accepted in the correct local/domain context and whether it is authorized for a usable session. <h2

title: 9.2.9.1 RDP baseline: authentication-only check
text: id="rdp-baseline-authentication-only-check">9.2.9.1 RDP baseline: authentication-only check xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore Some distributions expose the binary as xfreerdp . Omit /d:DOMAIN for the intended local-account context; use /u:TARGET\\USER if needed to make that context explicit. Decisive output: successful authentication -only validation supports that the credential is accepted for RDP/NLA. It does not prove an interactive desktop will be granted under every policy/session condition. <summary

title: 9.2.9.1.1 Variant — open an RDP desktop
text: id="variant-9-2-9-1-1">9.2.9.1.1 Variant — open an RDP desktop xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Let FreeRDP prompt for the password. /cert:ignore suppresses certificate validation and is suitable only in the controlled lab context; it removes server-identity protection. <summary

title: 9.2.9.1.2 Variant — identify RDP security requirements
text: id="variant-9-2-9-1-2">9.2.9.1.2 Variant — identify RDP security requirements nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-enum-encryption,rdp-ntlm-info TARGET This can disclose supported security layers, NLA and NTLM host/domain clues. It does not validate a credential. <h2

title: 9.2.9.2 WinRM baseline: interactive session
text: id="winrm-baseline-interactive-session">9.2.9.2 WinRM baseline: interactive session evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER evil-winrm -i TARGET -u 'DOMAIN\\USER' Omitting -p makes the established Ruby client prompt for the password. Decisive output: an interactive PowerShell prompt establishes WinRM authorization . Immediately verify identity and host context with whoami , hostname and Get-NetIPAddress . <summary

title: 9.2.9.2.1 Variant — WinRM over HTTPS
text: id="variant-9-2-9-2-1">9.2.9.2.1 Variant — WinRM over HTTPS evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -S -P 5986 Check evil-winrm -h because the established Ruby client and newer evil-winrm-py use different long-option spelling. Do not assume a copied command matches the installed implementation. <summary

title: 9.2.9.2.2 Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting
text: id="variant-9-2-9-2-2">9.2.9.2.2 Variant — Windows PowerShell remoting $cred = Get-Credential Enter-PSSession -ComputerName TARGET -Credential $cred PowerShell remoting uses the configured WinRM endpoint. Local trusted-host, Kerberos/name-resolution and endpoint authorization settings can fail independently of password validity. Failure cues: certificate warnings are different from authentication failure. RDP errors can reflect NLA, account context, expired/locked accounts or missing logon rights. WinRM 401 supports authentication/authorization failure; WinRM cannot process the request can be name resolution, trusted-host, listener or transport context. Valid SMB credentials do not guarantee RDP or WinRM rights. Next action: after a session, re-enumerate identity, groups, privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes. Password spraying, pass-the-hash and ticket use belong to later credential/AD blocks. <h2

title: 9.2.9.3 VNC
text: id="vnc">9.2.9.3 VNC nmap -Pn -sV --script vnc-info -p PORT TARGET vncviewer TARGET:PORT VNC may expose a desktop without Windows logon semantics; the VNC server's authentication and the resulting OS session identity are separate. Use realvnc-auth-bypass or password testing only for a confirmed compatible product and explicit authorized objective, then verify the desktop identity. <h2

title: 9.2.9.4 Telnet
text: id="telnet">9.2.9.4 Telnet nmap -Pn -sV -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT telnet TARGET PORT Telnet is plaintext and may expose a banner/login prompt. Validate only legitimately acquired credentials; do not make telnet-brute a baseline. After login, verify host and identity because appliance/application shells can differ from an OS shell. Source supplement: reviewed getSH Nmap VNC/Telnet blocks. <h2

title: 9.2.9.5 GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check
text: id="gnu-inetutils-telnetd--conditional-authentication-bypass-check">9.2.9.5 GNU Inetutils telnetd — conditional authentication-bypass check Use only after identifying the affected GNU Inetutils telnetd/login chain and its patch status. CVE-2026-24061 concerns how a supplied USER value reaches login; it does not apply to every Telnet server. Distribution backports matter. # Client supports sending the autologin USER environment value USER='-f root' telnet -a TARGET PORT Read: if a shell is obtained, verify hostname and id. A prompt or echoed username is not root access. A different daemon, fixed build, client negotiation mismatch or a rejected USER value → return to service identification. The affected upstream range and distribution fixes must be checked against the advisory rather than inferred from port 23. Sources: upstream 1 .

title: 9.2.10 HTTP and Web Application Mapping
text: id="http-and-web-application-mapping">9.2.10 HTTP and Web Application Mapping ← Stage index · Quick sheet · Mechanics | Strategy map | Study methods: Map useful web behavior Use when: an HTTP(S) endpoint must become a route, request, role, object and input map before exploitation. Enter with: SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp PORT | HTTP/TLS evidence | hostname clues | coverage limit . <h2

title: 9.2.10.1 Baseline the application identity
text: id="baseline-the-application-identity">9.2.10.1 Baseline the application identity curl -skL -D headers.txt -o body.html http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'code=%{http_code} bytes=%{size_download} type=%{content_type} redirect=%{redirect_url}\n' http://TARGET:PORT/ Decisive output: record the scheme, hostname/ Host header, port, redirects, page title, certificate names, server/framework clues and whether the view is anonymous or authenticated. <summary

title: 9.2.10.1.1 Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate
text: id="variant-9-2-10-1-1">9.2.10.1.1 Variant — explicit virtual-host candidate curl -sk -H 'Host: CANDIDATE.DOMAIN' http://TARGET:PORT/ Compare it with a random hostname. A different status alone is weak evidence; compare body, length, title and redirects. <summary

title: 9.2.10.1.2 Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects
text: id="variant-9-2-10-1-2">9.2.10.1.2 Variant — preserve cookies and follow redirects curl -skL -c cookies.txt -b cookies.txt http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Use a separate cookie jar per identity. Do not mix anonymous, ordinary-user and administrator evidence. <summary

title: 9.2.10.1.3 Variant — replay through Burp Community
text: id="variant-9-2-10-1-3">9.2.10.1.3 Variant — replay through Burp Community curl -sk -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Confirm the proxy listener is active on 127.0.0.1:8080 . Use -k only for the controlled lab because it disables destination-certificate verification. <h2

title: 9.2.10.2 Manual behavior map
text: id="manual-behavior-map">9.2.10.2 Manual behavior map For every visible function, capture one unchanged request in Burp Proxy history, send it to Repeater and record: METHOD PATH | CONTENT-TYPE | ACCESS CONTEXT/ROLE INPUT LOCATION + NAME | BASELINE VALUE STATUS | LENGTH/HASH | REDIRECT | MARKER/ERROR/TIME OBJECT/FUNCTION SELECTED | NEXT ONE-VARIABLE TEST Check login/registration/reset, profiles/objects, search/filter/pagination, download/export/preview, upload/import, administration and every JavaScript API call. Next: a browser-side restriction is not server authorization . Replay the raw request and change one field, object reference, method or access-context element at a time. <h2

title: 9.2.10.3 Inspect exposed artifacts
text: id="inspect-exposed-artifacts">9.2.10.3 Inspect exposed artifacts curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/robots.txt curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/sitemap.xml curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/.git/HEAD curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/openapi.json curl -sk http://TARGET:PORT/swagger.json Also inspect HTML comments, hidden inputs, form actions, linked JavaScript, route strings, source-map references, cookies and response headers. Decisive output: a path, parameter, API schema, object identifier, component or secret-bearing artifact that creates a specific next request. Source disclosure is not command execution. <h2

title: 9.2.10.4 Discover files and directories
text: id="discover-files-and-directories">9.2.10.4 Discover files and directories Request a random nonexistent path first and record its status, length and body marker. gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -t 10 -o gobuster-root.txt Decisive output: manually verified routes including useful 200 , redirect, 401 , 403 and 405 responses. <summary

title: 9.2.10.4.1 Variant — technology-aware extensions
text: id="variant-9-2-10-4-1">9.2.10.4.1 Variant — technology-aware extensions gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -x php,txt,bak,old,zip -t 10 -o gobuster-ext.txt Choose extensions from observed stack evidence; do not spray every extension. <summary

title: 9.2.10.4.2 Variant — authenticated discovery
text: id="variant-9-2-10-4-2">9.2.10.4.2 Variant — authenticated discovery gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST -c 'SESSION=VALUE' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -t 10 -o gobuster-auth.txt Use only the cookie or header that applies. An expired session can turn every result into the same login redirect. <summary

title: 9.2.10.4.3 Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length
text: id="variant-9-2-10-4-3">9.2.10.4.3 Variant — filter a confirmed wildcard body length gobuster dir -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -w WORDLIST --exclude-length NOISE_LENGTH -t 10 -o gobuster-filtered.txt Filtering without first confirming the noise response can hide a real path. <h2

title: 9.2.10.5 Discover virtual hosts
text: id="discover-virtual-hosts">9.2.10.5 Discover virtual hosts gobuster vhost -u http://DOMAIN:PORT/ --append-domain -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -o vhosts.txt Alternative with automatic calibration: ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/ -H 'Host: FUZZ.DOMAIN' -ac -o ffuf-vhosts.json Failure cue: uniform status/length may be the default vhost. Compare each candidate with a random host header before adding it to the application map. <h2

title: 9.2.10.6 Discover parameters and object values
text: id="discover-parameters-and-object-values">9.2.10.6 Discover parameters and object values GET parameter names: ffuf -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/burp-parameter-names.txt -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH?FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-get.json POST form parameter names: ffuf -w WORDLIST -u http://TARGET:PORT/PATH -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' -d 'known=value&FUZZ=test' -ac -o params-post.json Object values with an authenticated API: ffuf -w NUMBERS -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/api/objects/FUZZ' -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -mc all -fc 404 -o object-values.json Decisive output: a manually reproduced parameter or value that changes application behavior. Tool outliers are candidates, not confirmed access-control flaws. <summary

title: 9.2.10.6.1 ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request
text: id="variant-9-2-10-6-1">9.2.10.6.1 ffuf — preserve a captured authenticated request Save a working raw request from the proxy as request.txt, retain its Host/cookie/body, and put FUZZ at the single parameter name/value or path being tested. Replay it once manually first. The request file does not specify TLS: choose the transport explicitly. <h3

title: 9.2.10.6.2 HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers
text: id="variant-9-2-10-6-2">9.2.10.6.2 HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers # HTTPS request, including its original method and session headers ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto https -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-https.json <h3

title: 9.2.10.6.3 Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS
text: id="variant-9-2-10-6-3">9.2.10.6.3 Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS # Plain HTTP request: otherwise ffuf defaults to HTTPS ffuf -request request.txt -request-proto http -w WORDLIST -mc all -ac -t 10 -o request-http.json Read: compare an outlier's status/length/body with a known missing value, then replay that exact request. A login redirect for every value → refresh the session before continuing. A one-time CSRF token → repair token handling; the saved-request flag does not refresh it automatically. ffuf request configuration . <h2

title: 9.2.10.7 Map API methods, schema and authorization
text: id="map-api-methods-schema-and-authorization">9.2.10.7 Map API methods, schema and authorization curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/PATH curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/login Interpretation: 405 can establish that a route exists but rejects the method. Validation errors can reveal required fields. A token establishes only the authorization demonstrated by a later request. Build a matrix across anonymous, user A, user B and administrator contexts where available: PATH | METHOD | IDENTITY/ROLE | OBJECT/PROPERTY | RESULT | NEXT <h2

title: 9.2.10.8 Exit and handoffs
text: id="exit-and-handoffs">9.2.10.8 Exit and handoffs Exit condition: each interesting function has a baseline request, access context, controllable input, expected result, observed difference and cheapest next test. file/path selector -> file handling attacks ; shell/diagnostic or database-backed input -> command and SQL injection ; object/role/property or browser-script context -> access control and XSS ; product/plugin/version exploit candidate -> Block 6 public-exploit adaptation; new credential -> Block 5 credential handling and authenticated re-enumeration; verified server command execution -> Block 7 session handling. <h2

title: 9.2.10.9 wfuzz alternative for paths and form values
text: id="wfuzz-alternative-for-paths-and-form-values">9.2.10.9 wfuzz alternative for paths and form values Use when wfuzz is the available/familiar client for the same controlled-response test. Choose a nonexistent control first; preserve the actual Host and authenticated session. <h3

title: 9.2.10.9.1 Paths; hiding 404s is appropriate only after checking the site's failure behavior
text: id="variant-9-2-10-9-1">9.2.10.9.1 Paths; hiding 404s is appropriate only after checking the site's failure behavior # Paths; hiding 404s is appropriate only after checking the site's failure behavior wfuzz -c -z file,WORDLIST --hc 404 -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/FUZZ' <h3

title: 9.2.10.9.2 A form value in a working authenticated request
text: id="variant-9-2-10-9-2">9.2.10.9.2 A form value in a working authenticated request # A form value in a working authenticated request wfuzz -c -z file,WORDLIST -b 'session=COOKIE' \ -d 'name=FUZZ' --hc 404 -u 'http://TARGET:PORT/PATH' Read: status/length/body outliers need manual replay. Uniform redirects, wildcard bodies or expired cookies → fix the response/session controls before expanding the list. The presence of an outlier is not a vulnerability result. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.10.10 HTTP proxy variables — control which client request goes through Burp
text: id="http-proxy-variables--control-which-client-request-goes-through-burp">9.2.10.10 HTTP proxy variables — control which client request goes through Burp Use when a client honors HTTP proxy environment variables. Keeping them on a single invocation avoids accidentally proxying later unrelated traffic. <h3

title: 9.2.10.10.1 http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
text: id="variant-9-2-10-10-1">9.2.10.10.1 http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ http_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \ curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 9.2.10.10.2 Explicit proxy and empty bypass list for a request that otherwise skips the proxy
text: id="variant-9-2-10-10-2">9.2.10.10.2 Explicit proxy and empty bypass list for a request that otherwise skips the proxy # Explicit proxy and empty bypass list for a request that otherwise skips the proxy curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:8080 --noproxy '' -i http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Read: confirm the request in Burp history before trusting the replay. HTTP proxy settings do not tunnel arbitrary SMB/Kerberos traffic. For HTTPS, the client's certificate trust still matters; distinguish a local proxy/TLS error from an application response. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.10.11 Extract candidate paths from a downloaded JavaScript file
text: id="extract-candidate-paths-from-a-downloaded-javascript-file">9.2.10.11 Extract candidate paths from a downloaded JavaScript file Use after reading an actual application JS file. This is a quick string candidate pass; it does not execute the script or understand its routing logic. curl -f http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/app.js -o app.js python3 -c 'import re; print("\n".join(sorted(set(re.findall(r"/[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+",open("app.js").read())))))' > js-paths.txt Read: inspect the list and surrounding source for the correct hostname, API prefix, method, parameter names and required session. Comments, regular expressions and third-party URLs can create false candidates. Replay an observed function before turning strings into a fuzzing list; remove anything outside the assigned scope. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.10.12 Sources
text: id="sources">9.2.10.12 Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8, pp201-231; Hexdump web modules ; Burp Proxy ; curl ; Gobuster ; ffuf .

title: 9.2.11 LDAP and Kerberos Enumeration
text: id="ldap-and-kerberos-enumeration">9.2.11 LDAP and Kerberos Enumeration ← Stage index | AD procedures | Service cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services Recognition: LDAP commonly appears on TCP/389 or TCP/636; Global Catalog on TCP/3268 or 3269; Kerberos on TCP/UDP 88. Applications may listen elsewhere, so follow protocol evidence rather than port labels. <h2

title: 9.2.11.1 Baseline: discover naming contexts
text: id="baseline-discover-naming-contexts">9.2.11.1 Baseline: discover naming contexts Prerequisite: LDAP reachability. Coverage: RootDSE only; this can work even when directory searches require authentication . Decisive output: defaultNamingContext and dnsHostName . ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://TARGET:389 -s base -b '' \ defaultNamingContext rootDomainNamingContext configurationNamingContext dnsHostName Convert DC=corp,DC=example into corp.example for DNS/Kerberos work. Preserve the server's exact hostname because Kerberos is name-sensitive. <summary

title: 9.2.11.1.1 LDAPS and certificate-name inspection
text: id="variant-9-2-11-1-1">9.2.11.1.1 LDAPS and certificate-name inspection openssl s_client -connect TARGET:636 -servername DC_HOST </dev/null ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldaps://DC_HOST:636 -s base -b '' defaultNamingContext dnsHostName A certificate can disclose domain/DC names. A TLS validation error is a client trust/name issue, not proof that LDAP is unavailable. <h2

title: 9.2.11.2 Anonymous directory search
text: id="anonymous-directory-search">9.2.11.2 Anonymous directory search Prerequisite: known base DN and server permitting anonymous search. Failure cue: Inappropriate authentication or Insufficient access closes only the anonymous path. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_IP:389 -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(objectClass=group)' cn member description <h2

title: 9.2.11.3 Authenticated search
text: id="authenticated-search">9.2.11.3 Authenticated search Prerequisite: a valid directory identity. Decisive output: objects/attributes unavailable anonymously. Avoid placing a real password in shell history when an interactive prompt is available. ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 \ -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' \ '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user))' \ sAMAccountName userPrincipalName memberOf description servicePrincipalName userAccountControl <summary

title: 9.2.11.3.1 Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately
text: id="variant-9-2-11-3-1">9.2.11.3.1 Search computers, groups and SPN-bearing accounts separately ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=computer)' \ dNSHostName operatingSystem operatingSystemVersion servicePrincipalName ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(objectClass=group)' cn member ldapsearch -x -LLL -H ldap://DC_HOST:389 -D 'USER@DOMAIN.TLD' -W \ -b 'DC=DOMAIN,DC=TLD' '(&(objectCategory=person)(servicePrincipalName=*))' \ sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName memberOf <h2

title: 9.2.11.4 Kerberos prerequisites before an attack
text: id="kerberos-prerequisites-before-an-attack">9.2.11.4 Kerberos prerequisites before an attack Kerberos failures are often name/time/route failures rather than credential failures. Establish: getent hosts DC_HOST nc -nvz DC_IP 88 date -u nmap -Pn -sV -p 88,389,445,464,636,3268,3269 DC_IP -oN dc-services.txt Interpretation: resolve DOMAIN and DC_HOST consistently, keep clock skew within Kerberos tolerance, and ensure the KDC is reached through the selected route. KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN points to identity/domain naming; KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW points to time; KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED normally points to authentication material. <h2

title: 9.2.11.5 Handoff
text: id="handoff">9.2.11.5 Handoff New users, groups, computers, SPNs or domain names → domain mapping . A user confirmed without preauthentication → Kerberos and identity transitions . Valid credentials → rerun authenticated LDAP plus SMB/share/remote-access enumeration. Certificate templates/AD CS clues → AD CS and object-control abuse . <h2

title: 9.2.11.6 Sources
text: id="sources">9.2.11.6 Sources getSH Common Services: LDAP , source snapshot e1f62dd OpenLDAP ldapsearch manual Hexdump Active Directory modules

title: 9.2.12 SIP and IRC Triage
text: id="sip-and-irc-triage">9.2.12 SIP and IRC Triage ← Stage index | Service cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services These source-site topics contain only first-pass reconnaissance. Treat them as application-identification branches, not default exploitation paths. <h2

title: 9.2.12.1 SIP
text: id="sip">9.2.12.1 SIP Commonly UDP/TCP 5060 or TLS 5061; follow protocol evidence. nmap -Pn -sU -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET nmap -Pn -sT -sV --script sip-methods -p 5060 TARGET Decisive output: a SIP response and supported methods. open|filtered without application response remains ambiguous. Do not run sip-brute until the exact registrar, known test identities, lockout policy and explicit authorization are established. <h2

title: 9.2.12.2 IRC
text: id="irc">9.2.12.2 IRC nmap -Pn -sV --script irc-info -p PORT TARGET nc -nv TARGET PORT Minimal registration for an authorized test client: NICK testnick USER testuser 0 * :Test User QUIT Decisive output: IRC numeric replies, server/network name, version/capabilities or authentication requirement. Do not use irc-brute as identification; authenticate only with legitimately acquired credentials. <h2

title: 9.2.12.3 Sources
text: id="sources">9.2.12.3 Sources getSH Scan route , source snapshot e1f62dd Nmap NSE documentation

title: 9.2.13 Memcached and WebDAV
text: id="memcached-and-webdav">9.2.13 Memcached and WebDAV Stage index | Complete task index <h2

title: 9.2.13.1 Memcached — inspect cache data through TCP
text: id="memcached--inspect-cache-data-through-tcp">9.2.13.1 Memcached — inspect cache data through TCP Use when a listener identifies as Memcached, commonly TCP/11211. Start with the text protocol; do not confuse cache access with an OS shell. <h3

title: 9.2.13.1.1 Identify the service and inspect its counters
text:
id="variant-9-2-13-1-1">9.2.13.1.1 Identify the service and inspect its counters # Identify the service and inspect its counters printf 'version
stats
quit
' | nc -nv TARGET PORT <h3

title: 9.2.13.1.2 Discover available slab/key metadata, if these commands are enabled
text:
id="variant-9-2-13-1-2">9.2.13.1.2 Discover available slab/key metadata, if these commands are enabled # Discover available slab/key metadata, if these commands are enabled printf 'stats items
lru_crawler metadump all
quit
' | nc -nv TARGET PORT <h3

title: 9.2.13.1.3 Read one key learned from configuration or metadata
text: id="variant-9-2-13-1-3">9.2.13.1.3 Read one key learned from configuration or metadata # Read one key learned from configuration or metadata printf 'get KEY\r\nquit\r\n' | nc -nv TARGET PORT Read: VALUE KEY ... followed by content proves a readable item; END alone does not establish that every key is absent. Configuration, session data or account material → identify its application/account and test that context. ERROR can mean unsupported or disabled metadata commands. Authentication /TLS or a binary-only interface requires its matching client. UDP amplification recipes are not part of this workflow. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.2.13.2 WebDAV — list, retrieve and test the actual write boundary
text: id="webdav--list-retrieve-and-test-the-actual-write-boundary">9.2.13.2 WebDAV — list, retrieve and test the actual write boundary Use when OPTIONS advertises DAV/PROPFIND or a known DAV endpoint exists. Preserve the real hostname and authentication. <h3

title: 9.2.13.2.1 curl -i -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/
text: id="variant-9-2-13-2-1">9.2.13.2.1 curl -i -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/ curl -i -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/ curl -i -X PROPFIND -H 'Depth: 1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/ <h3

title: 9.2.13.2.2 Known-account version; curl prompts for the password
text: id="variant-9-2-13-2-2">9.2.13.2.2 Known-account version; curl prompts for the password # Known-account version; curl prompts for the password curl -i -u USER -X PROPFIND -H 'Depth: 1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/ <h3

title: 9.2.13.2.3 Interactive client; respond to the authentication prompt if required
text: id="variant-9-2-13-2-3">9.2.13.2.3 Interactive client; respond to the authentication prompt if required # Interactive client; respond to the authentication prompt if required cadaver http://TARGET:PORT/PATH/ In cadaver, choose the relevant operation: ls get FILE put probe.txt delete probe.txt quit Read: a 207 response needs actual resource entries; a 401/login page is not a listing.
