title: 9.6.6 Conditional AD infrastructure and trust checks
text: id="conditional-ad-infrastructure-and-trust-checks">9.6.6 Conditional AD infrastructure and trust checks Stage index | Complete task index | Object control and delegation | Lateral movement Use these checks when host or directory evidence identifies the feature. They identify the next prerequisite to investigate; they are not complete exploitation recipes for every product or version. <h2

title: 9.6.6.1 DNSAdmins: distinguish DNS configuration from a service trigger
text: id="dnsadmins-distinguish-dns-configuration-from-a-service-trigger">9.6.6.1 DNSAdmins: distinguish DNS configuration from a service trigger # Domain-joined source with the RSAT AD module and readable group membership Get-ADGroupMember -Identity DnsAdmins -Recursive :: Service queries use the current identity and can be denied separately sc.exe \\DC_HOST qc DNS sc.exe \\DC_HOST sdshow DNS Read → next: resolve whether the controlled identity really has DNS-server configuration rights, which server runs DNS, its service identity, and whether a usable plugin/configuration operation and restart trigger exist on that build. Group membership alone does not prove immediate execution or restart rights. Follow the service-control permission workflow . A DNS restart on a DC can interrupt the domain; do not use it as a discovery probe. <h2

title: 9.6.6.2 WSUS: identify the update authority from the current client
text: id="wsus-identify-the-update-authority-from-the-current-client">9.6.6.2 WSUS: identify the update authority from the current client reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate /v WUServer reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate /v WUStatusServer reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\AU /v UseWUServer Read → next: record the actual server URL, port, TLS and client policy. A client configured for WSUS does not grant update approval, content/signing control or server administration. Investigate server access and the exact privileged update consumer only after those rights are established. Missing registry values can mean another policy/configuration source; they do not prove the organization has no WSUS. <h2

title: 9.6.6.3 Configuration Manager / SCCM: recognize the client before choosing a server-side path
text: id="configuration-manager--sccm-recognize-the-client-before-choosing-a-server-side-path">9.6.6.3 Configuration Manager / SCCM: recognize the client before choosing a server-side path Get-Service CcmExec -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\ccm -ClassName SMS_Client Read → next: CcmExec / SMS_Client identifies a client context. It does not prove site-server access, SMS Provider authorization , deployment rights, accessible network-access-account credentials or permission to execute CMPivot. Record the site/management point from readable client configuration and test only the matching authenticated interface. Namespace absent and access denied are different outcomes. This reference does not yet contain a complete SCCM compromise procedure. <h2

title: 9.6.6.4 Trusts: inspect the boundary before treating another domain as reachable privilege
text: id="trusts-inspect-the-boundary-before-treating-another-domain-as-reachable-privilege">9.6.6.4 Trusts: inspect the boundary before treating another domain as reachable privilege nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts # RSAT alternative; query the domain in the current authenticated context Get-ADTrust -Filter * -Properties * | Format-List Name,Direction,TrustType,ForestTransitive,SelectiveAuthentication,SIDFilteringForestAware,SIDFilteringQuarantined Read → next: keep trust direction, same-forest versus cross-forest scope, SID filtering, selective authentication , target SPN and the accepted identity separate. A trust object or child-domain admin does not by itself prove a usable forest-compromise chain. Verify name resolution, service reachability and authorization in the destination using the movement preflight . Trust-key/SID-history forgery and cross-forest coercion are specialized paths, not complete procedures in this playbook. <h2

title: 9.6.6.5 Sources
text: id="sources">9.6.6.5 Sources Microsoft: dnscmd Microsoft: update-management troubleshooting Microsoft: Configuration Manager WMI programming Microsoft: Get-ADTrust

title: 9.6.0 Stage 06: Active Directory and Lateral Movement
text: id="stage-06-active-directory-and-lateral-movement">9.6.0 Stage 06: Active Directory and Lateral Movement ← Main index | AD cheatsheet | Master Notes | Strategy map | Study methods: Recover and use authentication material ; Map Active Directory attack paths ; Gain a more useful domain identity ; Move to another host Reasoning chain: Identity → Group → Rights → Host Access → Session/Credential → New Identity → Higher Privilege. Validate each edge and route; BloodHound proposes paths but does not prove them. Focused AD investigation guide — where to look, expected behavior, annotated synthetic observations and the next prerequisite to validate. Investigation command chooser . Task Open Identify the domain, objects, rights, shares, sessions and candidate paths Domain mapping Recover credentials/tickets from an already controlled host when privileges permit Credential access AS-REP roast, Kerberoast, password validation and ticket transitions Kerberos and identity transitions Convert validated user/group/ SPN / DACL rights and domain-replication rights; branch to AD CS/GPO/delegation only when evidence selects them Object control and domain compromise Match password/hash/ticket to a reachable remote service Lateral movement <h2

title: 9.6.0.1 Generic worked chain
text: id="generic-worked-chain">9.6.0.1 Generic worked chain A supplied low-privilege domain identity authenticates to LDAP and SMB. Native/LDAP/PowerView collection identifies computers, groups, SPNs, shares and ACL candidates. BloodHound suggests that the identity can control a group whose members administer an application server; manual checks validate both the directory right and host authorization . A remote session exposes an application configuration credential. Its identity/context is validated before reuse. The new identity has a roastable service account or a validated remote-management path to another host. A higher-privileged session produces a new credential/ticket or reveals replication rights. Every identity/host/route transition triggers re-enumeration and evidence capture. This is a reasoning example, not a target solution or claim of practical completion. Exit condition: the chosen relationship has been validated through compatible authentication and authorization, the new host/identity is verified, and the environment is re-enumerated from the new state. Conditional infrastructure and trusts : DNSAdmins, WSUS, SCCM and trust-boundary checks. Diagrams: AD capability transitions before mapping; credential routing before credential classification.

title: 9.7.1 Tunneling and Port Forwarding
text: id="tunneling-and-port-forwarding">9.7.1 Tunneling and Port Forwarding ← Stage index | Quick sheet | Master Notes | Lateral movement | Strategy map | Study methods: Reach internal services Selection rule: required application flow → reachable tunnel transport → pivot egress → client compatibility → return path. Exit: a protocol-appropriate client reaches the intended internal endpoint through a documented route; DNS/ SPN behavior and any callback route are independently verified. <h2

title: 9.7.1.1 Draw the route before choosing a command
text: id="1-draw-the-route-before-choosing-a-command">9.7.1.1 Draw the route before choosing a command APPLICATION TOOL -> local listener / SOCKS endpoint / TUN route -> tunnel transport endpoint -> pivot exit -> internal destination service CALLBACK TARGET -> pivot listener or routable address -> relay/tunnel -> final listener Record: TOOL_HOST -> ENTRY_SOCKET/ROUTE -> TRANSPORT -> PIVOT -> DESTINATION application protocol | TCP/UDP | initiator | bind address | DNS point credential/SPN name | callback route | privilege | cleanup objects Do not use “pivot works” as a single state. Confirm these layers separately: the tunnel process started; its listener/transport connection exists; the pivot can reach the intended destination socket; the local route, forward or proxy points at the right exit; the application actually uses that path; name resolution and authentication match the application; a callback, if required, has its own return path. <h2

title: 9.7.1.2 Discover the pivot's network position
text: id="2-discover-the-pivots-network-position">9.7.1.2 Discover the pivot's network position Linux: id ip -brief address ip route ip neigh ss -lntup cat /etc/resolv.conf Windows: whoami /all ipconfig /all route print arp -a netstat -ano PowerShell selected endpoints: Get-NetIPConfiguration Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 | Sort-Object DestinationPrefix,RouteMetric Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 An interface or route proves a possible network position, not destination reachability. Validate one justified socket from the pivot before building a tunnel. nc -nvz -w 3 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT curl -v --connect-timeout 5 http://INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT/ Test-NetConnection INTERNAL_HOST -Port INTERNAL_PORT <h2

title: 9.7.1.3 Choose the smallest compatible route
text: id="3-choose-the-smallest-compatible-route">9.7.1.3 Choose the smallest compatible route Need Baseline Choose when Main limitation One TCP service through an SSH pivot SSH local forward Kali can initiate SSH to pivot One destination socket per forward Many TCP destinations through SSH pivot SSH dynamic forward Kali can initiate SSH to pivot SOCKS/client compatibility Pivot can connect outward but inbound access is blocked SSH remote or remote-dynamic forward Pivot has OpenSSH client and can reach Kali SSH Kali SSH policy; OpenSSH version for remote dynamic SSH hop directly to internal SSH ProxyJump Both pivot and destination provide SSH SSH-only path Simple Linux TCP relay Socat Binary already exists and listener can be exposed Clear TCP relay; no authentication/encryption Transparent selected subnets through SSH sshuttle Suitable SSH server with Python; local privileges TCP/DNS-oriented, local firewall changes Windows SSH-based forward Built-in ssh.exe or Plink Compatible client exists and outbound SSH works Server policy and credential/host-key handling Windows native fixed TCP relay netsh interface portproxy Elevated token ; target modification acceptable TCP only; firewall/IP Helper/stateful cleanup Outbound HTTP/WebSocket-shaped tunnel Chisel Pivot can run matching binary and reach server Client/server compatibility and proxy/client transport limits Routed access for ordinary clients Ligolo-ng Agent can reach proxy and TUN/route setup is possible Userland stack is not identical to direct raw networking DNS is the only viable egress dnscat2 DNS path plus authoritative/direct server control Slow/noisy, infrastructure and client required Prefer one explicit forward for one known service. Use SOCKS when several TCP endpoints must be explored. Use a routed pivot when many ordinary tools must operate without proxy wrappers. Do not add a multi-host route when command execution directly on the pivot is sufficient. <h2

title: 9.7.1.4 Socat fixed TCP relay
text: id="4-socat-fixed-tcp-relay">9.7.1.4 Socat fixed TCP relay On a Linux pivot, expose one internal TCP service: socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT Loopback-only relay for another local tunnel stage: socat -ddd TCP-LISTEN:LOCAL_PORT,bind=127.0.0.1,reuseaddr,fork \ TCP:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT Verify the listener on the pivot with ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT . Run nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT from the intended client to test client-to-pivot reachability. These checks run on different machines: ss -lntp | grep LOCAL_PORT nc -nvz PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP LOCAL_PORT fork handles multiple connections. reuseaddr eases rebinding after restart. Socat does not add authentication or encryption to this relay; bind narrowly and remove the process when finished. A listener can exist even when the pivot-to-destination connection fails. <h2

title: 9.7.1.5 OpenSSH forwarding
text: id="5-openssh-forwarding">9.7.1.5 OpenSSH forwarding Add reliability and attributable failure to transport-only sessions: -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 ExitOnForwardFailure proves requested listening sockets were established. It does not prove the final destination is reachable through them. <h3

title: 9.7.1.5.1 Local forward: listener on the SSH client
text: id="51-local-forward-listener-on-the-ssh-client">9.7.1.5.1 Local forward: listener on the SSH client Run on Kali when Kali can SSH to the pivot: ssh -N \ -L 127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 Use the listener as though it were the internal service: nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 LOCAL_PORT curl -v http://127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT/ The SSH server/pivot resolves and connects to INTERNAL_HOST . Bind to 127.0.0.1 unless another authorized local host must use the forward; -g or a non-loopback bind expands exposure. <h3

title: 9.7.1.5.2 Dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH client
text: id="52-dynamic-forward-socks-listener-on-the-ssh-client">9.7.1.5.2 Dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH client ssh -N -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -p SSH_PORT USER@PIVOT \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 OpenSSH acts as a SOCKS4/5 server. The pivot makes destination connections selected by each SOCKS request. <h3

title: 9.7.1.5.3 Remote forward: listener on the SSH server
text: id="53-remote-forward-listener-on-the-ssh-server">9.7.1.5.3 Remote forward: listener on the SSH server Run on a pivot that can initiate an SSH connection back to Kali: ssh -N \ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT \ -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 Kali then uses: nc -nvz 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT The SSH client/pivot connects to INTERNAL_HOST . AllowTcpForwarding and server policy must permit the forward. A non-loopback remote bind additionally depends on GatewayPorts ; do not assume 0.0.0.0 was honored. <h3

title: 9.7.1.5.4 Remote dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH server
text: id="54-remote-dynamic-forward-socks-listener-on-the-ssh-server">9.7.1.5.4 Remote dynamic forward: SOCKS listener on the SSH server Run on the pivot: ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 -p KALI_SSH_PORT KALI_USER@LHOST \ -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 The SOCKS listener appears on Kali and destination connections exit through the pivot. Remote dynamic forwarding requires OpenSSH 7.6 or later on the client that issues -R . Run ssh -V on the pivot (the SSH client). Run ss -lntp | grep 1080 on Kali (the SSH server hosting the SOCKS listener). These checks run on different machines; do not paste both into one terminal: ssh -V ss -lntp | grep 1080 <h3

title: 9.7.1.5.5 SSH jump and proxy command
text: id="55-ssh-jump-and-proxy-command">9.7.1.5.5 SSH jump and proxy command Direct SSH through an SSH pivot: ssh -J PIVOT_USER@PIVOT TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST SSH through an existing SOCKS5 endpoint with Ncat: ssh -o ProxyCommand='ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' \ TARGET_USER@INTERNAL_HOST %h and %p are replaced with the destination host and port. Prefer this native proxy route when ProxyChains interposition is unreliable. <summary

title: 9.7.1.5.5.1 Use an SSH configuration for repeated access
text: id="variant-9-7-1-5-5-1">9.7.1.5.5.1 Use an SSH configuration for repeated access Host pivot HostName PIVOT User PIVOT_USER Host internal HostName INTERNAL_HOST User TARGET_USER ProxyJump pivot ssh internal scp FILE internal:DESTINATION_PATH <h2

title: 9.7.1.6 ProxyChains and SOCKS-aware clients
text: id="6-proxychains-and-socks-aware-clients">9.7.1.6 ProxyChains and SOCKS-aware clients Use a task-specific configuration rather than repeatedly editing a shared global file: strict_chain proxy_dns tcp_read_time_out 15000 tcp_connect_time_out 8000 [ProxyList] socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf curl http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST proxychains4 -q -f ./proxychains-pivot.conf impacket-smbclient \ 'DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@INTERNAL_HOST' Constraints: ProxyChains hooks socket calls in dynamically linked programs; some static binaries, scripts, child processes or dynamically loaded modules bypass or break the hook. ProxyChains supports TCP only. It does not proxy UDP, ICMP, SYN scans or pcap-based discovery. For Nmap use -sT -Pn -n with a focused port list. Proxy scanning is slow and is not a replacement for discovery from the pivot. proxy_dns moves supported hostname resolution through the proxy, but application behavior varies. -n prevents Nmap's local reverse lookups. Prefer an application's native proxy option when available. Native examples: curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ ncat --proxy-type socks5 --proxy 127.0.0.1:1080 INTERNAL_HOST INTERNAL_PORT <h2

title: 9.7.1.7 sshuttle transparent selected-subnet route
text: id="7-sshuttle-transparent-selected-subnet-route">9.7.1.7 sshuttle transparent selected-subnet route sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@PIVOT:SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET ANOTHER_SUBNET Through a previously established local forward to the SSH pivot: sudo sshuttle --dns \ -r SSH_USER@127.0.0.1:LOCAL_SSH_PORT \ INTERNAL_SUBNET sshuttle is useful when many TCP clients need transparent access. It requires privileges and firewall/redirection support on the client; the remote side needs a compatible Python execution path. It is not a general layer-2 VPN and does not make arbitrary raw-packet or UDP behavior equivalent to direct routing. Record the selected subnets so existing VPN routes are not accidentally captured. <h2

title: 9.7.1.8 Windows forwarding alternatives
text: id="8-windows-forwarding-alternatives">9.7.1.8 Windows forwarding alternatives <h3

title: 9.7.1.8.1 Built-in OpenSSH client
text: id="81-built-in-openssh-client">9.7.1.8.1 Built-in OpenSSH client where ssh.exe ssh.exe -V ssh.exe -N -R 127.0.0.1:1080 KALI_USER@LHOST -p KALI_SSH_PORT -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 The same -L , -D , -R , ProxyJump and ProxyCommand concepts apply to current Windows OpenSSH. Remote dynamic forwarding depends on the client version. <h3

title: 9.7.1.8.2 Plink
text: id="82-plink">9.7.1.8.2 Plink Remote fixed forward from Windows to Kali: plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l KALI_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\kali-password.txt ^ -R 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT ^ -P KALI_SSH_PORT LHOST Local dynamic SOCKS on Windows: plink.exe -ssh -N -batch -hostkey "HOST_KEY_FINGERPRINT" ^ -l SSH_USER -pwfile C:\PATH\ssh-password.txt ^ -D 127.0.0.1:1080 -P SSH_PORT PIVOT Current Plink supports -L , -R and -D , but not OpenSSH's remote-dynamic shorthand. -batch prevents an unseen prompt from hanging; pair it with a verified -hostkey . -pwfile avoids a literal password in the command line but creates a sensitive file that must be protected and removed. Prefer a key or existing authenticated context where feasible. <h3

title: 9.7.1.8.3 Netsh portproxy
text: id="83-netsh-portproxy">9.7.1.8.3 Netsh portproxy Elevated Windows shell: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT ^ connectaddress=INTERNAL_HOST connectport=INTERNAL_PORT netsh interface portproxy show all netstat -ano -p tcp | findstr ":LOCAL_PORT" If the existing firewall policy does not already allow the listener and a change is authorized: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" ^ dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=LOCAL_PORT Cleanup: netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 ^ listenaddress=PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP listenport=LOCAL_PORT netsh advfirewall firewall delete rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" portproxy requires an elevated token, forwards TCP rather than UDP, modifies persistent host configuration and may depend on the IP Helper service. A stored rule or listening socket still does not prove the destination is reachable. Record and remove both the proxy and any firewall rule. <h2

title: 9.7.1.9 Chisel HTTP/WebSocket tunnel
text: id="9-chisel-httpwebsocket-tunnel">9.7.1.9 Chisel HTTP/WebSocket tunnel <h3

title: 9.7.1.9.1 Reverse SOCKS: pivot initiates outward
text: id="91-reverse-socks-pivot-initiates-outward">9.7.1.9.1 Reverse SOCKS: pivot initiates outward On Kali: chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT Record the server fingerprint. On the pivot: chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:socks R:socks is the shorter equivalent using the default server-side 127.0.0.1:1080 listener. Traffic sent to Kali's SOCKS listener exits through the Chisel client/pivot. <h3

title: 9.7.1.9.2 Reverse fixed TCP forward
text: id="92-reverse-fixed-tcp-forward">9.7.1.9.2 Reverse fixed TCP forward <h4

title: 9.7.1.9.2.1 Kali
text: id="variant-9-7-1-9-2-1">9.7.1.9.2.1 Kali # Kali chisel server --reverse --port CHISEL_PORT <h4

title: 9.7.1.9.2.2 Pivot: expose an internal service on Kali loopback
text: id="variant-9-7-1-9-2-2">9.7.1.9.2.2 Pivot: expose an internal service on Kali loopback # Pivot: expose an internal service on Kali loopback chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' LHOST:CHISEL_PORT \ R:127.0.0.1:LOCAL_PORT:INTERNAL_HOST:INTERNAL_PORT <h3

title: 9.7.1.9.3 Forward SOCKS when the client is on the tool side
text: id="93-forward-socks-when-the-client-is-on-the-tool-side">9.7.1.9.3 Forward SOCKS when the client is on the tool side <h4

title: 9.7.1.9.3.1 Pivot/server side
text: id="variant-9-7-1-9-3-1">9.7.1.9.3.1 Pivot/server side # Pivot/server side chisel server --socks5 --port CHISEL_PORT <h4

title: 9.7.1.9.3.2 Kali/client side
text: id="variant-9-7-1-9-3-2">9.7.1.9.3.2 Kali/client side # Kali/client side chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' PIVOT:CHISEL_PORT \ 127.0.0.1:1080:socks <h3

title: 9.7.1.9.4 Current UDP-aware mode
text: id="94-current-udp-aware-mode">9.7.1.9.4 Current UDP-aware mode Current upstream Chisel distinguishes: socks / R:socks -> SOCKS5 TCP CONNECT only udpsocks / R:udpsocks -> TCP CONNECT plus SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE # Requires compatible current peers chisel client --fingerprint 'SERVER_FINGERPRINT' \ LHOST:CHISEL_PORT R:127.0.0.1:1080:udpsocks This does not make ProxyChains UDP-capable—ProxyChains remains TCP-only. The UDP application must support SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE, or another compatible adapter must be used. Current Chisel peers, TCP and UDP firewall access to the SOCKS listener, and its documented association/fragmentation limits all matter. <h3

title: 9.7.1.9.5 Chisel failure cues
text: id="95-chisel-failure-cues">9.7.1.9.5 Chisel failure cues chisel --version chisel server --help chisel client --help ss -lntp Cue Interpretation No connection at server Pivot egress, address, listener or WebSocket/proxy path HTTP reaches server but upgrade fails Intermediary may block WebSocket upgrade exec format error Wrong OS/architecture Missing GLIBC/version symbol Build/runtime incompatibility; choose a compatible official build Fingerprint mismatch Wrong server or changed key; do not bypass verification blindly SOCKS listener exists but endpoint fails Pivot-to-destination or application/proxy compatibility TCP works but UDP fails Ordinary socks , old peer, UDP bind/firewall or unsupported client <h2

title: 9.7.1.10 Ligolo-ng routed pivot
text: id="10-ligolo-ng-routed-pivot">9.7.1.10 Ligolo-ng routed pivot <h3

title: 9.7.1.10.1 Proxy and agent
text: id="101-proxy-and-agent">9.7.1.10.1 Proxy and agent On Kali: ./proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:LIGOLO_PORT In the proxy console, obtain the fingerprint: certificate_fingerprint On the pivot: ./agent -connect LHOST:LIGOLO_PORT -accept-fingerprint CERT_FINGERPRINT -ignore-cert is a controlled-lab/debug fallback, not the baseline. <h3

title: 9.7.1.10.2 Current managed interface and route
text: id="102-current-managed-interface-and-route">9.7.1.10.2 Current managed interface and route In the Ligolo console: interface_create --name ligolo session ifconfig interface_add_route --name ligolo --route INTERNAL_SUBNET tunnel_start --tun ligolo Manual Linux alternative: sudo ip tuntap add user "$USER" mode tun ligolo sudo ip link set ligolo up sudo ip route add INTERNAL_SUBNET dev ligolo Then use normal clients: ip route get INTERNAL_HOST nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS INTERNAL_HOST curl -v http://INTERNAL_HOST:PORT/ Ligolo translates connections through a userland network stack. Ordinary TCP clients generally work without ProxyChains, but raw-packet assumptions, ICMP details and some UDP behavior can differ from direct access. Use connect-based validation first. <h3

title: 9.7.1.10.3 Pivot loopback services
text: id="103-pivot-loopback-services">9.7.1.10.3 Pivot loopback services Ligolo maps its special 240.0.0.0/4 range to the selected agent's loopback. Add one narrow route: sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo nmap -sT -Pn -n -p PORTS 240.0.0.1 Use this only when the desired service is bound to 127.0.0.1 on the agent. <h3

title: 9.7.1.10.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent
text: id="104-callback-or-file-server-listener-on-the-agent">9.7.1.10.4 Callback or file-server listener on the agent In the selected Ligolo session: listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT --to 127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT --tcp listener_list Kali listener: ncat -lvn 127.0.0.1 KALI_PORT An internal target connects to PIVOT_REACHABLE_IP:PIVOT_PORT ; Ligolo relays it to Kali's loopback listener. Cleanup: listener_stop LISTENER_ID <h2

title: 9.7.1.11 DNS and Kerberos across pivots
text: id="11-dns-and-kerberos-across-pivots">9.7.1.11 DNS and Kerberos across pivots Decide whether the application resolves the name locally, ProxyChains intercepts it, the SOCKS exit resolves it, or the pivot's configured resolver handles it. Use numeric addresses for route validation; then restore the confirmed hostname when the application protocol requires it. Kerberos needs an SPN-compatible hostname, realm/ KDC route and correct time. A working IP connection does not prove Kerberos naming works. A temporary host mapping is acceptable only for a confirmed in-scope address/name pair and must be recorded. getent hosts INTERNAL_FQDN curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://INTERNAL_FQDN:PORT/ klist KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr kvno cifs/TARGET_HOST The first command checks Kali's normal resolver. The curl form deliberately delegates the destination hostname through SOCKS. Do not assume a generic resolver utility will be intercepted by ProxyChains: NSS implementation and process behavior vary. For Impacket, preserve the target hostname while routing to an IP when the tool supports it: impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass -dc-ip DC_IP -target-ip TARGET_IP \ 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET_HOST' <h2

title: 9.7.1.12 Callback and delivery routing
text: id="12-callback-and-delivery-routing">9.7.1.12 Callback and delivery routing A forward path and callback path are different graphs: Kali -> tunnel -> internal service # access path internal target -> pivot -> Kali listener # callback path Options: make the callback directly to an address the internal host already reaches; expose a listener on the pivot and relay it to Kali; use a Ligolo agent listener or SSH/Chisel remote forward; choose a non-callback technique such as authenticated remote execution. Fixed SSH callback relay, run from the pivot: ssh -N -g -L 0.0.0.0:PIVOT_PORT:127.0.0.1:KALI_PORT \ KALI_USER@LHOST -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes This creates the listener on the SSH client/pivot and makes the destination connection from Kali's SSH server to Kali loopback. -g permits other hosts to use the pivot-side local forward. Verify the actual bind with ss ; do not infer it from command syntax. Also route payload delivery separately. An internal host may reach the pivot but not Kali's HTTP server; relay the delivery service or serve from the pivot when justified. <h2

title: 9.7.1.13 Multi-hop routes
text: id="13-multi-hop-routes">9.7.1.13 Multi-hop routes For every additional hop, write another complete segment: Kali -> tunnel A -> PIVOT_A -> tunnel B -> PIVOT_B -> INTERNAL_HOST:PORT Rules: validate one hop before adding the next; avoid overlapping local/VPN/internal routes; use unique listener and SOCKS ports; record which session owns each route; ensure the deeper agent/client can reach the upstream listener; re-evaluate DNS and callback direction at every hop; prefer a routed method for several deep services instead of stacking many opaque wrappers. An upstream tunnel failure invalidates every deeper observation. Do not troubleshoot target credentials until the complete path is restored. <h2

title: 9.7.1.14 DNS tunneling with dnscat2
text: id="14-dns-tunneling-with-dnscat2">9.7.1.14 DNS tunneling with dnscat2 Use only when ordinary transports are unavailable and DNS is demonstrably permitted. This is a conditional advanced route, but it remains in the current official BOK. Prerequisites: command execution sufficient to run a compatible client; either authoritative control/NS delegation for TUNNEL_DOMAIN or direct UDP/53 reachability to the server; a resolver chain that forwards the chosen domain externally; permission to bind/listen on the required DNS port; tolerance for low throughput and conspicuous DNS patterns. Authoritative-domain mode: dnscat2-server --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN Client: ./dnscat --secret=SHARED_SECRET TUNNEL_DOMAIN Direct DNS-server mode shown by the server's own usage output: ./dnscat --dns server=DNS_SERVER,port=53 --secret=SHARED_SECRET Server console: windows window -i SESSION_ID help A DNS query reaching the server proves only the resolver path. Match the pre-shared secret or independently verify the negotiated authentication string. Cache, recursion, EDNS, TCP fallback, DNS security controls and response-size limits can affect the channel. DNS tunneling is not DNS spoofing; spoofing remains prohibited by the current exam guide. <h2

title: 9.7.1.15 Failure router
text: id="15-failure-router">9.7.1.15 Failure router Evidence Failing layer Next decision Pivot cannot reach destination Internal route/firewall/service Fix or choose another pivot before tunneling Tunnel client cannot reach server Transport/egress/listener Test the exact server address/port from pivot SSH says forwarding disabled Server policy Use an authorized alternative; do not keep changing client flags Local/remote port does not bind Address in use, privilege or bind policy Inspect listeners and ExitOnForwardFailure output Listener exists; simple TCP test fails Pivot-to-destination or wrong destination Test from pivot and inspect tunnel logs Simple TCP works; application fails Client/protocol/authentication Check native proxy support, hostname/SPN and application prerequisites ProxyChains shows no hook/connection Static/incompatible client or config Use native proxy option, explicit forward or routed pivot Nmap through SOCKS finds nothing Wrong scan type/discovery/DNS/latency Use focused -sT -Pn -n ; verify with Ncat/curl Kerberos works by IP only for TCP, auth fails DNS/SPN/KDC/time Separate route address from service hostname Forward access works; callback absent Reverse path/listener bind Draw target-to-listener route independently Chisel starts but server sees nothing Egress/URL/WebSocket/binary execution Capture stderr and inspect transport Ligolo session exists; route misses tunnel OS route/interface/session Check route selection and selected agent/tunnel TCP works, UDP fails Tool/client transport limitation Identify a genuine UDP-capable path; do not assume SOCKS/ProxyChains DNS queries never reach authority Delegation/resolver/egress Prove the DNS path before debugging dnscat2 crypto Deep route suddenly fails everywhere Upstream tunnel/session Repair from the first hop outward <h2

title: 9.7.1.16 Verification and cleanup
text: id="16-verification-and-cleanup">9.7.1.16 Verification and cleanup Kali/Linux: ss -lntup ip -brief address ip route ps -ef | grep -E '[s]sh .*-[LDR]|[c]hisel|[l]igolo|[s]ocat|[s]shuttle' Windows: netstat -ano tasklist netsh interface portproxy show all netsh advfirewall firewall show rule name="OSCP Pivot LOCAL_PORT" Record: exact process/command and version; bind address and port; transport direction and initiator; pivot and destination; routes/name mappings/configuration files added; simple TCP proof and final application proof; callback proof where applicable; cleanup command and result. Stop tunnel processes and remove TUN routes, Ligolo listeners, temporary mappings, password files, Netsh rules and firewall exceptions after the authorized task. <h2

title: 9.7.1.17 Tooling for this section
text: id="tooling-for-this-section">9.7.1.17 Tooling for this section Tool Purpose Required context Baseline Decisive output Failure cue ip / route / ss / netstat Discover and verify each hop Shell on relevant host Sections 2 and 16 Correct route and listener Listener exists on wrong interface Ncat/curl/Test-NetConnection Prove one socket Route from test source Sections 2 and 16 TCP handshake/application response Complex tool fails before baseline proof Socat Simple fixed TCP relay Binary and bind permission Section 4 Listener plus remote connection Clear relay exposed too broadly OpenSSH Fixed, dynamic, remote and jump routes SSH authentication/policy Section 5 Requested listener and successful client flow Forwarding or bind denied ProxyChains Wrap compatible TCP clients SOCKS endpoint + dynamic linking Section 6 Connection log through proxy UDP/raw/static client unsupported sshuttle Transparent selected-subnet TCP/DNS route SSH, client privileges, remote Python Section 7 Ordinary client reaches selected subnet Route collision/firewall backend issue Windows ssh.exe /Plink SSH forwards from Windows Client present and server reachable Section 8 Kali/Windows listener established Hidden host-key/password prompt Netsh portproxy Native Windows fixed TCP relay Elevated token Section 8 Stored rule + listener + remote flow Firewall/IP Helper/destination failure Chisel HTTP/WebSocket reverse SOCKS/forwards Compatible binary and egress Section 9 Session + SOCKS/forward listener WebSocket, fingerprint or runtime error Ligolo-ng Routed access and agent listeners Agent/proxy + TUN route Section 10 OS route and ordinary client flow Wrong session/interface/route dnscat2 Conditional DNS channel Resolver/authority or direct DNS path Section 14 Authenticated encrypted session DNS never reaches server Package names and command behavior vary. Check local --help /versions before use. Do not install tooling or alter host/network configuration without scope and authorization . <h2

title: 9.7.1.18 Exam restriction
text: id="exam-restriction">9.7.1.18 Exam restriction The current OSCP+ exam guide explicitly states that Metasploit cannot be used for pivoting because that would involve more than one target. The current guide does not individually approve every other tool; the learner remains responsible for restrictions and must recheck the guide before a mock or exam. <h2

text: id="sources">9.7.1.19 Sources Supplied PEN-200, Chapter 19 pp. 583–629 and Chapter 20 pp. 630–652. OffSec OSCP+ Body of Knowledge and current exam guide OpenSSH client manual Socat documentation ProxyChains-NG sshuttle PuTTY/Plink manual Microsoft Netsh interface/portproxy Chisel Ligolo-ng quickstart , listeners and agent loopback access dnscat2 getSH tunneling route , source snapshot e1f62dd Hexdump OSCP repository and Port Forwarding and Pivoting video index . The upstream module provides the four SSH-forwarding categories; current syntax and tool behavior above were checked independently.

title: 9.7.0 Stage 07: Pivoting and Tunneling
text: id="stage-07-pivoting-and-tunneling">9.7.0 Stage 07: Pivoting and Tunneling ← Main index | Pivoting cheatsheet | Master Notes | Strategy map | Study methods: Reach internal services Purpose: build an explicit route from the tool to an internal service, including every listener, initiator, bind address, name-resolution point and return path. Task Open Choose a fixed, SOCKS, routed, HTTP/WebSocket or DNS route Tunneling and port forwarding Use Socat, all SSH directions, sshuttle, Windows clients/Netsh, Chisel or Ligolo-ng Tunneling and port forwarding Diagnose DNS/ SPN , callbacks, transport limits and multihop failures Tunneling and port forwarding Exit condition: a protocol-appropriate client reaches the intended internal endpoint through the documented route, and callback traffic (if needed) has a separate verified return path.

title: 9.8.1 Integrated Attack Tracking and Evidence
text: id="integrated-attack-tracking-and-evidence">9.8.1 Integrated Attack Tracking and Evidence ← Stage index | Quick sheet | Master Notes | Strategy map | Study methods: Complete attacks and retain reproducible evidence Goal: finish an unfamiliar scoped target by keeping the current attack state, candidate paths and required evidence synchronized. This is the integration procedure for the earlier stages; it does not replace their service- and technique-specific procedures. <h2

title: 9.8.1.1 Establish the operating contract
text: id="establish-the-operating-contract">9.8.1.1 Establish the operating contract Before interacting with a target, record: scope and explicit exclusions objective and required evidence starting identity/credential and whether it is local, domain or application scoped source host, interface, route and DNS context allowed/restricted tools and the current Metasploit target decision case directory and note/evidence locations cleanup or restoration obligations An interesting vulnerability is not automatically the objective. The attack is complete only when the required access or privilege is verified and the reproduction/evidence chain is retained. Create a private case workspace using target-neutral names until the real scope is known: mkdir -p case/{00-admin,01-scans,02-services,03-web,04-exploits,05-loot,06-sessions,07-screenshots,08-report} touch case/00-admin/{scope.md,state.md,credentials.md,routes.md,hypotheses.md,transitions.md} Do not put exam or private target material in a public repository. <h2

title: 9.8.1.2 Maintain a live state map
text: id="maintain-a-live-state-map">9.8.1.2 Maintain a live state map Keep target-specific values in a private case/lab record, not this public repository. HOSTS - host/IP | role | reachable from | open services | evidence file IDENTITIES - local/domain identity | credential type | validated services | privilege | source ROUTES - source -> listener/tunnel -> pivot -> destination | DNS point | callback path HYPOTHESES - observation | hypothesis | prerequisite | next discriminating test | status TRANSITIONS - old state -> action -> new access/identity/route | decisive output | evidence EVIDENCE COVERAGE - objective | reproduction complete? | identity/IP proof? | screenshot? | panel/task state Label each claim observed , inferred , possible , confirmed , disproven or inconclusive . Close a path only with a test that addressed its prerequisite; do not confuse a tool error with a disproven attack hypothesis. <h2

title: 9.8.1.3 Run the attack as a state machine
text: id="run-the-attack-as-a-state-machine">9.8.1.3 Run the attack as a state machine Observe → Enumerate → Interpret → Hypothesize → Validate prerequisite → Exploit the confirmed primitive → Verify the new state → Re-enumerate from that state → Escalate, move or pivot → Capture evidence and cleanup The sequence is a loop, not a one-time checklist. A state change routes work back to the relevant earlier stage: New state Mandatory re-entry Hostname, address, interface, listener or route Discovery and service identification from the source position that can reach it Credential, key, hash or ticket Classify identity/material, validate compatible access, then authenticated enumeration Application role/session Revisit the same application and objects through the new authorization view Command execution or shell Verify host/identity/network, repair the session, transfer only what is needed, start local enumeration Administrator/root/SYSTEM Re-enumerate protected files, credentials, services, sessions, routes and domain context Domain identity/group/right Rebuild reachable host/service/object paths and validate the specific right Pivot or proxy Repeat discovery from the new vantage point; separately design callback and delivery routes <h3

title: 9.8.1.3.1 Keep two queues
text: id="keep-two-queues">9.8.1.3.1 Keep two queues The coverage queue prevents missed surfaces: host/source position → endpoint → confirmed application → required enumeration → state The hypothesis queue prevents random exploitation: observation → possible transition → prerequisite → cheapest discriminating test → decisive success/failure → next action Do not spend the whole assessment deepening one hypothesis while high-value coverage remains unknown. Conversely, do not keep scanning after a confirmed path only to avoid validating it. <h2

title: 9.8.1.4 Rank candidate paths
text: id="rank-candidate-paths">9.8.1.4 Rank candidate paths Create one card per distinct mechanism: Observation: Desired state transition: Required prerequisites: Already confirmed: Still unknown: Cheapest discriminating test: Success means: Failure means: Noise/change/cleanup: Handoff if successful: Status/evidence: Rank without false numerical precision: Confirmed prerequisite, direct objective transition. Test first. Strong observation, one cheap missing prerequisite. Validate next. Useful information path. Prefer when it can unlock several branches. Multiple unsupported assumptions or disruptive action. Defer. Disproven prerequisite. Close until new evidence changes it. Evidence strength overrides technique popularity. Prefer low-cost tests that split plausible explanations and create reusable information. A path that succeeds only after several unverified assumptions is not yet a high-priority path. <h2

title: 9.8.1.5 Standalone attack workflow
text: id="standalone-attack-workflow">9.8.1.5 Standalone attack workflow Use the earlier procedure linked at each transition; the integration layer owns order and state: Record scope, objective, source position and evidence requirements. Establish TCP coverage, bounded UDP coverage and confirmed application identities. Enumerate every confirmed service in its anonymous/current context; map web requests, hosts, parameters, content and roles. Search files, configuration, repositories and application data for identities or prerequisites. Build candidate cards for manual application weaknesses, compatible credentials and exact public-exploit prerequisites. Validate one prerequisite at a time and prove the smallest useful effect. Convert execution into a verified session; record host, identity, privilege, interfaces and routes. Capture the initial-access transition and any required unprivileged objective before changing state. Enumerate local privilege paths as controlled object → effective permission → privileged consumer → trigger → effect. Verify the elevated identity, capture required evidence, re-enumerate protected context and remove exercise artifacts. Reconstruct the ordered reproduction path while the commands and assumptions are still known. Failure at a step returns to its owning block. Do not skip service enumeration because one banner suggests a CVE, and do not start privilege escalation before proving which host and identity the shell represents. <h2

title: 9.8.1.6 Assumed-breach AD workflow
text: id="assumed-breach-ad-workflow">9.8.1.6 Assumed-breach AD workflow starting credential → local/domain identity + DNS/time/DC context → reachable host/service map → users/groups/computers/shares/SPNs/ACLs/sessions → ranked identity or host transition → compatible password/hash/ticket use → verified session/new identity → re-enumeration → route/movement to next host → higher domain privilege/objective Keep five variables together for every edge: controlled identity effective group/right target object or host required protocol/route resulting identity/access BloodHound and enumerators generate candidate edges. Validate the underlying group membership, ACL, session, service right, route and authentication material before acting. After every new identity or host session, repeat authenticated enumeration rather than continuing from the old authorization view. For multihop work, maintain a route diagram and a separate callback diagram. A route that permits an operator tool to reach a service does not prove that a payload can return to its handler. <h2

title: 9.8.1.7 Capture every state transition
text: id="capture-every-state-transition">9.8.1.7 Capture every state transition Linux: date -Is hostname id ip addr ip route Windows: echo %DATE% %TIME% hostname whoami /all ipconfig /all route print For each access or escalation, retain: the observation that selected the path; the exact command/request with secrets redacted in the reusable copy; relevant output or response; host and identity verification; the effect/new capability; cleanup/restoration; and the next re-enumeration result. Use a compact transition packet: time/timezone | source host/interface | target host/service | starting identity observation | prerequisite | exact action | decisive output new identity/access/route | evidence files | cleanup | next re-enumeration Capture the transition when it happens. Reconstructing it later risks losing a required token , request, route, working directory, listener or source identity. <h2

title: 9.8.1.8 Save tool output deliberately
text: id="save-tool-output-deliberately">9.8.1.8 Save tool output deliberately mkdir -p evidence/nmap evidence/web evidence/loot evidence/screenshots nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p PORTS TARGET -oA evidence/nmap/TARGET-services script -q -f evidence/session.txt Run exit when finished so the transcript closes and flushes. Do not record unrelated secrets in a broad transcript. Start-Transcript -Path .\evidence\powershell-session.txt # commands Stop-Transcript Hash important transferred or generated artifacts: sha256sum FILE | tee FILE.sha256 Never publish credentials, flags, target IPs, full private transcripts or copyrighted course text to this repository. <h2

title: 9.8.1.9 Proof/evidence checkpoint
text: id="proofevidence-checkpoint">9.8.1.9 Proof/evidence checkpoint Current official exam guidance requires proof-file content to be displayed from its original location in an interactive target shell and included in a screenshot with the target IP. The control-panel submission is separate and must occur before the exam ends. Recheck the guide immediately before an exam because these rules can change. Linux example layout: hostname; id; ip addr cat /root/proof.txt Windows example layout: hostname & whoami & ipconfig type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt Use the actual objective-provided path and required identity. Do not use AI on actual exam targets, proofs or reports; the current guide prohibits AI chatbots during the exam. <h2

title: 9.8.1.10 Public exploit evidence
text: id="public-exploit-evidence">9.8.1.10 Public exploit evidence For an unmodified exploit, retain its source URL rather than pasting pages of code. For a modified exploit, retain: original URL and version/commit; local modified copy; a focused diff/highlight of changes; why each change was necessary; build/interpreter command and dependencies; payload-generation command, if any; and exact execution and result verification. git diff --no-index original.py modified.py > exploit-changes.diff sha256sum original.py modified.py <h2

title: 9.8.1.11 Reproduction-path template
text: id="reproduction-path-template">9.8.1.11 Reproduction-path template ### Objective / result **Starting state:** source host, network position and identity. 1. Observation and evidence. 2. Enumeration command/request and decisive output. 3. Vulnerability/prerequisite validation. 4. Exploitation command/request, including required listener/route. 5. Session verification: host, identity and privilege. 6. Escalation evidence and final verification. 7. Cleanup/restoration. **Artifacts:** screenshots, saved output, hashes and exploit source/diff. Write steps in execution order. Explain why a command was needed and what the output established; a transcript alone is not a report. <h2

title: 9.8.1.12 Dead-end recovery
text: id="dead-end-recovery">9.8.1.12 Dead-end recovery Treat stagnation as a state problem, not an instruction to try more commands. Warning signs include unchanged evidence, repeated disproven tests, increasingly exotic mechanisms, tool switching without a new hypothesis, and work whose success would not advance the objective. When progress stalls: Freeze the current host/identity/route/credential map. Mark each path with the last decisive result. Recheck scan/service/application coverage and authenticated views. Separate environment/tool failure from a disproven prerequisite. Choose the cheapest test that can change the decision. Switch paths when the expected information gain is higher. Return only when new evidence changes an assumption. Use this failure router: Symptom Classification Next action Tool cannot reach any known-good endpoint Environment/route failure Repair source interface, proxy, DNS or tool configuration Test did not exercise the claimed prerequisite Inconclusive Replace it with a discriminating test Exact prerequisite is absent Disproven path Close the card until state changes Authentication works but action is denied Authorization boundary Enumerate service/object rights under that identity New credential or route exists but old enumeration is unchanged Stale state Re-enumerate from the new identity/vantage point Many weak possibilities, no decisive observation Coverage gap Return to surface/service/application enumeration <h2

title: 9.8.1.13 Build the report from transitions
text: id="build-the-report-from-transitions">9.8.1.13 Build the report from transitions For every achieved objective, the report path should read: starting state and scope → decisive enumeration → prerequisite/vulnerability validation → exact exploitation action → session/identity verification → privilege or movement transition → final objective evidence → cleanup/restoration Include only enough non-decisive enumeration to make the selection understandable. Screenshots need captions and nearby interpretation; they do not replace commands or prose. Raw transcripts are supporting artifacts, not the final narrative. Current official exam grading follows the target order used in the report. Keep target/objective labels aligned with the control panel and place each target's complete chain together. <h2

title: 9.8.1.14 Final PDF and archive validation
text: id="final-pdf-and-archive-validation">9.8.1.14 Final PDF and archive validation Recheck the current guide immediately before a mock or exam. The current baseline is one PDF inside a non-password-protected .7z , exact case-sensitive filenames and an archive no larger than 200 MB: 7z a OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf 7z l OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z 7z t OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z md5sum OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z Windows hash fallback for a local rehearsal: Get-FileHash -Algorithm MD5 -LiteralPath '.\OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z' Inspect every exported PDF page before archiving. Confirm that code is not clipped, screenshots remain readable, captions match the correct target and the archive contains only the required PDF. Required scripts and PoCs belong as text inside that PDF, not as extra archive members. The current guide recommends creating/uploading from Kali and warns of a Windows 11 archive compatibility issue. Compare the local MD5 with the upload site's value, click the final submission control and retain the acknowledgement. The official Word or LibreOffice template is the reliable baseline. A Markdown/Pandoc pipeline, including Hexdump's report/ generator, is a viable alternative only after a complete dummy export/archive rehearsal; do not install or debug a new report stack during an assessment. <h2

title: 9.8.1.15 Final quality checks
text: id="final-quality-checks">9.8.1.15 Final quality checks Commands are copyable and placeholders/secrets are resolved in the private report. Screenshots are legible and show required identity/IP/proof context. Every claim is supported by nearby evidence. Target order and objective labels match the control panel. Exploit modifications and payload-generation steps are documented. The final PDF is visually reviewed after export. Archive name/format/size and upload hash match current official requirements. <h2

title: 9.8.1.16 Tooling for this section
text: id="tooling-for-this-section">9.8.1.16 Tooling for this section Tool or utility Purpose Required context Baseline Decisive output Failure cue Plain Markdown/editor Portable live state and reproduction notes Private case directory Six ledgers and transition packets above Current state and next action can be recovered without memory Notes contain commands but no interpretation/state Nmap -oA and client-native output options Preserve raw enumeration evidence Authorized scoped target Save output beside target/service record Raw and human-readable result exists Terminal-only output cannot be reconstructed reliably script / PowerShell transcript Record interactive command sequences Local shell; avoid recording unrelated secrets script -q -f evidence/session.txt / Start-Transcript Timestamped command/output stream Transcript is not a report and may omit GUI/HTTP state Screenshot utility Capture required visual proof and decisive GUI/request state Readable display and private storage Capture one objective/context per image Legible proof, IP, identity/context as required Cropped, unreadable or wrong-host image sha256sum / Get-FileHash Integrity for artifacts and evidence Local files Hash original/modified/transferred files Matching expected digest A hash does not establish exploit success Official Word/LibreOffice template Baseline report composition/export Template and tested local editor Export dummy report to PDF before assessment Visually correct PDF Broken code wrapping/images after export 7z plus md5sum / Get-FileHash Package and verify final report Final reviewed PDF and exact OSID naming Commands above One PDF, archive test succeeds, local/upload MD5 match Wrong name, extra files, password or size over limit No new attack tool is required for Block 15.
